### 2. Sacubitril/Valsartan (Entresto) — NDA 207620 (original approval)

**Sponsor:** Novartis Pharmaceuticals

**Indication approved:** Reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II-IV) and reduced ejection fraction

**Approval date:** July 7, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** PARADIGM-HF, NCT01035255

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, early-stopped for efficacy
- *Endpoints:* CV death/HF-hospitalization composite (primary), all-cause death, KCCQ score, new-onset AF, renal composite (secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* Cox regression (treatment + region), repeated-measures ANCOVA (KCCQ)
- *Multiplicity:* Bonferroni-Holm sequentially rejective procedure (secondary endpoints)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design (3 planned interim analyses), Haybittle-Peto boundary, DMC-driven early stop

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Phase III, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled (vs. enalapril) trial; N=8,442 patients with HFrEF, NYHA class II-IV
- Primary endpoint: time to first heart failure hospitalization or CV death (composite)
- Secondary endpoints: time to all-cause death; change from baseline in KCCQ clinical summary score at 8 months; time to new-onset atrial fibrillation; time to a renal composite (≥50% eGFR decline, >30 mL/min/1.73m² eGFR decline to below 60, or ESRD)
- Analysis method: Cox regression (treatment + region) for the primary composite and the three time-to-event secondary endpoints; repeated-measures ANCOVA (treatment + region + timepoint) for the KCCQ secondary endpoint
- Sample size: designed for ~2410 primary endpoint events and ~1229 CV-death events at maximum duration
- Group-sequential design: three interim analyses planned at 1/3, 1/2, and 2/3 information time (~804, 1205, 1607 patients with a primary event), with actual timing adjusted to DMC meeting schedule; Haybittle-Peto-type efficacy boundary, spending ~0.0001 (one-sided) at the first interim analysis and ~0.001 (one-sided, nominal) at the second and third
- Secondary-endpoint multiplicity: if the primary endpoint was significant at trial stop, the 4 secondary endpoints were tested at the same alpha using a Bonferroni-Holm sequentially rejective procedure with pre-specified endpoint-ordering/weighting

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/207620orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/207620orig1s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (original NDA) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/207620Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01035255 (no protocol/SAP documents posted; trial record shows status "Terminated" — early stop for efficacy, not a safety termination)
- Pivotal publication: McMurray JJV, et al. "Angiotensin-Neprilysin Inhibition versus Enalapril in Heart Failure." *N Engl J Med.* 2014;371:993-1004. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1409077), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25176015/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Angiotensin-Neprilysin%20Inhibition%20versus%20Enalapril%20in%20Heart%20Failure)

**Other resources**

- Novartis IPD access via Vivli.org; trial-specific PARADIGM-HF availability not individually confirmed here.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, §1.4.2 "Statistical Methodologies," p.8]*

> "The study was designed to have approximately 2410 primary endpoint events and 1229 CV-death events if the study reached the maximum study duration. Three interim analyses were planned at 1/3, 1/2 and 2/3 of information time (i.e. approximately 804, 1205 and 1607 patients, respectively, with a primary event). However, some adjustment to the frequency and time for interim analyses was made to coincide with the DMC meetings. Appropriate statistical adjustments for the interim analyses actually performed were made to control the overall type-I error of 0.025 (one-sided)... The Haybittle-Peto type of boundary was used for the interim efficacy analyses to assess superiority. The interim efficacy analysis with the boundary spent approximately an alpha of 0.0001 (one-sided) at the first IA and 0.001 (one-sided and nominal) at the second and third interim analyses.
>
> Whatever time point the study stopped, if the primary endpoint was statistically significant, then the secondary endpoints were to be tested using the same alpha as used for the primary endpoint. The testing of the four secondary endpoints was to be done using the Bonferroni-Holm's method."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, §1.4.4 "Results and Conclusions," p.11]*

> "The trial was stopped at the third interim analysis by the DMC because the efficacy boundary was crossed. The combination was superior to the control on the primary endpoint... The p-value was less than 0.0001, which was statistically significant and smaller than the boundary pre-specified by the Haybittle-Peto rule (0.001)."

### 3. Dapagliflozin (Farxiga) — NDA 202293/S-018

**Sponsor:** AstraZeneca (trial co-led with the TIMI Study Group)

**Indication approved:** Reduce the risk of hospitalization for heart failure in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple CV risk factors

**Approval date:** October 18, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** DECLARE-TIMI 58, NCT01730534

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, non-inferiority-then-superiority, mid-trial SAP amendment (secondary endpoint elevated to dual-primary), co-primary endpoints
- *Endpoints:* 3-point MACE, HHF/CV-death composite (dual primary), renal composite (secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* stratified Cox proportional-hazards model (hematuria, CV risk category)
- *Multiplicity:* closed testing procedure, alpha recycling
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design, O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending rule, 2 interim analyses
- *Regulatory:* reviewer-documented mid-trial endpoint elevation (FDA feedback-driven)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Phase IIIb, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial; N=17,160 (59.4% multiple risk factors, 40.6% established ASCVD)
- Originally designed with a single primary endpoint (3-point MACE) and a co-primary safety non-inferiority objective; **the statistical testing hierarchy was substantially changed mid-trial**: SAP Edition 6.0 (17-Dec-2015) elevated the composite of heart failure hospitalization/CV death to a second, dual primary efficacy endpoint alongside MACE, and added a renal composite as a secondary endpoint in the closed testing procedure — a change made in response to FDA feedback, before database lock (locked 16-Sep-2018; SAP finalized as Edition 8.0 on 31-May-2018)
- Analysis method: Cox proportional hazards model stratified by baseline hematuria and baseline CV risk category
- Sample size: event-driven, 1390 MACE events planned for 85% power (HR 0.85); trial ultimately accrued 1559 MACE events
- Two interim analyses (conducted by an independent statistical group at Stanford, reviewed by the DMC) at 1/3 and 2/3 of MACE events, using an O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending rule: first interim analysis one-sided α=0.000095, second interim analysis one-sided α=0.00614, leaving one-sided α=0.023095 for the final analysis
- Final testing hierarchy: test MACE for non-inferiority first (margin 1.3); if superiority shown for *either* dual-primary endpoint (MACE or HHF/CV-death), the full one-sided alpha could be "recycled" to test the other; only if both dual-primary endpoints were significant could alpha be recycled further to the secondary renal composite

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2019/202293Orig1s018,%20205649Orig1s011ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label (2019, S-018) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/202293s018lbl.pdf
- FDA combined review package (Clinical Review by Michelle Carey, MD, MPH, with the full SAP amendment history and testing hierarchy) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2021/202293Orig1s018.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01730534 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Wiviott SD, et al. "Dapagliflozin and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes." *N Engl J Med.* 2019;380:347-357. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1812389), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30415602/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Dapagliflozin%20and%20Cardiovascular%20Outcomes%20in%20Type%202%20Diabetes)

**Other resources**

- AstraZeneca IPD access via Vivli.org; trial-specific DECLARE-TIMI 58 availability not individually confirmed here.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA combined review, "Statistical Analysis Plan" section, p.45]*

> "The initial SAP (Edition 1.0) was dated November 19, 2012 and was revised several times based on feedback from the Agency. A major change to the statistical testing hierarchy was submitted in SAP Edition 6.0, dated December 17, 2015, in which the composite of heart failure hospitalization/CV death was elevated to a dual primary efficacy endpoint along with MACE, and a renal composite endpoint was added to the closed testing procedure as a secondary endpoint... The SAP was finalized on May 31, 2018 (Edition 8.0) and contained additional exploratory analyses of eGFR slope that were not included in the final CSP. The trial database was locked on September 16, 2018."

*[verbatim, from FDA combined review, interim analysis description, p.45-46]*

> "There were two interim analyses performed by an independent statistical group (Stanford University) and reviewed by the DMC/DSMB. These interim analyses assessed superiority for MACE and all-cause mortality after 1/3 and 2/3 of the MACE events had occurred and used an O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending rule... The first interim analysis had a one-sided alpha level of 0.000095; the second interim analysis had a one-sided alpha level of 0.00614. This left a one-sided alpha of 0.023095 for the final analysis... Neither interim analysis presented to the DMC demonstrated superiority of dapagliflozin to placebo for MACE, and therefore the trial continued to completion."

*[verbatim, from FDA combined review, final testing hierarchy and MACE result, p.62]*

> "The final confirmatory testing hierarchy (Table 3) elevated the composite of time-to-first heart failure hospitalization or CV death to a dual primary efficacy endpoint, along with the time-to-first occurrence of 3-point MACE. If dapagliflozin were non-inferior to placebo for MACE, testing could proceed down the hierarchy to test for superiority for 3-point MACE and hospitalization for heart failure/CV death. If either of these demonstrated statistical superiority of dapagliflozin, the entire one-sided alpha could be recycled to test the other primary efficacy endpoint... The hazard ratio (HR) based on the Cox proportional hazards model for dapagliflozin vs. placebo was 0.93 (95% CI 0.84, 1.03)... dapagliflozin is non-inferior to placebo for MACE... superiority of dapagliflozin over placebo was not demonstrated [for MACE]."

This is a clean real-world example of a testing hierarchy paying off exactly as designed: MACE superiority failed, but because non-inferiority on MACE was established, the full alpha recycled down to the HHF/CV-death dual-primary endpoint, which *did* reach significance — and that recycled-alpha result is the entire basis for the approved indication.

### 4. Evolocumab (Repatha) — BLA 125522/S-013

**Sponsor:** Amgen Inc.

**Indication approved:** Reduce the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and coronary revascularization in adults with established cardiovascular disease

**Approval date:** December 1, 2017

**Pivotal trial:** FOURIER, NCT01764633

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven
- *Endpoints:* 5-component MACE+ composite (primary), 3-point MACE (key secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* [inferred] hierarchical primary→key-secondary gatekeeping — see Reverse-engineered SAP below

**No FDA statistical review specific to this supplement was found publicly posted.** Drugs@FDA lists only the label and approval letter for BLA 125522/S-013. (A "Statistical Review and Evaluation" document does exist for BLA 125522, but it is a subgroup-analysis snapshot tied to the *original* 2015 hyperlipidemia approval, not the 2017 FOURIER-based CV supplement — included below only as a note, not as a source for this indication.) No protocol or SAP was found posted on ClinicalTrials.gov for NCT01764633. This entry relies on the approved label and the pivotal NEJM publication, with a reverse-engineered SAP for analysis details not stated in either.

**Trial design & endpoints** *(from label + publication)*

- Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial; N=27,564 (13,784 evolocumab, 13,780 placebo) with established ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL and/or non-HDL-C ≥100 mg/dL despite statin therapy
- Randomized 1:1 to evolocumab (140 mg q2w or 420 mg monthly) or placebo; median follow-up 26 months
- Primary composite endpoint: time to first CV death, MI, stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina, or coronary revascularization
- Key secondary composite endpoint: time to first CV death, MI, or stroke (a subset of the primary composite's components)

- Pivotal publication: Sabatine MS, et al. "Evolocumab and Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Cardiovascular Disease." *N Engl J Med.* 2017;376:1713-1722. **SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from the approved Package Insert, "Clinical Studies" section]*

> "Study 1 (FOURIER, NCT01764633) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial in 27,564... adult patients with established cardiovascular disease... REPATHA significantly reduced the risk for the primary composite endpoint (time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina, or coronary revascularization; p<0.0001) and the key secondary composite endpoint (time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke; p<0.0001)."

**Reverse-engineered SAP** *(inferred — not genuine FOURIER SAP text)*

- **Hierarchical primary → key secondary testing** [inferred from: the label's own vocabulary explicitly labels the second composite a "key secondary" endpoint tested with its own p-value, and the fact both are reported as significant at p<0.0001 without any multiplicity caveat]. This phrasing strongly implies a fixed-sequence gatekeeping procedure (test the primary composite first; only formally test the "key" secondary at full alpha if the primary is significant) rather than a split-alpha or Bonferroni approach — this is the near-universal convention for a single primary/single key-secondary pairing of this kind in cardiology CVOTs of this period, but the exact gatekeeping language is not itself quoted in the label and cannot be confirmed without the SAP.
- **Likely group-sequential monitoring given the trial's event-driven, multi-year enrollment** [inferred from: FOURIER's structure (event-driven, ~27,564 patients, median follow-up 26 months, run by an independent academic-adjacent trial infrastructure) closely parallels EMPA-REG, PARADIGM-HF, and DECLARE-TIMI 58 above, all of which used a group-sequential design with a DMC and a pre-specified alpha-spending function for interim monitoring]. It is very likely FOURIER used a similar interim-monitoring scheme, but no interim analysis is mentioned anywhere in the label, and the specific spending function, interim timing, and boundary values cannot be reconstructed from public sources without the SAP or protocol.

### 5. Semaglutide (Wegovy) — NDA 215256/S-011

**Sponsor:** Novo Nordisk A/S

**Indication approved:** Reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight

**Approval date:** March 8, 2024

**Pivotal trial:** SELECT (Novo Nordisk trial ID EX9536-4388), NCT03574597

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, group-sequential (per SAP v3.0; later reportedly changed to a fixed design)
- *Endpoints:* 3-point MACE (primary), HF composite / all-cause death / CV death (confirmatory secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* Cox proportional-hazards model (score test), ITT estimand
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* Lan-DeMets alpha-spending function approximating O'Brien-Fleming
- *Missing data/bias:* competing-risk censoring, tipping-point sensitivity analysis (multiple imputation)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial; semaglutide 2.4 mg s.c. once weekly vs. placebo, both added to standard of care, 1:1 randomization, N=17,500 planned (17,604 enrolled) with established CV disease and overweight/obesity, no prior diabetes
- Primary endpoint: time to first 3-point MACE (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke)
- Confirmatory secondary endpoints (time-to-event): CV death; a composite heart-failure endpoint (HF hospitalization, urgent HF visit, or CV death); all-cause death
- Estimand: intention-to-treat, evaluating the randomized treatment effect irrespective of adherence or background-medication changes
- Sample size: 90% power to reject H0: HR≥1.0 (one-sided) against Ha: HR<1.0, at design HR=0.83; 1,225 primary endpoint events required, 1:1 randomization
- Design (per SAP v3.0, dated 22-Apr-2022): group-sequential, one interim analysis for superiority at two-thirds of planned primary-endpoint events, no futility stopping; Lan-DeMets alpha-spending function approximating O'Brien-Fleming boundaries, controlling overall one-sided type I error at 2.5%. (A later public description of the trial states the design was ultimately changed to a fixed design without interim testing while keeping the same sample size — the SAP version obtained here still specifies the interim-analysis design, so the final, as-executed monitoring plan should be confirmed against the trial's final CSR before relying on this detail.)
- Primary analysis: Cox proportional hazards model (treatment group as sole fixed factor), score test for the hypothesis test, two-sided 95% CI alongside the one-sided fixed-design p-value; competing risk from non-CV death handled via censoring

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[reconstructed — see caveat below, from SAP §2.1 "Sample size determination," p.6]*

> "The trial is designed with 90% power to confirm superiority for the primary endpoint, i.e., reject the null-hypothesis of a hazard ratio (HR) ≥1.0 against the one-sided alternative of HR<1.0... The trial is designed with one interim testing for superiority of the primary endpoint when two thirds of the total planned number of primary endpoint events has been accrued. Testing for futility is not included. The Lan-DeMets alpha spending function, approximating the O'Brien-Fleming's stopping boundaries, is used to test superiority at a study-wise one-sided type I error rate of 2.5%... Based on a randomisation ratio of 1:1 and a design HR of 0.83 a total of 1,225 primary endpoint events are required."

*[reconstructed — see caveat below, from SAP §2.3.1 "Primary analysis," p.14]*

> "The primary analysis will address the primary estimand (intention-to-treat). The HR for comparing semaglutide 2.4 mg versus semaglutide placebo is estimated from a Cox proportional hazards model with treatment group... as fixed factor together with the two-sided 95% CI and one-sided fixed design p-value for hypothesis testing. The score test from the Cox model is used for testing... The nominal significance level is calculated using the alpha spending function and the actual observed number of events available for the analysis."

**Extraction caveat:** the posted SAP and protocol PDFs for this trial were produced by a redaction/anonymization tool that strips inter-word spacing from the extracted text layer (every character is individually positioned, with no reliable word-boundary information). The passages above were manually reconstructed word-by-word from that corrupted extraction. The technical content and wording are believed faithful to the source, but — unlike the other **[verbatim]** quotes in this document — this should be treated as a careful reconstruction, not a character-for-character-guaranteed quote, and re-checked against the original PDF before being cited elsewhere.

### 6. Azilsartan medoxomil (Edarbi) — NDA 200796

**Sponsor:** Takeda Pharmaceuticals North America, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of hypertension (an angiotensin II receptor blocker), alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents

**Approval date:** February 25, 2011

**Pivotal trial:** Two identically-designed co-pivotal trials — Study 491-019 ("Study 1" in labeling), NCT00696436, and Study 491-008 ("Study 2" in labeling), NCT00696241

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; randomized, double-blind, active-controlled (olmesartan and/or valsartan comparator arms); dose up-titration design; two identically-designed co-pivotal trials required for substantial evidence
- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in 24-hour mean ambulatory systolic blood pressure by ABPM at Week 6 (primary, agreed with FDA at the End-of-Phase-2 meeting); trough (Hour 22-24) ABPM SBP/DBP, clinic (cuff) SBP/DBP, 24-hour mean ABPM DBP (secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* placebo-subtracted least-squares mean treatment comparison (ANCOVA-type model)
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing, terminated once a comparison in the sequence was non-significant, with later comparisons treated as exploratory

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Two 6-week, randomized, double-blind, multi-arm trials in patients with stage 1-2 hypertension (clinic SBP 150-180 mmHg and 24-hour mean SBP 130-170 mmHg at entry); each used a 2-week starting dose followed by up-titration for the remaining 4 weeks
- Study 491-019 (N=1291): TAK-491 (azilsartan medoxomil) 20→40 mg or 40→80 mg vs. valsartan 160→320 mg, olmesartan 20→40 mg, or placebo
- Study 491-008 (N=1275): TAK-491 20, 40, or 80 mg (fixed, no up-titration arm structure noted) vs. olmesartan 40 mg or placebo (no valsartan arm)
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline in 24-hour mean ABPM SBP at Week 6, the endpoint FDA agreed to at the End-of-Phase-2 meeting
- Secondary endpoints: trough (Hour 22-24) ABPM SBP/DBP, clinic (cuff) SBP/DBP at Weeks 4 and 6, 24-hour mean ABPM DBP
- Statistical method: placebo-subtracted LS-mean treatment differences from an ANCOVA-type model; Type I error was controlled using a pre-specified stepwise (fixed-sequence) hierarchical testing procedure — in Study 491-019, TAK-491 80 mg was tested vs. olmesartan then valsartan, followed by TAK-491 40 mg vs. olmesartan; the sequence terminated at a non-significant comparison (TAK-491 40 mg vs. olmesartan), rendering the next scheduled comparison (TAK-491 40 mg vs. valsartan) exploratory despite its own nominal p=0.001
- ABPM data were missing post-baseline in about 20% of subjects in Study 491-019; the sponsor ran multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses that were consistent with the primary result, and a robust ~95%-of-randomized clinic-cuff BP (ITT-LOCF) analysis supported the same conclusion
- No formal group-sequential/interim-analysis design was used in either trial

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2011/200796s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/200796s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review / Summary Review (Shari L. Targum, M.D., Jan 21, 2011 — contains the per-study statistical methodology and results quoted below) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/200796Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — note: the only Statistical Review posted for this NDA (Matthew Jackson, PhD) addresses the nonclinical rat/mouse carcinogenicity studies, not clinical efficacy; the clinical-statistical reviewers of record (Maryann Gordon, M.D. and John Lawrence, Ph.D., per the CDTL memo) do not appear to have a separately posted efficacy statistical review document — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/200796Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record, Study 491-019 — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00696436 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)

- Takeda's general participation in an IPD-sharing program (e.g., Vivli/YODA-type platform) was not individually confirmed for these trials.
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was identified for this application (standard review, no CRL).

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review Memo (Targum), §7.1.2, p.9]*

> "The placebo-controlled phase 3 studies utilized clinic SBP 150-180 mmHg, inclusive, and 24-hour SBP 130-170 mm Hg, inclusive, as entry criteria. The primary endpoint for these studies was the change from baseline in 24-hour mean ABPM SBP. Secondary endpoints included other ABPM and clinic measures of SBP and DBP. During the End of Phase 2 meeting, the Agency accepted the 24-hour mean systolic BP by ABPM for the Phase 3 primary endpoint."

*[verbatim, from FDA Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review Memo (Targum), §7.1.2.1, p.10]*

> "Study 491-019 randomized 1291 subjects to TAK-491 20 or 40 mg, valsartan 160 mg, olmesartan 20 mg or placebo for 2 weeks, followed by up-titration to TAK-491 40 mg or 80 mg (respectively), valsartan 320 mg, olmesartan 40 mg or placebo (respectively) for the next 4 weeks. Type I error was controlled using a stepwise testing procedure."

*[verbatim, from FDA Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review Memo (Targum), §7.1.2.1, pp.10-11]*

> "Significant decreases from baseline vs. placebo were observed for all treatment groups (p < 0.001) for the change in mean 24-hour ABPM SBP. In the context of sequential testing, TAK-491 80 mg was superior to olmesartan (treatment difference -2.54; p = 0.009) and valsartan (treatment difference -4.31 mm Hg; p < 0.001). However, the testing sequence was terminated at the comparison of TAK-491 40 mg vs. olmesartan (p= NS); thus, the ensuing comparison of TAK-491 40 mg vs. valsartan (treatment difference -3.20 mm Hg; p = 0.001) should be considered exploratory."

*[verbatim, from FDA Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review Memo (Targum), §7.1.2.1, p.11]*

> "The statistical reviewer has commented on the lack of post-baseline ABPM data in about 20% of subjects. However, the sponsor's sensitivity analyses (with multiple imputations) were consistent in supporting efficacy; in addition, cuff BP results (ITT LOCF population about 95% of randomized patients) showed robust, consistent results."

This is a case where the fixed-sequence hierarchy actually bit: because the TAK-491 40 mg vs. olmesartan step in the pre-specified order came back non-significant, the *next* scheduled comparison (40 mg vs. valsartan, which had its own nominally significant p=0.001) had to be relabeled exploratory rather than confirmatory — a clean illustration of what a step-down procedure costs a sponsor when an earlier link in the chain fails.

### 7. Linagliptin (Tradjenta) — NDA 201280

**Sponsor:** Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** As an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (a DPP-4 inhibitor)

**Approval date:** May 2, 2011

**Pivotal trial:** Four co-pivotal, 24-week, placebo-controlled Phase III trials — Study 1218.16 (monotherapy), NCT00621140; Study 1218.17 (add-on to metformin), NCT00601250; Study 1218.18 (add-on to metformin+sulfonylurea), NCT00602472; Study 1218.15 (add-on to pioglitazone), NCT00641043 — plus supportive trials 1218.20 (active-controlled vs. glimepiride, 52-week interim of a planned 104-week trial), NCT00622284; 1218.35 (add-on to sulfonylurea), NCT00819091; and 1218.50 (monotherapy in metformin-ineligible patients), NCT00740051

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; four identically-structured co-pivotal monotherapy/add-on trials required for substantial evidence; randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, non-inferiority-then-superiority (supportive Study 1218.20 vs. glimepiride, on a common metformin background)
- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in HbA1c (primary, all trials); fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose (meal tolerance test), treat-to-target response (HbA1c <7.0%/<6.5%) (secondary); body weight change and hypoglycemia incidence (key secondary, Study 1218.20)
- *Primary analysis:* sponsor's ANCOVA (treatment and prior antidiabetic therapy as fixed effects, baseline HbA1c as linear covariate) on the LOCF-imputed Full Analysis Set; FDA statistical reviewer's independent MMRM (with visit-week as an additional fixed effect) on the observed-cases population, used as FDA's primary sensitivity analysis
- *Multiplicity:* Bonferroni split of the two-sided α=0.05 across a pre-planned 52-week interim analysis (α=0.025) and a 104-week final analysis (α=0.025) within Study 1218.20; no protocol-defined multiplicity adjustment was applied across the four separately-tested co-pivotal placebo-controlled trials themselves
- *Missing data/bias:* last observation carried forward (LOCF) imputation for the sponsor's primary FAS analysis; FDA statistical reviewer ran an independent MMRM-based analysis on observed data as a check on the LOCF result

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Four co-pivotal, 24-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trials, each stratified by baseline HbA1c (< or ≥8.5%) and prior antidiabetic therapy: Study 1218.16, monotherapy in drug-naïve or washed-out patients (N=503, 2:1 linagliptin:placebo randomization); Study 1218.17, add-on to metformin in patients inadequately controlled on metformin (N=701); Study 1218.18, add-on to metformin+sulfonylurea (N=1058); Study 1218.15, add-on to pioglitazone in drug-naïve/washed-out patients (N=389)
- Supportive trials: Study 1218.50, monotherapy in patients ineligible/intolerant to metformin, 18 weeks (N=227); Study 1218.35, add-on to sulfonylurea, 18 weeks (N=245); Study 1218.20, active-controlled non-inferiority trial vs. glimepiride (both arms on a metformin background), planned for 104 weeks with only the 52-week interim data submitted in this NDA (N=1559 randomized 1:1)
- Primary endpoint in all trials: change from baseline in HbA1c at the trial's pre-designated primary timepoint (24 weeks for the four co-pivotal trials, the 52-week interim for Study 1218.20)
- Secondary endpoints: fasting plasma glucose and 2-hour postprandial glucose (meal tolerance test), proportion achieving treat-to-target HbA1c <7.0% or <6.5%; in Study 1218.20, change in body weight and hypoglycemia incidence were designated key secondary endpoints
- Sponsor's primary analysis: ANCOVA with treatment and prior antidiabetic therapy as fixed classification effects and baseline HbA1c as a linear covariate, on the Full Analysis Set with LOCF imputation for missing values (patients requiring rescue therapy for FPG >240 mg/dL were discontinued and their pre-rescue LOCF data used)
- FDA's statistical reviewer (Wei Liu, PhD) additionally applied MMRM with an added visit-week fixed effect on the observed-cases population as the primary FDA sensitivity analysis, plus per-protocol/LOCF/FAS-completers MMRM analyses, all evaluated at the last timepoint
- Study 1218.20 non-inferiority margin: 0.35% in HbA1c change from baseline vs. glimepiride, tested at one-sided α=0.025 (2-sided 95% CI) at the 52-week interim; the total two-sided α=0.05 was divided by Bonferroni correction between the 52-week interim (α=0.025) and the planned 104-week final analysis (α=0.025)

**Other resources**

- Boehringer Ingelheim's general participation in an IPD-sharing program (e.g., Vivli) was not individually confirmed for these trials.
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was identified for this application (standard review, first-cycle approval); as a postmarketing requirement, FDA required a dedicated cardiovascular-safety trial to show the upper bound of the two-sided 95% CI for the risk ratio of important CV events vs. comparator is <1.3.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Wei Liu, PhD), §1.2, p.5]*

> "There are 4 pivotal efficacy and safety placebo-controlled phase III trials over 24 weeks (1218.15, 1218.16, 1218.17, and 1218.18). Information on long-term efficacy and safety is derived from a double-blind active-controlled phase III study which compared linagliptin with glimepiride added to a metformin background over 104 weeks (1218.20) of which only the 52 week interim data available from the sponsor... Supportive evidence of efficacy was provided by two double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trials with a treatment duration of 18 weeks: Study 1218.35 compared linagliptin with placebo added to an SU background, whereas study 1218.50 was conducted in patients ineligible for treatment with metformin."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Wei Liu, PhD), §3.1, p.8]*

> "The primary endpoint for these studies is the change from baseline of HbA1c after pre-designed weeks of the treatments as specified in each trial... The sponsor's primary analyses used an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) method with the treatment and previous anti-diabetes therapy as fixed classification effects and baseline HbA1c as linear covariate on the full analysis set (FAS)... The last observation carried forward method (LOCF) was applied to the FAS... Unlike the sponsor's method for the primary analysis, this reviewer applied MMRM method with an additional fixed effect 'visit week' to the general model on the actually observed data, the OC population."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Wei Liu, PhD), §3.1.2.10, pp.25-26]*

> "As an adjustment for the multiple testing of endpoints after 52 weeks (for the interim analysis) and after 104 weeks (for the final analysis), the sponsor applied a Bonferroni correction. The total alpha (α) at 0.05 level (two-sided) was divided between the testing done at 52 weeks (α=0.025) and that done at 104 weeks (α=0.025). The primary endpoint, HbA1c change from baseline to 52 weeks of treatment, was analyzed to test non-inferiority of linagliptin versus glimepiride at the level of α=0.025 (2-sided). The pre-set non-inferiority margin is 0.35%."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Wei Liu, PhD), §1.1.1, p.6]*

> "The non-inferiority of linagliptin 5 mg treatment against the glimepiride in HbA1c improvement is supported by a non-inferiority margin 0.35% in the interim efficacy analysis after 52 weeks treatment. In fact, linagliptin 5 mg is statistically worse than glimepiride in HbA1c change from baseline at every time point measured up to 78 weeks... On the safety side, the hypoglycemia incidence rate in the lina 5 mg treated patients is significantly smaller than that in the glimepiride treated patients."

The FDA reviewer's conclusion is a textbook non-inferiority result landing exactly where non-inferiority margins are designed to allow: linagliptin was numerically and statistically *worse* than glimepiride on the primary glycemic measure at every timepoint, yet within the pre-specified 0.35% margin — with the trade-off (much lower hypoglycemia, weight loss vs. weight gain) forming the actual basis for calling the result acceptable.

### 8. Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) — NDA 22406

**Sponsor:** Johnson and Johnson Pharmaceutical Research and Development, LLC

**Indication approved:** Prophylaxis of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which may lead to pulmonary embolism (PE), in patients undergoing knee or hip replacement surgery

**Approval date:** July 1, 2011

**Pivotal trial:** Four identically-designed co-pivotal Phase III trials (RECORD program) — RECORD1 (Study 11354, total hip replacement), NCT00329628; RECORD2 (Study 11357, extended-duration vs. short-course enoxaparin, total hip replacement), NCT00332020; RECORD3 (Study 11356, total knee replacement), NCT00361894; RECORD4 (Study 11355, total knee replacement), NCT00362232

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, multinational; non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchy (per-protocol population tested first for non-inferiority, then modified-intent-to-treat population for superiority); four identically-designed co-pivotal trials across two surgical settings required for substantial evidence
- *Endpoints:* total VTE — composite of any DVT (proximal/distal, symptomatic/asymptomatic), non-fatal PE, or all-cause death (primary); major VTE, symptomatic VTE or death, net clinical benefit (secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* exact-method and Mantel-Haenszel-weighted risk-difference confidence intervals (non-inferiority margin 3.5%), followed by superiority testing on the modified intent-to-treat population; logistic regression used for exploratory risk-factor/covariate analyses
- *Multiplicity:* unadjusted secondary/supportive testing (single formal primary endpoint) — the sponsor's SAPs did not include strong control of Type I error for the secondary endpoints, including the clinically important "symptomatic VTE or death" endpoint
- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval; FDA Advisory Committee meeting held; FDA Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) site-integrity finding, resolved via a reviewer sensitivity analysis excluding unreliable sites
- *Missing data/bias:* sponsor sensitivity analyses across multiple scenarios for handling missing/inadequate thromboembolism-assessment data, all supporting the primary conclusion

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Four Phase III, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-comparator-controlled, multicenter, multinational trials, all similarly designed with identical efficacy/safety parameters: RECORD1 (N=4541, elective total hip replacement, rivaroxaban 10 mg QD for ~35 days vs. enoxaparin); RECORD2 (N=3148, total hip replacement, rivaroxaban 10 mg QD for 5 weeks vs. enoxaparin 40 mg QD for 10-14 days followed by placebo — an extended-vs-short-duration comparison); RECORD3 (N=2531, total knee replacement, rivaroxaban vs. enoxaparin); RECORD4 (N=2509, total knee replacement, rivaroxaban vs. enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily, the US-approved TKR regimen)
- Primary efficacy endpoint (all four trials): total VTE — composite of any DVT (proximal and/or distal, symptomatic or asymptomatic, generally ascertained by mandatory bilateral venography), non-fatal PE, or death from any cause
- Major secondary endpoints: major VTE (proximal DVT, non-fatal PE, or VTE-related death), incidence of DVT, incidence of symptomatic VTE, and "net clinical benefit" (efficacy composite plus major bleeding)
- Analysis populations: the per-protocol (PP) population was used to test non-inferiority of rivaroxaban vs. enoxaparin first; if non-inferiority was established, the modified intent-to-treat (MITT) population was used to test superiority (non-inferiority margin: 3.5% risk difference)
- Primary results (original 2009 NDA review, total VTE, MITT): RECORD1, rivaroxaban 1.1% vs. enoxaparin 3.7% (p<0.0001); RECORD2, 2.0% vs. 9.3% (p<0.0001); RECORD3, 9.6% vs. 18.9% (p<0.0001); RECORD4, 6.9% vs. 10.1% (p=0.012) — each trial independently met superiority
- FDA's reviewer flagged that the SAPs did not strongly control Type I error across secondary endpoints, and that "symptomatic VTE or death" (a clinically important endpoint) was only nominally significant (p<0.05) in RECORD2 and RECORD3 — the two trials FDA identified as using non-US-standard enoxaparin regimens (shorter duration in RECORD2, an unapproved lower dose in RECORD3), which the reviewer judged likely to have underestimated enoxaparin's true benefit
- FDA's reviewer also found rivaroxaban increased major/clinically-relevant bleeding vs. enoxaparin, using an Andersen-Gill counting-process formulation of the Cox model (rather than the sponsor's simple time-to-first-event Cox model) to properly account for multiple bleeding events per subject
- The original NDA (submitted July 2008) received a Complete Response Letter (May 27, 2009) citing CMC issues, a potential serious-liver-toxicity safety signal, and data-integrity findings from FDA's Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) at specific RECORD-program sites/investigators; the sponsor resubmitted January 3, 2011, and FDA's reviewer re-ran the primary efficacy analysis excluding all DSI-identified unreliable sites, finding the original efficacy conclusion unchanged

- FDA Statistical Review — a combined PDF containing the original efficacy Statistical Review (Qing Xu, PhD, signed May 8, 2009, covering RECORD1-4 study design/results in full), a 2011 Statistical Review Addendum (Qing Xu, PhD, re-analyzing efficacy after excluding DSI-identified unreliable sites), and a separate Statistical Safety Review of potential liver toxicity (John Stephen Yap, PhD) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022406Orig1s000StatR.pdf

**Other resources**

- FDA Advisory Committee meeting: the Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee met on March 19, 2009, and voted 15 (yes) to 2 (no) that the available data demonstrated a favorable risk-benefit profile for rivaroxaban in this indication; the drug was nonetheless issued a CRL two months later on CMC/safety/data-integrity grounds unrelated to the efficacy vote.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Qing Xu, PhD, original, signed May 8, 2009), §1.1, p.5]*

> "Four Phase III pivotal clinical studies were included in this New Drug Application (NDA) submission. Statistical analysis results, based on the data of the 4 pivotal studies, demonstrate the drug efficacy using Rivaroxaban in the treatment of major VTE when compared with Enoxaparin control... However, the primary efficacy endpoint was the incidence of total VTE that defined as the composite of any DVT, non-fatal PE, or all cause death. Among the 3 components of the composite endpoint, only incidence of DVT in Rivaroxaban group was significantly lower than that in active-control group. In all four pivotal studies, incidences of PE and all cause death were rare."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Qing Xu, PhD, original), §1.1, pp.5-6]*

> "All RECORD study protocols included several secondary efficacy endpoints. However, the study statistical analysis plans or SAPs did not include strong control Type I error rate for confirmatory evidence of benefit based on secondary endpoints. A clinically important endpoint in these patient populations is Symptomatic VTE or Death. However Nominal p-values for this secondary endpoints were <0.05 only for RECORD 2 and RECORD 3 studies which used shorter duration of treatment in RECORD 2 and used unapproved lower Enoxaparin regimen in RECORD 3 study. Data from these trials are likely to have resulted in underestimation of Enoxaparin's benefit in terms of Symptomatic VTE."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review (Qing Xu, PhD, original), §1.3, p.7]*

> "Sponsor used Cox model for time to first event for bleeding analyses, although bleeding events are time dependent with multiple observations per subject and it is more appropriate to use time-to-event data in the multiple event setting. In this review, the Andersen-Gill (AG) formulation of the proportional hazards model as a counting process is used for the assessment of benefit in terms of bleeding... administration of Rivaroxaban for prophylaxis of DVT and PE increases the incidence of bleeding in comparison with the active control Enoxaparin."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review Addendum (Qing Xu, PhD, May 2011), §1]*

> "Primary efficacy analyses results from reviewing original NDA of four multi-center, randomized controlled trials (RECORD 1-4) indicated statistical superiority of rivaroxaban over enoxaparin in the primary efficacy outcome (composite endpoint of any DVT, nonfatal PE, and death from all cause). In this resubmission, the reviewer conducted analysis by excluding all unreliable sites identified by the Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI); and the results did not alter the original efficacy conclusion."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review Addendum (Qing Xu, PhD, May 2011), §4]*

> "The review analysis results for the primary efficacy endpoint of total VTE by excluding unreliable sites for each of the RECORD study did not alter the original efficacy conclusion that rivaroxiaban is statistically superior over enoxaparin in the primary efficacy outcome of total VTE in the treatment of patient with VTE."

The 2009 statistical review is unusually blunt for a document that ultimately supported approval: FDA's own reviewer flagged that two of the four "identically designed" co-pivotal trials used enoxaparin regimens that were shorter (RECORD2) or lower-dose (RECORD3) than the US-approved comparator regimen — a design choice that would tend to inflate rivaroxaban's apparent advantage — and that the sponsor's SAPs made no attempt to control Type I error across secondary endpoints, so the one endpoint most clinically relevant to patients (symptomatic VTE or death) never had a multiplicity-protected claim built around it.

### 9. Ticagrelor (Brilinta) — NDA 22433

**Sponsor:** AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals

**Indication approved:** Reduce the rate of thrombotic cardiovascular events in patients with acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, NSTEMI, or STEMI)

**Approval date:** July 20, 2011

**Pivotal trial:** PLATO (PLATelet inhibition and patient Outcomes), NCT00391872

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, event-driven trial
- *Endpoints:* MACE composite (3-point: CV death, MI, stroke; primary)
- *Primary analysis:* unstratified Cox proportional-hazards model, single treatment-group term only, no covariates or stratification factors
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (5-endpoint secondary sequence)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* Haybittle-Peto boundary (single interim analysis at ~1,200 events; critical p=0.001 interim, p=0.0497 final)
- *Missing data/bias:* post hoc treatment-by-region / treatment-by-aspirin-dose interaction investigation mandated by a Complete Response Letter
- *Regulatory:* FDA Advisory Committee meeting held; Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Phase III, multicenter, international, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled (vs. clopidogrel) trial; 18,624 patients randomized within 24 hours of non-ST or ST-elevation ACS, across 43 countries (per the FDA Advisory Committee transcript, "almost 1,000 centers")
- Randomized 1:1 to ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily (180 mg loading dose, plus an additional 90 mg before PCI if >24h post-randomization) or clopidogrel 75 mg once daily (300 mg loading dose); both arms received background aspirin per investigator discretion — a fact that became central to the trial's regulatory controversy (see below); notably, contrary to a claim made by the sponsor's presenter at the FDA Advisory Committee meeting, randomization was **not** stratified by planned invasive-vs-medical management, a point FDA staff (Marciniak) forced the sponsor to correct on the record
- Primary efficacy endpoint: time to first occurrence of the composite of CV death, MI, or stroke
- Secondary endpoints tested in a fixed hierarchical (step-down) sequence of five hypotheses (invasive-intent subgroup MACE; all-cause-mortality/MI/stroke composite; a broader ischemic composite; each MACE component individually in order MI→CV death→stroke; all-cause mortality), continuing only until the first non-significant result
- Sample size: event-driven, target of 1,780 primary endpoint events over a 6-12 month treatment period (average ~10 months/patient); one formal interim analysis at ~1,200 adjudicated events (2/3 of target)
- Primary analysis method: Cox proportional-hazards model with only a treatment-group factor (no covariates, no stratification) on the full analysis set (all randomized patients, ITT); nominal 2-sided significance level of 4.97% to account for the interim look; Peto-Haybittle group-sequential boundaries (critical p=0.001 at interim, p=0.0497 at final) preserved overall 2-sided alpha of 5%
- **Regulatory history is unusually eventful for this census**: original NDA submitted November 13, 2009; reviewed at a July 28, 2010 FDA Advisory Committee meeting (voted 7-1 for approval) that focused heavily on an unexplained divergence between US and non-US (OUS) treatment effects (US point estimate HR≈1.27, i.e., numerically favoring clopidogrel, vs. clear OUS benefit); FDA issued a Complete Response Letter on December 16, 2010 requiring the sponsor to conduct an extensive set of analyses testing whether concurrent aspirin dose explained the regional heterogeneity; the sponsor's January 20, 2011 complete response included 13 different "representative aspirin dose" definitions crossed with 6 imputation methods, reviewed in a dedicated FDA statistical re-review; approved July 20, 2011

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2011/022433Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/022433s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (post-CRL resubmission, aspirin-dose/regional-heterogeneity re-analysis; Jialu Zhang, PhD) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022433Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review (Clinical Efficacy Review by Robert Fiorentino, MD, MPH, with an embedded Cross-Discipline Team Leader "Review of Complete Response" by Thomas Marciniak, MD, dated May 14, 2011) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022433Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (Division Director memo, Norman Stockbridge, MD, PhD, July 8, 2011) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022433Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00391872 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Wallentin L, Becker RC, Budaj A, et al. "Ticagrelor versus Clopidogrel in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndromes." *N Engl J Med.* 2009;361(11):1045-1057. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0904327), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19717846/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Ticagrelor%20versus%20Clopidogrel%20in%20Patients%20with%20Acute%20Coronary%20Syndromes)

**Other resources**

- AstraZeneca IPD access via Vivli.org; trial-specific PLATO availability not individually confirmed here.
- An FDA Advisory Committee (Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee) meeting was held July 28, 2010, which voted 7-1 for approval; the meeting transcript itself became part of the regulatory record after FDA staff publicly disputed statements made by the sponsor's presenter (see SAP section).
- FDA's Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) audited six clinical sites in Hungary and Poland; the audit report did not identify major problems that would invalidate use of the data.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Medical Review, Clinical Efficacy Review by Robert Fiorentino, MD, MPH, §5.3.1.13 "Primary Efficacy Objective," pp.30-31]*

> "The primary efficacy variable was the time to first occurrence of any event from the composite of CV death, MI, and stroke... Hypothesis testing was at the nominal significance level of 4.97% (2-tailed) in order to account for the planned interim analysis... The primary analysis was performed on the full analysis set: All patients who have been randomized to study treatment were to be included irrespective of their protocol adherence and continued participation in the study. In order to address the issue of multiplicity, a prespecified hierarchical test sequence was performed. Once the null hypothesis concerning the primary composite efficacy endpoint is rejected, the secondary composite efficacy endpoints will be tested separately in the order given below: [1. invasive-intent MACE subgroup; 2. all-cause mortality/MI/stroke; 3. broader ischemic composite; 4. MI, CV death, stroke individually; 5. all-cause mortality]... Statistical hypothesis testing was continued until the first statistically non-significant treatment difference was observed. The confirmatory analysis also included a formal interim analysis of the primary composite efficacy endpoint after approximately 1200 events (2/3rds of the total target number of 1780 events) had been observed. Multiplicity between the interim and final analyses was controlled using Peto-Haybittle group sequential boundaries corresponding to critical p-values of 0.001 and 0.0497, respectively."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (post-CRL resubmission), Jialu Zhang, PhD, "Executive Summary," p.4]*

> "The original application was submitted on November 13, 2009. One major issue in the application was the regional difference in the observed treatment effect between North America and the rest of the world... The issue was further discussed in the Advisory Committee meeting on August 28 [sic], 2010... The division subsequently issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL) on December 16, 2010 requesting additional analyses to examine the aspirin hypothesis... A total of 13 different ASA definitions and 6 imputations were proposed and analyses were performed in a number of Cox proportional hazards models under these scenarios... There appeared a consistently adverse trend for ticagrelor with high dose of ASA in US, while there did not in OUS."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary (Division Director) Review, Norman Stockbridge, MD, PhD, "Divisional memo," July 8, 2011, pp.1-2]*

> "As shown below, effects were heterogeneous with respect to region with the US results being the main driver of the North American anomaly... In the US the point estimate of the hazard ratio was about 1.27. The point estimates for the hazard ratios in placebo-controlled studies of clopidogrel are in the ballpark of 1/1.27, so, by the most generous of non-inferiority calculations, based solely on point estimates, the US results are entirely consistent with there being no effect whatsoever of ticagrelor in the US. No single or combination of baseline covariates was found to explain the US-foreign differences in outcome. However, post-randomization dose of aspirin does appear to account for regional differences, at least in the statistical sense."

*[verbatim, FDA Medical Review, Cross-Discipline Team Leader "Review of Complete Response," Thomas Marciniak, MD (14 May 2011), §8 "Advisory Committee Meeting," pp.48-50]*

> "We presented ticagrelor at the July 28, 2010, meeting of the Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee. The members voted 7 to 1 for approval... COMMENT: I believe the advisory committee proceedings were marred by a major problem: misrepresentation of some facts by the sponsor's representatives... 'DR. TEMPLE: Dr. Harrington said that there was stratification by the intent to intervene or not intervene. Tom Marciniak showed me a statement in what appeared to be the protocol that said it was not stratified by that... which was it? DR. FOX:...they were given a randomization code. DR. TEMPLE: And stratified by that question. DR. FOX: That's correct.'... Because the protocol, statistical analysis plan, and study report do not mention stratification of the randomization, I queried the sponsor in writing after the meeting. The sponsor responded... 'While there was no intent whatsoever to misguide the committee, AstraZeneca acknowledge it would have been helpful to have been more precise in this regard...'... PLATO did not have only five patients with missing vital status at study end. The sponsor's presenter also made the following assertion: 'we have vital status at the end of the trial for all but five patients. This is a tremendous achievement'... If one considers having vital status 'at the end of trial' to be having it on or after the targeted study completion date for a patient — the only definition that I consider valid — then the sponsor reports 54 ticagrelor and 52 clopidogrel patients as not having vital status known at the end of the trial. So by the sponsor's count 106 patients — not 5 — are missing follow-up at the end of the study."

This is a genuinely striking data point for the census: the same reviewer, Thomas Marciniak, MD, who filed the ticagrelor CDTL review above would go on 18 months later to raise a near-identical missing-vital-status/fragility argument against apixaban's ARISTOTLE trial (see below) — suggesting a reviewer-level pattern of concern about vital-status ascertainment across FDA's cardiovascular outcomes-trial reviews in this era, not a drug-specific artifact.
