[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1209657), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23883377/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Riociguat%20for%20the%20treatment%20of%20chronic%20thromboembolic%20pulmonary%20hypertension)
- Pivotal publication (PATENT-1): Ghofrani HA, Galiè N, Grimminger F, et al. "Riociguat for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension." *N Engl J Med.* 2013;369(4):330-340. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1209655), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23883378/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Riociguat%20for%20the%20treatment%20of%20pulmonary%20arterial%20hypertension)

**Other resources**

- Bayer's general clinical-trial-data-sharing commitments cover IPD requests via Vivli.org; trial-specific CHEST-1/PATENT-1 availability not individually confirmed here.
- An FDA Advisory Committee meeting (Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee) was held on August 5, 2013; the Committee voted unanimously in favor of approval for both CTEPH and PAH, reasoning that the relevance of the PAH data supported approving the CTEPH indication on the basis of a single trial.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary, p.1]*

> "This submission contains two phase 3 trials to support two separate but related indications. Trial 12934 (PATENT-1) was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center, multinational study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral riociguat (1 mg, 1.5 mg, 2 mg, or 2.5 mg tid) in patients with symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Trial 11348 (CHEST-1) was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter, multinational study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral riociguat (1 mg, 1.5 mg, 2 mg, or 2.5 mg tid) in patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Both studies met their primary objective of showing an improvement compared to placebo in 6-minute walk distance, a symptomatic benefit. No statistical issues were identified with these trials."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §1.4.2 "Statistical Methodologies"]*

> "In trial 12934, the primary efficacy analysis was the analysis of the change in 6MWD from baseline to week 12 (last observation until week 12) in subjects valid for ITT, with imputation of missing values for subjects who withdrew or died before 12 weeks. The riociguat 1.0-2.5 mg and placebo groups were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)... The primary statistical method would be the stratified Wilcoxon test if the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality of residuals was statistically significant... Superiority of the riociguat 1.0-2.5 mg group over the placebo group was to be declared if the two-sided p-value was less than or equal to 0.05."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §1.4.4.1, on the actual analysis used]*

> "Note that the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality of the ANCOVA residuals was significant (p=0.0001). Therefore, the stratified Wilcoxon p-value was formally used for determining statistical significance, as pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan... The LS mean difference shown in the table is not a good estimate of the treatment effect for the same reason that the ANCOVA is not a good test (errors not normally distributed). A better estimate would be the Hodges-Lehmann estimate associated with the stratified Wilcoxon test, which I calculated as 29 m with a 95% CI of (18 m, 40 m)" [PATENT-1]; the analogous CHEST-1 estimate is "39 m with a 95% CI of (25 m, 54 m)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §1.12, labeling recommendation]*

> "Since the assumptions for ANCOVA were not met, the statistical analysis plan stated that formal testing would be done using the stratified Wilcoxon test... I recommend the label does not show the LS mean estimated by ANCOVA; instead, it should show the median change from baseline in both groups or the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the difference in medians."

This is a clean real-world example of a trial's own pre-specified contingency rule firing: the sponsor's SAP treated ANCOVA as the primary analysis only if a normality check passed, and named the stratified Wilcoxon/Hodges-Lehmann approach as the fallback — the fallback is what actually determined the approved claim, and FDA's reviewer pushed back on the sponsor's continued use of the ANCOVA LS-mean estimate in labeling once that contingency had been triggered.

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review (Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review), "Advisory Committee Meeting"]*

> "An Advisory Committee meeting was held on 5 August 2013 to discuss the approvability of riociguat, dosing, and risk of hypotension. The Committee voted unanimously in favor of approval for both CTEPH and PAH, feeling that there was enough relevance of PAH to approve CTEPH on the basis of a single trial. There were no significant concerns about trial designs or execution."

### 17. Macitentan (Opsumit) — NDA 204410

**Sponsor:** Actelion Pharmaceuticals

**Indication approved:** Delay disease progression in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, WHO Group I)

**Approval date:** October 18, 2013

**Pivotal trial:** SERAPHIN, NCT00660179

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial, three-arm dose-ranging design
- *Endpoints:* PAH morbidity/mortality composite (time to first event of death, disease-specific hospitalization/intervention, or other disease worsening)
- *Primary analysis:* stratified log-rank test, Cox proportional-hazards model (stratified or with covariates)
- *Multiplicity:* Bonferroni split-alpha allocation across two active-dose arms vs. placebo, fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (secondary endpoints)
- *Missing data/bias:* early treatment-discontinuation censoring (EOT+7 days rather than end-of-study) flagged as a review issue by the FDA reviewer
- *Regulatory:* reviewer-documented deviation from agreed analysis plan

**Trial design & endpoints**

- SERAPHIN: multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven Phase 3 trial in 742 patients with symptomatic WHO Functional Class II-IV PAH, randomized 1:1:1 to placebo (n=250), macitentan 3 mg (n=250), or macitentan 10 mg (n=242); sponsor planned to collect 285 primary events
- Primary endpoint: time from start of study treatment to the first morbidity/mortality event up to end of treatment (EOT), a composite of death, a treatment-emergent fatal adverse event within 4 weeks of drug discontinuation, atrial septostomy or hospitalization for atrial septostomy, lung transplantation or hospitalization for lung transplantation, initiation of intravenous/subcutaneous prostanoids, or other adjudicated worsening of PAH
- Sample size: 285 events needed to detect a hazard ratio of 0.5472 for macitentan vs. placebo at a nominal two-sided type-I error of 0.005 per dose group, 90% power, using the log-rank test
- Multiplicity: study-wise two-sided alpha of 0.01 was preserved by testing each active-dose-vs-placebo comparison at a nominal two-sided alpha of 0.005 (Bonferroni approach); secondary endpoints (6-minute walk distance change at month 6, WHO Functional Class change at month 6, time to death/PAH-hospitalization, time to all-cause death through EOT+7 days, time to all-cause death through end of study) were tested hierarchically in that pre-specified order
- No interim analysis on efficacy was performed, despite the event-driven design
- Primary endpoint events were censored at end-of-treatment plus 7 days rather than end-of-study; 93 patients discontinued treatment early and were censored without a primary event, which the FDA reviewer flagged as a review issue requiring sensitivity analyses
- Result (10 mg vs. placebo): HR 0.55 (97.5% CI 0.39-0.76; log-rank p<0.0001); critical secondary endpoint (PAH death or PAH hospitalization): HR 0.50 (97.5% CI 0.34-0.75; p<0.0001); the FDA reviewer noted the composite primary result was "driven by the single component 'other worsening of PAH' with no effect shown for mortality"

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2013/204410Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2013/204410s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204410Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (Cross-Discipline Team Leader Review) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204410Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204410Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00660179 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Pulido T, Adzerikho I, Channick RN, et al; SERAPHIN Investigators. "Macitentan and morbidity and mortality in pulmonary arterial hypertension." *N Engl J Med.* 2013;369(9):809-818. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1213917), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23984728/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Macitentan%20and%20morbidity%20and%20mortality%20in%20pulmonary%20arterial%20hypertension)

**Other resources**

- Actelion (a Johnson & Johnson company since 2017) participates in sponsor data-sharing programs including Vivli.org; trial-specific SERAPHIN availability not individually confirmed here.
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held for this application, per the FDA Summary Review.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2 "Study Design and Endpoints"]*

> "This was a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel group, event-driven, Phase 3 study. A total of 742 patients were randomized (1:1:1 ratio) to the three treatment groups, i.e., macitentan 3 mg (250 patients), macitentan 10 mg (242 patients), or placebo (250 patients)... This study was designed as an event-driven trial and the sponsor planned to collect 285 primary events."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, primary endpoint definition]*

> "The primary endpoint was defined as time from start of study treatment to the first morbidity or mortality event up to EOT. The first composite event included: Death, or onset of a treatment-emergent AE with a fatal outcome occurring within 4 weeks of study treatment discontinuation, or Atrial septostomy or hospitalization for atrial septostomy, or Lung transplantation or hospitalization for lung transplantation, or Initiation of intravenous (i.v.) or subcutaneous (s.c.) prostanoids... or Other worsening of PAH."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, "Statistical Methodologies"]*

> "To keep the study-wise type-I error to a two-sided 0.01 level, each comparison of active dose versus placebo was tested at a nominal type-I error level of 0.005 (two-sided) using Bonferroni's approach. The secondary endpoints were analyzed hierarchically in the following order. [Change from baseline to Month 6 in 6MWD; Change from baseline to Month 6 in modified WHO FC; Time to death due to PAH or hospitalization for PAH; Time to death of all causes up to EOT + 7 days; Time to death of all causes up to EOS]... A total of 285 events were determined to be needed to detect a hazard ratio of 0.5472 for macitentan versus placebo with a nominal type-I error of 0.005 (two-sided) for each dose group of macitentan (3 mg and 10 mg) and 90% power using the logrank test."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, filing checklist]*

> "Interim analyses (if present) were pre-specified in the protocol and appropriate adjustments in significance level made. DSMB meeting minutes and data are available." — marked "No," with reviewer comment: "No interim analysis on efficacy was performed."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §5.1 "Statistical Issues and Collective Evidence," on the reviewer-documented censoring concern]*

> "The subjects were followed for the primary events until the end of treatment + 7 days instead of the end of study. As a result, 93 patients discontinued treatment early and censored at EOT + 7 days without any primary endpoint events. The sponsor and the reviewer performed a number of sensitivity analyses to assess the impact on the study results from these patients... At least 18 more events out of the 34 patients in the high dose group were needed to change the p-value of logrank test to 0.005."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary, on the composite endpoint's component driver]*

> "The primary endpoint of the study was a composite morbidity/mortality endpoint with multiple components, including death, lung transplantation, initiation of prostanoids, atrial septostomy and other worsening of PAH. The primary endpoint showed highly significant results. However, it was driven by the single component 'other worsening of PAH' with no effect shown for mortality."

The FDA reviewer's censoring critique is a good illustration of how an event-driven trial's power depends on where the "clock stops" for patients who discontinue early: SERAPHIN's protocol-specified EOT+7-day censoring rule (rather than following patients to a common end-of-study date) removed potential follow-up time and events from 93 early discontinuers, and the review explicitly quantifies how few additional events in the high-dose arm alone would have been needed to erase significance — a rare example of FDA publishing that kind of fragility calculation.

### 18. Droxidopa (Northera) — NDA 203202

**Sponsor:** Chelsea Therapeutics International, Ltd.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of orthostatic dizziness, lightheadedness, or the "feeling that you are about to black out" in adults with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension caused by primary autonomic failure (Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure), dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, or non-diabetic autonomic neuropathy — approved under accelerated approval (Subpart H)

**Approval date:** February 18, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** Study 306B (NOH306B), NCT01176240 (also discussed: Study 301/NOH301, NCT00782340)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, mid-trial SAP amendment changing endpoint status (primary endpoint redefined twice before database lock), FDA reviewer suspected site-level data fraud/implausible results excluded from efficacy conclusions
- *Endpoints:* single-item patient-reported symptom severity score (OHSA Item 1) as primary endpoint
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing
- *Missing data/bias:* baseline-observation-carried-forward (BOCF) sensitivity analysis exposing an informative-dropout imbalance between arms
- *Regulatory:* accelerated approval based on a short-term symptom-score effect reasonably likely to predict long-term clinical benefit (non-oncology indication), confirmatory trial required, FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (two cycles)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Droxidopa's development program included four Phase 3 trials before approval: Study 301 (NOH301, NCT00782340) and Studies 302/303 (NOH302/NOH303) were negative on their pre-specified primary endpoints, or positive only until a data-integrity problem was identified at one site; a fifth trial ("Study 304"/NOH304, NCT01132326) was a single-arm long-term safety extension, not an efficacy trial
- Study 301 (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled) was initially reported positive on the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire (OHQ) composite score, but FDA's review found data from one site (Site 507) "implausible, and quite remarkable, different from all other data," raising an unresolved possibility of fraud that undermined reliance on the trial as sole pivotal evidence
- Study 306B (NOH306B), submitted only after an initial Complete Response and a denied formal-dispute-resolution appeal, was the trial FDA ultimately relied on: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, all-U.S. trial restricted to Parkinson's-disease-associated neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, N=174 (89 droxidopa/85 placebo), with a 14-day dose titration (100-600 mg tid) followed by an 8-week fixed-dose period
- The primary endpoint for Study 306B was changed twice during the trial's conduct before database lock: from the OHQ composite score at Week 8, to patient-reported falls at Week 8, to the final endpoint of change in OHSA Item 1 (the dizziness/lightheadedness item of the Orthostatic Hypotension Symptom Assessment) from baseline to Week 1
- Pre-specified primary analysis: ANCOVA adjusting for baseline OHSA Item 1 score, with a pre-specified switch to a non-parametric analysis if ANCOVA assumptions (including residual normality) were violated, assessed by visual inspection of diagnostic plots rather than a formal normality test
- Secondary endpoints (six, tested sequentially only if the primary endpoint was significant at the 0.05 level): change in OHSA Item 1 at Weeks 2/4/8, standing systolic blood pressure change at Week 1, patient-reported falls, and change in OHQ at Week 8
- Result: 147 of 174 randomized patients contributed to the primary Full Analysis Set (69 droxidopa/78 placebo) because of differential dropout; LS mean difference in OHSA Item 1 change was -0.94 (95% CI -1.78, -0.1), p=0.028 (FDA reviewer's ANCOVA recalculation; the sponsor's non-parametric analysis gave -1.0, p=0.018)
- Missing-data concern: dropout was substantially more common in the droxidopa arm, driven by adverse events and treatment failures — an imbalance the FDA statistical reviewer characterized as evidence that missingness was informative rather than random; a baseline-observation-carried-forward sensitivity analysis reduced the estimated treatment effect to -0.45 (95% CI -1.2, 0.3), which one clinical reviewer cited in formally regarding Study 306B as a negative trial once informative censoring was accounted for
- Approved on the accelerated-approval (Subpart H) pathway, with a post-marketing requirement for a confirmatory trial to verify durable clinical benefit

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter (labeled "ACCELERATED APPROVAL") — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2014/203202Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/203202lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/203202Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (Office Director Decisional Memo) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/203202Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/203202Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record (Study 306A/306B) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01176240 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- ClinicalTrials.gov record (Study 301) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00782340 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication (Study 301): Kaufmann H, Freeman R, Biaggioni I, et al; NOH301 Investigators. "Droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: a randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial." *Neurology.* 2014;83(4):328-335. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000000615), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24944260/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Droxidopa%20for%20neurogenic%20orthostatic%20hypotension%20a%20randomized%20placebo-controlled%20phase%203%20trial)
- Pivotal publication (Study 306B): Hauser RA, Isaacson S, Lisk JP, Hewitt LA, Rowse G. "Droxidopa for the short-term treatment of symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson's disease (nOH306B)." *Mov Disord.* 2015;30(5):646-654. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/mds.26086), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25487613/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Droxidopa%20for%20the%20short-term%20treatment%20of%20symptomatic%20neurogenic%20orthostatic%20hypotension%20in%20Parkinson%27s%20disease) — note this publication postdates the February 2014 approval

**Other resources**

- Chelsea Therapeutics was acquired by H. Lundbeck A/S in 2014, shortly after this approval; trial-specific IPD access was not individually confirmed here.
- Two FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee meetings were held: February 23, 2012 (voted 7-4 in favor of approval, based on Study 301 alone, before the Site 507 data-integrity issue fully entered the risk-benefit calculus) and January 14, 2014 (voted 16-1 in favor of approval, after Study 306B had been submitted).

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review (Office Director Decisional Memo), on the accelerated-approval basis]*

> "The NDA will be approved under Subpart H, where the short-term effect is construed as 'reasonably likely' to predict the long-term effect that would be clinically meaningful."

> "One could take the position that the existence of prior studies that failed to show durability of treatment effect essentially make the short-term demonstration of efficacy reasonably unlikely to predict a long-term treatment effect here. It is possible that the applicant's theory about carryover effect is incorrect. But 'reasonably likely' isn't tantamount to 'substantial evidence.'"

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the primary endpoint's two changes]*

> "The primary endpoint was the OHQ composite score at Week 8." [initial version] — then, after two changes — "the 1° endpoint was changed a second time: from patient-reported falls at Week 8 to OHSA Item 1 at Week 1."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the pre-specified analysis contingency]*

> "According to the final statistical analysis plan, the 1° endpoint would be tested using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model adjusting for baseline OHSA Item 1 score. However, if any of the ANCOVA assumptions (including normality of the residuals) were not met, then the 1° analysis was to be changed to a non-parametric model. The violation of assumptions was to be determined by visual inspection of the plots, without a formal test of normality."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on secondary-endpoint gatekeeping]*

> "The secondary endpoints were tested sequentially in the order listed above if the primary efficacy endpoint won at significance level of 0.05."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the missing-data concern]*

> "The missing data, and particularly the substantial imbalance between treatment groups, was a concern to all on the review team. Subjects dropped out predominantly in the droxidopa group because of adverse events and treatment failures, strongly suggesting that missingness was not random."... "Dr. Zhang imputed the missing data by carrying forward the baseline observations, and found a treatment effect of -0.45 with 95% CI -1.2, 0.3."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, reviewer dissent]*

> "Dr. Stockbridge views Study 306B as a negative trial... He noted that the p-value of 0.028 cannot stand up against any adjustments that might be made for informative censoring, i.e., the trial is negative at a p-value of 0.028 because of the imbalance in dropouts."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the Study 301 Site 507 data-integrity finding]*

> "These results were considered to be implausible, and quite remarkable, different from all other data. Although fraud is difficult to prove in clinical trials, many on the review team were concerned about this possibility."

Droxidopa is a genuinely unusual case for this census: the drug reached approval only on its fourth attempted pivotal trial, on an endpoint that had already been changed twice within that same trial's SAP, via a contingency (visual-inspection-triggered non-parametric fallback) similar in spirit to riociguat's Shapiro-Wilk-triggered fallback above but with a much looser, non-formal trigger criterion — and even the reviewing team was internally split on whether the result should be read as positive once dropout-driven informative censoring was accounted for.

### 19. Metreleptin (Myalept) — BLA 125390

**Sponsor:** Amylin Pharmaceuticals (development originated at Amgen/the NIH; commercialized by Amylin/Bristol-Myers Squibb at approval)

**Indication approved:** Adjunct to diet as replacement therapy to treat the complications of leptin deficiency in patients with congenital or acquired generalized lipodystrophy (partial lipodystrophy was considered and not approved)

**Approval date:** February 24, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** No randomized controlled trial — approval rested on pooled open-label, single-arm data from an NIH proof-of-concept/extension study (Study 991265 and its extension, internally numbered inconsistently within FDA's own documents as either 20010769 or 20010796) and a separate treatment-IND expanded-access program, Study FHA101 (NCT00677313)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* single-arm, open-label trial; non-randomized, open-label treatment program combining an NIH proof-of-concept/natural-history-adjacent cohort and a separate treatment-IND expanded-access cohort, pooled for efficacy
- *Endpoints:* metabolic biomarker change from baseline (HbA1c, fasting triglycerides) as efficacy endpoints, without formal hypothesis testing
- *Primary analysis:* descriptive single-arm continuous-endpoint analysis (means/medians + 95% CI, no formal hypothesis test; analogous to the existing "descriptive single-arm response-rate analysis" concept but for continuous biomarkers)
- *Missing data/bias:* complete-case analysis under an unverifiable missing-completely-at-random assumption, with no control arm available to support imputation-based sensitivity or tipping-point analyses
- *Regulatory:* FDA restriction of the approved indication to one disease subtype following a split Advisory Committee vote (generalized vs. partial lipodystrophy)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- The efficacy case rested on 72 patients treated in an NIH-run proof-of-concept study (991265) and its long-term open-label extension, plus 28 patients treated under a treatment IND (Study FHA101) opened in 2008 — 100 total efficacy patients, of whom the generalized-lipodystrophy subset supported the approved indication
- No control group, randomization, or blinding was used at any stage; all comparisons were before-after within each patient relative to their own pre-treatment baseline
- "Primary endpoints" as specified across the program's protocols/SAP were change from baseline in HbA1c and fasting triglycerides at Months 4, 8, and 12; the FDA statistical reviewer noted the SAP additionally listed fasting plasma glucose as a primary endpoint, inconsistent with the protocols, and that no single milestone visit was pre-specified as the definitive efficacy timepoint
- No formal hypothesis testing was pre-specified anywhere in the program; results were summarized descriptively (means/medians with 95% confidence intervals), and the FDA statistical reviewer explicitly stated the sponsor's use of "intent-to-treat (ITT)" terminology for the analysis population was "inappropriate as this convention is defined only in the context of a randomized control trial"
- Missing data were substantial and grew over calendar time in the longer-running NIH extension study (up to 60% missing at Month 4 for later-enrolled patients); the primary FDA analysis used complete-case exclusion of patients with missing values at baseline or follow-up
- Because no formal efficacy hypothesis existed, the FDA reviewer noted that standard missing-data sensitivity tools (e.g., a tipping-point analysis) could not be constructed, since there was no pre-specified "win" criterion for the analysis to tip away from
- A boxed-warning-level safety signal (lymphoma) was also assessed only descriptively, with the FDA review explicitly flagging that the underlying incidence estimates were based on a very small sample and carried very wide confidence intervals

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter (BLA approval; explicitly names "pivotal clinical trials NIH 991265/20010769 and trial FHA101") — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2014/125390Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/125390s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125390Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125390Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125390Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record (NIH extension study, likely corresponding to the 20010769/20010796 protocol referenced in the BLA, though the exact protocol-number match is not independently confirmed) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00025883 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- ClinicalTrials.gov record (Study FHA101, expanded-access/treatment-IND program, not a registered interventional efficacy trial) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00677313 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- No single peer-reviewed publication reports the exact pooled dataset (991265/extension + FHA101) that FDA reviewed; the closest related publications are cited below as context, not as "the" pivotal-trial report

**Other resources**

- No confirmed IPD/dataset-sharing program for this ultra-rare-disease dataset was identified.
- An FDA Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee (EMDAC) meeting was held on December 11, 2013. The Committee voted 11-1 that benefits outweighed risks for generalized lipodystrophy, but 2-10 against approval for partial lipodystrophy — directly explaining why the approved indication is restricted to generalized lipodystrophy only.
- Related (non-pivotal) publications describing overlapping cohorts: Petersen KF, Oral EA, Dufour S, et al. "Leptin reverses insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis in patients with severe lipodystrophy." *J Clin Invest.* 2002;109(10):1345-1350. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI15001), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12021250/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leptin%20reverses%20insulin%20resistance%20and%20hepatic%20steatosis%20in%20patients%20with%20severe%20lipodystrophy); and Diker-Cohen T, Cochran E, Gorden P, Brown RJ. "Partial and generalized lipodystrophy: comparison of baseline characteristics and response to metreleptin." *J Clin Endocrinol Metab.* 2015;100(5):1802-1810 (published after approval). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2014-4491), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25734254/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Partial%20and%20generalized%20lipodystrophy%20comparison%20of%20baseline%20characteristics%20and%20response%20to%20metreleptin)

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the design history]*

> "The metreleptin-lipodystrophy development program began in 2000 with a proof-of-concept study (991265) conducted under an investigator IND. This initial evaluation involved a small number of patients... Given these dramatic results and the rarity of lipodystrophy, the Division agreed with continued study of metreleptin in an open-label single-arm fashion."

> "The BLA submission includes efficacy data from 72 patients treated in studies 991265/20010796 at the NIH, and 28 patients from study FHA101 conducted under a treatment IND opened in 2008."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the ITT terminology critique and the single-arm design's evidentiary limits]*

> "The sponsor's referral to this analysis population as an intent-to-treat (ITT) population, however, is inappropriate as this convention is defined only in the context of a randomized control trial."

> "Due to formal hypotheses tests not being performed per the SAP, descriptive statistics are used to summarize visits and to compare the change in baseline levels at month 4 and month 12; 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the mean change from baseline are also presented... Importantly, the lack of formal testing coupled with the single-arm design makes the evaluation of study results rely on clinical judgment and information external to the study."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on missing data]*

> "Patients with missing values (at baseline or at follow-up) were excluded in the calculation of descriptive summaries and CIs. Extrapolating findings from the group with data to the full sample requires the strong assumption that the missing data is missing completely at random... Without a control arm any approach would require making assumptions that would be difficult to justify empirically or clinically."

> "The informative and alternative 'tipping-point' strategy to investigate the impact of missing data could not be performed due to the absence of formal study hypotheses. That is, a judgment on whether responses in patients that were not included in the analysis could be such that the analysis based on patients with available data would transition from 'win' to 'lose' cannot be done since there is no 'win' criteria."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on a protocol/SAP inconsistency]*

> "Several issues exist around the primary endpoints. First, while both protocols list HbA1c and fasting triglyceride as primary endpoints, the SAP additionally lists fasting plasma glucose as a primary endpoint. Second, instead of specifying a specific visit to evaluate the efficacy of metreleptin (in either the SAP or the protocols), the SAP states comparisons with baseline will be done at certain milestone visits (months 4, 8, 12)."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the small-sample safety caveat]*

> "While the incidence of lymphoma in patients from the NIH and FHA101 clinical studies was 5900 per 100,000 in males and 1900 per 100,000 in females, these crude estimates are based on a very small sample of patients and therefore have very wide confidence intervals."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the indication restriction]*

> "The BLA lacked sufficient evidence to support approval of metreleptin for the treatment of patients with partial lipodystrophy... Because the sponsor has not provided sufficient evidence of metreleptin's efficacy in patients with partial lipodystrophy, the benefit-risk assessment in this population is unfavorable and does not support approval."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, Advisory Committee vote]*

> "For the most part, the committee did not believe that the sponsor had provided adequate evidence that the benefits of metreleptin outweighed the risks for the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with metabolic disorders associated with partial lipodystrophy... (Vote: Yes=2, No=10). In contrast, the majority of the committee agreed that the benefits of metreleptin outweighed the risks for the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with generalized lipodystrophy (Vote: Yes=11, No=1)."

Metreleptin is the clearest illustration in this census of what a genuine ultra-rare-disease evidentiary basis looks like when it is documented honestly rather than forced into a randomized-trial template: no control arm ever existed, "primary endpoints" were never formally tested, and the FDA statistical review is candid that essentially every standard tool for judging a trial's reliability — a normality-contingent test, a multiplicity procedure, a tipping-point sensitivity analysis — was simply unavailable given the single-arm design, leaving the approval decision to rest on descriptive statistics plus clinical judgment.

---

### 20. Albiglutide (Tanzeum) — BLA 125431

**Sponsor:** GlaxoSmithKline

**Indication approved:** Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist)

**Approval date:** April 15, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** No single pivotal trial — approval rested on a program of 8 Phase 3 trials (GSK protocol numbers GLP112756, GLP112753, GLP112757, GLP112754, GLP112755, GLP114179, GLP108486, GLP114130; publicly known as HARMONY 1-8), most prominently HARMONY 7, NCT01128894

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (5 of 8 trials), randomized, open-label, active-controlled (3 of 8 trials, vs. insulin lispro/glargine or liraglutide), non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchy, multi-trial program (8 independently protocoled trials against varied comparators) as the collective evidentiary basis rather than one single pivotal trial, approval granted despite one program trial (HARMONY 7, vs. liraglutide) failing its pre-specified non-inferiority margin, based on totality-of-evidence across the broader program
- *Endpoints:* HbA1c change from baseline (glycemic-control primary endpoint)
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA on LOCF-imputed ITT population, adjusted for baseline value and stratification factors
- *Missing data/bias:* FDA reviewer concern about LOCF imputation adequacy given substantial, calendar-time-increasing missingness at later study visits

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Program consisted of 8 Phase 3 trials against varied comparators: placebo (monotherapy and multiple add-on settings), pioglitazone, glimepiride/sitagliptin, insulin glargine, insulin lispro, and liraglutide, plus a dedicated renal-impairment trial (vs. sitagliptin); designs ranged from 26 to 104 weeks, double-blind for 5 trials and open-label for 3 (the insulin- and liraglutide-comparator trials)
- Primary endpoint in every trial: change from baseline in HbA1c at each trial's pre-specified primary timepoint (26, 32, 52, or 104 weeks depending on trial)
- Primary analysis: ANCOVA model on the ITT population using last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) imputation, with main effects for treatment, region, and trial-specific stratification factors (e.g., prior MI history, age category, background therapy) and baseline HbA1c as a covariate; active/insulin-comparator trials used a non-inferiority margin of 0.4%, oral-comparator trials 0.3%, each tested via a one-sided contrast at alpha=0.025, followed by two-sided superiority testing at alpha=0.05 if non-inferiority was established
- HARMONY 7 (albiglutide vs. liraglutide, open-label, N=805) did not meet its pre-specified non-inferiority margin and was statistically inferior to liraglutide on HbA1c reduction; this trial was not "the" pivotal trial relied upon, but one component of the overall program considered in the totality-of-evidence approval decision
- The FDA statistical reviewer flagged that missing data grew substantially at later timepoints (particularly the Week 104 endpoint in the longest trial) and that LOCF is a method generally disfavored relative to modern alternatives, concluding this "may undermine the reliability and confidence in the results"
- No dedicated interim-analysis/alpha-spending plan was described across the program; each trial's testing hierarchy (non-inferiority, then superiority) constituted its own multiplicity control

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2014/125431Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/125431s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (includes a Secondary Statistical Review Memo by Mark Rothmann, Ph.D.) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125431Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125431Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125431Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record (HARMONY 7) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01128894 (no protocol/SAP documents posted; the other 7 program trials — NCT00849017, NCT00838903, NCT00839527, NCT00838916, NCT00849056, NCT00976391, NCT01098539 — were also checked and none have posted protocol/SAP documents)
- Pivotal publication (HARMONY 7): Pratley RE, Nauck MA, Barnett AH, et al; HARMONY 7 study group. "Once-weekly albiglutide versus once-daily liraglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral drugs (HARMONY 7): a randomised, open-label, multicentre, non-inferiority phase 3 study." *Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol.* 2014;2(4):289-297. [DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(13)70214-6>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24703047/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Once-weekly%20albiglutide%20versus%20once-daily%20liraglutide%20in%20patients%20with%20type%202%20diabetes%20inadequately%20controlled%20on%20oral%20drugs)

**Other resources**

- GlaxoSmithKline participates in sponsor data-sharing programs generally; trial-specific HARMONY-program IPD availability was not individually confirmed here. (Albiglutide was voluntarily withdrawn from the market by GSK in 2017-2018 for commercial reasons unrelated to safety or efficacy findings — not itself part of this SAP-focused entry, but relevant context.)
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held: the Summary Review states albiglutide was "the fourth member of the GLP-1 agonist class of anti-diabetic drugs" and that "no new efficacy or safety issue identified in the application rose to the level of requiring the input from an advisory panel."

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the overall program framing]*

> "This submission is for the use of albiglutide in patients with Type 2 diabetes. The submission consists of results from eight active- and placebo-controlled clinical trials... The primary endpoint in each trial was HbA1c change from baseline."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, representative primary-analysis methodology (from the insulin lispro-comparator trial)]*

> "The primary analysis of the HbA1c change from Baseline response at Week 26 was applied to the ITT Population using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with main effects for treatment group, region, history of prior MI, age category, and current oral antidiabetic therapy and with baseline HbA1c as a continuous covariate. The difference in treatment-effect between the albiglutide group and the lispro group was evaluated within this ANCOVA model as least squares means contrast. The contrast was evaluated with a 1-sided t test at the 0.025 significance level with a noninferiority margin of 0.4% on the change of HbA1c. With significance on the noninferiority hypothesis, the superiority hypothesis will be tested using a 2-sided, superiority with significance level of 0.05."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the LOCF/missing-data concern]*

> "The report states 'The panel believes that in nearly all cases, there are better alternatives to [LOCF]…which are based on more reasonable assumptions and hence result in more reliable inferences about treatment effects.' There was little information in Dr. Choudhury's review on the potential impact of the missing data. The high amount of missing data for the later endpoints (in particular the week 104 end point) may undermine the reliability and confidence in the results."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the absence of an Advisory Committee]*

> "Albiglutide is the fourth member of the GLP-1 agonist class of anti-diabetic drugs. No new efficacy or safety issue identified in the application rose to the level of requiring the input from an advisory panel. Therefore no advisory committee was convened."

Albiglutide illustrates a program-level rather than single-trial approval logic: no individual trial in the 8-trial HARMONY program is "the" pivotal trial in the sense used elsewhere in this census, one of the eight (HARMONY 7) was an outright non-inferiority failure against an active GLP-1 comparator, and the FDA reviewer's own methodological critique (LOCF's disfavored status, worsening missingness at the longest timepoint) was folded into a totality-of-evidence approval rather than blocking it.

### 21. Vorapaxar (Zontivity) — NDA 204886

**Sponsor:** Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp.

**Indication approved:** Reduction of thrombotic cardiovascular events in patients with a history of myocardial infarction or with peripheral arterial disease, added to standard of care (not approved for patients with a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, because of intracranial hemorrhage risk)

**Approval date:** May 8, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** TRA 2P-TIMI 50, NCT00526474

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial, label population narrowed post-unblinding to exclude a subgroup identified by an interim DSMB safety signal (intracranial hemorrhage in patients with prior stroke), with TIA history excluded in parallel by the sponsor's Executive Committee after database lock
- *Endpoints:* MACE composite (3-point, plus urgent coronary revascularization) (primary), MACE composite (3-point) (key secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* Cox proportional-hazards model (stratified or with covariates), Kaplan-Meier estimation
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (primary→key secondary)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design (one planned interim analysis at ~50% of events); unplanned additional unblinded efficacy examinations with no pre-specified alpha-spending function, addressed post-hoc via a conservative Bonferroni-type multiplier (x11) applied by the FDA reviewer
- *Regulatory:* reviewer-documented deviation from agreed analysis plan, FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- TRA 2P-TIMI 50 (Protocol P04737): multicenter, international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial in patients with a history of atherosclerotic disease (MI, ischemic stroke, or PAD), randomized within 2 weeks to 12 months of the qualifying event (median 77 days), stratified by qualifying condition (hierarchically MI > stroke > PAD) and planned thienopyridine use; 26,449 patients randomized 1:1 to vorapaxar 2.5 mg daily or placebo, added to standard of care
- Primary endpoint: composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and urgent coronary revascularization; key secondary endpoint: composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke (tested only if the primary endpoint was significant)
- Original design: ~85% power to detect a 15% relative risk reduction at two-sided alpha=0.05, planned N=19,500; blinded sample-size re-estimation led to two protocol amendments (January and March 2009) increasing planned enrollment to approximately 25,000
- One interim efficacy analysis was formally planned, at approximately 50% of primary and key-secondary events, conducted February 24, 2010
- During the trial, a DSMB review of unblinded safety data identified an increased incidence and relative risk of intracranial hemorrhage in patients with a prior history of stroke; the DSMB recommended discontinuing study drug in all patients with a history of stroke (and any stroke occurring during the trial); after database lock and unblinding, the sponsor's Executive Committee further decided patients with a history of TIA should be treated the same way, removing that subgroup from the proposed label population as well
- The FDA statistical reviewer identified that, beyond the one pre-specified interim analysis, there were three additional unblinded examinations of the efficacy data during the trial, for which no pre-specified alpha-spending function existed; in the absence of one, the reviewer applied a conservative Bonferroni-type adjustment (multiplying final p-values by 11) as a sensitivity check, finding the primary and key secondary endpoints remained significant (p≈0.0116 and p≈0.0108, respectively) even under this penalty
- Result (overall population): primary endpoint HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.82-0.95, p=0.001); key secondary HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.80-0.94, p<0.001). In the approved label population (post-MI/PAD, no history of stroke or TIA): primary endpoint HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.76-0.90, p<0.001)

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2014/204886Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/204886s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (includes an addendum memo on a body-weight subgroup interaction) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204886Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204886Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204886Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- FDA Other Review (regulatory/project-management timeline, including the Advisory Committee record) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204886Orig1s000OtherR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00526474 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Related companion trial (non-positive, ACS population, discussed extensively in the FDA review as supportive context): TRACER, NCT00527943
- Pivotal publication: Morrow DA, Braunwald E, Bonaca MP, et al; TRA 2P-TIMI 50 Steering Committee and Investigators. "Vorapaxar in the secondary prevention of atherothrombotic events." *N Engl J Med.* 2012;366(15):1404-1413. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1200933), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22443427/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Vorapaxar%20in%20the%20secondary%20prevention%20of%20atherothrombotic%20events)

**Other resources**

- Merck's clinical-trial-data-sharing commitments cover IPD requests generally (via the Yale Open Data Access/YODA Project, which Merck has historically used for some compounds); trial-specific TRA 2P-TIMI 50 availability was not individually confirmed here.
- An FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held on January 15, 2014. Asked "Should vorapaxar be approved?", the Committee voted 10 (yes) to 1 (abstain). Given the reviewing division (Division of Cardiovascular and Renal Drug Products), this was very likely the Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee, though the FDA documents reviewed here refer to it only as "the Advisory Committee (ADCOM)" without spelling out the full committee name in the extracted text — the specific committee name should be treated as a well-supported inference rather than a verbatim-confirmed fact.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary]*

> "The vorapaxar's efficacy in addition to the standard of care for preventing patients' atherothrombotic ischemic events appears to be demonstrated in TRA 2◦P-TIMI 50 trial for the overall study population and also for the proposed label population, i.e., post MI patients without history of stroke or TIA. We are concerned about several unplanned interim analyses, sample size increase and change of patient population, even though these analyses are performed by an independent statistician through the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB). Whether these analyses might have impacted the trial integrity is uncertain."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.1, study design and primary objective]*

> "Primary Objective: To evaluate the hypothesis that vorapaxar added to standard of care will reduce the incidence of atherothrombotic ischemic events relative to standard of care alone, as measured by the composite of cardiovascular (CV) death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and urgent coronary revascularization... TRA 2οP – TIMI 50 (Protocol P04737) was a multicenter, international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, balanced-parallel-groups, events-driven investigation... Up to 25,000 subjects were anticipated to participate at approximately 1000 centers. This sample size was required to provide adequate power to test the hypothesis of a 15% relative risk reduction... One interim efficacy analysis was planned for when approximately 50% of the primary and 50% of the key secondary efficacy endpoints... were available and was conducted on 24 FEB 2010."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the safety-driven population change]*

> "...during an interim analysis, the DSMB observed an increased incidence and relative risk of ICH in subjects with prior history of stroke and thus recommended discontinuing the study drug in all subjects with a prior history of stroke or a stroke occurring during the course of the study. The sponsor decided to update and pre-define in the data analysis plan the following supplementary secondary objectives... Following data-base lock and unblinding, the sponsor and trial's Executive Committee determined that, for the purpose of clinical clarity and patient safety, subjects with a history of TIA be granted the same consideration as subjects with a history of stroke... This TIA subgroup was then removed from the pre-specified post MI with no history of stroke population, yielding this definition for the proposed label population: Proposed Label Population (post MI with no history of stroke or TIA)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the unplanned unblinded looks and the reviewer's post-hoc adjustment]*

> "there were 3 examinations of the efficacy data in an unblinded fashion, in addition to the planned interim analysis... there was no pre-specified alpha spending function necessary, leading to lack of such a function to provide a basis for a post-hoc adjustment. In lieu of a pre-specified alpha-spending function, a conservative methodology, such as a Bonferonni adjustment, could be utilized... Utilizing a Bonferonni adjustment by multiplying the final p-values by 11, yields a p-value for the primary endpoint of ≈ 0.01164, and a p-value for the key secondary endpoint of ≈0.01079, both of which are still less than 0.05."

> "In this reviewer's opinion, it can be argued that the single trial TRAP-2P may need to achieve a p-value of 0.01 or less for vorapaxar's efficacy on atherothrombotic ischemic events, especially that Study TRACER is non-positive... Therefore, TRAP-2P seems to have achieved statistical significance at 0.01 level for both the primary and the secondary endpoints."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the clinical review team's recommendation and headline result]*

> "The primary clinical reviewers, Dr. Martin Rose (efficacy) and Jonathan Levine (safety), recommend that vorapaxar be approved for the reduction of atherothrombotic events in patients with a history of MI or with PAD. (While their initial filed review recommends approval only with a history of MI, Dr. Rose presented at the advisory committee meeting arguments favoring approval with PAD and subsequently they have changed their recommendation to include with PAD.)... The hazard ratio (HR) for the primary endpoint was 0.88 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.82 to 0.95, p=0.001.)"

Vorapaxar is a rare case where the FDA statistical reviewer's own words state discomfort with trial-integrity risk from repeated unblinded looks, yet resolve it not by rejecting the result but by independently constructing a worst-case multiplicity penalty (an 11-fold Bonferroni multiplier) and showing the result survives it — a transparent, quantified answer to "how much does this really cost us" rather than an unquantified caveat.

### 22. Dulaglutide (Trulicity) — BLA 125469

**Sponsor:** Eli Lilly and Company

**Indication approved:** Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist)

**Approval date:** September 18, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** No single pivotal trial — approval rested on a program of 5 Phase 3 trials (Lilly protocol numbers H9X-MC-GBDA/GBDB/GBDC/GBDD/GBCF, publicly known as AWARD-1 through AWARD-5); AWARD-6 (vs. liraglutide) was not part of the original approval package and was submitted later

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (AWARD-5, add-on metformin), randomized, double-blind, active-controlled (AWARD-3, vs. metformin monotherapy), randomized, open-label, active-controlled (AWARD-1/2/4, vs. exenatide, insulin glargine, or prandial-insulin-lispro combinations), non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchy, pre-specified pooled cardiovascular meta-analysis across program trials to rule out a 1.8 CV-risk margin per 2008 FDA T2DM CV-safety guidance
- *Endpoints:* HbA1c change from baseline (glycemic-control primary endpoint)
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing / tree-gatekeeping strategy (non-inferiority then superiority, two doses)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* Pocock alpha-spending function for the pooled cardiovascular-safety meta-analysis
- *Regulatory:* no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Five pivotal Phase 3 trials evaluated dulaglutide 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg once weekly: AWARD-1 (add-on metformin+pioglitazone, 26 wk, vs. placebo/open-label exenatide 10mcg BID); AWARD-2 (add-on metformin+glimepiride, 52 wk, vs. open-label titrated insulin glargine); AWARD-3 (monotherapy, 26 wk, double-blind vs. metformin); AWARD-4 (add-on prandial insulin lispro, 26 wk, vs. open-label titrated insulin glargine); AWARD-5/GBCF (add-on metformin, 104-week two-stage adaptive design with a 52-week primary analysis, double-blind vs. placebo and sitagliptin 100mg)
- Primary endpoint in each trial: change from baseline in HbA1c at the trial's pre-specified primary timepoint (26 or 52 weeks)
- Non-inferiority margins were prespecified at 0.4% (vs. insulin comparators, most trials) or 0.25% (AWARD-5/GBCF vs. sitagliptin), consistent with 2008 FDA draft guidance for type 2 diabetes trials
- Multiplicity structure (illustrated by AWARD-3): a tree-gatekeeping strategy tested, in sequence, (1) dulaglutide 1.5mg non-inferiority to metformin (p≤0.025), then, if rejected, (2) dulaglutide 0.75mg non-inferiority (p≤0.0125) and (3) dulaglutide 1.5mg superiority (p≤0.0125), with dulaglutide 0.75mg superiority tested under a further conditional rule
- Separately from the individual-trial glycemic analyses, a pooled cardiovascular meta-analysis across the program trials was pre-specified to rule out a hazard ratio upper bound of 1.8, per then-current FDA guidance for new diabetes drugs, using a Pocock alpha-spending rule to account for two planned looks at the pooled CV data; the first meta-analysis met this requirement, so no data from the subsequent dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial (REWIND, then still underway) were included in the BLA submission
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held; per the FDA Summary Review, dulaglutide was "the fifth member of the GLP-1 agonist class" and no efficacy or safety issue was judged to require advisory-panel input

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2014/125469Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/125469s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (combined: cardiovascular-safety review by Janelle K. Charles, PhD, plus overall efficacy/safety review by Bradley W. McEvoy, DrPH) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125469Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125469Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Clinical/Medical Review (redacted) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/125469Orig1s000MedRedt.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov records — AWARD-1 NCT01064687, AWARD-2 NCT01075282, AWARD-3 NCT01126580, AWARD-4 NCT01191268, AWARD-5 NCT00734474 (none have posted protocol/SAP documents)
- Pivotal publications: Wysham C, et al. (AWARD-1) *Diabetes Care.* 2014;37(8):2159-2167. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc13-2760), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24879836/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=AWARD-1%20dulaglutide%20Wysham); Giorgino F, et al. (AWARD-2) *Diabetes Care.* 2015;38(12):2241-2249. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc14-1625), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26089386/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=AWARD-2%20dulaglutide%20Giorgino); Umpierrez G, et al. (AWARD-3) *Diabetes Care.* 2014;37(8):2168-2176. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc13-2759), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24842985/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=AWARD-3%20dulaglutide%20Umpierrez); Blonde L, et al. (AWARD-4) *Lancet.* 2015;385(9982):2057-2066. [DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)60936-9>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26009229/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=AWARD-4%20dulaglutide); Nauck M, et al. (AWARD-5) *Diabetes Obes Metab.* 2014;16(11):1101-1110. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.12305), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24762094/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=AWARD-5%20dulaglutide%20Nauck)

**Other resources**

- Eli Lilly participates in sponsor clinical-trial-data-sharing programs (including its own LillyTrialGuide/Vivli-affiliated access); trial-specific AWARD-program IPD availability was not individually confirmed here.
- AWARD-6 (NCT01624259, dulaglutide vs. liraglutide), published by Dungan et al. in *Lancet* 2014 ([DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60976-4>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25018121/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Dungan%20AWARD-6%20dulaglutide%20liraglutide%20type%202%20diabetes)), was not part of the original approval package and is noted here only because it is sometimes assumed to be the pivotal trial — it is not, per the FDA review documents for this original BLA.
- The pooled cardiovascular meta-analysis requirement reflects the FDA's 2008 industry guidance (issued after the rosiglitazone cardiovascular-safety controversy) requiring new type 2 diabetes drugs to rule out excess cardiovascular risk before approval; REWIND, dulaglutide's dedicated post-marketing cardiovascular outcomes trial, was still underway at the time of this BLA and not included in it.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the pivotal trial program]*

> "To support the indication of improved glycemic control, the medium to long term glucose lowering effect of dulaglutide 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg was evaluated in 5 completed phase 3 clinical trials."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on non-inferiority margins]*

> "Non-inferiority Margin was prespecified as 0.25% for trial GBCF and 0.4% for the other four trials. These margins are similar to margins used in other T2DM trials and consistent with the 2008 FDA draft guidance for diabetes mellitus."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Table 9, on the AWARD-3 multiplicity structure]*

> "The prespecified primary endpoint was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26. The key secondary endpoint was change in HbA1c from baseline at 52 weeks. Table 9 lists the prespecified hypotheses and the tree-gatekeeping strategy to control the family-wise type-I error rate. The non-inferiority margin was prespecified as 0.4%."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the cardiovascular meta-analysis alpha-spending]*

> "The Pocock spending rule was used for alpha adjustment to account for two planned meta-analyses for testing the 1.8 risk margin."... "According to the study report, the first meta-analysis met the FDA requirement by demonstrating that the upper bound of the alpha-adjusted confidence interval for the hazard ratio (HR) was less than 1.8. Therefore, no data from REWIND were included in the meta-analysis included in the BLA submission that is currently under review."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the absence of an Advisory Committee]*

> "Dulaglutide is the fifth member of the GLP-1 agonist class of anti-diabetic drugs. No new efficacy or safety issue identified in the application rose to the level of requiring the input from an advisory panel. Therefore no advisory committee was convened." Confirmed independently in the approval letter: "Your application for Trulicity (dulaglutide) was not referred to an FDA advisory committee..."

Dulaglutide's approval package shows the "two-track" statistical structure common to later GLP-1/diabetes drugs in this period: an ordinary per-trial non-inferiority/superiority hierarchy for the glycemic claim, running alongside a separately alpha-spent, pooled cardiovascular-safety meta-analysis required purely to rule out a harm signal (not to support any efficacy claim) — a regulatory-science artifact of the FDA's 2008 post-rosiglitazone diabetes-drug guidance rather than a scientific feature of the drug itself.

### 23. Edoxaban tosylate (Savaysa) — NDA 206316

**Sponsor:** Daiichi Sankyo Inc.

**Indication approved:** Reduction of stroke and systemic embolism risk in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, not to be used in patients with creatinine clearance (CrCL) >95 mL/min due to reduced efficacy relative to warfarin at that renal function level

**Approval date:** January 8, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, NCT00781391

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, event-driven trial, non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchy, dose-adjusted regimen based on pre-specified renal function/weight/P-gp-inhibitor criteria, two-dose parallel non-inferiority comparisons (high-dose and low-dose arms each independently tested against warfarin)
- *Endpoints:* stroke/systemic embolic event (SEE) composite
- *Primary analysis:* Cox proportional-hazards model (stratified or with covariates)
- *Multiplicity:* Bonferroni approach to control overall type-I error across two simultaneous dose-arm-vs-comparator comparisons, fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (secondary endpoints, gated behind high-dose superiority)
- *Missing data/bias:* on-treatment (rather than intention-to-treat) population used as the primary analysis population in this active-controlled non-inferiority trial, with an FDA reviewer dissent favoring ITT as primary
- *Regulatory:* FDA reviewer qualitative-interaction analysis by renal-function subgroup, leading to a labeled efficacy restriction (Boxed Warning, CrCL>95 mL/min), FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (Study DU176B-C-U301): Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group, multicenter, multinational, event-driven trial in 21,105 patients age ≥21 with documented atrial fibrillation within the prior 12 months and CHADS2 score ≥2, randomized to warfarin (target INR 2.0-3.0), edoxaban 60 mg once daily (dose-reduced to 30 mg if CrCL<50, weight≤60kg, or concomitant P-gp inhibitor use), or edoxaban 30 mg once daily (dose-reduced to 15 mg under the same criteria); randomization stratified by CHADS2 category (2-3 vs. 4-6) and dose-adjustment eligibility
- Primary endpoint: time to first stroke (any type) or systemic embolic event (SEE) while on treatment
- Event-driven design targeting approximately 672 total primary events, with 448 on-treatment primary events required for each of two pairwise comparisons (edoxaban 30mg vs. warfarin; edoxaban 60mg vs. warfarin)
- Primary analysis: proportional-hazards model estimating the hazard ratio for each edoxaban arm vs. warfarin, with a two-sided 97.5% CI (Bonferroni-type adjustment for the two simultaneous comparisons); non-inferiority declared if the upper bound of this CI was below a pre-specified margin of 1.38 (derived from the historical estimated effect of warfarin vs. placebo)
- If the high-dose arm was non-inferior, it was tested for superiority to warfarin on the primary endpoint at two-sided alpha=0.01 (ITT analysis); if superiority was shown, three hierarchically ordered secondary endpoints (stroke/SEE/CV-mortality composite; MACE; stroke/SEE/all-cause-mortality composite) were tested in sequence at the same alpha; no superiority testing was planned for the low-dose arm
- The FDA statistical reviewer explicitly disagreed with the trial's use of an on-treatment (rather than intention-to-treat) analysis population as primary, arguing ITT should be primary "even in an active control, non-inferiority trial" and that on-treatment analysis should instead be a sensitivity analysis
- A key post-hoc regulatory finding: a qualitative treatment-by-renal-function-subgroup interaction, in which the high-dose edoxaban arm showed a favorable hazard ratio in patients with estimated CrCL 50-<80 mL/min (HR 0.53) but an unfavorable one in patients with CrCL≥80 mL/min (HR 1.41) relative to warfarin — this became the basis for the label's restriction against use in patients with CrCL>95 mL/min
- Result (overall ITT): edoxaban high-dose non-inferior and directionally favorable vs. warfarin for stroke/SEE; full quantitative results by dose and renal-function subgroup are detailed in the label and the FDA statistical review

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter (NVAF indication) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/206316Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/206316lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (combined, covering both the NVAF and DVT/PE indications) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206316Orig1Orig2s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206316Orig1Orig2s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review (redacted) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206316Orig1Orig2s000MedRedt.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00781391 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Giugliano RP, Ruff CT, Braunwald E, et al; ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 Investigators. "Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation." *N Engl J Med.* 2013;369(22):2093-2104. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1310907), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24251359/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Edoxaban%20versus%20warfarin%20in%20patients%20with%20atrial%20fibrillation)

**Other resources**

- Daiichi Sankyo's IPD data-sharing status was not individually confirmed for this trial.
- An FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee meeting was held October 30, 2014, and voted 9-1 in favor of approval; most of the 9 in favor recommended restricting the 60 mg dose in patients with normal/high renal function, and one of the nine dissented from even that restricted use.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the trial design]*

> "Study DU176B-C-U301, also called the ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 trial, was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group, multi-center, multi-national study for evaluation of efficacy and safety of du-176b (edoxaban) versus warfarin in subjects with atrial fibrillation (AF)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the primary endpoint and event-driven sample size]*

> "The primary endpoint was time to first stroke (of any kind) or systemic embolic event (SEE) while on treatment."... "This was an event-driven study. The statistical considerations and plan for the study required approximately 672 primary endpoints overall, with 448 on-treatment primary endpoint (composite of stroke and SEE) events for each of the following 2 pairwise comparisons: i) edoxaban 30 mg group versus warfarin ii) edoxaban 60 mg group versus warfarin."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the multiplicity/non-inferiority framework]*

> "Because there were two treatment arms being compared simultaneously to the active control group, a Bonferroni type approach was used to control the overall error rate. The two-sided 97.5% confidence interval (CI) for the hazard ratios (each edoxaban treatment group versus warfarin) was estimated using the proportional hazards model. If the upper limit of this CI of the hazard ratio was below 1.38, then non-inferiority to warfarin was considered established... The margin of 1.38 was appropriate and has been used in many other studies for this indication. It was derived from the estimated effect of warfarin compared to placebo in historical trials."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the superiority/secondary-endpoint hierarchy]*

> "If the high dose arm was noninferior to warfarin, then the high dose would be compared to warfarin for superiority on the primary endpoint using two-sided error rate of α=0.01... If superiority was concluded, then the three secondary endpoints would be tested in order using the same approach (ITT analysis with α=0.01). No testing for superiority of the primary or any secondary endpoints was planned for the low dose arm."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, reviewer dissent on the primary analysis population]*

> "In my opinion, the intention to treat analysis should be used for the primary analysis, even in an active control, non-inferiority trial... The on treatment analysis should be a sensitivity analysis."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, on the renal-function qualitative-interaction finding]*

> "If we look at the treatment effect in those two subgroups (high dose vs. warfarin only) adjusting only for chads score variable and treatment, the estimated hazard ratios are 0.53 (50≤eCrCL<80 subgroup) and 1.41 (eCrCL≥80 subgroup)... A qualitative interaction with respect to the noninferiority margin of 1.38 would happen if one confidence interval was below 1.38 (edoxaban was effective) and the other was completely above 1.38 (edoxaban was not effective)."

*[verbatim, approved Package Insert, Boxed Warning]*

> "REDUCED EFFICACY IN NONVALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION PATIENTS WITH CRCL > 95 mL/min... SAVAYSA should not be used in patients with CrCL > 95 mL/min. In the ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 study, nonvalvular atrial fibrillation patients with CrCL > 95 mL/min had an increased rate of ischemic stroke with SAVAYSA 60 mg once daily compared to patients treated with warfarin. In these patients another anticoagulant should be used."

Edoxaban is the clearest example in this batch of a subgroup interaction directly reshaping the approved label rather than just appearing as a forest-plot caveat: the qualitative reversal of effect by renal function became a Boxed Warning restricting use altogether in high-renal-function patients — a stronger regulatory consequence than the routine "interpret with caution" treatment most subgroup findings receive.
