### 24. Ivabradine (Corlanor) — NDA 206143

**Sponsor:** Amgen Inc. (licensed from Servier, which conducted SHIFT)

**Indication approved:** Reduce the risk of hospitalization for worsening heart failure in patients with stable, symptomatic chronic heart failure with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%, who are in sinus rhythm with resting heart rate ≥70 bpm and either are on maximally tolerated doses of beta-blockers or have a contraindication to beta-blocker use

**Approval date:** April 15, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** SHIFT, NCT02441218

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial, heart-rate/rhythm-selected population (resting HR ≥70 bpm, sinus rhythm)
- *Endpoints:* CV death / HF-hospitalization composite
- *Primary analysis:* Cox proportional-hazards model (stratified or with covariates), Kaplan-Meier estimation
- *Multiplicity:* unadjusted secondary/supportive testing (single formal primary endpoint; component/subgroup analyses explicitly not adjusted for multiplicity per the label)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design, Haybittle-Peto boundary (Peto-type procedure, fixed 0.1% interim type-I error), efficacy boundary crossed at a pre-planned interim analysis without early stopping — trial continued and was later closed only for slow enrollment
- *Regulatory:* FDA-conducted Cui-Hung-Wang adjustment for potential Type I error inflation from data-influenced sample-size/event-count amendments, FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- SHIFT: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 6,558 adults with stable NYHA class II-IV heart failure, LVEF ≤35%, resting heart rate ≥70 bpm and sinus rhythm, hospitalized for heart failure within the prior 12 months and on an optimized, stable background regimen (maximally tolerated beta-blockers plus, in most cases, ACE inhibitor/ARB, spironolactone, diuretics)
- Randomized 1:1 to ivabradine (titrated between 2.5 mg and 7.5 mg BID to a resting heart rate of 50-60 bpm) or matching placebo, both added to background therapy; median follow-up 22.9 months
- Primary endpoint: time to first occurrence of hospitalization for worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death (composite), intention-to-treat, tested with a Cox proportional-hazards model adjusted for baseline beta-blocker intake (yes/no), two-sided Wald test
- Analyses were performed on both the full Randomized Set (RS) and a subset receiving at least half the guideline target beta-blocker dose (RSBBdose), described as a hierarchical procedure across the two analysis sets
- The initial protocol (April 2006) specified 5,500 patients/1,220 events; Amendment 5 (September 2008), prompted by disappointing results from a separate trial (BEAUTIFUL) in a related population, increased the target to 7,000 patients and ≥1,600 composite events; Amendment 6 (June 2009) stopped randomization at 6,500 patients, citing lower-than-expected recruitment
- Three Data Monitoring Committee interim analyses were planned (20%, 40%, 70% of expected events), using a Peto-type group-sequential procedure with interim efficacy/harm boundaries fixed at a 0.1% type-I error level; the third interim analysis (March 2009, ~3 months before Amendment 6) crossed the efficacy stopping boundary (p<0.0001), but the trial was not stopped for efficacy — Amendment 6 attributed the later enrollment closure solely to recruitment shortfall
- Result: HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.75-0.90; p<0.0001) for the composite primary endpoint, driven entirely by the hospitalization-for-HF component; no significant effect on the CV-death component alone
- FDA's statistical reviewer flagged that the sample-size/event-count amendments (1,220→1,600 events) occurred without documentation ruling out that the changes were influenced by internal trial data, and independently re-derived a Cui-Hung-Wang-adjusted p-value to test whether this could have inflated the overall Type I error rate

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/206143Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/206143Orig1s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206143Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206143Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/206143Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02441218 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Swedberg K, Komajda M, Böhm M, et al; SHIFT Investigators. "Ivabradine and outcomes in chronic heart failure (SHIFT): a randomised placebo-controlled study." *Lancet.* 2010;376(9744):875-885. [DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61198-1>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20801500/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Ivabradine%20and%20outcomes%20in%20chronic%20heart%20failure%20SHIFT%20a%20randomised%20placebo-controlled%20study)

**Other resources**

- Servier (SHIFT's sponsor) and Amgen (NDA holder) IPD-sharing status not individually confirmed for this trial; Amgen participates in Vivli.org generally.
- An FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee meeting was scheduled for January 14, 2015, per the FDA Summary Review; the specific vote outcome was not found in the documents reviewed here and should be confirmed separately before citing a tally.
- A related trial, BEAUTIFUL (ivabradine in stable coronary artery disease without clinical heart failure), did not meet its primary endpoint and prompted SHIFT's sample-size amendment; a post-marketing safety trial, SIGNIFY (ivabradine in stable CAD without heart failure, target HR 60 bpm), later showed no benefit and a signal of harm in a subgroup with angina, both discussed in the FDA review as external context rather than part of the SHIFT SAP itself.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, "Efficacy Endpoints"]*

> "The primary composite endpoint is the first event of cardiovascular death (including death from unknown cause) or hospitalization for worsening HF."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2 "Statistical Methodologies"]*

> "The initial SHIFT protocol was written on April 18, 2006. There were six amendments in the following three years. The original protocol proposed a sample size of 5,500 patients for the detection of a 17% relative risk reduction of the PCE (90% power and 1220 events)... According to Amendment 5, in September 2008, the sample size was increase to 7,000 patients and the study will continue until at least 1600 composite endpoints had occurred. Per the Amendment, the changes were caused by the unfavorable results of another study, BEAUTIFUL, which suggested a possible lower treatment effect of Ivabradine on heart failure endpoints than expected. Per Amendment 6, in June 2009, SHIFT was to be stopped when 6,500 patients have been randomized due to lower than expected recruitment rate. SHIFT had only one version of the Statistical Analysis Plan, which was finalized prior to study unblinding, per the study report."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, "Efficacy Analysis Methods"]*

> "The primary composite endpoint was tested using a survival analysis conducted on a time-to-first event basis using the intention-to-treat principle. A Cox's proportional hazards model adjusted for previous beta-blocker intake at randomization was used to estimate the treatment effect and calculate the associated two-sided p-value (significance level: 5%)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, "Interim Analyses and Multiplicity"]*

> "Three interim analyses were performed by the Data Monitoring Committee: the first one (20% of the expected events) dedicated only to prematurely detect an eventual harmful effect, the two other ones (40% and 70% of the expected events) were to investigate both premature efficacy and harmful effects. The alpha spending for the latter two interim analyses were based on the Peto group sequential procedure, the type I error rates used for interim efficacy analyses were fixed at 0.1% and have no significant impact on the type I error rate used for the final analysis."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.4.3.1, reviewer's independent check on the sample-size amendments]*

> "The trial sample size and number of primary events were modified in Amendments 5 and 6. The total number of primary events is increased from 1220 to 1600, specifically. Hence, there are concerns regarding possible inflation of the Type I error probability if such sample size adjustments are influenced by the internal trial data. To address this potential concern (noting that there is no document that can be used to check if the adjustments of sample size or number of pre-planned number of events was ever influenced by the internal trial data), this reviewer performed an analysis to adjust p-value using the valid statistical test method of Cui, Hung, and Wang (1999, Biometrics)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Table 3-9 discussion, on the boundary-crossing-without-stopping episode]*

> "Table 3-9 listed the result of each interim analysis. There are two interesting observations from the following results: 1. The poor Ivabradine efficacy results from BEAUTIFUL trial prompted the sample size/event increase with SHIFT Amendment No. 5 in September of 2008..., but the second interim analysis on the SHIFT's primary endpoint provided a very promising result (p=0.0458) just three months prior to the amendment. 2. According to the stopping rule of the 3rd interim analysis, SHIFT had crossed the early stopping boundary for the overwhelming efficacy (p<0.0001) in March of 2009. This interim analysis was conducted, again, three months prior to the Amendment No. 6, which stopped SHIFT recruitment when 6500 patients were randomized. The amendment did not stop the trial for the reason of overwhelming efficacy, but stated that the sample size change was made due to the lower than expected recruitment rate."

The reviewer's juxtaposition of these two facts — a promising interim result preceding an event-count increase, and an efficacy-boundary crossing preceding an enrollment-closure amendment attributed only to recruitment — is the review's way of flagging, without directly accusing the sponsor, that both protocol amendments happened to follow favorable unblinded-committee-level signals, which is exactly the scenario the Cui-Hung-Wang adjustment exists to guard against.

### 25. Cangrelor (Kengreal) — NDA 204958

**Sponsor:** The Medicines Company

**Indication approved:** As an adjunct to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to reduce the risk of periprocedural myocardial infarction, repeat coronary revascularization, and stent thrombosis in patients who have not been treated with a P2Y12 platelet inhibitor and are not being given a GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor

**Approval date:** June 22, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** CHAMPION PHOENIX, NCT01156571

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled; redesigned confirmatory trial following two prior unsuccessful same-program trials (revised endpoint definition and eligibility criteria); single-trial regular approval accepted in place of two independent successful trials, per prospective sponsor-FDA agreement on a low p-value threshold
- *Endpoints:* periprocedural composite endpoint (48-hour death/MI/ischemia-driven revascularization/stent thrombosis)
- *Primary analysis:* logistic regression model (odds ratio) for a binary short-term composite endpoint, adjusted for loading dose and baseline status
- *Multiplicity:* unadjusted secondary/supportive testing (single formal primary endpoint)
- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval, FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- CHAMPION PHOENIX: randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial in 10,942 patients with coronary artery disease (stable angina, UA/NSTEMI, or STEMI) requiring PCI and receiving standard aspirin plus heparin or bivalirudin, who had not previously taken an oral P2Y12 inhibitor and for whom GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor use was not planned; randomized 1:1 to cangrelor (30 mcg/kg bolus + 4 mcg/kg/min infusion for 2-4 hours, n=5,472) or clopidogrel 300/600 mg (n=5,470)
- Primary endpoint: first occurrence, within 48 hours of randomization, of the composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, ischemia-driven revascularization, or stent thrombosis, in the modified-ITT population (all randomized subjects who received study drug and underwent the index PCI)
- Primary analysis: logistic regression model comparing cangrelor vs. clopidogrel, adjusted for intended loading dose and baseline clinical-presentation status, yielding an odds ratio and p-value
- Result: primary composite event rate 4.7% (cangrelor) vs. 5.9% (clopidogrel), OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.66-0.93), p=0.005; most of the treatment effect was concentrated in post-procedural MIs detected solely by CK-MB elevation (type 4a MI)
- Supplementary/sensitivity analysis, pre-specified: a narrower composite omitting intraprocedural stent thrombosis (IPST, an angiographic finding during PCI rather than a post-procedural clinical event) and low-magnitude CK-MB-only MIs, still favoring cangrelor (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.92)
- CHAMPION PHOENIX was the third trial in cangrelor's development program: two earlier Phase 3 trials, CHAMPION PCI and CHAMPION PLATFORM, had both failed to demonstrate superiority to clopidogrel; PHOENIX revised the primary-endpoint MI definition, restricted enrollment to P2Y12-naive patients, and prospectively obtained the Division's agreement that a single successful trial at a low p-value (<0.01) could support approval, given the established pharmacologic-class precedent of P2Y12 inhibition
- Sponsor first submitted the NDA based on PHOENIX's success (p≈0.005), but FDA issued a Complete Response Letter (April 30, 2014) citing concerns about the clinical relevance of the IPST/CK-MB-only MI subcomponents, a discrepancy between adjudicated and site-reported primary events, classification of clinical presentation subgroups, use of cangrelor in stable angina, and database-unlocking/bioequivalence-documentation issues; the sponsor resubmitted with additional landmark, sensitivity, and site-reported-event analyses, leading to approval on the second review cycle

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/204958Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/204958Orig1s000Lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (resubmission-cycle review, addressing landmark/sensitivity/site-reported-event analyses) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/204958Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (includes the original Complete Response Letter issues and Advisory Committee vote) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/204958Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01156571 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Bhatt DL, Stone GW, Mahaffey KW, et al; CHAMPION PHOENIX Investigators. "Effect of platelet inhibition with cangrelor during PCI on ischemic events." *N Engl J Med.* 2013;368(14):1303-1313. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1300815), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23473369/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Effect%20of%20platelet%20inhibition%20with%20cangrelor%20during%20PCI%20on%20ischemic%20events)

**Other resources**

- The Medicines Company (acquired by Chiesi Group in 2020) IPD-sharing status not individually confirmed for this trial.
- An FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee meeting was held for the second time on April 15, 2015, to reconsider the resubmitted application; the Committee voted 9-2 (one abstention) in favor of approval. Members voting against cited concern that PHOENIX alone did not provide strong enough evidence, given that CHAMPION PCI and PLATFORM should arguably be viewed as similarly-designed trials whose failure weakens rather than merely "generates hypotheses" about PHOENIX's result.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3720818, §1.1 "Overview"]*

> "Reference is made to the Agency's Complete Response for the Cangrelor New Drug Application NDA 204958 on April 30, 2014. After subsequent meetings, the sponsor resubmitted the NDA with additional analyses and information to address the issues raised in the Complete Response letter. The statistical review for this re-submission mainly focuses on several items in CHAMPION PHOENIX trial: 1. Landmark analysis. 2. Sensitivity analyses on the primary composite endpoint (removing intraprocedural stent thrombosis from the primary composite endpoint, using more conservative definition of MI, et al). 3. Efficacy analyses on site-reported primary endpoint. 4. Discrepancies between Sponsor's results and Dr. Marciniak's results."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the Division's prospective single-trial agreement]*

> "The applicant prospectively consulted the Division about the ability of PHOENIX as a single trial to provide sufficient evidence of efficacy to support approval of an NDA. The Division agreed that if successful at a low p-value (< 0.01), it could be sufficient. The Division viewed PHOENIX as sufficiently different from the first two trials so that their failure would not be viewed as impugning a positive result from PHOENIX. Also, the Division did not request two trials successful at p < 0.05 because 1) the pharmacology and clinical profile of the drug class is well understood... and 2) clopidogrel reduces the risk of stent thrombosis and superiority to an active control provides strong evidence that a drug is effective."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the original Complete Response Letter's six issues]*

> "PHOENIX was successful on its prespecified primary endpoint at a p-value of ~ 0.005 but the Office declined to approve because it doubted the clinical relevance. The issues listed in the complete response letter included: 1. Concern that two subcomponents of the primary endpoint, intraprocedural stent thrombosis (IPST) and small post-procedural myocardial infarctions (MIs) identified solely by increases in serum biomarkers of myocardial necrosis, were not events whose avoidance were clinical benefits. 2. Concern about an apparent difference in the outcome of PHOENIX if site-reported events are used for the primary analysis instead of adjudicated events. 3. Concern about the classification of subjects' clinical presentation as ST-elevation MI (STEMI), non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS), or stable coronary disease and the effect of cangrelor in each presentation type. 4. Concern about the appropriateness of using cangrelor in patients with stable angina... 5. Concern about unlocking of the PHOENIX data base after unblinding. 6. Concern about whether the over-encapsulated clopidogrel administered to clopidogrel subjects in PHOENIX was bioequivalent to clopidogrel approved in the USA."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, on the composition of the primary endpoint]*

> "The primary endpoint in PHOENIX was a composite of death, MI, ischemia driven revascularization, and stent thrombosis. The clinical import of two subcomponents, IPST and small peri-procedural MIs detected solely by increases by markers of myocardial necrosis, is unclear. First, the applicant definition of stent thrombosis included 'intraprocedural stent thrombosis' (IPST), which represents an angiographic finding identified during PCI. Stent thrombosis is generally considered to be an event that occurs after completion of PCI. The Division has not previously considered a similar claim and the applicant did not seek the Division's concurrence to its inclusion as a subcomponent of the primary endpoint."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, §10 "Advisory Committee Meeting"]*

> "This application was discussed for a second time by the Cardiovascular and Renal Advisory Committee on April 15 2015. The Committee voted 9-2 with one abstention for approval. Committee members who voted against approval expressed a number of concerns: PLATFORM and PCI should not be viewed as hypothesis generating but rather as trials similar to PHOENIX; their lack of success should therefore be viewed as weakening the conclusions of PHOENIX. PHOENIX did not provide strong enough support for efficacy to support approval on the basis of a single trial."

Cangrelor is an unusually explicit real-world case of a sponsor negotiating its statistical burden of proof in advance: rather than being held to the usual two-independent-trials standard, the Division prospectively agreed a single trial succeeding at p<0.01 could suffice, reasoning from the established pharmacology of the P2Y12-inhibitor class — and even then, the first successful trial (PHOENIX, p≈0.005) still drew a Complete Response Letter over endpoint-composition and adjudication concerns, resolved only on a second review cycle with a fairly narrow Advisory Committee vote.

### 26. Alirocumab (Praluent) — BLA 125559

**Sponsor:** Sanofi-Aventis U.S. LLC (developed with Regeneron Pharmaceuticals)

**Indication approved:** Adjunct to diet and maximally tolerated statin therapy for the treatment of adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) or clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease who require additional lowering of LDL-cholesterol

**Approval date:** July 24, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** ODYSSEY program (10 Phase 3 trials; largest and safety-sizing trial ODYSSEY LONG TERM, NCT01507831)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled or active-controlled (ezetimibe and/or statin up-titration), dose up-titration within trial
- *Endpoints:* percent change in LDL-C from baseline to week 24 (primary, all 10 trials), percent change in ApoB/non-HDL-C/total-C/Lp(a)/HDL-C/ApoA1/triglycerides (key secondary), adjudicated MACE (safety, underpowered)
- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM), pattern-mixture model (FDA-preferred sensitivity analysis for missing data), robust regression/M-estimation (non-normally distributed secondary endpoints: TG, Lp(a)), Hodges-Lehmann estimator (FDA-added alternative to robust regression)
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence hierarchical testing across a long ordered list of primary/key-secondary endpoint-population-estimand combinations per trial, family-wise two-sided α=0.05 (per trial); within the two factorial-design trials (OPTIONS I, OPTIONS II), each pairwise comparison additionally tested at a per-comparison two-sided alpha (1% and 1.25% respectively)
- *Missing data/bias:* FDA reviewer disputed the sponsor's missing-at-random (MAR) assumption in the primary MMRM, given that treatment adherence was not accounted for; pattern-mixture model imputing non-adherent patients' post-discontinuation LDL-C toward their own baseline value was adopted as FDA's preferred analysis
- *Regulatory:* FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (EMDAC, June 9, 2015), FDA-restricted approved population narrower than the sponsor's proposed indication (approval limited to patients on a maximally tolerated statin, pending the ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Ten Phase 3 trials (ODYSSEY FH I, FH II, HIGH FH, COMBO I, COMBO II, LONG TERM, OPTIONS I, OPTIONS II, ALTERNATIVE, MONO) supported the BLA, all randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo- or active-controlled, with treatment periods of 6-24 months and a total of 5,296 subjects randomized (3,188 to alirocumab); eight trials used 75 mg every-2-weeks with up-titration to 150 mg at week 12 if a pre-defined LDL-C target was not met at week 8, and two trials used a fixed 150 mg dose throughout
- Five trials (FH I, FH II, HIGH FH, COMBO I, LONG TERM) were placebo-controlled on top of a maximally tolerated background statin (with FH I/FH II/HIGH FH restricted to heterozygous FH patients); the other five were active-controlled — ALTERNATIVE and MONO studied alirocumab without a background statin (vs. ezetimibe), and OPTIONS I/OPTIONS II were multi-arm factorial trials comparing alirocumab-plus-statin against statin up-titration, a different statin, or ezetimibe-plus-statin, at two statin-intensity levels each
- Primary endpoint in all 10 trials: percent change in LDL-C from baseline to week 24 (ITT estimand, ITT population), analyzed via an MMRM including treatment, randomization strata, timepoint, treatment-by-time and strata-by-time interactions, baseline LDL-C, and baseline-LDL-C-by-time interaction, with missing values assumed missing-at-random and not explicitly imputed
- FDA's statistical reviewer directly disputed the sponsor's MAR assumption, reasoning that patients who discontinued treatment early were systematically different from those with observed data (LDL-C reduction was not sustained after stopping the drug in earlier Phase 2 follow-up data), and required a pattern-mixture model (PMM) sensitivity analysis as its preferred primary-endpoint analysis: patients' on-treatment missing values were imputed as MAR, but post-discontinuation missing values were imputed centered on the patient's own baseline value (i.e., assuming no persisting drug benefit) — this PMM was FDA's preferred estimate, not the sponsor's on-treatment MMRM estimand, which FDA's reviewer considered clinically irrelevant "due to the underlying implausibility of achieving perfect treatment adherence"
- Multiplicity: study-wise two-sided type I error (5%) was controlled per trial via a long pre-specified fixed-sequence hierarchy across combinations of endpoint, timepoint, analysis population (ITT/mITT), and estimand (ITT/on-treatment) — e.g., in FH I/FH II/HIGH FH/COMBO I/COMBO II/LONG TERM the hierarchy ran to 25 ordered hypotheses; in the two factorial trials (OPTIONS I, OPTIONS II) each of several pre-specified pairwise comparisons was tested hierarchically within itself, at a per-comparison two-sided alpha of 1% (OPTIONS I) or 1.25% (OPTIONS II)
- Key secondary endpoints assumed non-normally distributed (triglycerides, Lp(a)) were analyzed via robust regression (M-estimation) per the sponsor's SAP; FDA's reviewer criticized this choice as an unjustified, arbitrarily-parameterized down-weighting of extreme values and added median-based Hodges-Lehmann location-shift estimates as an alternative, consistent with how other approved products' labels summarize triglyceride treatment differences
- Cardiovascular safety: only 93 adjudicated MACE events occurred across all 10 trials (58 alirocumab, 35 control), the majority (52) from ODYSSEY LONG TERM; FDA's reviewer concluded this was too few events to support a robust conclusion of CV benefit, and — because patients not on a maximally tolerated statin have a known-effective alternative (statin up-titration) for further LDL-C lowering — recommended restricting approval to the maximally-tolerated-statin population pending the ongoing dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial (ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, approved as a separate supplement years later, not part of this original BLA)

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/125559Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label (2015 original) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/125559Orig1s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3734042 (the primary source for the excerpts below) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/125559Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (Deputy Division Director Summary Review, documents the Advisory Committee meeting and FDA's population-restriction rationale) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/125559Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record for ODYSSEY LONG TERM — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01507831 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Robinson JG, Farnier M, Krempf M, et al. (ODYSSEY LONG TERM Investigators). "Efficacy and Safety of Alirocumab in Reducing Lipids and Cardiovascular Events." *N Engl J Med.* 2015;372(16):1489-1499. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501031), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25773378/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy%20and%20Safety%20of%20Alirocumab%20in%20Reducing%20Lipids%20and%20Cardiovascular%20Events)

**Other resources**

- Sanofi and Regeneron generally participate in clinical-trial data-sharing via Vivli.org; trial-specific availability not individually confirmed here.
- FDA Advisory Committee (EMDAC) meeting held June 9, 2015 — the same broad regulatory period as evolocumab's (Repatha's) parallel EMDAC review of the same PCSK9-inhibitor class, though evolocumab's original approval and this alirocumab entry are separate submissions; the evolocumab/FOURIER entry already in this census concerns evolocumab's later 2017 cardiovascular-outcomes supplement, not its original hyperlipidemia approval, so the two entries are not directly comparable trial-for-trial.
- Cross-reference: this is the same PCSK9-inhibitor pharmacologic class as evolocumab/FOURIER already in the census; alirocumab's own cardiovascular-outcomes trial (ODYSSEY OUTCOMES) was completed and separately reviewed years after this original approval and is out of scope for this entry.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3734042, Executive Summary, p.5]*

> "Ten phase 3 trials were conducted to evaluate LDL-C reduction at week 24 in different patient populations and across different levels of background statin intensity... The excess reduction was statistically significant at the prespecified alpha level for all primary hypotheses tested in nine trials and for two of four tested in the tenth trial... However, the submission had too few outcome events to allow a robust evaluation of cardiovascular (CV) benefit. Because patients not on a maximally tolerated background statin have treatment options for additional LDL-C lowering with known clinical benefit (i.e., up-titrating the statin), I support the approval of alirocumab in a more restricted population than the one proposed by the applicant."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3734042, §3.2.2 "Statistical analysis," p.19-20]*

> "Analysis of the primary efficacy endpoint: Percent change in LDL-C from baseline to week 24 was analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM)... Missing LDL-C values were assumed to be missing at random (MAR) and were not imputed. In my opinion, given that treatment adherence is not accounted for in the MMRM, the MAR assumption is questionable and likely leads to an over-estimate of the ITT effect... those with data were primarily on study drug, whereas those without data were primarily no longer receiving study drug... In the PMM different imputation strategies were applied to missing LDL-C values during the on-treatment period and after treatment discontinuation... For patients that stopped their study treatment it was assumed they would no longer benefit from study drug, and their LDL-C values would return to baseline. For these patients the imputed LDL-C values were centered on the patient's baseline value."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3734042, §3.2.2, "Controlling study-wise type-I error," p.17]*

> "Study-wise type-I error rate was maintained at the two-sided 5% level by testing the primary and key secondary endpoints hierarchically according to the order in Table 6. Each hypothesis is defined by four quantities: the endpoint, weeks from randomization, analysis population (ITT or mITT) and statistical estimand (on-treatment or ITT). For OPTIONS I and OPTIONS II testing was done hierarchically within each pairwise comparison; in OPTIONS I each pairwise comparison was performed at the two-sided 1% alpha level and 1.25% level for OPTIONS II."

*[verbatim, from FDA Summary Review, Reference ID 3797092, §9 "Advisory Committee Meeting," p.26]*

> "This BLA was discussed with the Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee (EMDAC) on 9 June 2015. The committee was asked to discuss the safety of alirocumab as observed in the clinical development program, to which the general consensus was that there were no serious safety signals observed with alirocumab treatment at this time. However, several members noted that the current safety database is limited to a relatively short duration of exposure and small number of patients relative to the very large target population... therefore, the applicant's ongoing CVOT was considered very important to help inform benefit/risk."

This is one of the richest missing-data disputes in the census: FDA's reviewer did not merely flag the sponsor's MMRM/MAR approach as a caveat but substituted its own pattern-mixture model as the preferred primary analysis, reasoning explicitly from an observed post-discontinuation LDL-C rebound pattern in earlier Phase 2 data — a genuinely mechanistic, trial-external justification for overriding the sponsor's assumed missing-data mechanism, distinct from the more common practice (seen elsewhere in this census) of adding a sensitivity analysis alongside, rather than in place of, the sponsor's own primary estimate.

### 27. Insulin degludec (Tresiba) — BLA 203314

**Sponsor:** Novo Nordisk A/S

**Indication approved:** Improve glycemic control in adults with diabetes mellitus

**Approval date:** September 25, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** BEGIN Once Long, NCT00982644 (with the BEGIN program broadly, plus DEVOTE, NCT01959529, as the postmarketing-commitment cardiovascular outcomes trial)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, open-label, active-controlled, treat-to-target, non-inferiority-then-superiority, dose-arm pooling
- *Endpoints:* change in HbA1c from baseline (primary, BEGIN program), 3-point MACE (primary, DEVOTE)
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA (treatment, antidiabetic therapy at screening, sex, region as fixed factors; age and baseline HbA1c as covariates), Cox proportional-hazards model (DEVOTE)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* single pre-planned interim analysis in DEVOTE gated against a CRL-specified 1.8 risk margin
- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter for a cardiovascular safety signal, resolved by a dedicated postmarketing cardiovascular outcomes trial *(closest existing taxonomy entries — "Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) rescinded by FDA" and "Voluntary withdrawal... after confirmatory-trial failure" — describe a different regulatory pattern; this one is a pre-approval CRL driven by a pooled meta-analysis signal, resolved via an interim risk-margin gate on a dedicated CVOT before resubmission, not an SPA rescission or a post-approval withdrawal)*, FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (unanimous 12-0 vote requiring a dedicated CVOT)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- The original 2012 submission (NDA 203314, alongside the insulin degludec/aspart combination NDA 203313) was supported by nine Phase 3a "BEGIN" trials: BEGIN Basal-Bolus Type 1 (NCT00982228, N=629), BEGIN Basal-Bolus Type 2 (NCT00972283, N=992), BEGIN Once Long (NCT00982644, N=1030), plus six further BEGIN trials — all randomized, open-label, treat-to-target designs comparing insulin degludec 3:1 against insulin glargine (or, in one trial, sitagliptin) as an active comparator, with mealtime insulin aspart co-administered in the basal-bolus trials
- Primary endpoint across the BEGIN program: change in HbA1c from baseline to trial end (26 or 52 weeks), analyzed via an ANCOVA model with treatment, antidiabetic therapy at screening, sex, and region as fixed factors, and age and baseline HbA1c as covariates, on the full analysis set with LOCF for missing data; pre-specified non-inferiority margin of 0.4% HbA1c (the standard FDA Diabetes Guidance margin for an insulin active comparator), confirmed if the upper bound of the two-sided 95% CI on the treatment difference was ≤0.4%
- All nine BEGIN trials met the non-inferiority margin; a November 8, 2012 FDA Advisory Committee (Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee) voted unanimously (12-0) that a pooled cardiovascular meta-analysis of the BEGIN program showed a signal warranting a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial before approval; FDA issued a Complete Response Letter on February 8, 2013 on that basis
- The resulting trial, DEVOTE (NCT01959529), randomized 7,638 patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk 1:1, double-blind, to insulin degludec or insulin glargine, event-driven, with a 3-component MACE composite (adjudicated CV death including death of unknown cause, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) as the primary endpoint, analyzed via a Cox proportional-hazards model
- DEVOTE's design (as specified in the CRL-driven resubmission) called for a single pre-planned interim analysis once 150 adjudicated MACE events had accrued, requiring the upper bound of the HR's 95% CI to rule out a risk margin of 1.8 to support resubmission/approval; the trial was to continue to a final analysis at 633 MACE events, testing against a tighter margin of 1.3
- The interim analysis (data cutoff January 19, 2015) ruled out the 1.8 margin, supporting the 2015 resubmission and approval; the full DEVOTE result (633 events, HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.78-1.06, non-inferior on the 1.3 margin) was published only after approval, as the completion of the postmarketing commitment

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/203314Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label (2015 original) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/203314lbl.pdf
- FDA combined Statistical Review (Novo Nordisk's joint NDA 203313/203314 submission; contains both the original October 2012 BEGIN-program efficacy statistical review, Ref ID 3216499, and the 2015 DEVOTE-interim-analysis statistical review, Ref ID 3813664) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/203313Orig1s000_203314Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (contains the 2012 Advisory Committee vote record) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/203313Orig1s000_203314Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov records: BEGIN Basal-Bolus Type 1 (NCT00982228), BEGIN Basal-Bolus Type 2 (NCT00972283), BEGIN Once Long (NCT00982644), DEVOTE (NCT01959529) — no protocol/SAP documents posted for any of the four
- Pivotal publications: Heller S, et al. "Insulin degludec, an ultra-longacting basal insulin, versus insulin glargine in basal-bolus treatment with mealtime insulin aspart in type 1 diabetes (BEGIN Basal-Bolus Type 1)." *Lancet.* 2012;379(9825):1489-1497. [DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60204-9>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22521071/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Insulin%20degludec%2C%20an%20ultra-longacting%20basal%20insulin%2C%20versus%20insulin%20glargine%20in%20basal-bolus%20treatment%20with%20mealtime%20insulin%20aspart%20in%20type%201%20diabetes); Marso SP, et al. "Efficacy and Safety of Degludec versus Glargine in Type 2 Diabetes." *N Engl J Med.* 2017;377(8):723-732 (DEVOTE, full postmarketing result). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1615692), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28605603/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy%20and%20Safety%20of%20Degludec%20versus%20Glargine%20in%20Type%202%20Diabetes)

**Other resources**

- Novo Nordisk generally participates in clinical-trial data-sharing via its own portal and Vivli.org; trial-specific availability not individually confirmed here.
- FDA Advisory Committee meeting held November 8, 2012 (Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee), unanimous 12-0 vote that a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial should be conducted based on the pooled BEGIN-program CV meta-analysis signal — this vote directly produced the February 2013 CRL.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA combined Statistical Review, Executive Summary of the 2015 DEVOTE-interim review, Ref ID 3813664, p.5-6]*

> "On February 8, 2013, the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL) to the applicant (Novo Nordisk), which outlined the cardiovascular safety deficiency of insulin degludec and requested additional clinical trial data from a dedicated, double-blind, cardiovascular outcomes trial (CVOT)... DEVOTE was designed and initiated as a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial... The study objective is to be supported by a non-excessive risk analysis to demonstrate that the hazard ratio (HR) of a primary MACE composite endpoint... for IDeg versus IGlar is no greater than 1.8 before resubmission of IDeg/IDegAsp NDAs, assessed by a pre-planned single interim analysis when 150 adjudicated primary MACEs have been accrued. The study will continue until the planned trial conclusion when 633 MACE events have been collected and confirmed. A final analysis will then be performed to further demonstrate non-excessive risk of MACE against a risk margin of 1.3... The upper bound of the 95% confidence interval ruled out the risk margin of 1.8 set forth in the Complete Response Letter. No component of the primary MACE endpoint raised any statistical concerns."

*[verbatim, from FDA combined Statistical Review, original October 2012 efficacy review, Ref ID 3216499, p.7-9]*

> "Except for Study 3580 (a superiority trial), all others were designed to show non-inferiority (NI) of IDeg to their comparator, with the NI margin of 0.4%... The primary efficacy endpoint was analyzed using an ANCOVA model with treatment, antidiabetic therapy at screening, sex, and region as fixed factors, and age and baseline HbA1c as covariates for all trials."

*[verbatim, from FDA Summary Review, Ref ID 3253410, p.40]*

> "These two NDAs were presented at an Advisory Committee Meeting on Thursday, November 8, 2012... 5. Based on the results from the CV meta-analysis, should a cardiovascular outcomes trial be conducted for degludec and degludec/aspart? (Vote) — 12 yes to require a dedicated CVOT... All twelve members voted in favor of a dedicated CVOT be conducted to further investigate the signal arising from the meta-analysis."

This is a genuinely unusual regulatory-process case for the census: rather than an SPA rescission or a post-approval confirmatory-trial failure, insulin degludec was blocked at the pre-approval stage by a pooled cardiovascular signal across the *glycemic-efficacy* trial program, resolved only after a dedicated CVOT (DEVOTE) was run specifically to satisfy a CRL, with an interim-analysis risk-margin gate (1.8) built into that trial's design to permit resubmission before the trial's own final, tighter-margin (1.3) analysis was complete.

### 28. Idarucizumab (Praxbind) — BLA 761025

**Sponsor:** Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Reversal of the anticoagulant effects of dabigatran (Pradaxa) for use when reversal of the anticoagulant effects is needed for emergency surgery/urgent procedures or in life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding

**Approval date:** October 16, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** RE-VERSE AD (Trial 1321.3), NCT02104947

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* single-arm, open-label trial *(genuinely a single-arm reversal-effect study, not a randomized/placebo-controlled efficacy trial — there is no comparator arm and no formal between-group hypothesis test)*
- *Endpoints:* maximum percentage reversal of dabigatran's anticoagulant effect within 4 hours, measured via dilute thrombin time (dTT) or ecarin clotting time (ECT) (primary; a pharmacodynamic surrogate, not a clinical-outcome endpoint), time to bleeding cessation and intraoperative hemostasis assessment (descriptive secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* descriptive single-arm response-rate analysis (point estimate, no formal hypothesis test) *(same taxonomy term already used for single-arm oncology response-rate trials in this census, e.g. Carfilzomib, Ponatinib — applies equally well here even though the clinical context is reversal of anticoagulation rather than tumor response)*
- *Regulatory:* Accelerated Approval (21 CFR 601.41) based on a pharmacodynamic surrogate endpoint, approval granted on a planned interim analysis (123 of an eventual larger enrollment) rather than a completed trial, postmarketing requirement to complete the same trial as confirmation, no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- RE-VERSE AD was an open-label, multicenter, single-arm Phase III "case series" trial (the FDA Summary Review's own description) enrolling adult patients being treated with dabigatran who had either uncontrolled/life-threatening bleeding (Group A) or an urgent need for surgery or an invasive procedure (Group B); there is no placebo or active-comparator arm — every enrolled patient received idarucizumab
- Fixed dose: 5.0 g idarucizumab, administered as two 2.5 g intravenous doses 15 minutes apart
- Primary efficacy endpoint: maximum percentage reversal of dabigatran's anticoagulant effect within 4 hours of administration, measured by dilute thrombin time (dTT) or ecarin clotting time (ECT) — a pharmacodynamic/coagulation-assay surrogate for clinical hemostatic benefit, not a clinical outcome itself
- Approval was granted on the basis of a planned interim analysis of 123 patients (66 in the bleeding group, 57 in the urgent-surgery group), out of a larger planned enrollment (up to several hundred, redacted in the public FDA document); this interim cohort achieved 100% (maximal) dTT reversal in 98% of bleeding patients and 93% of urgent-surgery patients, and maximal ECT reversal in 89% and 88% respectively, sustained for 24 hours after administration
- Because there is no comparator arm and no pre-specified null hypothesis to test statistically, the primary and secondary results (dTT/ECT reversal rates, time to bleeding cessation, intraoperative hemostasis assessment) were reported descriptively — point estimates and, where relevant, percentages of patients achieving a threshold response — rather than via a formal single-arm hypothesis test or a between-arm comparison; the FDA Summary Review notes explicitly that clinical hemostasis/bleeding-cessation assessments were inherently subjective, given the absence of a control group against which to benchmark expected untreated bleeding course
- This was an Accelerated Approval (21 CFR 601.41) on the coagulation-assay surrogate rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit endpoint (e.g., reduced mortality or a validated bleeding-outcome scale); the postmarketing requirement (PMR 2977-1) was simply to complete the same ongoing RE-VERSE AD trial (Trial 1321.3) to its full planned enrollment, which the sponsor did, publishing a full-cohort analysis (n=503) in 2017

- FDA Approval Letter (states the Accelerated Approval basis and postmarketing requirement) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/761025Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/761025lbl.pdf
- FDA Summary Review (Deputy Division Director Summary Review for Regulatory Action; the statistical/efficacy detail for this BLA is folded into this combined review rather than a separate Statistical Review document) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/761025Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/761025Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02104947 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publications: Pollack CV Jr, Reilly PA, Eikelboom J, et al. "Idarucizumab for Dabigatran Reversal." *N Engl J Med.* 2015;373(6):511-520 (interim analysis supporting accelerated approval). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1502000), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26095746/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Idarucizumab%20for%20Dabigatran%20Reversal); Pollack CV Jr, Reilly PA, van Ryn J, et al. "Idarucizumab for Dabigatran Reversal - Full Cohort Analysis." *N Engl J Med.* 2017;377(5):431-441 (full-enrollment result completing the postmarketing requirement). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1707278), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28693366/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Idarucizumab%20for%20Dabigatran%20Reversal%20Full%20Cohort%20Analysis)

**Other resources**

- Boehringer Ingelheim generally participates in clinical-trial data-sharing; no trial-specific IPD/Vivli availability confirmed here.
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held: per the FDA Summary Review, "This BLA was not presented at an Advisory Committee because the application did not raise significant safety or efficacy issues that were unexpected for a biologic of this class."

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Summary Review, Reference ID 3834251, §7 "Clinical/Statistical-Efficacy"]*

> "The Clinical review team reviewed the results of the Clinical Pharmacology trials and the preliminary results of the Phase 3 trial entitled 'A Phase III, Case Series Clinical Study of the Reversal of the Anticoagulant Effects of Dabigatran by Intravenous Administration of 5.0 g of Idarucizumab in Patients Treated with Dabigatran Etexilate Who Have Uncontrolled Bleeding or Require Emergency Surgery or Procedures, the REVERSE-AD Trial'. The trial is an open label, multicenter, safety and efficacy trial with projected enrollment of up to 300 adult patients... The maximum reversal of dilute thrombin time (dTT) or ecarin clotting time (ECT) in the 4 hours after idarucizumab administration is the primary efficacy endpoint."

*[verbatim, from FDA Summary Review, Reference ID 3834251, §7, results of the 123-patient interim cohort]*

> "A maximal reversal (100%) of dTT was achieved in 98% of bleeding patients and 93% of patients needing urgent surgery. A maximal reversal of ECT was achieved in 89% of bleeding patients and 88% of patients needing urgent surgery. Both dTT and ECT decreased to normal levels within 10-30 minutes after idarucizumab administration and were sustained for a period of 24 hours. Reversal of elevated coagulation tests is considered a surrogate for clinical efficacy... Assessments of hemostasis and of bleeding cessation were subjective; however, these data are useful in considerations of efficacy of the reversal agent."

*[verbatim, from FDA Approval Letter, "Accelerated Approval Requirements"]*

> "Products approved under the accelerated approval regulations, 21 CFR 601.41, require further adequate and well-controlled clinical trials to verify and describe clinical benefit. You are required to conduct such a clinical trial with due diligence... PMR 2977-1 Trial 1321.3 titled, 'A Phase III, Case Series Clinical Study of the Reversal of the Anticoagulant Effects of Dabigatran by Intravenous Administration of 5.0 g Idarucizumab in Patients Treated with Dabigatran Etexilate Who Have Uncontrolled Bleeding or Require Emergency Surgery or Procedures, the REVERSE-AD trial.'"

Idarucizumab is the clearest example in this census of a submission that simply does not fit the RCT-with-hypothesis-testing template the rest of this project's methodology sections are built around: there is no randomization, no comparator, no formal alpha, and no multiplicity or interim-monitoring framework in the usual sense — approval instead rested on an Accelerated Approval pathway granted from an interim look at a single-arm surrogate-endpoint case series, with the "confirmatory" postmarketing requirement satisfied simply by finishing enrollment in the same trial rather than by running an independent confirmatory study, since a placebo-controlled trial of a life-threatening-bleeding reversal agent would be difficult to justify ethically.

---

### 29. Patiromer (Veltassa) — NDA 205739

**Sponsor:** Relypsa, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of hyperkalemia

**Approval date:** October 21, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** OPAL-HK (RLY5016-301), NCT01810939

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized withdrawal design, single-blind, Special Protocol Assessment
- *Endpoints:* change in serum potassium from baseline (Part A, single-arm treatment phase), change in serum potassium during randomized withdrawal (Part B, primary), recurrence of hyperkalemia (Part B, secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* longitudinal repeated-measures model (Part A), ANOVA on ranked change scores with Hodges-Lehmann estimator (Part B)
- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation across 10 datasets (Part B)
- *Regulatory:* Special Protocol Assessment agreement

**Trial design & endpoints**

- OPAL-HK was a two-part, single-blind trial conducted under a Special Protocol Assessment (agreement letter dated December 26, 2012); Part A was a single-arm, open-label 4-week treatment phase (N=243 enrolled, in two baseline-potassium dose groups: 5.1-<5.5 mEq/L and 5.5-<6.5 mEq/L by local lab) in which all patients received patiromer; Part B was a randomized withdrawal phase in which Part A responders (serum K+ in target range 3.8-<5.1 mEq/L at week 4 without rescue medication) were re-randomized 1:1, stratified by type 2 diabetes status and Part A baseline potassium (<5.8 vs. ≥5.8 mEq/L), to continue patiromer or switch to placebo for 8 weeks (108 randomized, 107 analyzed)
- Part A primary endpoint: mean change in serum potassium (central lab) from Part A baseline to week 4; per the SPA, the trial would be considered pivotal only if the decrease was ≥0.7 mEq/L (double the maximum expected hemolysis-artifact magnitude of 0.36 mEq/L) with p<0.05 against a null of zero change; the observed result was -1.01 mEq/L (SE 0.031, 95% CI -1.07 to -0.95, p<0.001), meeting the SPA criterion
- Part B primary endpoint: change in serum potassium from Part B baseline to Part B week 4 (or the earliest visit with K+ <3.8 or ≥5.5 mEq/L); median difference (placebo minus patiromer) was 0.72 mEq/L (95% CI 0.46-0.99, p<0.001)
- Part B secondary "recurrence of hyperkalemia" endpoints: proportion of patients with K+ ≥5.5 mEq/L through week 8 (60% placebo vs. 15% patiromer, difference 45%, p<0.001) and K+ ≥5.1 mEq/L (91% vs. 43%, difference 48%, p<0.001)
- Statistical methods: Part A used a longitudinal repeated-measures model with covariates for baseline heart failure (yes/no), baseline type 2 diabetes (yes/no), and continuous Part A baseline potassium; Part B ranked the changes from baseline and compared treatment groups via an ANOVA model including randomization strata as covariates plus a treatment indicator, with the between-group difference tested by a two-sided t-test on the mean ranks and the median difference/CI estimated via the Hodges-Lehmann method; missing Part B data (4 of 107 subjects) were handled via multiple imputation across 10 datasets, with results combined across the imputed datasets
- A second, supportive trial — AMETHYST-DN (RLY5016-205, NCT01371747) — was a multicenter, randomized, open-label, dose-ranging trial in hypertensive patients with diabetic kidney disease and hyperkalemia on ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy (with or without spironolactone); it served a supportive dose-ranging/safety role in the submission rather than as one of the SPA-agreed pivotal analyses

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/205739Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/205739s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/205739Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Medical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/205739Orig1s000MedR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov records — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01810939 (OPAL-HK) and https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01371747 (AMETHYST-DN); neither has a protocol/SAP posted
- Pivotal publication: Weir MR, Bakris GL, Bushinsky DA, et al. (OPAL-HK Investigators). "Patiromer in Patients with Kidney Disease and Hyperkalemia Receiving RAAS Inhibitors." *N Engl J Med.* 2015;372(3):211-221. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1410853), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25415805/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Patiromer%20in%20Patients%20with%20Kidney%20Disease%20and%20Hyperkalemia%20Receiving%20RAAS%20Inhibitors); supportive: Bakris GL, Pitt B, Weir MR, et al. "Effect of Patiromer on Serum Potassium Level in Patients With Hyperkalemia and Diabetic Kidney Disease: The AMETHYST-DN Randomized Clinical Trial." *JAMA.* 2015;314(2):151-161. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.7446), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172895/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Effect%20of%20Patiromer%20on%20Serum%20Potassium%20Level%20in%20Patients%20With%20Hyperkalemia%20and%20Diabetic%20Kidney%20Disease)

**Other resources**

- Relypsa was acquired by Galenica/Vifor Pharma in 2016 (later part of CSL Vifor); no trial-specific IPD/Vivli availability confirmed here.
- No evidence of an FDA Advisory Committee meeting for this NDA was found in the sources reviewed.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3777872, Introduction/Overview]*

> "The original Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) was developed on February 15, 2013. It was amended on March 20, 2013. A memorandum was added on August 2, 2013, and an addendum was added on September 30, 2013."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3777872, §3.2.2 "Statistical Methodologies"]*

> "In Part A, as the primary efficacy analysis, the mean change will be estimated using a longitudinal repeated measures model that includes two binary covariates for the presence of heart failure (HF) at baseline (yes/no) and T2DM at baseline (yes/no) and a continuous covariate containing the Baseline Part A level of serum K+... In Part B, changes from baseline serum potassium were ranked, and the treatment groups were compared using an ANOVA model with strata used at randomization... included as covariates and a treatment indicator. To compare Veltassa with placebo, the difference between the mean ranks was tested using a two-sided t-test. The difference and 95% CI between the treatment groups in median change from baseline was estimated using a Hodges-Lehmann estimator. The statistical tests and estimates were calculated for each of the 10 complete observation datasets and combined using multiple imputation methods."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3777872, §3.2.4 "Results and Conclusions"]*

> "The reviewer confirmed the efficacy results for both Part A and Part B of the study using the analysis data that were provided by the sponsor. The reviewer also used other nonparametric test statistical methods such as Wilcoxon test to verify the primary efficacy results in Part B. The missing data in these two parts of the study seem to be minor and do not lead to a different conclusion of the primary efficacy results."

The two-part randomized-withdrawal design here is a distinctive structure in this census: rather than a single-stage RCT, the SPA required a first-stage, uncontrolled dose-response demonstration (Part A) to clear a pre-specified minimum-effect-size bar before the genuinely comparative randomized-withdrawal stage (Part B) could carry the label claim — a design suited to a drug whose plausible placebo-controlled alternative (withholding treatment from severely hyperkalemic patients) would be difficult to justify ethically over a full treatment course.

### 30. Selexipag (Uptravi) — NDA 207947

**Sponsor:** Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH; WHO Group I) to delay disease progression and reduce risk of hospitalization for PAH

**Approval date:** December 21, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** GRIPHON (AC-065A302), NCT01106014

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven, group-sequential design, mid-trial SAP amendment (primary endpoint changed from a symptomatic 6MWD measure to a morbidity/mortality composite, and sample size substantially increased, both before unblinding)
- *Endpoints:* morbidity/mortality composite (primary: death, PAH hospitalization, lung transplant/atrial septostomy, initiation of parenteral prostanoid/chronic oxygen therapy, or disease progression), change in 6-minute walk distance (key secondary), absence of NYHA/WHO functional-class worsening (secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* unstratified log-rank test, Hodges-Lehmann estimator (6MWD), Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test (functional-class endpoint)
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing across the primary and ordered secondary endpoints, family-wise one-sided alpha of 0.005
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design with a single interim analysis, Haybittle-Peto-type fixed nominal boundary (one-sided α=0.00005 at interim regardless of observed information fraction), non-binding futility rule
- *Missing data/bias:* single-imputation rule for missing 6MWD (later changed from multiple imputation per FDA advice), supportive competing-risks analysis (Gray's method) for the primary composite

**Trial design & endpoints**

- GRIPHON was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, event-driven Phase III trial; N=1,156 randomized 1:1 (574 selexipag, 582 placebo) at 181 sites in 39 countries, stratified by site with a block size of 4, in adults with symptomatic PAH (NYHA/WHO functional class I-IV), either treatment-naive or on background PAH-specific therapy (ERAs and/or PDE-5 inhibitors)
- The trial's design evolved substantially across six protocol amendments: the original 2009 protocol's primary endpoint was change from baseline to week 16 in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD); Amendment 1 (March 2010) changed the primary endpoint to time to first "clinical worsening" and moved 6MWD to a secondary endpoint assessed at week 26; Amendment 4 (August 2011) revised the target hazard ratio from 0.5729 to 0.65, increasing the planned primary-endpoint event count from 202 to 332 and the sample size from 670 to 1,150, and added a single interim analysis; Amendment 5 (December 2011) set the interim analysis's one-sided alpha at 0.0001 per a Haybittle-Peto-type rule and, to eliminate any concern that Amendment 4 was informed by unblinded data, pre-specified that the 46 events observed before Amendment 4 (up to August 16, 2011) would be censored in the primary analysis; Amendment 6 (January 2013) renamed the "clinical worsening" endpoint the "morbidity/mortality (MM) event" endpoint
- Final primary endpoint: time to first CEC-adjudicated MM event up to 7 days after last study drug intake — a composite of death (all causes), hospitalization for PAH worsening, lung transplantation or balloon atrial septostomy, initiation of parenteral prostanoid or chronic oxygen therapy, or disease progression (a ≥15% decrease in 6MWD confirmed on two separate days plus worsening functional class)
- Sample size/power: designed for 331 CEC-confirmed MM events to give 90% power, under assumed constant hazard rates of 0.2231/year (placebo) and 0.145/year (selexipag, target HR 0.65); the group-sequential design fixed the overall one-sided type-I error at α=0.005, with a single interim analysis planned at 202 events (61% information fraction) but with the interim's one-sided significance level fixed at 0.00005 regardless of the actual event count at the time of the interim look — a Haybittle-Peto-type fixed boundary rather than an information-fraction-driven spending function — paired with a non-binding futility stopping option
- Primary analysis: one-sided unstratified log-rank test on the Full Analysis Set (all randomized patients), with a supportive competing-risks analysis (Gray's method, implemented via the R `cmprsk` package) also pre-specified in the SAP; result: 140 selexipag vs. 212 placebo patients with a CEC-confirmed MM event, HR 0.61 (99% CI 0.46-0.81), 1-sided log-rank p<0.0001, a 39% relative risk reduction
- Multiplicity: secondary endpoints were tested in a conditional, fixed-sequence hierarchy at the full one-sided family-wise alpha of 0.005, with a later hypothesis rejected only if the primary endpoint and all preceding secondary hypotheses were also rejected; the key secondary endpoint (change from baseline to week 26 in 6MWD at trough) used a non-parametric ANCOVA (rank-transformed residuals, one-sided Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test with continuity correction) and reached significance (Hodges-Lehmann location shift 12.0 m, 99% CI 1-24, p=0.0027); the next endpoint in the hierarchy (absence of NYHA/WHO functional-class worsening at week 26, Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by baseline functional class) also reached significance, after which the FDA statistical review states testing of further secondary endpoints was not presented because "the statistical significance stopped" there

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2015/207947Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2015/207947s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/207947Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2015/207947Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01106014 (no protocol/SAP documents posted)
- Pivotal publication: Sitbon O, Channick R, Chin KM, et al. (GRIPHON Investigators). "Selexipag for the Treatment of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension." *N Engl J Med.* 2015;373(26):2522-2533. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1503184), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26699168/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Selexipag%20for%20the%20Treatment%20of%20Pulmonary%20Arterial%20Hypertension)

**Other resources**

- Actelion was acquired by Johnson & Johnson in 2017; no trial-specific IPD/Vivli availability confirmed here.
- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was held for this NDA (per the FDA Summary Review: "an Advisory Committee meeting... none was held").

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3798968, §3.2.3 "Statistical Methodologies," Table 3-1 and surrounding text]*

> "The original study protocol was written on September 17, 2009. The primary endpoint in this study was 'Change from Baseline to Week 16 in 6MWD.'... Amendment 1 (3/11/2010): Changed the primary endpoint to time to first clinical worsening. Moved change from baseline to week 16 in 6MWD to secondary endpoint and changed to be assessed at Week 26... Amendment 4 (08/10/2011): Changed initial target hazard ratio of 0.5729 to 0.65. The amended treatment effect increased the number of primary events from 202 to 332. The sample size was increased from 670 to 1150 patients. Added an interim analysis after observing 202 primary events. Amendment 5 (12/14/2011): In order to eliminate any concern that the protocol change (Amendment 4) could be considered informed, the 46 events observed until 16 August 2011 are censored in the primary endpoint analysis. For the interim analysis, the type-I error was set to 0.0001 (1-sided) according to the Haybittle-Peto stopping rule."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3798968, §3.2.3, "Efficacy Analysis Methods"]*

> "Study GRIPHON employed a group-sequential design for the primary efficacy endpoint with options to recommend stop for futility or for compelling and robust efficacy at the interim analysis... the one-sided overall type-I-error probability is fixed to α= 0.005... the one-sided type-I-error probability at the interim analysis is fixed to 0.00005... the interim analysis is planned with 202 MM events (an information fraction of 202/331 = 61%); however, if there are less or more events available for the interim analysis, the one-sided significance level used for the interim analysis is kept unchanged at 0.00005."

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Reference ID 3798968, §3.2.3, "Analysis of secondary efficacy data"]*

> "In case of rejection of the null hypothesis in the main statistical analysis of the primary efficacy endpoint, the null hypotheses for the secondary efficacy endpoints were tested in a conditional hierarchical manner. A null hypothesis was rejected if and only if the main analysis of the endpoint and all main analyses of preceding secondary efficacy endpoints resulted in rejection of respective null hypotheses. This procedure restricted the family-wise type-I-error rate to the overall assigned one-sided alpha of 0.005... In the FAS, the statistical significance stopped at Absence of worsening from baseline in NYHA/WHO FC at Week 26. This review did not present the results of any further secondary endpoints."

GRIPHON is a clean illustration of a pre-specified fixed-alpha (Haybittle-Peto-style) interim boundary rather than an information-fraction-adaptive spending function like Lan-DeMets/O'Brien-Fleming used elsewhere in this census (FLAURA, SELECT): the interim significance threshold (0.00005 one-sided) was fixed at protocol-amendment time and held constant regardless of how many events had actually accrued by the time of the interim look, which is characteristic of the original Haybittle-Peto approach.

### 31. Lixisenatide (Adlyxin) — BLA 208471

**Sponsor:** Sanofi-Aventis U.S. LLC

**Indication approved:** Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

**Approval date:** July 27, 2016

**Pivotal trial:** GetGoal program (11 Phase 3 trials; representative trial EFC6014, "GetGoal-M," NCT00712673, a morning/evening add-on-to-metformin comparison), plus ELIXA, NCT01147250, as the required cardiovascular outcomes trial

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (9 of 11 GetGoal trials) or open-label, active-controlled (2 of 11), non-inferiority-then-superiority (ELIXA), event-driven (ELIXA)
- *Endpoints:* change in HbA1c from baseline (primary, GetGoal program), 4-component MACE+ (primary, ELIXA)
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA (GetGoal, as pre-specified), mixed model for repeated measurements with all available data (GetGoal, as FDA recommended for labeling), Cox proportional-hazards model with treatment and region as factors (ELIXA)
- *Missing data/bias:* last-observation-carried-forward (GetGoal, sponsor's original analysis, FDA-criticized), multiple imputation for missing values (GetGoal, FDA sensitivity analysis that reversed a non-inferiority conclusion in one trial)
- *Regulatory:* FDA Advisory Committee meeting held, dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial required before US approval under the 2008 FDA Diabetes Guidance (approval delayed several years relative to earlier EU approval for this reason)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- The efficacy claim rested on 11 Phase 2/3 trials (e.g., EFC6018, EFC10743, EFC6014, EFC6019, EFC11321, EFC6015, EFC6017, EFC6016, EFC10781, EFC10887, EFC12626), multicenter, multinational, randomized trials with a screening period, single-blind run-in, a 12- or 24/26-week treatment period, and a 4-week post-treatment follow-up; nine were double-blind, placebo-controlled and two were open-label, active-controlled (vs. exenatide twice daily or insulin glulisine three times daily), covering monotherapy and add-on settings to metformin, sulfonylurea, pioglitazone, and basal insulin
- Primary endpoint across the 11 trials: change in HbA1c from baseline to the end of the main treatment period (24/26 weeks, or 12 weeks for one trial), pre-specified to be analyzed via an ANCOVA model (terms for treatment, and randomization strata for baseline HbA1c, country, background antidiabetic drug(s), and BMI, with baseline HbA1c as a covariate) on the modified intent-to-treat population
- FDA's statistical review documented a substantive missing-data dispute: the sponsor's original analyses used last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) to handle 5%-16% missing data at the landmark visit across the 11 trials; FDA's own reviewer instead performed an ANCOVA with multiple imputation for missing values, and while the overall conclusions were unchanged for 10 of the 11 trials, the reanalysis reversed the conclusion for EFC12626 (lixisenatide vs. insulin glulisine three-times-daily) — the multiple-imputation-based analysis could no longer support non-inferiority of lixisenatide to glulisine TID at the pre-specified 0.4% margin (LS mean treatment difference 0.28%, 95% CI 0.157-0.408), where the sponsor's MMRM-based analysis had shown non-inferiority; the label ultimately reflects the FDA-preferred MMRM-with-all-available-data estimates, and states plainly that Adlyxin was less effective than insulin glulisine TID
- A dedicated cardiovascular safety trial, ELIXA (NCT01147250), was required before US approval under the post-2008 FDA Diabetes Guidance requiring CV-risk exclusion for new antidiabetic therapies; ELIXA randomized 6,068 patients with type 2 diabetes and a recent (≤180 days) acute coronary syndrome event 1:1, double-blind, to lixisenatide or placebo added to standard of care, at 828 sites in 49 countries
- ELIXA's primary endpoint was time to first adjudicated MACE+ (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal ischemic stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina), analyzed via a Cox proportional-hazards model with treatment and region as factors, tested against the 2008 Guidance's 1.3 non-inferiority risk margin at a pre-specified 805 MACE+ events; the result (406 lixisenatide vs. 399 placebo events, HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.89-1.17) ruled out the 1.3 margin, establishing cardiovascular safety without showing benefit or excess harm
- A May 25, 2016 FDA Advisory Committee meeting discussed both the efficacy/safety package and the fixed-dose lixisenatide/insulin glargine combination, focusing on anti-drug antibody findings and rare severe allergic reactions; the committee's concerns were not judged sufficient to recommend against marketing

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2016/208471Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2016/208471Orig1s000lbl.pdf
- FDA Statistical Review (covers the ELIXA cardiovascular-safety evaluation in detail) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2016/208471Orig1s000StatR.pdf
- FDA Division Director (Summary) Review (covers the GetGoal efficacy program's missing-data reanalysis and the Advisory Committee meeting) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2016/208471Orig1s000SumR.pdf
- ClinicalTrials.gov records — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01147250 (ELIXA) and https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00712673 (GetGoal-M); no protocol/SAP documents posted for either
- Pivotal publications: Ahrén B, Leguizamo Dimas A, Miossec P, Saubadu S, Aronson R. "Efficacy and safety of lixisenatide once-daily morning or evening injections in type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (GetGoal-M)." *Diabetes Care.* 2013;36(9):2543-2550. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc12-2006), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23536584/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy%20and%20safety%20of%20lixisenatide%20once-daily%20morning%20or%20evening%20injections%20in%20type%202%20diabetes%20inadequately%20controlled%20on%20metformin); Pfeffer MA, Claggett B, Diaz R, et al. (ELIXA Investigators). "Lixisenatide in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes and Acute Coronary Syndrome." *N Engl J Med.* 2015;373(23):2247-2257. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1509225), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26630143/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Lixisenatide%20in%20Patients%20with%20Type%202%20Diabetes%20and%20Acute%20Coronary%20Syndrome)

**Other resources**

- Sanofi generally participates in clinical-trial data-sharing via Vivli.org; trial-specific availability not individually confirmed here.
- FDA Advisory Committee meeting held May 25, 2016.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, from FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary, Ref ID 3913919]*

> "The cardiovascular safety of lixisenatide was evaluated based on the final results of the ELIXA trial. The pre-specified primary endpoint for the trial was the time until first major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE+), defined as any of the following adjudicated events: cardiovascular (CV) death, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), non-fatal ischemic stroke and hospitalization for unstable angina... The pre-specified Cox proportional hazards model-based hazard ratio estimate for MACE+ was 1.02 with an associated 95% confidence interval of (0.89, 1.17). The upper bound of 1.17 ruled out the risk margin of 1.3 in accordance with the 2008 FDA Diabetes Guidance."

*[verbatim, from FDA Division Director Review, Ref ID 3964062, p.8-9]*

> "The applicant had pre-specified the primary efficacy assessment to be the change in hemoglobin A1c (i.e., HbA1c) from baseline to the end of the main treatment period... and relies on an ANCOVA model with terms for treatment, and randomization strata for HbA1c, country, background antidiabetic drug(s), and BMI as fixed effects and baseline HbA1c value as covariate. In reality, the primary analysis was not strictly speaking based on the change in HbA1c from baseline to the landmark visit but reflected the change from baseline to either the landmark visit, the onset of rescue (for subjects rescued) or the last on study visit... The amount of missing data at the landmark visit ranged from 5% to 16% across the phase 3 trials and missing data were handled in the sponsor's original analyses by carrying forward the last available on-treatment observation (LOCF method). Assumptions made in handling missing data in this way are unlikely to be valid and the Agency has been recommending since 2009 that applicants use methods to handle missing values that are based on a set of more plausible and valid assumptions... Missing data handling in this way did however affect the conclusion of study EFC12626, the study comparing lixisenatide to insulin glulisine TID. Using a multiple imputation for missing values model, a conclusion of non-inferiority of lixisenatide to glulisine TID (using a NI margin of 0.4%) could no longer be made (LS mean treatment difference [95% CI]: 0.28 [0.157, 0.408]) calling into question the persuasiveness of the reported results based on the sponsor's MMRM analysis."

This is a clear real-world example of missing-data handling changing a formal regulatory conclusion for one trial within a larger program: FDA's own multiple-imputation-based sensitivity analysis, not the sponsor's original LOCF or MMRM approach, is what determined that lixisenatide could not be labeled as non-inferior to insulin glulisine three-times-daily.
