### 39. Lasmiditan (Reyvow) — NDA 211280

**Sponsor:** Eli Lilly and Company

**Indication approved:** Acute treatment of migraine, with or without aura, in adults

**Approval date:** October 11, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** SAMURAI (Study 301, NCT02439320) and SPARTAN (Study 302, NCT02605174)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, single-attack acute-treatment trials (SAMURAI: 2 active dose arms; SPARTAN: 3 active dose arms), stratified by concomitant migraine-preventive medication use

- *Endpoints:* co-primary endpoints — pain-free at 2 hours and most-bothersome-symptom (MBS)-free at 2 hours, corrected modified intent-to-treat population

- *Primary analysis:* logistic regression with treatment group and background preventive-medication use as covariates, Wald test for the treatment-effect estimate

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (gatekeeping) hierarchical testing across two doses and two co-primary endpoints, maintaining overall two-sided type I error at 0.05

- *Missing data/bias:* missing 2-hour response data counted as treatment failure (non-responder imputation)

- *Regulatory:* no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held, explicitly because the trial designs and evidentiary basis were considered similar to those of previously approved drugs in the class, without controversial issues; no REMS or boxed warning, but a driving-precaution labeling statement (avoid driving for 8 hours post-dose)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- SAMURAI (Study 301, US-only, 99 sites): 2-arm active-dose design (100 mg, 200 mg vs. placebo), single-attack acute treatment. SPARTAN (Study 302, US/UK/Germany, 125 sites): 3-arm active-dose design (50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg vs. placebo). Both randomized 1:1:1 (SAMURAI) or 1:1:1:1 (SPARTAN), stratified by concomitant use of migraine-preventive medication

- Co-primary endpoints (both trials): pain-free at 2 hours and MBS-free at 2 hours, in the corrected modified intent-to-treat population

- Sample size: planned per-group enrollment of approximately 570 subjects per arm, powered at >90% to detect differences in pain-free response rates of 7.4%, 13.6%, and 18.8% between placebo, 100 mg, and 200 mg respectively, based on rates observed in the Phase 2 study COL-MIG-202

- Primary analysis: logistic regression with treatment group and background preventive-medication use as covariates; missing 2-hour data were imputed as non-responses (treatment failures); point estimates and p-values (Wald test) reported for the response-rate difference

- Multiplicity: a gatekeeping procedure pre-specified to maintain the overall two-sided study-wise type I error at 0.05 across the two doses and two co-primary endpoints, tested in a fixed sequence: (1) 200 mg vs. placebo, pain-free at 2h; (2) 200 mg vs. placebo, MBS-free at 2h; (3) 100 mg vs. placebo, pain-free at 2h; continuing through the 100 mg comparisons only if the preceding tests were significant

- Results (SAMURAI, Study 301): pain-free at 2h — placebo 15.34%, 100 mg 28.31% (p<0.001), 200 mg 31.81% (p<0.001); MBS-free at 2h — placebo 29.58%, 100 mg 41.16% (p<0.001), 200 mg 40.69% (p<0.001). A sensitivity analysis excluding 29 patients whose migraine severity did not meet dosing criteria at the time of dosing did not change the conclusions. SPARTAN (Study 302) followed the same design/analysis structure across its four arms with consistent results

**Documents**

- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/211280s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Statistical Review (reviewer Jinnan Liu, PhD, Division of Biometrics 1) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211280Orig1s000StatR.pdf

- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211280Orig1s000SumR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov records — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02439320 (SAMURAI), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02605174 (SPARTAN) (neither has posted protocol/SAP documents)

- Pivotal publication (SAMURAI): Kuca B, Silberstein SD, Wietecha L, Berg PH, Dozier G, Lipton RB; COL MIG-301 Study Group. "Lasmiditan is an effective acute treatment for migraine: A phase 3 randomized study." *Neurology.* 2018;91(24):e2222-e2232. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000006641), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30446595/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Lasmiditan%20effective%20acute%20treatment%20migraine%20phase%203%20randomized%20SAMURAI)

- Pivotal publication (SPARTAN): Goadsby PJ, Wietecha LA, Dennehy EB, Kuca B, Case MG, Aurora SK, Gaul C. "Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study of lasmiditan for acute treatment of migraine." *Brain.* 2019;142(7):1894-1904. **Other resources**

A sample size of 570 per group were needed to detect with power >90% a difference in pain free response rates of 7.4%, 13.6% and 18.8% between placebo, 100mg and 200mg respectively. ### 40. Cenobamate (Xcopri) — NDA 212839

**Sponsor:** SK Life Science, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of partial-onset (focal) seizures in adults

**Approval date:** November 21, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** Study C013 (YKP3089C013, NCT01397968, Phase 2) and Study C017 (YKP3089C017, NCT01866111, Phase 2/3 dose-response)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trials with a prospective baseline period, titration phase, and maintenance phase; C017 used a 4-arm parallel dose-response design (placebo, 100/200/400 mg)

- *Endpoints:* percent change in seizure frequency per 28 days during the treatment period compared to baseline (primary); ≥50% responder rate (secondary)

- *Primary analysis:* rank ANCOVA on percent-change seizure-frequency endpoint (C017: covariate-adjusted rank-based ANCOVA with ranked baseline seizure rate as a covariate; C013: two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test as the primary analysis) ("Rank ANCOVA on percent-change seizure-frequency endpoint," distinct from the existing stratified-Wilcoxon/Hodges-Lehmann term)

- *Missing data/bias:* last observation carried forward (LOCF) for the primary endpoint

- *Regulatory:* dedicated post-hoc safety study (Study C021) with a pre-specified upper-95%-CI-bound safety threshold (0.3%) for DRESS incidence, run under a slower titration schedule to characterize and mitigate a previously observed serious hypersensitivity signal, including one fatal DRESS case in a thorough-QT healthy-volunteer study ("Post-hoc dedicated safety study with a pre-specified upper-CI-bound safety threshold, run under a modified risk-mitigation protocol"); no formal REMS — risk instead managed via mandatory slow titration labeling, a Warnings and Precautions statement (not a Boxed Warning), and a Medication Guide; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study C013 (NCT01397968, Phase 2): multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial with an 8-week prospective baseline, 6-week titration, and 6-week maintenance phase; n=222 randomized (~113 cenobamate/108 placebo at the ITT level after exclusions). Study C017 (NCT01866111, Phase 2/3): multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial with an 8-week prospective baseline and an 18-week double-blind treatment period; n=437 randomized 1:1:1:1 to placebo, 100 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg

- Primary endpoint (both trials): percent change in seizure frequency per 28 days in the treatment period compared to baseline, in the ITT population, using LOCF for missing data

- Primary analysis: C013 used a two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test (sample size of 100 subjects per group planned to detect a 16-percentage-point difference in median percent reduction at two-sided alpha=0.05, assuming SD=40%, 80% power). C017 used an analysis of covariance model with terms for ranked baseline seizure rate and randomized treatment group (rank ANCOVA) — a related but distinct method from C013's unadjusted rank-sum test

- Results: C013 — median % reduction in seizure frequency, cenobamate 55.6% vs. placebo 21.5%, p<0.0001 (Wilcoxon rank-sum); responder rate (≥50% reduction) 50.4% vs. 22.2%. C017 — median % change from baseline: 100 mg -36.3% (p=0.006), 200 mg -55.2% (p<0.001), 400 mg -55.3% (p<0.001), vs. placebo -24.3%

- SAP amendments: C013's SAP was amended (Amendment 3, dated July 26, 2013); C017's SAP (Amendment 2, dated March 20, 2015) removed a previously planned interim analysis and added detail on the statistical procedures

- GCP: FDA's Office of Scientific Investigations inspected two C013 sites (Philadelphia, Bangalore) plus the C017 sponsor/CRO; data were judged acceptable at all inspected sites

- DRESS safety history and risk mitigation: a fatal case of Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) occurred in a thorough-QT healthy-volunteer study; two additional DRESS cases (both recovered, requiring hospitalization and corticosteroid treatment) occurred in the open-label extension of Study C017. A dedicated safety study (Study C021), using a slower titration schedule, enrolled 1339 subjects (1110 under the modified/slower titration) with no DRESS cases observed, and was sized so that, with no new cases, the upper limit of the 95% CI for the DRESS rate under the modified titration would be 0.3%

- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/212839Orig1s000SumR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov records — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01397968 (C013), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01866111 (C017) (neither has posted protocol/SAP documents)

- Pivotal publication (C013): Chung SS, French JA, Kowalski J, et al. "Randomized phase 2 study of adjunctive cenobamate in patients with uncontrolled focal seizures." *Neurology.* 2020;94(22):e2311-e2322. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000009530), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32409485/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Randomized%20phase%202%20study%20adjunctive%20cenobamate%20uncontrolled%20focal%20seizures)

- Pivotal publication (C017): Krauss GL, Klein P, Brandt C, et al. ### 41. Lumateperone (Caplyta) — NDA 209500

**Sponsor:** Intra-Cellular Therapies, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of schizophrenia in adults

**Approval date:** December 20, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** Study ITI-007-301 (NCT02282761) — the positive, FDA-designated pivotal Phase 3 trial; Study ITI-007-302 (NCT02469155) — a second Phase 3 trial submitted in the same NDA that FDA classified as a "failed" (not "negative") study; supportive Phase 2 Study ITI-007-005 (NCT01499563) also contributed positive data at the approved dose

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-arm dose-comparison trial (Study 301: lumateperone 28 mg vs. 42 mg vs. placebo, no active comparator); randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled, four-arm trial with the active arm included only for assay-sensitivity, not for a formal efficacy claim (Study 302: lumateperone 14 mg vs. 42 mg vs. risperidone 4 mg vs. placebo); single efficacious dose (42 mg) identified across a four-dose (14/28/42/84 mg), three-trial development program with no consistent monotonic dose-response relationship

- *Endpoints:* change from baseline to Day 28 (Study 301) / Day 42 (Study 302) in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) total score (primary); change from baseline in Clinical Global Impressions-Severity (CGI-S) scale (secondary in Study 301, key secondary in Study 302)

- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance matrix, modeling treatment, visit, baseline PANSS score, baseline-by-visit interaction, and treatment-by-visit interaction, under a missing-at-random assumption (distinct from the taxonomy's sandwich-variance-estimator MMRM entry)

- *Multiplicity:* mixture-based gatekeeping procedure (Dmitrienko et al.) across two doses and two endpoints (Study 301); fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing across dose/endpoint pairs (Study 302)

- *Missing data/bias:* placebo-based multiple imputation under a missing-not-at-random pattern-mixture model, pre-specified as a sensitivity analysis in both trials; tipping-point analysis (multiple imputation) and non-responder imputation applied post hoc by the sponsor to argue Study 302 lacked assay sensitivity

- *Regulatory:* FDA classification of a negative confirmatory trial as "failed" rather than "negative," based on an inconclusive assessment of assay sensitivity, so as not to weigh it fully against the totality-of-evidence conclusion; FDA Advisory Committee meeting scheduled, then cancelled after the sponsor filed a Major Amendment addressing nonclinical carcinogenicity safety questions, extending the PDUFA date without a Complete Response Letter

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Both pivotal trials enrolled adults (18-60) with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia (DSM-5, confirmed by SCID-CT, with eligibility confirmed by an independent Eligibility Adjudication Committee), conducted entirely on inpatient units at US sites, with a baseline PANSS total score ≥70 and CGI-S ≥4 required for entry
- Study 301 (12 US sites): 450 patients randomized 1:1:1 to lumateperone 28 mg, lumateperone 42 mg, or placebo once daily for 4 weeks; no active comparator; no stratification factors were specified in the FDA review beyond treatment assignment
- Study 302 (13 US sites): 696 patients randomized 1:1:1:1 to lumateperone 14 mg, lumateperone 42 mg, risperidone 4 mg (titrated 2 mg on Day 1, then 4 mg), or placebo once daily for 6 weeks; risperidone was included, per FDA, solely to demonstrate the trial's assay sensitivity, not as a formal comparator arm in the multiplicity procedure
- Primary endpoint (both trials): change from baseline to end of treatment (Day 28 for Study 301, Day 42 for Study 302) in PANSS total score (30-item clinician-rated scale, range 30-210, higher = more severe), analyzed in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population (randomized subjects with ≥1 dose and ≥1 valid baseline and post-baseline PANSS assessment)
- Key secondary endpoint (both trials): change from baseline to end of treatment in CGI-S
- Primary analysis model: MMRM including PANSS change from baseline as the response, with terms for study visit, baseline PANSS total score, baseline-by-visit interaction, treatment, and treatment-by-visit interaction, and an unstructured covariance matrix for within-subject correlation; this assumes data are missing at random (MAR)
- Sample size: Study 301 planned ~440 subjects (1:1:1) for 90% power to detect a 6-point PANSS difference at two-sided alpha=0.05 (SD=15), using an effect size of 0.4 estimated from Study 005; Study 302 was originally planned at 587 subjects based on Study 301's interim effect size (0.4), then increased to 680 (696 ultimately enrolled) once Study 301's final, smaller effect size (0.3) for the 42 mg dose became available — a sample-size increase FDA's statistical reviewer noted was permissible without analysis adjustment because it was driven by external (Study 301) data, not by unblinded Study 302 data
- Multiplicity: Study 301 pre-specified a mixture-based gatekeeping procedure (Dmitrienko, Kordzakhia et al. 2016) to control the familywise error rate across two doses and two endpoints (PANSS, CGI-S); Study 302 pre-specified a fixed-sequence test order: 42 mg PANSS → 42 mg CGI-S → 14 mg PANSS → 14 mg CGI-S
- Missing-data sensitivity: both trials pre-specified a placebo-based multiple-imputation pattern-mixture model (missing-not-at-random) as a sensitivity analysis to the MMRM/MAR primary analysis; in Study 301 this produced an estimate close to the primary analysis (pattern-mixture: -3.9 [-7.4, -0.4] vs. MMRM: -4.2 [-7.8, -0.6] for 42 mg)
- Result — Study 301: LS mean placebo-subtracted PANSS change was -4.2 (95% CI -7.8, -0.6; nominal p=0.014, multiplicity-adjusted p=0.045) for lumateperone 42 mg (superior to placebo) and -2.6 (95% CI -6.2, 1.1; not significant) for 28 mg; on CGI-S, the 42 mg placebo-subtracted difference was -0.3 (95% CI -0.5, -0.1; unadjusted p=0.003, multiplicity-adjusted p=0.045)
- Result — Study 302: neither lumateperone dose separated from placebo on the primary endpoint (14 mg: +0.1 [-3.4, 3.5]; 42 mg: +0.5 [-2.9, 3.8]; both not significant, p=0.789 for 42 mg per the Summary Review), while the risperidone assay-sensitivity arm did separate from placebo (-5.4 [-8.9, -1.9], nominal p=0.003) — the study was therefore the largest and longest of the three placebo-controlled trials yet showed no lumateperone effect at either dose
- The sponsor conducted extensive post hoc sensitivity analyses of Study 302 (responder analysis treating missing Day-42 data as non-response; multiple-imputation variants with an added shift, akin to a tipping-point analysis) arguing the MMRM/MAR primary model was poorly suited to the risperidone arm's higher discontinuation rate (37%, vs. 21% placebo and 25% lumateperone 42 mg) and that, under these assumptions, "all active treatments, including risperidone, very likely have no efficacy versus placebo" in that trial — i.e., that Study 302 was a failed (assay-insensitive) rather than a negative study; FDA's own supporting non-parametric sensitivity analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test with worst-observed-value imputation for missing Day-42 scores) could not reject the null hypothesis of no difference between risperidone and placebo (two-sided p=0.4), which FDA said "aligns with the Applicant's assertion" but was not fully dispositive
- Across the three placebo-controlled trials (005, 301, 302), only the 42 mg dose was ever superior to placebo (Study 005: -5.8 [-10.5, -1.1], adjusted p=0.040; Study 301: -4.2 [-7.8, -0.6], adjusted p=0.045); the 84 mg dose (Study 005), 28 mg dose (Study 301), and 14 mg dose (Study 302) were never superior to placebo, so labeling recommends only the 42 mg dose

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, NDA 209500, p.18-19]* — "The Applicant provided results of two clinical studies (Studies 005 and 301) that met their primary efficacy endpoint for the 42-mg lumateperone dose. Both Studies 005 and 301 are considered to be adequate and well-controlled investigations... Of note, the results from a third adequate and well-controlled trial described in this review (Study 302) did not provide evidence that lumateperone was superior to placebo for the treatment of schizophrenia. Although the results from Study 302 raised questions about the magnitude and reliability of the lumateperone treatment effect, these findings did not change the overall conclusion of effectiveness for the 42-mg dose as demonstrated by Studies 005 and 301."

*[verbatim, p.23-24]* — "Lumateperone 42 mg was found to be superior to placebo on the primary efficacy endpoint in Studies 005 and 301... In Study 302, lumateperone 42 mg was not found to be superior to placebo on the primary efficacy endpoint (p=0.789). In addition, the 84-mg, 28-mg, and 14-mg doses of lumateperone were not found to be superior to placebo in the three studies. On the key secondary endpoint (CGI-S) in Study 301, lumateperone 42 mg was found to be superior to placebo... It is not entirely clear why lumateperone 42 mg was not superior to placebo in Study 302, which had the largest sample size and the longest treatment duration. The active comparator, risperidone 4 mg, separated from placebo based on the primary efficacy model... suggesting the study had assay sensitivity... Based on post-hoc sensitivity analyses, the Applicant considers Study 302 to be a failed, rather than a negative, study (i.e., a study lacking assay sensitivity)."

*[verbatim, p.177, Study 301 Statistical Analysis Plan]* — "The treatment effect on the primary efficacy endpoint, change from baseline to Day 28 in PANSS total score, was evaluated using a MMRM model. The model includes the PANSS change from baseline as response variable and study visit, baseline PANSS total score, baseline PANSS total score-by-study visit interaction, treatment (lumateperone 28 mg, lumateperone 42 mg, placebo), and treatment-by-study visit interaction. An unstructured covariance matrix was used to model the correlation among repeated measures within subject... A mixture-based gatekeeping procedure was pre-specified to adjust for multiplicity due to testing two doses and two efficacy endpoints. This method proposed by Dmitrienko et al is a valid approach for controlling the familywise error rate (Dmitrienko, Kordzakhia et al. 2016)... A pattern-mixture model using a placebo-based multiple imputation method was pre-specified in the SAP to explore the impact of a different assumption regarding missing data... (Study 301 SAP page 27)."

*[verbatim, p.185, Table 66]* — Study 301 Primary Efficacy Results: Lumateperone 28 mg, N=150, LS mean change -12.9 (1.3), placebo-subtracted difference -2.6 (-6.2, 1.1); Lumateperone 42 mg*, N=150, LS mean change -14.5 (1.3), placebo-subtracted difference -4.2 (-7.8, -0.6); Placebo, N=150, LS mean change -10.3 (1.3). "* Dose statistically significantly superior to placebo."

*[verbatim, p.189]* — "The point estimate of the difference in change from baseline in the CGI-S score at Day 28 (analyzed via MMRM) for the 42 mg lumateperone dose versus placebo is -0.3 (95% CI: -0.5, -0.1) with an unadjusted p-value of 0.003 (multiplicity adjusted p-value=0.045). Note, that the CGI-S results were not replicated in other studies in this program... Efficacy was demonstrated for lumateperone 42 mg but not for lumateperone 28 mg. None of the other registration studies included a 28-mg treatment arm; therefore, the data on the 28-mg dose are limited to this study."

*[verbatim, p.197, Study 302 Statistical Analysis Plan]* — "The treatment effect on the primary efficacy endpoint, change from baseline to Day 42 in PANSS total score, was evaluated using an MMRM model. The model included the change from baseline at each pre-specified timepoint as the response variable and study visit, baseline PANSS total score, baseline PANSS total score-by-study visit interaction, treatment (lumateperone 14 mg, lumateperone 42 mg, risperidone 4 mg, and placebo) and treatment-by-study visit interaction... A fixed sequence testing strategy was pre-specified (primary endpoint for 42 mg lumateperone versus placebo followed by key secondary endpoint 42 mg lumateperone versus placebo followed by primary endpoint for 14 mg lumateperone versus placebo and lastly key secondary endpoint for 14 mg lumateperone versus placebo)... Originally, the overall planned sample size (i.e., 587 randomized subjects) was based on the interim results of Study 301 (observed effect size of 0.4). Once the final results for Study 301 including the smaller effect size for the 42 mg lumateperone dose (observed effect size of 0.3) were available, the Applicant decided to increase the overall sample size to 680. Statistical reviewer note: Increasing the sample size while Study 302 was ongoing is permissible without any adjustments to the analysis because the decision is based on external data and not on accumulating data from Study 302."

*[verbatim, p.205, Table 74]* — Study 302 Primary Efficacy Results: Lumateperone 14 mg, N=174, LS mean change -15.0 (1.3), placebo-subtracted difference 0.1 (-3.4, 3.5); Lumateperone 42 mg, N=174, LS mean change -14.6 (1.2), placebo-subtracted difference 0.5 (-2.9, 3.8); Risperidone 4 mg (footnoted "Included for assay sensitivity, not included in multiple comparison procedure"), N=174, LS mean change -20.5 (1.3), placebo-subtracted difference -5.4 (-8.9, -1.9); Placebo, N=174, LS mean change -15.1 (1.2).

*[verbatim, pp.207-209]* — "Study 302 provides no evidence of efficacy for lumateperone 42 mg, and the lack of a treatment effect is concerning... the question is whether the study demonstrates assay sensitivity. A positive finding for risperidone (vs. placebo) would demonstrate assay sensitivity, such the study would be deemed 'negative' with respect to lumateperone. Conversely, if the effect of risperidone were statistically indistinguishable from placebo, the study would lack assay sensitivity and be deemed a 'failed' study... In response to the Division's concerns... the Applicant conducted numerous post-hoc sensitivity analyses... under varying Missing Not At Random assumptions (e.g., a responder analysis treating all patients without a Day 42 assessment as non-responders and several variants of multiple imputation with a shift added (akin to a tipping point analysis))... the Applicant states that 'all active treatments, including risperidone, very likely have no efficacy versus placebo' in Study 302... The statistical reviewer conducted an additional sensitivity analysis (Wilcoxon rank sum test)... assigning the worst change value observed to patients with missing PANSS scores at Day 42... This hypothesis could not be rejected (two-sided p-value=0.4)... This analysis aligns with the Applicant's assertion about viewing Study 302 as 'failed' study."

*[verbatim, p.210, Table 75]* — cross-trial summary of placebo-subtracted PANSS change (95% CI, multiplicity-adjusted p): Study 005 (n=335) 84 mg -0.9 (NS), 42 mg -5.8 (-10.5,-1.1) p=0.040, risperidone 4 mg -6.0; Study 301 (n=450) 28 mg -2.6 (NS), 42 mg -4.2 (-7.8,-0.6) p=0.045; Study 302 (n=696) 14 mg +0.1 (NS), 42 mg +0.5 (NS), risperidone 4 mg -5.4.

*[verbatim, p.35]* — "In order to incorporate outside expertise into our assessment of whether the benefits of lumateperone outweigh its risks, an Advisory Committee Meeting was scheduled for July 31, 2019. A late-cycle meeting was held with the Applicant on July 18, 2019... We reached an agreement that the data the Applicant pledged to provide would allow the Division to reach a conclusion on the safety of lumateperone without the assistance of an Advisory Committee. The Division cancelled the Advisory Committee Meeting."

### 42. Lemborexant (Dayvigo) — NDA 212028

**Sponsor:** Eisai Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of adult patients with insomnia, characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance

**Approval date:** December 20, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** SUNRISE-1 (Study E2006-G000-304), NCT02783729 — 1-month, polysomnography-based trial with a zolpidem active-comparator arm; and SUNRISE-2 (Study E2006-G000-303), NCT02952820 — 6/12-month, diary-based (subjective) trial, placebo-controlled only

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* four-arm randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-comparator-controlled design (lemborexant 5 mg/10 mg vs. placebo vs. zolpidem tartrate ER 6.25 mg, 5:5:5:4 randomization, 1-month treatment) paired with a separate three-arm randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design (lemborexant 5 mg/10 mg vs. placebo, 1:1:1 randomization, 6-month placebo-controlled period plus 6-month active-treatment extension) — complementary short-duration objective (PSG) and long-duration subjective (diary) pivotal-trial pairing for the same drug; randomization stratified by country and age group (<65 vs. ≥65, or 55-64 vs. ≥65) in both trials

- *Endpoints:* polysomnography-measured latency to persistent sleep (LPS), sleep efficiency (SE), and wake after sleep onset (WASO)/WASO in the second half of the night (WASO2H) (SUNRISE-1, objective); patient sleep-diary-based subjective sleep onset latency (sSOL), subjective sleep efficiency (sSE), and subjective wake after sleep onset (sWASO) (SUNRISE-2, subjective) (objective PSG-based and subjective diary-based sleep-onset/maintenance endpoints, not covered by existing taxonomy rows)

- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measurements (MMRM) on the log-transformed endpoint (unstructured covariance matrix, with Toeplitz then AR(1) as non-convergence fallbacks), adjusted for baseline value, region, age group, treatment, time, and treatment-by-time interaction, reported as least-squares geometric mean ratios to placebo (this MMRM variant does not use the sandwich variance estimator tied to the existing MMRM taxonomy row)

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing / sequential gate-keeping procedure (LEM10 vs. placebo tested first, then LEM5 vs. placebo, then key secondaries in a fixed order; testing stops at the first non-significant result)

- *Interim/alpha-spending:* non-binding administrative interim analysis (SUNRISE-1 only) — a single interim look at ~50% enrollment limited to a conditional-power calculation for LEM10 vs. zolpidem on WASO2H, with no stopping rule and no alpha adjustment

- *Missing data/bias:* pattern-mixture multiple imputation assuming missing-not-at-random (MNAR) via a complete-case missing-value (CCMV) pattern, used as the primary (not merely sensitivity) missing-data method ahead of the MMRM analysis (MNAR-based imputation used as the primary rather than a sensitivity analysis); tipping-point analysis (multiple imputation) and MMRM-without-imputation (MAR) as sensitivity analyses

**Trial design & endpoints**

- SUNRISE-1 (Study E2006-G000-304): a 1-month, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-comparator-controlled, parallel-group trial in adults ≥55 (women) / ≥65 (men) with insomnia disorder (DSM-5), also enrolling adults 21-64 for the driving/PK substudy population framing; 1,006 subjects randomized 5:5:5:4 to lemborexant 10 mg, lemborexant 5 mg, zolpidem tartrate ER 6.25 mg (Ambien CR), or placebo, stratified by country and age group (55-64 vs. ≥65); primary endpoint: change from baseline in mean latency to persistent sleep (LPS, minutes from lights-off to the first 20 consecutive epochs of non-wakefulness), measured by overnight PSG on treatment nights 29/30; three prespecified key secondary endpoints: change from baseline in sleep efficiency (SE) and in WASO (both LEM vs. placebo) and in WASO in the second half of the night (WASO2H, LEM vs. zolpidem)
- SUNRISE-2 (Study E2006-G000-303): a 12-month (6-month placebo-controlled Core period plus 6-month active-treatment Extension), multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in adults with insomnia disorder (~40% planned ≥65 years); 971 subjects randomized 1:1:1 to lemborexant 10 mg, lemborexant 5 mg, or placebo, stratified by country and age group (<65 vs. ≥65); placebo-arm subjects were re-randomized to LEM5 or LEM10 at Month 6 for the Extension; primary endpoint: change from Study Baseline to Month 6 in mean subjective (patient sleep-diary) sleep onset latency (sSOL); two prespecified key secondary endpoints: change from baseline to Month 6 in subjective sleep efficiency (sSE) and subjective wake after sleep onset (sWASO)
- Sample size/power: SUNRISE-1 was powered (SD assumptions from dose-finding Study 201) for ≥95% power (2-sided t-test, α=0.05) to detect the assumed LEM5/LEM10-vs-placebo effect on log(LPS) with ~250/250/200 subjects per arm; SUNRISE-2 targeted ~300 subjects/arm (900 total) for >90% power to detect an 8.7-minute sSOL treatment difference and for 90% power on an 11.4-minute sWASO difference, at a 2-sided α=0.05
- Statistical methods: both trials used MMRM on the log-transformed primary endpoint (unstructured covariance, Toeplitz/AR(1) fallback), with missing data imputed before the MMRM step via pattern-mixture multiple imputation under an MNAR/CCMV assumption; both used a sequential gate-keeping (fixed-sequence step-down) procedure — primary endpoint LEM10 vs. placebo, then LEM5 vs. placebo, then (only if both primary comparisons were significant) the key secondaries in a fixed order — to control overall type I error at 0.05, with no adjustment for other secondary/exploratory analyses
- FDA statistical concerns raised pre-NDA (June 14, 2018 pre-NDA meeting): the Agency objected to the sponsor's originally proposed primary-analysis missing-data method (a "complete case missing value" [CCMC] assumption) and to the interpretability of the sponsor's proposed tipping-point analysis (TPA); the sponsor amended the SAP to the MNAR/CCMV pattern-mixture MI approach ultimately used as primary, with a revised TPA presented as a post hoc sensitivity analysis in both trials
- FDA's independent sensitivity analyses (both trials) — MMRM without imputation (MAR assumption) and pattern-mixture imputation using "jump to placebo" (MNAR) — reproduced the sponsor's primary conclusions in both studies
- Both primary endpoints were statistically significant for lemborexant 5 mg and 10 mg vs. placebo in both trials; in SUNRISE-1, zolpidem ER numerically underperformed placebo on the primary LPS endpoint at Days 29/30 (LS-geometric-mean ratio to baseline 0.85 for zolpidem vs. 0.70 for placebo), which the FDA clinical reviewer attributed to zolpidem ER's labeled efficacy window (weeks, not a full month) rather than to a flaw in the lemborexant comparison
- Next-day/driving-impairment data considered in review (not from an Advisory Committee, since none was convened): a separate Phase 1 driving-performance study (Study 106; healthy and elderly subjects, incomplete-block crossover, doses 2.5/5/10 mg vs. zopiclone positive control vs. placebo) found lemborexant's 95% CI for placebo-corrected change in standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) fell below the 2.4 cm threshold associated with a 0.5 g/L blood-alcohol-equivalent impairment level at both doses tested in the label-relevant range, but 2 of 32 subjects on lemborexant 10 mg had SDLP changes exceeding the 4.4 cm threshold associated with 0.8 g/L, leading FDA and the label to flag next-morning driving impairment as possible in some patients at the 10 mg dose

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, ClinicalTrials.gov-posted Statistical Analysis Plan, Study E2006-G000-304 (SUNRISE-1), Final V3.0, p.17]* — "A sequential gate-keeping procedure will be used for the primary and the key secondary endpoint comparisons to control for the overall type I error at the 0.05 significance level... The primary endpoints will be tested in the following order: • Change from baseline of the mean LPS of Days 29 and 30 of LEM10 compared to PBO • Change from baseline of the mean LPS of Days 29 and 30 of LEM5 compared to PBO."

*[verbatim, SUNRISE-1 SAP, p.22]* — "The null hypothesis of primary objective is that no difference exists in the mean change from baseline of LPS of Days 29/30 for treatment with LEM10 (or LEM5) as compared with PBO... The change from baseline of LPS on Days 1/2 and Days 29/30, will be analyzed using the mixed effect model repeated measurement analysis (MMRM) with factors of age group (55 to 64, and ≥ 65 years old), region (North America and Europe), treatment, visit (Days 1/2 and Days 29/30), and treatment-by-visit interaction as fixed effect, and baseline LPS as a covariate based on FAS... Before the implementation of the MMRM model, the missing values will be imputed using pattern-mixture model multiple imputation (MI) assuming the missing values are missing not at random (MNAR) utilizing the complete case missing value pattern (CCMV - subjects who completed primary efficacy assessments without missing values)."

*[verbatim, SUNRISE-1 SAP, p.10]* — sample-size justification: "a sample size of 250 subjects for LEM5, 250 subjects for LEM10, and 200 subjects for PBO has at least 95% power for each treatment comparison, LEM10 with PBO, and LEM5 with PBO, based on 2-sided 2-sample t-test at 5% significance level."

*[verbatim, ClinicalTrials.gov-posted Statistical Analysis Plan, Study E2006-G000-303 (SUNRISE-2), Final V2, p.10]* — "The primary objective of the study is to: Determine the efficacy of lemborexant 5 mg (LEM5) and 10 mg (LEM10) compared to placebo (PBO) on subjective sleep onset latency (sSOL) after 6 months of treatment in subjects with insomnia disorder."

*[verbatim, SUNRISE-2 SAP, p.25]* — "Null Hypothesis: No difference exists in the mean change from Study Baseline to Month 6 of treatment with LEM10 (or LEM5) as compared with PBO... The model will be adjusted for the corresponding Study Baseline value, region (North America, Europe and New Zealand, Asia), age group (<65 years old, ≥65 years old), treatment, time (1st 7 nights, Month 1, Month 2, Month 3, Month 4, Month 5 and Month 6) and the interaction of treatment by time... a log-transformation will be used in the analysis."

*[verbatim, SUNRISE-2 SAP, p.20-21]* — "A sequential gate-keeping procedure will be used for primary endpoint and secondary endpoint comparisons to control for the overall type 1 error at the 0.05 significance level... The primary endpoints will be tested in the following order: • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sSOL, LEM10 compared to PBO • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sSOL, LEM5 compared to PBO. The key secondary endpoints will only be tested if both primary analyses are statistically significant at the 0.05 level... • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sSE, LEM10 compared to PBO • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sSE, LEM5 compared to PBO • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sWASO, LEM10 compared to PBO • Change from Study Baseline at Month 6 in sWASO, LEM5 compared to PBO."

*[verbatim, SUNRISE-2 SAP, p.12-13]* — sample-size justification: "To detect a treatment difference in sSOL of at least -8.7 minutes, a sample size of 300 per treatment group at 5% (2-sided) level of significance had >90% power for comparing a dose of lemborexant with PBO... Study 303 providing subjective (patient-reported) data from the home setting of 6 months of treatment and Study 304 providing objective (laboratory PSG-measured) data following 30 days of treatment."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, p.136-137, Study 303 (SUNRISE-2)]* — on the FDA-directed SAP amendment: "At the pre-NDA meeting held on June 14, 2018, the Agency raised concerns about the proposed primary analysis method which was based on missing data imputation using a complete case missing value (CCMC) assumption. The Agency also raised concerns on the interpretability of Eisai's proposed tipping point analysis (TPA). The Applicant agreed to amended statistical analysis plan with the details of the revised TPA."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, p.149, Table 37, Study 303 primary efficacy results on sSOL]* — Placebo LS-geometric-mean ratio to baseline 0.62 (95% CI 0.56, 0.68); lemborexant 5 mg 0.45 (0.41, 0.50), active/placebo ratio 0.73 (0.64, 0.84), unadjusted p<0.001; lemborexant 10 mg 0.43 (0.39, 0.48), active/placebo ratio 0.70 (0.61, 0.81), unadjusted p<0.001; both significant after multiplicity adjustment.

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, p.179, Table 50, Study 304 primary efficacy results on LPS]* — Placebo LS-geometric-mean ratio to baseline 0.70 (0.62, 0.78); zolpidem ER 6.25 mg 0.85 (0.77, 0.94), active/placebo ratio 1.22 (1.06, 1.40), unadjusted p=0.006 (numerically worse than placebo); lemborexant 5 mg 0.54 (0.49, 0.60), active/placebo ratio 0.77 (0.67, 0.89), unadjusted p<0.001; lemborexant 10 mg 0.51 (0.46, 0.56), active/placebo ratio 0.72 (0.63, 0.83), unadjusted p<0.001; both lemborexant doses significant after multiplicity adjustment.

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, p.169, Study 304]* — on the non-binding interim look: "An interim analysis was planned to be conducted after approximately 50% of subjects (approximately n=475 subjects) had been randomized and either completed Day 31 assessments or discontinued from the study... The interim analysis was limited to the comparison of LEM10 versus ZOL on the change from baseline in WASO2H for the mean of Days 29 and 30. The study was not planned to be terminated for either futility or efficacy. Therefore no adjustment to the type I error rate was planned."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, p.112, driving-performance Study 106]* — "The 95% confidence intervals of SDLP change in lemborexant groups (2.5, 5 and 10 mg) are below 2.4 cm (associated with blood alcohol limit of 0.5 g/L)... Notably, 2 out of 32 subjects had SDLP > 4.4 cm (associated with blood alcohol limit of 0.8 g/L) in 10 mg lemborexant group, indicating the presence of inter-subject variability in the driving test. Therefore, there is a potential for next-day residual effects in some patients taking 10 mg lemborexant."

### 43. Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy) — NDA 211765

**Sponsor:** Allergan (Allergan Sales, Inc.; acquired by AbbVie in 2020)

**Indication approved:** Acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults

**Approval date:** December 23, 2019

**Pivotal trial:** ACHIEVE I (UBR-MD-01, NCT02828020) and ACHIEVE II (UBR-MD-02, NCT02867709) — two identically-designed Phase III single-attack trials analyzed separately by FDA (not pooled), each with its own genuine posted protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan on ClinicalTrials.gov

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group; single-attack acute-treatment design (one qualifying moderate/severe migraine attack treated per randomized subject within a 60-day window, with a blinded optional second dose/rescue medication); two identically-designed trials with different dose arms per trial (ACHIEVE I: 50 mg and 100 mg vs. placebo; ACHIEVE II: 25 mg and 50 mg vs. placebo); co-primary endpoints

- *Endpoints:* binary responder co-primary endpoints — pain freedom at 2 hours after initial dose, and absence of the self-identified most-bothersome migraine-associated symptom (MBS: photophobia, phonophobia, or nausea) at 2 hours after initial dose (acute-treatment binary responder endpoint at a fixed post-dose timepoint); key secondary endpoints — pain relief at 2 hours, sustained pain relief 2-24h, sustained pain freedom 2-24h, absence of photophobia/phonophobia/nausea at 2 hours

- *Primary analysis:* logistic regression model for each binary responder endpoint, adjusted for treatment group and the randomization stratification factors (historical triptan response, use of migraine-preventive medication) plus baseline headache severity (and, for symptom endpoints, baseline presence/absence of that symptom), with Firth's penalized-likelihood method as a fallback for (quasi-)complete separation (logistic regression model for a binary responder endpoint, adjusted for stratification factors)

- *Multiplicity:* Graphical alpha-propagation method (Maurer-Bretz) — a weighted Bonferroni-based closed testing procedure (Bretz et al. 2009) in which the two co-primary endpoints for each dose serve as gatekeepers of the secondary endpoints, with alpha recycling allowed between the two doses and among the three individual migraine-associated-symptom secondaries

- *Missing data/bias:* last observation carried forward (LOCF) for missing on-schedule diary assessments feeding the primary responder endpoints, with a non-responder-imputation sensitivity analysis (non-responder imputation for missing binary/diary efficacy data) for participants missing the 2-hour assessment

- *Regulatory:* no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held; reviewer-vs-clinical-team dissent over whether to approve/label a dose (ubrogepant 25 mg in ACHIEVE II) that reached nominal significance on one but not both co-primary endpoints, resolved by excluding that dose from labeling (FDA declines to label a dose that wins only one of two gatekept co-primary endpoints, over clinical-team objection)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Two Phase III, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, single-attack trials in adults 18-75 years with ≥1-year history of migraine with or without aura per ICHD-3 beta criteria; each trial randomized (1:1:1) participants to placebo or one of two ubrogepant doses to treat one qualifying moderate/severe migraine attack within a 60-day window, with an optional blinded second dose (active or placebo, per original randomization) or usual rescue medication permitted 2-48 hours after the initial dose for a non-responding or recurrent headache
- ACHIEVE I (UBR-MD-01): doses were 50 mg and 100 mg vs. placebo; randomized N=456 placebo / 423 (mITT 422) ubrogepant 50 mg / 448 ubrogepant 100 mg
- ACHIEVE II (UBR-MD-02): doses were 25 mg and 50 mg vs. placebo; randomized N=456 placebo / 435 ubrogepant 25 mg / 464 ubrogepant 50 mg
- Randomization stratification factors: historical triptan response (responder/insufficient responder/naive) and use of migraine-preventive medication (yes/no)
- Co-primary endpoints (identical definitions in both trials): (1) pain freedom at 2 hours after the initial dose, defined as reduction of headache severity from moderate/severe at baseline to no pain; (2) absence, at 2 hours after the initial dose, of the migraine-associated symptom (photophobia, phonophobia, or nausea) the participant identified at baseline as most bothersome
- Key secondary endpoints (same order across trials, gated behind the co-primaries): pain relief at 2 hours; sustained pain relief 2-24h; sustained pain freedom 2-24h; absence of photophobia at 2h; absence of phonophobia at 2h; absence of nausea at 2h
- Analysis populations: Intent-to-Treat (ITT, all randomized) and modified ITT (mITT: randomized, received ≥1 dose, had a baseline severity measurement and ≥1 postdose measurement at or before 2 hours) — primary analysis conducted in the mITT population
- Sample size: each trial was amended (Amendment 3, 19-May-2017) to increase planned enrollment from 450 to 550 patients per arm (~1650 total) based on a sample-size re-estimation using updated response-rate assumptions; no interim analysis was planned in either trial
- Primary analysis method: logistic regression model per endpoint (treatment group, stratification factors, baseline severity/symptom covariates), with pairwise odds-ratio contrasts of each ubrogepant dose vs. placebo and two-sided p-values; Firth's penalized-likelihood method used if the model failed to converge from separation
- Multiplicity control: overall familywise error rate held at α=0.05 per trial via a graphical (Bretz et al. 2009) weighted Bonferroni-based closed testing procedure; each dose's two co-primary endpoints each start with local significance level α/2=0.025 and act as gatekeepers releasing alpha to the ordered secondary endpoints, with weight-recycling allowed between doses and among the three symptom-absence secondaries
- Missing data: LOCF for missing on-schedule diary/severity assessments driving the primary responder classification, with a pre-specified non-responder-imputation sensitivity analysis for participants missing the 2-hour assessment (provided ≥1 earlier postdose value existed); FDA additionally required clarification of how rescue-medication timing was applied and ran its own timing-window sensitivity analyses on ACHIEVE II's primary pain-freedom endpoint

### 44. Eptinezumab-jjmr (Vyepti) — BLA 761119

**Sponsor:** Lundbeck Seattle BioPharmaceuticals, Inc. (originator: Alder BioPharmaceuticals, Inc., acquired by H. Lundbeck A/S in December 2019 before approval)

**Indication approved:** Preventive treatment of migraine in adults

**Approval date:** February 21, 2020

**Pivotal trial:** PROMISE-1 (ALD403-CLIN-006, episodic migraine), NCT02559895, and PROMISE-2 (ALD403-CLIN-011, chronic migraine), NCT02974153

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; multiple randomized dose arms (30/100/300 mg in PROMISE-1, 100/300 mg in PROMISE-2) each tested pairwise vs. placebo; intravenous (IV) infusion route of administration — the first IV-administered migraine preventive, distinguishing eptinezumab from the subcutaneously-injected anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) approved just before it (IV-infusion route as a design-distinguishing feature)

- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in monthly migraine days over Weeks 1-12, diary-derived (primary) (no existing taxonomy row covers a diary-based continuous frequency endpoint); 50%/75% migraine responder rate and 75% migraine responder rate at Weeks 1-4, percentage of subjects with a migraine the day after dosing (key secondaries); Patient-reported outcomes / HRQoL (HIT-6, PROMISE-2 only — matches existing taxonomy term)

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA model on change-from-baseline migraine days, single timepoint (Weeks 1-12 average), covariates = treatment + randomization-stratification factors (distinct from the existing "Repeated-measures ANCOVA" row, which is a longitudinal multi-timepoint model); Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) / extended-CMH test, stratified by randomization factors, for responder-rate and day-after-dosing secondaries (matches existing taxonomy term)

- *Multiplicity:* Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing across dose levels — 300 mg → 100 mg → 30 mg, each gated behind the prior dose's full endpoint set (PROMISE-1); Bonferroni-Holm sequentially rejective procedure nested within a fixed dose-level gate (300 mg → 100 mg), i.e. Holm's procedure applied within each dose's key-secondary-endpoint group before moving to the next dose (PROMISE-2)

- *Missing data/bias:* completion-rate normalization and prior-interval-weighted blending for partially-missing eDiary data ("Missing Data Rule 1" / "Missing Data Rule 2"); baseline-carried-forward sensitivity imputation for subjects who withdrew due to adverse event, study burden, lack of efficacy, or death

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Two independently conducted, near-simultaneous Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, each in a distinct migraine population: PROMISE-1 (episodic migraine, 4-14 migraine days/28-day period) and PROMISE-2 (chronic migraine, ≥15 headache days/month with ≥8 migraine days/month).
- PROMISE-1: 898 subjects randomized 1:1:1:1 to eptinezumab 30 mg, 100 mg, 300 mg, or placebo, all given as four IV infusions at 12-week intervals; randomization stratified by baseline migraine days (≤9 vs. >9 in a 28-day period). PROMISE-2: 1,121 subjects randomized 1:1:1 to eptinezumab 100 mg, 300 mg, or placebo, given as two IV infusions 12 weeks apart; randomization stratified by baseline migraine days (<17 vs. ≥17 days) and prophylactic-medication use.
- Both trials administered study drug/placebo as a single IV infusion (not subcutaneous injection), diluted in 100 mL 0.9% saline and infused over approximately 30 minutes — the approved label's Dosage and Administration section reflects this IV-only route, the feature that most distinguishes eptinezumab from the SC-injected anti-CGRP mAb class.
- Primary endpoint (both trials): change from baseline in monthly (28-day) migraine days averaged over Weeks 1-12 following the first infusion, derived from a daily eDiary.
- Key secondary endpoints (both trials): 75% migraine responder rate at Weeks 1-4, 75% migraine responder rate at Weeks 1-12, 50% migraine responder rate at Weeks 1-12, and percentage of subjects with a migraine the day after dosing; PROMISE-2 added further key secondaries (reduction in migraine prevalence Baseline-to-Week 4, HIT-6 change, acute migraine medication days Weeks 1-12).
- Analysis population: Full Analysis Population (FAS/FAP) — all randomized subjects who received study drug/placebo.
- Sample size: PROMISE-1 planned for ~800 (200/arm) subjects, giving ≥95% power per pairwise dose-vs-placebo comparison assuming a 1-day treatment effect and SD ≤2.7 days; PROMISE-2 planned for ~1,050 (350/arm), giving ≥90% power assuming the same 1-day effect and SD ≤4 days.
- Primary analysis: ANCOVA model of change-from-baseline migraine days, testing each dose vs. placebo (two-sided, α=0.05), covariates = treatment plus randomization-stratification factors (baseline migraine days in both trials; prophylactic-medication use, additionally, in PROMISE-2).
- Multiplicity: both trials used a serial, dose-level-gated hierarchy (300 mg tested first, then 100 mg, then — in PROMISE-1 only — 30 mg), with the primary endpoint gating a fixed ordered subset of key secondaries within each dose. PROMISE-2 additionally applied the Holm step-down procedure within each key-secondary "block" once that block was reached; if any one endpoint in a block failed, the entire remaining hierarchy stopped for that dose. Because the ALD403 100 mg group's 75% responder rate over Weeks 1-12 in PROMISE-1 was not statistically significant, the hierarchy stopped there for both 100 mg and (once 100 mg failed) the 30 mg arm was tested only for the primary endpoint (nominally significant, not formally significant per the pre-specified decision rule).
- Missing eDiary data: a two-tier rule set — if the eDiary was completed ≥21 of 28 days, results were normalized to 28 days by the inverse completion rate; if completed <21 days, the 28-day result was a weighted blend of the observed current-interval data and the prior interval's (imputed) data, weighted by completion rate. A pre-specified sensitivity analysis substituted baseline values for the "prior interval" term for subjects who withdrew due to an adverse event, study burden, lack of efficacy, or death.

Moreover, the safety profile was acceptable for the preventive treatment of migraine."

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, PROMISE-1 Statistical Analysis Plan (ALD403-CLIN-006), Version 1.4, Section 2.5 "Statistical Assessment of the Trial Objectives," p.19]* — "Hypothesis testing will be performed for the primary endpoint: change from baseline in migraine days from Weeks 1-12... An ANCOVA model will be used to test for a difference between treatment arms. This model will include the change from baseline measure as the response variable. Treatment and the stratification variable: baseline migraine days (continuous covariate) will be the independent variables."

*[verbatim, PROMISE-1 SAP, Section 2.7.5 "Multiple Comparisons/Multiplicity," p.24]* — "A serial procedure will be used to account for multiplicity of dose level for the primary endpoint and the secondary endpoints. This procedure will start with the 300 mg vs placebo comparison for the primary endpoint. If this is significant, testing will continue to a subset of the key secondary endpoints for 300 mg (first the Weeks 1-4 75% responder endpoint, then the Weeks 1-12 75% responder endpoint, and then the Weeks 1-12 50% responder endpoint). The procedure will then move on to the primary endpoint for the 100 mg group and subsequently to the same subset of key secondary endpoints as tested for the 300 mg dose... Only if all of these secondary endpoints reach statistical significance will the 30 mg group be tested. Statistical testing will be conducted at the 5% alpha level."

*[verbatim, PROMISE-1 SAP, Section 2.7.2 "Handling of Dropouts or Missing Data," p.21-22]* — "If the eDiary has been completed at least 21 days in a 28 day interval, then a normalization procedure will be used. The results will be normalized to 28 days by multiplying the observed results by the inverse of the completion rate (e.g. if a subject does not complete the eDiary on 5 days they will have completed the diary on 82% of the days and the normalized results will be the observed results times 1.22)... If the eDiary has been completed on less than 21 days in the 28 day interval then the results for the 28 day interval will be a weighted function of the observed data for the current four week interval and the results from the previous interval."

*[verbatim, PROMISE-2 Statistical Analysis Plan (ALD403-CLIN-011), Version 1.0, Section 2.3 "Multiple Comparisons/Multiplicity," p.19-20]* — "Multiplicity control will be used for the primary and key secondary endpoints. A combination of gate keeping and the Holm's procedure will be used to control the study wide Type-I error rate. At a high level this procedure will start with the 300 mg vs placebo comparison for the primary endpoint. If this is significant, testing will continue to the first group of key secondary endpoints for 300 mg where Holm's multiplicity procedure will be used. Testing will then continue to the second group of key secondary endpoints and then move on to the 100 mg group for the primary endpoint and subsequently the key secondary endpoints using the same methodology (Holm's within each group)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Section 3.2.1.4 "Efficacy Results and Conclusions," p.12, Table 3-3, PROMISE-1]* — "With a mean difference of -1.11 days (95% CI: -1.68, -0.54), the ALD403 300-mg dose demonstrated a statistically significant improvement (P=0.0001) from placebo. The ALD403 100-mg dose demonstrated a statistically significant (P=0.0182) improvement from placebo with a mean difference of -0.69 days (95% CI: -1.25, -0.12) for Weeks 1-12... The ALD403 30-mg group was nominally significant (P=0.0046) from placebo with a mean difference of -0.82 days (95% CI: -1.39, -0.25)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Section 3.2.1.4, p.14, on the responder-rate hierarchy failure]* — "The 75% migraine responder rate over Weeks 1-12 demonstrated a statistically significant improvement (P=0.0007) for ALD403 300 mg over placebo group. The ALD403 100mg was not statistically significant vs. placebo... The remaining key secondary endpoints in the ALD403 300-mg and 100-mg groups were not statistically significant despite unadjusted p-values being <5%, due to the decision rules of multiple testing."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Section 3.2.2.4 "Efficacy Results and Conclusions," p.22-23, Table 3-11, PROMISE-2]* — "With a mean difference of -2.59 days (95% CI: -3.45, -1.74), the ALD403 300 mg dose demonstrated a statistically significant improvement (P<0.0001) from placebo. The ALD403 100 mg dose also demonstrated a statistically significant improvement (P<0.0001) from placebo with a mean difference of -2.03 days (95% CI: -2.88, -1.18) for Weeks 1-12."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Section 5.1 "Statistical Issues and Collective Evidence," p.30]* — "It is notable that to address multiplicity, a serial, fixed-sequence procedure was used to consecutively and conservatively test hierarchically-ordered hypotheses at level α until the first non-rejection in both pivotal studies. Many other less conservative multiplicity procedures will also conclude the statistically significant finding in the primary endpoint for 30-mg group in Study 006. Collective evidence is not formally considered in this review since there was one double-blind, controlled trial in Chronic Migraine and one in Episodic Migraine which are considered distinct populations."

*[verbatim, approved Package Insert, Dosage and Administration]* — "Recommended dosage is 100 mg as an intravenous infusion over approximately 30 minutes every 3 months. Some patients may benefit from a dosage of 300 mg."

The label's approved 100 mg / 300 mg dosing (omitting the 30 mg arm tested only in PROMISE-1) is directly traceable to the StatR's documented hierarchy outcome: 30 mg reached only nominal, not formally hierarchy-protected, significance in PROMISE-1, and was not studied at all in PROMISE-2.

### 45. Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) — NDA 212728

**Sponsor:** Biohaven Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults (not indicated for preventive treatment of migraine)

**Approval date:** February 27, 2020

**Pivotal trial:** Study 303 (BHV3000-303, NCT03461757, ODT formulation); supportive: Study 302 (BHV3000-302, NCT03237845) and Study 301 (BHV3000-301), both using a conventional oral tablet formulation cross-referenced from a concurrently reviewed, separately numbered tablet NDA

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; single-attack, single-dose-per-migraine treatment design (no second dose assessed); cross-formulation supportive efficacy evidence via a bioequivalence bridge between an ODT and a tablet formulation, cross-referenced from a concurrently reviewed but separately numbered NDA

- *Endpoints:* co-primary endpoints (freedom from headache pain at 2 hours; freedom from patient-identified most-bothersome-symptom [MBS] at 2 hours) — both required to be statistically significant for the study to be considered supportive

- *Primary analysis:* Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test (sample-size weights), stratified by prophylactic/preventive migraine medication use

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing of secondary endpoints (each tested at p=0.05; testing stopped at the first non-significant endpoint in the sequence)

- *Missing data/bias:* non-responder imputation (missing 2-hour data and post-rescue-medication data counted as treatment failure); sensitivity analyses using last-available-value imputation and complete-case analysis

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study 303: multicenter (69 US centers), randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase 3 trial in adults ≥18 years with ≥1-year history of migraine with or without aura, migraine onset before age 50, 2–8 moderate/severe attacks per month, <15 headache days/month; patients with uncontrolled/unstable/recently diagnosed cardiovascular disease were excluded. Randomized 1:1 to a single sublingual/oral dose of rimegepant 75 mg ODT or matching placebo to treat one qualifying migraine attack within 45 days of randomization; patients were instructed not to take a second dose (the program never assessed a second-dose regimen). Randomization stratified by use of prophylactic migraine medication (yes/no).
- Co-primary endpoints (both trials 303, 302, and supportive Study 301): pain freedom at 2 hours (reduction from moderate/severe pain at baseline to no pain) and freedom from most-bothersome-symptom (MBS: nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia, identified by the patient before dosing) at 2 hours. The statistical analysis plan specified both co-primary endpoints had to reach statistical significance for the study to be considered supportive of a treatment effect.
- Secondary endpoints were sequentially tested under a fixed-sequence hierarchical gatekeeping procedure (each at p=0.05); Study 303's protocol listed an extensive ordered list of 21 secondary endpoints (pain relief at 2h, normal function at 2h, sustained pain relief 2–24h, sustained MBS freedom 2–24h, rescue-medication use within 24h, etc.); Studies 301/302 used a shorter 9-endpoint ordered list. Testing stopped at the first non-significant endpoint in the sequence (in Studies 301/302 this was freedom from nausea at 2 hours).
- Efficacy analyses used the modified intent-to-treat (mITT) population: randomized patients who received ≥1 dose of study drug and had ≥1 evaluable efficacy measurement. Patients taking rescue medication were counted as failures for endpoints coincident with or after the rescue use; patients who identified their MBS after dosing (or not at all) were counted as MBS-analysis failures; missing 2-hour data were imputed as failures (non-responder imputation).
- Sample size history (FDA statistical reviewer's account): Study 303's protocol was amended (version 2→3) to increase planned sample size by ~37% (380 to 600 per arm) without ever specifying the underlying assumed effect size in any protocol/SAP version, and with no interim analyses planned or performed; the reviewer calculated the trial was "overpowered by design" (>99.9% power at both 380 and 600/arm against the effect size observed in the completed Phase 2b study), noting a possible (unstated) reason was that Studies 301/302's observed effect sizes were smaller than the Phase 2b estimate.
- Study conduct issues documented by the FDA statistical reviewer: (1) the final SAP version predated study unblinding by only 8 days; (2) one study site (Site 002, Nashville, TN) was placed on enrollment hold after a sponsor-initiated audit found improper drug storage, consent-form dating irregularities, unverifiable vital-signs/medical-history data, and under/late reporting of protocol deviations — the reviewer found removing this site had no effect on the efficacy results; (3) an e-Diary software malfunction affected Studies 301 and 302 shortly after study start, producing 3–7% missing primary-endpoint data, addressed via sensitivity analyses (LAV imputation, complete-case) that were consistent with the primary result.
- No FDA advisory committee meeting was held; per the approval letter, this was because "the clinical trial design was acceptable, the efficacy findings were clear, and the safety profile was acceptable for use in the intended population."
- Regulatory pathway: NDA 212728 (ODT formulation only) was reviewed on a priority-review timeline using a rare pediatric disease priority review voucher; a separate, concurrently submitted NDA for the tablet formulation was under standard review and was cross-referenced for the Study 301/302 efficacy and long-term open-label safety data, relying on demonstrated bioequivalence between the ODT and tablet formulations.

The MBS was decided before the dosing."

If one of the analyses was not statistically significant, then all subsequent analyses would be exploratory rather than confirmatory."

*[verbatim, FDA Approval Letter, NDA 212728]* — "Your application for rimegepant was not referred to an FDA advisory committee because the clinical trial design was acceptable, the efficacy findings were clear, and the safety profile was acceptable for use in the intended population."

There is no evidence to suggest that rimegepant is more effective than other FDA-approved drugs for the acute treatment of migraine; however, rimegepant as an ODT formulation may offer a treatment alternative to some patients."

### 46. Ozanimod (Zeposia) — NDA 209899

**Sponsor:** Celgene Corporation (a wholly owned subsidiary of Bristol-Myers Squibb, whose acquisition of Celgene completed November 2019; ozanimod was originally discovered by Receptos, Inc., acquired by Celgene in 2015)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (RMS), to include clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease, in adults

**Approval date:** March 25, 2020 (date of the electronic signature on the NDA approval letter; Drugs@FDA's approval-package cover sheet separately lists March 20, 2020)

**Pivotal trial:** SUNBEAM (Study RPC01-301, NCT02294058) and RADIANCE Part B (Study RPC01-201B, NCT02047734), both conducted under Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) agreements with FDA

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* Randomized, double-blind, active-controlled (two identically-designed trials, each double-dummy, comparing ozanimod 0.5 mg and 1 mg oral capsules once daily against interferon β-1a 30 µg intramuscular weekly [Avonex]; SUNBEAM ran until the last-enrolled patient completed a minimum of 12 months, RADIANCE Part B ran a fixed 24 months); randomization stratified by baseline EDSS (≤3.5 vs. >3.5) and country

- *Endpoints:* Annualized relapse rate (ARR) of protocol-defined relapse, primary (not yet in Keyword_Taxonomy.md §2); key secondary endpoints (rank-ordered): cumulative number of new/enlarging T2-weighted brain MRI lesions, number of Gd-enhancing (GdE) brain MRI lesions, and time to onset of 3-month- and 6-month-confirmed disability progression (sustained ≥1.0-point EDSS worsening)

- *Primary analysis:* Poisson regression for ARR (offset = natural log of time on study; covariates region, age, baseline GdE lesion count); negative binomial regression as the primary method for the MRI-lesion key secondary endpoints, and as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis for ARR; Cox proportional-hazards model (existing term) and log-rank test for disability progression

- *Multiplicity:* Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing — each ozanimod dose tested against IFN β-1a at α=0.025 for the primary endpoint, then (if significant) the 1 mg dose tested before the 0.5 mg dose down the rank-ordered key-secondary list, each comparison at the 5% level, stopping at the first non-significant comparison

- *Missing data/bias:* LOCF and same-treatment-group mean-value imputation as sensitivity analyses for missing MRI lesion counts, alongside an observed-cases primary analysis (not yet in Keyword_Taxonomy.md §6)

- *Regulatory:* Special Protocol Assessment (SPA)-agreed pivotal trial design for both trials; reviewer-documented deviation from the agreed pooled-analysis plan for disability progression (existing term) — pooling of the two trials' disability-progression data was pre-specified/agreed to boost power, but the FDA statistical reviewer determined pooling was not appropriate given divergent within-study directionality, and based conclusions on the two studies' individual (unpooled) results instead; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Two Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-group trials of ozanimod in adults with relapsing forms of MS (EDSS 0–5.0 at baseline, ≥1 relapse in the prior year or ≥1 relapse in the prior 2 years with a GdE lesion in the prior year; primary progressive MS excluded), each comparing ozanimod 0.5 mg and 1 mg (as the HCl salt; equivalent to the approved free-base doses of 0.46 mg and 0.92 mg) against interferon β-1a 30 µg IM weekly, randomized 1:1:1
- SUNBEAM (RPC01-301): planned enrollment 1,200; 1,346 subjects actually randomized (448 IFN β-1a, 451 ozanimod 0.5 mg, 447 ozanimod 1 mg) at sites in North America, Europe, and New Zealand; treatment continued until the last-randomized patient completed ≥12 months
- RADIANCE Part B (RPC01-201B): planned enrollment 1,200; 1,320 subjects actually randomized (441/439/433 across the same three arms) at 150 sites in North America, Europe, and South Africa; fixed 24-month treatment period
- Primary endpoint (both trials): annualized relapse rate (ARR) of protocol-defined relapse (new/worsening neurological symptoms, confirmed by the treating investigator per EDSS/Functional-System-score criteria assessed by a blinded evaluator, following ≥30 days of stability) over the treatment period (SUNBEAM) or at Month 24 (RADIANCE)
- Key secondary endpoints, rank-ordered identically in both trials: (1) cumulative number of new/enlarging T2-weighted MRI lesions over 12 months (SUNBEAM) / 24 months (RADIANCE); (2) number of GdE lesions at Month 12/24; (3) time to onset of disability progression (sustained ≥1.0-point EDSS increase, confirmed after 3 and after 6 months) — pre-specified to be analyzed on data pooled across the two trials to increase power
- Other (non-key) secondary/exploratory objectives: proportion of patients GdE-lesion-free / new-T2-lesion-free, percent change in brain volume (atrophy), Multiple Sclerosis Functional Composite (MSFC), low-contrast letter acuity, patient-reported quality of life (MSQOL), safety/tolerability
- Primary efficacy population: Intent-to-Treat (ITT) — all randomized patients confirmed to have received ≥1 dose of study drug, analyzed as randomized regardless of treatment actually received
- Statistical methods: primary ARR analysis by Poisson regression (covariates: region, age, baseline GdE lesion count; offset = natural log of time on study), reporting adjusted rates, rate ratios, CIs, and p-values; two pre-specified sensitivity analyses — (a) repeating the primary analysis counting confirmed + unconfirmed relapses, and (b) substituting a negative binomial regression model for the same comparison, run twice (confirmed-only and confirmed+unconfirmed); the two key-secondary MRI lesion endpoints analyzed by negative binomial regression (covariates: treatment, region, age, baseline GdE count; offset = natural log of number of available MRI scans), with three sensitivity analyses (mean-value imputation from the same treatment group, LOCF, and observed-cases-only) each substituting exposure time for scan count as the offset; disability progression analyzed via log-rank test (primary p-value), Kaplan-Meier estimation, and a Cox proportional-hazards model (covariates region, age, baseline EDSS), each endpoint assessed separately at 3-month and 6-month confirmation
- Multiplicity: statistical testing for the primary endpoint was split 2-ways (each ozanimod dose vs. IFN β-1a) with each comparison tested at α=0.025; the three rank-ordered key secondary endpoints were then tested in a closed, sequential hierarchical procedure with the 1 mg dose tested before the 0.5 mg dose for each endpoint in turn (5% level per comparison), continuing down the list only while comparisons kept reaching significance, and reverting to a single-dose (surviving-dose-only) hierarchy at the 2.5% level if only one dose met the primary endpoint
- Results (FDA Statistical Review, reviewer's analyses): SUNBEAM — adjusted ARR 0.35 (IFN β-1a) vs. 0.24 (ozanimod 0.5 mg, rate ratio 0.688, 31.2% reduction, p=0.0013) vs. 0.18 (ozanimod 1 mg, rate ratio 0.518, 48.2% reduction, p<0.0001); RADIANCE Part B — adjusted ARR 0.276 (IFN β-1a) vs. 0.218 (0.5 mg, rate ratio 0.791, 20.9% reduction, p=0.0167) vs. 0.172 (1 mg, rate ratio 0.623, 37.7% reduction, p<0.0001); both trials showed statistically significant reductions in MRI lesion counts (T2 and GdE) for both doses; neither trial (individually, nor the pre-specified pooled analysis) showed a statistically significant effect on 3-month or 6-month confirmed disability progression
