In this study, the median time to onset of symptom relief was 2.5 hours for icatibant and 4.6 hours for placebo."

*[verbatim, same review, "Statistical Methodologies," p.8, quoting the applicant's report]* — "A subject was considered evaluable if they had moderate to very severe cutaneous and/or abdominal angioedema (as judged by the investigator in the Global Assessment at pretreatment), VAS ≥ 30mm for any symptom pretreatment and completes the 8 hour assessment post dose or reaches the symptom relief as determine by 50% reduction in the composite VAS... A Peto-Peto Wilcoxon test with a global 2-sided significance level of 5% was used to test the null hypothesis for the non-laryngeal ITT, non-laryngeal per-protocol, ITT, and laryngeal populations. The Peto-Peto Wilcoxon test was selected for this analysis as it gives more weight to earlier achievement of symptom relief. To control for study design factors, time to symptom relief was analyzed using a Cox proportional hazards model which included covariates for treatment and stratification factors, edema location and previous use of C1-INH."

*[verbatim, same review, "Statistical Methodologies," p.8, rescue-medication sensitivity analysis]* — "To evaluate the use of rescue medications, time to symptom relief was analyzed censoring subjects who took rescue medications before the onset of symptom relief. This analysis was conducted using the non-laryngeal ITT population. Subjects were censored at the time of administration of rescue medication, if symptom relief had not already occurred. Kaplan-Meier methods were used to estimate the median time to symptom relief and corresponding sign-test based 2-sided 95% confidence interval."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, Badrul A. Chowdhury, MD, PhD, "Primary efficacy variable," p.9]* — "The unpredictable, fluctuating nature of HAE attacks complicates the conduct of clinical trials for HAE, and there is limited regulatory precedent in terms of drug development programs for HAE. In the absence of an accepted standard endpoint, Jerini developed a new patient-reported outcome (PRO) instrument for use as primary efficacy variable in the pivotal studies... The Agency asked for additional validation of the VAS in the Not Approval action letter of the original NDA."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, "Choice of active control," p.9-10]* — "The selection of TA as an active control is questionable. The efficacy of antifibrinolytic agents such as TA or EACA for the treatment of acute attack of HAE is not established... The existing data do not support use of TA as a valid active control."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, "9. Advisory Committee Meeting," p.15]* — "The panel concluded that icatibant was efficacious, although there was some concern expressed regarding the adequacy of blinding and the use of a median time point to summarize efficacy results with such a limited sample size. Overall, the voting favored that the efficacy data for icatibant were sufficient to support the proposed indication (12 Yes, 1 No)... Consistent with these views on efficacy and safety, the panel members voted in favor of approval (12 Yes, 1 No)."

**Reverse-engineered SAP** (no independently posted sponsor SAP/protocol exists for any of the three trials; the following extend beyond what FDA's reviewers reproduced verbatim, and are traced to specific reported results)

- *[inferred]* FAST-1 and FAST-2 were almost certainly analyzed and reported as two independent trials with no multiplicity adjustment spanning the pair, each at its own two-sided alpha of 0.05 — inferred from the fact that FDA's original 2008 review treats FAST-2's p<0.001 and FAST-1's p=0.142 as two separately-interpreted results (with the Division's Not Approvable rationale resting on FAST-1 alone failing, not on a combined test across both trials), and no cross-trial alpha-allocation procedure is described anywhere in either the 2008 or 2011 statistical reviews.

- *[inferred]* The unstated treatment-effect assumption behind FAST-1/FAST-2's "80 evaluable subjects, 80% power" sample-size target was very likely back-derived from early open-label/Phase 2 data suggesting a multi-hour median time-to-relief advantage for icatibant, since the FDA reviewer explicitly noted the sponsor's own stated sample-size text gave alpha, power, and the required N but never named the assumed effect size — the closest analogous stated assumption anywhere in the documents is FAST-3's later, more transparent Query Advisor calculation keyed to FAST-1's observed 2.5h-vs-4.6h medians.

- *[inferred]* The per-protocol population's "major protocol deviation" criteria (referenced by the FDA reviewer as being "listed in Appendix 1 of the statistical analysis plan," but never reproduced in either FDA review) most likely centered on late dosing relative to attack onset and rescue-medication timing violations, given that (a) FAST-3's eligibility itself required dosing within 6 hours of at least moderate symptom onset, (b) 4-7 patients per arm were excluded from the PP population in each trial, comparable in scale to the 6-14 patients per arm using rescue medication during the double-blind phase (Table 4 of the original 2008 review), and (c) no other deviation category is discussed anywhere in either statistical review.

### 2. Ivacaftor (Kalydeco) — NDA 203188

**Sponsor:** Vertex Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of cystic fibrosis (CF) in patients age 6 years and older who have a G551D mutation in the CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene

**Approval date:** January 31, 2012

**Pivotal trial:** STRIVE (Study 102 / VX08-770-102), NCT00909532 (ages ≥12) and ENVISION (Study 103B / VX08-770-103), NCT00909727 (ages 6-11); both randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase 3 trials with an identical design and primary endpoint, reviewed together by FDA as the joint efficacy basis for approval

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (STRIVE, ENVISION; quadruple-masked per ClinicalTrials.gov, 14-day run-in, 24-week double-blind efficacy period followed by a second 24-week double-blind "extension" period preserving the blind through Week 48 to assess durability); small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (ENVISION enrolled only 52 subjects, and the approved indication — CF patients with a G551D-CFTR gating mutation — represented only about 4% of the overall CF population per FDA's Medical Review, i.e., a rare mutation-defined subgroup within an already-rare disease); a third, separately reviewed Phase 2 trial (Study 104/VX08-770-104A, NCT00953706) tested the same drug and endpoints in CF patients homozygous for the more common F508del-CFTR mutation and was negative, serving as a mechanistic/genotype-specificity negative control rather than part of the approved indication's evidentiary basis

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint was absolute change from baseline in percent predicted FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) through Week 24, a continuous pulmonary-function biomarker endpoint (continuous spirometric/pulmonary-function change-from-baseline endpoint — distinct from the psychiatric/neurological continuous rating-scale endpoints already in the taxonomy); key secondary endpoints were absolute change from baseline in sweat chloride concentration (a CFTR-activity pharmacodynamic biomarker), patient-reported outcomes / HRQoL (CFQ-R Respiratory Domain score, pooled adolescent/adult and 12-13-year versions in STRIVE; separate child- and parent/caregiver-reported versions in ENVISION), time to first pulmonary exacerbation through Week 48 (STRIVE only), and change from baseline in weight

- *Primary analysis:* Mixed Model Repeated Measures (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance ("R-matrix") structure and covariates of age and baseline percent predicted FEV1, with no imputation for missing observations given a low (~6%) dropout rate (MMRM with unstructured covariance as the sole primary analysis for a small-trial continuous efficacy endpoint, with sensitivity analyses — not the primary model — carrying the imputation burden); sensitivity analyses included alternative covariance structures, ANCOVA, and a stratified Wilcoxon rank-sum test, plus last-observation-carried-forward and within-subject worst-case imputation

- *Multiplicity:* Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing combined with Hochberg step-up procedure within tiers — a 2-3-stage gatekeeping structure (Test 1: primary FEV1 endpoint at α=0.05; Test 2, gated on Test 1: two co-equal key secondaries tested via Hochberg step-up at α=0.05 — CFQ-R + sweat chloride in STRIVE, weight + sweat chloride in ENVISION; Test 3, gated on Test 2: the remaining key secondaries via Hochberg step-up — pulmonary exacerbation + weight in STRIVE, CFQ-R in ENVISION); in ENVISION, CFQ-R (child, key secondary) was tested last in the chain and did not reach significance (p=0.11 at Week 24), which FDA's statistical reviewer attributed explicitly to its position in the gatekeeping order rather than to a true lack of effect

- *Missing data/bias:* standard right-censoring/analysis-as-observed given minimal dropout (94% of STRIVE and ENVISION subjects completed dosing through Week 24); FDA's statistical reviewer independently examined "non-responders" (STRIVE subjects who did not achieve a ≥5-percentage-point FEV1 change by Week 48) and found no covariate pattern (age, genotype) explaining them; FDA conducted its own supplementary subgroup/interaction analyses (age <18 vs. ≥18, gender, G551D/F508del vs. G551D/other genotype) for the primary endpoint, finding no significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction in any

- *Regulatory:* No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened ("the Agency decided that the efficacy and safety were sufficiently robust that holding up approval to discuss at an advisory committee meeting was not necessary" — Summary Review); Fast Track designation (granted May 4, 2006) and Orphan Drug designation (granted December 20, 2006), the latter also serving as the basis for a PREA exemption (PREA exemption derived from orphan-drug designation rather than a case-by-case waiver); an initial Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) submission for the Phase 3 program was never agreed — FDA placed the studies on clinical hold in January 2009 for insufficient nonclinical (chronic toxicity) support, Vertex withdrew those SPA protocols the same day, and the trials that were actually run (Studies 102/103/104) proceeded without an SPA; a 505(o)(3) postmarketing requirement (in vivo P-gp drug-interaction study with a sensitive substrate such as digoxin) was imposed at approval; no REMS required; approved ~2.5 months ahead of the April 18, 2012 PDUFA goal date

**Trial design & endpoints**

- STRIVE (Study 102) enrolled subjects ≥12 years old (mean age 26) with FEV1 40-90% predicted and at least one G551D-CFTR allele; 167 randomized (84 ivacaftor/83 placebo), 161 dosed and included in the Full Analysis Set, across sites in North America, Europe, and Australia. ENVISION (Study 103B/Part B) used an identical design in subjects 6-11 years old (mean age 9) with FEV1 40-105% predicted; 52 randomized and dosed (26/26). Both trials were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group studies of ivacaftor 150 mg orally every 12 hours with fat-containing food, with a 14-day run-in, a 24-week double-blind treatment/efficacy period, and a second 24-week double-blind extension period (to Week 48) preserving the blind to assess durability of response; completers were eligible to roll over into an open-label long-term safety study (Study 105).

- Sample-size rationale (per FDA's Statistical Review, Appendix 1 and §2.1): STRIVE was designed to enroll a minimum of 80 subjects to provide ≥80% power to detect a 4.5-percentage-point treatment effect in absolute change in percent predicted FEV1; ENVISION was designed to enroll a minimum of 30 subjects (a formal power calculation for the smaller pediatric trial was considered adequate because, per FDA's Cross Discipline Team Leader Review of the End-of-Phase-1 meeting record, "given the small number of patients with CF who have a G551D mutation, the proposed small pediatric study showing a positive trend would be adequate to support a positive result" given the already-demonstrated adult/adolescent efficacy).

- Primary analysis population: Full Analysis Set (all randomized subjects who received ≥1 dose), analyzed by MMRM as described above.

- Results (FDA Statistical Review, Tables 4-5, confirming sponsor's Clinical Study Report tables): in STRIVE, the treatment difference in mean absolute change in percent predicted FEV1 was 10.6 percentage points at Week 24 and 10.5 points at Week 48 (both P<0.0001; ivacaftor +10.4 pp vs. placebo −0.2 pp through Week 24). In ENVISION, the treatment difference was 12.5 points at Week 24 and 10.0 points at Week 48 (both P<0.0001). Key secondary results in STRIVE: CFQ-R respiratory domain +8.1 points through Week 24 and +8.6 through Week 48 (both P<0.0001, exceeding the 4-point MCID); sweat chloride −47.9 mmol/L (Week 24) and −48.1 mmol/L (Week 48); pulmonary exacerbation risk reduced 60% through Week 24 and 54% through Week 48 (HR 0.40 [95% CI 0.2-0.7], P=0.0016 and HR 0.46 [0.3-0.7], P=0.0012, respectively); weight +2.8 kg (Week 24, P<0.0001) and +2.7 kg (Week 48, P=0.0001). In ENVISION: sweat chloride −54.3 mmol/L (Week 24)/−53.5 mmol/L (Week 48); weight +1.9 kg (Week 24, P=0.0004)/+2.8 kg (Week 48, P=0.0002); CFQ-R (child) treatment difference was numerically positive but not statistically significant at either timepoint (P=0.1092 at Week 24), and the parent/caregiver-reported version was significant at Week 24 only.

- Study 104 (Phase 2, VX08-770-104A, F508del-homozygous CF patients, N≈140, 16-week duration) was negative: "the trial failed to demonstrate efficacy of ivacaftor in subjects with this genotype" (FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.2), with no significant FEV1, sweat chloride, symptom, or weight improvement — used by FDA and the sponsor as confirmatory evidence that ivacaftor's mechanism (CFTR channel-gating potentiation) requires the specific gating defect produced by G551D, not the trafficking/processing defect of F508del.

- FDA's statistical reviewer (David Hoberman, PhD, concurred by Joan Buenconsejo, PhD, and Thomas Permutt, PhD) concluded: "During my review of the clinical studies, I found no statistical issues in the applicant's analyses of the data," and that both Phase 3 trials showed consistent, robust, statistically significant benefit (P-values "consistently less than .001") across the primary endpoint and nearly all key secondary endpoints.

**Other resources**

- No Vivli/YODA Project/Project Data Sphere participation specific to this program was identified for Vertex Pharmaceuticals; not independently confirmed.

- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened for this application (FDA Summary Review, §9: "An advisory committee was not convened for this application. After initial review of the data the Agency decided that the efficacy and safety were sufficiently robust that holding up approval to discuss at an advisory committee meeting was not necessary").

- FDA's Office of Scientific Investigation (OSI) audited two clinical sites (chosen for relatively high enrollment and favorable outcomes) plus the Vertex sponsor site itself as part of a data-integrity review specifically motivated by the small per-site enrollments typical of this ultra-rare-mutation population; no deficiencies were found at either clinical site or the sponsor site (FDA Medical Review, §3.1).

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §2.1 "Overview," p.6]* — "The Phase 3 studies, referred to as 102 and 103b, are randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled studies to assess the efficacy and safety of 24 weeks of treatment with Ivacaftor 150 mg q12h in subjects age 12 years and older (Study 102) and 6 to 11 years (Study 103b)... A sequential procedure for testing the primary and secondary endpoints was pre-specified to control the overall Type 1 error rate due to multiple key secondary endpoints. Study 102 was designed to enroll a minimum of 80 subjects to provide at least 80% power to detect a treatment effect of 4.5 percentage points in absolute change in percent predicted FEV1 (refer to Appendix 1 for power calculation) and Study 103b was designed to enroll a minimum of 30 subjects."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.1.1 "Study Design and Endpoints," p.7]* — "In both Phase 3 studies, the primary efficacy endpoint was the absolute change from baseline in % predicted FEV1 through week 24. The primary method of analysis was Mixed Model Repeated Measures (MMRM) with an 'unstructured' R- matrix and with no imputed data for missing observations. Covariates were age and baseline % predicted FEV1. The sponsor conducted various sensitivity analyses including using various specified R- matrix structures, ANCOVA and stratified Wilcoxon tests. Other analyses using imputations included last observation carried forward, (LOCF) and worse-case (within subject)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.1.1, p.8-9]* — "To control the overall type I error rate, the primary and key secondary endpoints were analyzed in sequence using the following multi-stage gate keeping procedure: Test 1: The primary efficacy endpoint was tested at significance level α=0.05... Test 2: If a statistically significant result was obtained from test 1 then absolute change from baseline in CFQ-R respiratory domain score through Week 24 and change from baseline in sweat chloride through Week 24 was tested using Hochberg's step-up procedure at significance level α=0.05. Test 3: If a statistically significant result was obtained from test 2, time to first pulmonary exacerbation through Week 48 and change from baseline in weight through Week 48 was tested using Hochberg's step-up procedure."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.1.3, p.13]* — "In both studies, the results from the analysis of the primary endpoint (absolute change in percent predicted FEV1 through Week 24) showed a statistically significant treatment effect both through Weeks 24 and 48. Analysis of all key secondary endpoints were also statistically significant in favor of ivacaftor in both studies, with the exception of the improvement in CFQ-R respiratory domain score through Week 24 (p = 0.11) in Study 103b. Of note, CFQ-R respiratory domain score was the last variable to be tested based on the gatekeeping procedure in Study 103b."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.2, p.29]* — "Overall, the trial failed to demonstrate efficacy of ivacaftor in subjects with this genotype (i.e. CF homozygous for the F508del-CFTR mutation)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §5.1-5.2, pp.33]* — "During my review of the clinical studies, I found no statistical issues in the applicant's analyses of the data... For the G551D subjects in trials 102 & 103, statistically significant results against placebo were found for the primary endpoint (absolute change in percent predicted FEV1 through week 24) and key secondary endpoints... P-values were consistently less than .001."

*[verbatim, FDA Cross Discipline Team Leader Review, "Background," pp.2-3]* — "Fast Track designation was requested in March, and granted on May 4, 2006. On December 20th, 2006, Orphan drug product designation was also granted to VX-770 for the treatment of patients with CF... In December 2008, Vertex submitted 3 protocols under a Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) for phase 3 clinical trials. However, review of the non-clinical data showed that there was not adequate non-clinical support for the proposed trials because of a lack of chronic toxicity data to support the proposed duration of the trial. On January 9, 2009, the Division placed the clinical studies on clinical hold for lack of non-clinical support and Vertex withdrew the studies the same day."

*[verbatim, FDA Medical Review, §3.1 "Submission Quality and Integrity," p.~985]* — "Due to the rarity of this orphan disease, and that only 4% of the CF population carries a G551D mutation, there were a large number of US and international clinical trial sites, with few subjects enrolled at each site."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, §13(b) "Risk Benefit Assessment"]* — "In terms of efficacy, the potential benefits of ivacaftor in CF patients with a copy of the G551D mutation in the CFTR gene are substantial and outweigh the identified safety concerns... Ivacaftor will be the first treatment for patients with CF that actually addresses the defective ion channel that is the cause of CF."

**Reverse-engineered SAP** (no genuine sponsor protocol/SAP is publicly posted on ClinicalTrials.gov for STRIVE or ENVISION as of this writing; the following points are inferred from FDA's Statistical Review, Medical Review, and Cross Discipline Team Leader Review):

- *[inferred]* The choice of percent predicted FEV1 (rather than sweat chloride) as the primary endpoint reflects FDA's End-of-Phase-1 pushback recorded in the Cross Discipline Team Leader Review — the Division "raised concerns regarding the use of sweat chloride as a primary efficacy variable because the clinical relevance of sweat chloride as a biomarker/clinical endpoint in CF has not been demonstrated and recommended FEV1 or another clinically meaningful endpoint instead" — meaning the trials' primary-endpoint choice was itself an FDA-driven design decision made before Phase 3 began, not purely a sponsor election.

- *[inferred]* The MMRM-based primary analysis with no imputation was chosen (and adequate) specifically because of the low observed dropout (~6% through Week 24 in both trials); had dropout been higher, the pre-specified secondary imputation methods (LOCF, worst-case within-subject) suggest the sponsor anticipated needing a formal missing-data strategy but treated it as a sensitivity check rather than the primary approach given how the trials actually enrolled and retained subjects.

- *[inferred]* ENVISION's smaller planned sample size (minimum 30 vs. STRIVE's minimum 80) and its status as a co-pivotal (not merely supportive) trial reflect the FDA End-of-Phase-1 meeting record's stated rationale that, "given the small number of patients with CF who have a G551D mutation," a smaller pediatric trial showing a positive trend would be considered adequate to extend the adult/adolescent efficacy finding downward in age — i.e., the sample-size logic for the pediatric trial was explicitly a rare-population accommodation agreed with FDA in advance, not a standard power calculation for an independently conclusive trial.

- *[inferred]* The decision to run Study 104 (F508del-homozygous cohort) as a parallel Phase 2 program, rather than to attempt an all-comers CF trial, reflects a mechanistic hypothesis (specified prospectively per the End-of-Phase-1 meeting record) that ivacaftor's channel-potentiation mechanism would show efficacy only in a gating mutation like G551D and not in the processing/trafficking defect of F508del; the negative Study 104 result reported in the Statistical Review functions as the reverse-engineered confirmatory/mechanistic evidence for restricting the approved indication to G551D (and, by later label expansions not covered in this entry, other gating mutations).

### 3. Taliglucerase alfa (Elelyso) — BLA 22458

**Sponsor:** Protalix Biotherapeutics, Ltd. (developed the product; Pfizer, Inc. holds the exclusive worldwide marketing license and is listed as the labeler)

**Indication approved:** long-term enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) for adults with a confirmed diagnosis of Type 1 Gaucher disease (label §1); pediatric use not established at approval

**Approval date:** May 1, 2012

**Pivotal trial:** PB-06-001, NCT00376168 (randomized, double-blind, dose-ranging trial in treatment-naive patients — FDA's statistical reviewer designated this the sponsor's sole adequate and well-controlled study); supported by PB-06-002, NCT00712348 (open-label switchover trial from imiglucerase/Cerezyme) and PB-06-003, NCT00705939 (blinded long-term extension of both PB-06-001 and PB-06-002)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1) — PB-06-001 enrolled only 33 randomized treatment-naive patients, the entire addressable population for a from-scratch Gaucher ERT trial; randomized, double-blind, two-active-dose parallel-group trial with no placebo or active-comparator arm, primary efficacy assessed by two separate within-dose one-sample tests rather than a between-arm comparison; open-label, single-arm switchover trial in patients stable on an already-approved enzyme replacement therapy, with efficacy judged as absence of pre-specified clinical deterioration rather than improvement — PB-06-002; FDA-conducted independent expansion of the efficacy analysis population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1) — FDA's statistical reviewer rejected the sponsor's pre-specified Intent-to-Treat definition as under-inclusive for a rare-disease trial and constructed a "Corrected ITT" set restoring 2 excluded randomized patients (31→33) as the basis for all primary analyses; Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §7) — original NDA submitted April 26, 2010, CR action issued February 25, 2011, Class 2 resubmission August 1, 2011, approved May 1, 2012

- *Endpoints:* organ-volume (spleen and liver, by centrally-read blinded MRI) percentage-change-from-baseline endpoint paired with hematologic (hemoglobin concentration, platelet count) change-from-baseline endpoints, analyzed per dose arm rather than as a between-arm comparison — PB-06-001 primary endpoint was percentage change from baseline in spleen volume at 9 months/38 weeks, with hemoglobin, liver volume, and platelet count as key secondaries; in the supportive switchover/extension trials (PB-06-002, PB-06-003) the same four parameters were instead framed as binary "clinically relevant deterioration" criteria (e.g., >20% increase in spleen volume, >20% decrease in hemoglobin) assessed by clinical judgment rather than formal inferential testing

- *Primary analysis:* one-sample t-test for within-dose-arm change-from-baseline in a randomized dose-comparison trial, with a two-independent-sample t-test as an explicitly non-primary/exploratory dose comparison — FDA's statistical review states plainly that this within-group design "is not traditionally an acceptable approach for establishing efficacy" and that its p-values "are not statistically valid" and "should not be emphasized"; descriptive-statistics-only analysis with no inferential/hypothesis-testing framework (PB-06-002, PB-06-003) — FDA review states efficacy in these two studies is "based on clinical judgment" with "no inferences made from formal statistical methodology"

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §4) — spleen volume (α=0.025 per dose) → hemoglobin → liver volume → platelet count, each subsequent endpoint tested only if the prior one reached significance in that dose arm; this sequence halted before platelet count in the 30 Units/kg arm

- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation (100 imputations, averaged) for missing 9-month spleen-volume data in a small-sample orphan trial; last observation carried forward (LOCF) for missing hemoglobin/platelet values; no-change-from-baseline imputation applied by FDA to two patients the sponsor had excluded from its own analysis set entirely

- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter followed by resubmission and approval (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §7); no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held ("did not raise significant safety or efficacy issues that were unexpected for a drug in this class," per the approval letter); FDA statistical reviewer's recommendation for an additional randomized, active-controlled head-to-head confirmatory trial (vs. Cerezyme and/or VPRIV) not adopted as a condition of approval, with the Division instead resting approval on clinical judgment given Gaucher-ERT product shortages and orphan-disease enrollment constraints; Orphan Drug Designation (OOPD, September 3, 2010) and Fast Track designation (August 24, 2009); nine 505(o)(3) postmarketing requirements imposed at approval (validated neutralizing-antibody and anti-plant-sugar-antibody assays, a long-term ≥10-year patient registry, completion of the ongoing pediatric trial PB-06-005, and completion of PB-06-002 itself)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- PB-06-001 was a Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel dose-group trial in 33 treatment-naive adults (19-74 years) with Type 1 Gaucher disease, conducted at 11 sites in 9 countries (first patient enrolled August 5, 2007; last patient completed September 11, 2009); eligibility required splenomegaly >8x normal by MRI and thrombocytopenia (platelet count <120,000/mm³), with prior exclusion of any patient with severe neurologic (neuronopathic) involvement; randomization was simple 1:1, non-stratified, in blocks of 4, to taliglucerase alfa 30 Units/kg or 60 Units/kg IV every 2 weeks for 9 months (38 weeks/20 infusions), with eligible completers offered rollover into the PB-06-003 extension.

- Primary endpoint: percentage change from baseline in spleen volume (by centrally-read, blinded, dual-reader MRI) at 9 months/38 weeks. Key secondary endpoints: change from baseline in hemoglobin concentration, percentage change in liver volume, and change in platelet count, all at 9 months.

- Sample-size rationale (FDA Statistical Review, original cycle, §3.1.3): with 12 evaluable patients per dose arm there was ">95% power to detect a percentage change from baseline in spleen volume after nine months of treatment of 20% or more utilizing a one-sample two-sided t-test at α=0.025," assuming a 12% SD for percent change; 15 patients per arm were enrolled to ensure 12 completers per arm given anticipated dropout.

- Analysis sets: the sponsor's pre-specified SAP defined an Intent-to-Treat (ITT) set (randomized, dosed, with a baseline MRI) and a Per-Protocol (PP) set; the sponsor's ITT excluded 2 randomized patients (one who withdrew before dosing, one who received a trivial partial first dose), yielding n=31 (15/16). FDA's statistical reviewer determined this exclusion violated the ICH E9 ITT principle for a rare-disease trial and constructed a "Corrected ITT" set of all 33 randomized patients (16 at 30 U/kg, 17 at 60 U/kg) as the basis for all primary (non-sensitivity) analyses; the sponsor's PP set (29 patients) was accepted as-is and used for sensitivity analyses.

- Primary analysis methodology (FDA Statistical Review, original cycle, §3.1.5.2): two separate one-sample t-tests (one per dose arm) of H0: μ=0 vs. HA: μ≠0 for the mean percentage/absolute change from baseline at 9 months, each with a 95% t-distribution CI, tested independently at α=0.025 per arm; a two-independent-sample t-test comparing the 60 vs. 30 Units/kg arms was pre-specified as an "additional exploratory analysis," not part of the primary inferential claim.

- Multiplicity (FDA Statistical Review, original cycle, §3.1.5.4): a sequential step-down procedure gated hemoglobin testing on a significant spleen-volume result (either dose), liver-volume testing on a significant hemoglobin result, and platelet-count testing on a significant liver-volume result, each step at α=0.025 per dose independently.

- Missing data (FDA Statistical Review, original cycle, §3.1.5.3): of the corrected-ITT population, 4 patients (2 per arm) had missing post-baseline data; spleen volume used multiple imputation (100 imputations, averaged) for 2 patients and a no-change-from-baseline carry-forward for the 2 patients added back by FDA's ITT correction; liver volume used LOCF for 2 patients and the same no-change carry-forward (with the cross-sectional mean baseline liver volume of the other 31 patients substituted, since these 2 patients had no recorded screening liver volume) for the other 2; hemoglobin and platelet count used LOCF throughout, including for all post-dropout timepoints.

- Results (FDA Statistical Review, original cycle, §3.1.6, Corrected ITT, screening to Week 38/9-month): spleen volume changed −25.2% (30 U/kg, 95% CI −30.61 to −19.85, one-sample p<0.0001) and −35.8% (60 U/kg, 95% CI −42.43 to −29.12, p<0.0001); the exploratory two-sample comparison between doses was significant (mean difference −10.6, 95% CI −18.82 to −2.27, p=0.0142), favoring 60 U/kg. Hemoglobin rose 1.37 g/dL (30 U/kg, p=0.0020) and 2.01 g/dL (60 U/kg, p<0.0001); the dose comparison was non-significant (p=0.2147). Liver volume changed −9.7% (30 U/kg, p=0.0026) and −9.9% (60 U/kg, p<0.0001); dose comparison non-significant (p=0.9587). Platelet count rose 10,713/mm³ (30 U/kg, p=0.0464) and 39,053/mm³ (60 U/kg, p=0.0033); per the pre-specified step-down rule, the 30 U/kg platelet result did not clear the α=0.025 threshold, and the exploratory two-sample dose comparison was significant (mean difference 28,340, 95% CI 2,604-54,077, p=0.0317), again favoring 60 U/kg. A pre-specified subgroup analysis by gender showed no qualitative difference from the overall spleen-volume result.

- PB-06-002 (switchover trial): 28 adult/pediatric patients (2 to 66 years) stable on imiglucerase ≥2 years were switched to taliglucerase alfa at their existing dose for 9 months, with efficacy defined by absence of pre-specified "clinically relevant deterioration" thresholds in the same 4 parameters (e.g., ≥20% increase in spleen volume, >20%/>40% decrease in platelet count depending on baseline level) rather than by improvement; of evaluable patients, deterioration occurred in 1/20 (5.0%) for spleen volume, 0/26 for hemoglobin, 1/23 (4.3%) for liver volume, and 2/26 (7.7%) for platelet count at Month 9. FDA's statistical reviewer explicitly noted the open-label single-arm design could instead "have been designed as a double-blind randomized withdrawal or double-blind randomized add-on study which would have resulted in much more useful and supportive efficacy data," calling the results "marginally supportive at best."

- PB-06-003 (extension trial, interim data cut May 1, 2011): PB-06-001 completers continuing double-blind at their original assigned dose showed, at Month 24 (n=12 at 30 U/kg, n=14 at 60 U/kg), mean spleen-volume reduction from original baseline of −40.5% and −54.9% respectively (descriptive only, no formal test); PB-06-002 rollover patients (open-label, n≤18, sparse follow-up) showed little further change, consistent with maintenance of the switchover-trial result.

- FDA's overarching statistical conclusion (original review cycle) was that the development program was "incomplete," recommending an additional randomized, adequately powered, active-controlled ("head-to-head") trial against Cerezyme and/or VPRIV before approval; this recommendation was not adopted. The final (resubmission-cycle) statistical review instead concluded that, "[d]ue to the orphan nature of Type I Gaucher Disease, and the limitations of the submitted clinical studies, the determination of the clinical effectiveness of ELELYSO will rely more on clinical judgment than on the statistical rigor usually required for larger controlled studies," and that PB-06-002/PB-06-003 data were sufficient to support approval alongside PB-06-001.

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, original review cycle, §3.1.5.2 "Analysis Methodology"]* — "The primary analysis for each of the four study endpoints previously presented in Section 3.1.2 above will be two separate one-sample t-tests (one for each dose group) to determine if the sample mean percent change from baseline (in spleen and liver volume) at 9 months/38 weeks or the sample mean change from baseline (in hemoglobin concentration and platelet count) at 9 months/38 weeks is significantly different than zero... A two independent sample t-test will be administered as an additional exploratory analysis of each endpoint for dose comparison purposes."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, original review cycle, §3.1.5.4 "Multiplicity"]* — "First, the primary efficacy analysis is performed at each dose level using an α level of 0.025 to allow each dose to be tested independently. If spleen volume as the primary endpoint is shown to be significant for either one or both doses, then the mean change in hemoglobin concentration will be tested for that dose (or doses) using an α level of 0.025... Next, if the change in hemoglobin is shown to be significant for either one or both doses, then the percent change in liver volume will be tested... Finally, if the percent change in liver volume is shown to be significant for either one or both doses, then the mean change in platelet count will be tested."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, original review cycle, Executive Summary, "PB-06-001 Study Design"]* — "This study design is more observational in nature. The use of a within-dose comparison (formally assessed by a one sample t-test) is not traditionally an acceptable approach for establishing efficacy. Inferential results (e.g. p-values) from this within-group comparison are not statistically valid, therefore have no basis regarding any efficacy claim and thus should not be emphasized. *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, original review cycle, Executive Summary, "PB-06-002 Study Design"]* — "The efficacy results from study PB-06-002 are marginally supportive at best due to the open-label switchover design utilized by the sponsor. These changes are considered to be clinically meaningful in light of the natural history of untreated Gaucher disease."

### 4. Elosulfase alfa (Vimizim) — BLA 125460

**Sponsor:** BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.

**Indication approved:** Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA (MPS IVA; Morquio A syndrome), 2 mg/kg IV once weekly; efficacy was established in patients ≥5 years old, the age range enrolled in the pivotal trial

**Approval date:** February 14, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** MOR-004, NCT01275066, phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (the pivotal publication's author group is named the "STRIVE Investigators," but no acronym is registered for the trial on ClinicalTrials.gov)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-arm parallel-group trial (elosulfase alfa 2 mg/kg once weekly vs. 2 mg/kg once every other week vs. placebo); small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1) — MPS IVA US prevalence estimated at 520-800 patients, with 177 randomized into the entire pivotal program; sponsor sought a Special Protocol Assessment (submitted December 3, 2010) but FDA issued a formal **No-Agreement letter** (January 20, 2011) rather than reaching SPA agreement, so the trial proceeded to completion without SPA protection (*SPA sought, No-Agreement Letter issued — trial proceeds without SPA protection*, distinct from the taxonomy's existing "SPA rescinded" and "SPA formally amended" rows, both of which presuppose an agreement was reached first)

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint was change from baseline to Week 24 in six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance, a continuous functional-endurance endpoint (not yet covered by the taxonomy's psychiatric/neurological continuous-scale row); secondary endpoints were change from baseline in three-minute stair climb test (3MSCT) rate and percentage change from baseline in normalized urine keratan sulfate (KS); randomization (1:1:1) was stratified by screening 6MWT category (≤200 meters and >200 meters) and age group (5-11, 12-18, ≥19 years)

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA model of Week 24 change from baseline in 6MWT with treatment, baseline 6MWT category, and age group as factors — a single-timepoint change-from-baseline ANCOVA with categorical stratification covariates (distinct from the taxonomy's existing "Repeated-measures ANCOVA" row, which covers a longitudinal multi-visit model); each active dose compared pairwise to placebo, with a Hochberg step-up procedure (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §3) applied within each endpoint step to the two dose-vs-placebo comparisons

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §4) across the endpoint family in order 6MWT → 3MSCT → urine KS, with the Hochberg step-up procedure nested within each step; FDA found the applicant's step-down rule "pre-specified in a dubious manner" because it did not state whether the step-down began at the primary-endpoint level, an ambiguity FDA deemed "inherently flawed" though it did not change the study's conclusions since the first secondary endpoint (3MSCT) was already non-significant for both doses

- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation via Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo sampling under a missing-at-random assumption (SAS PROC MI, 5 imputations, seed 38867) for missing 6MWT/3MSCT/urine-KS values, with a no-change-from-baseline imputation and an All-Randomized/Per-Protocol analysis-set repeat as sensitivity analyses; only 2 of 177 randomized patients discontinued, so missing data had negligible impact on conclusions; three studentized-residual outliers were identified and removed as a sensitivity analysis with no change in conclusions

- *Regulatory:* FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee, November 19, 2013, convened specifically on the appropriateness of the 6MWT as an efficacy endpoint; majority of members considered 6MWT adequate, but no formal approval-recommendation vote tally is recorded in the Summary Review); Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis; exploratory (non-confirmatory) subgroup findings favoring White, age 12-18, North American, and ≤200m-baseline-6MWT patients were identified during the review cycle and, per FDA, could only be described descriptively in labeling, not as an efficacy claim

**Trial design & endpoints**

- MOR-004 was a 24-week, multinational (17 countries), multicenter (33 sites), outpatient, randomized (1:1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in patients ≥5 years old with confirmed MPS IVA able to walk ≥30 and ≤325 meters in the 6MWT; patients received elosulfase alfa 2 mg/kg once weekly (n=58), 2 mg/kg once every other week (n=59), or placebo (n=59) as a 4-hour IV infusion; the protocol was finalized October 4, 2010, the trial ran January 25, 2011-August 23, 2012, and the SAP was finalized August 24, 2012 (with an October 3, 2012 addendum solely defining the Per-Protocol analysis set), after database hard-lock and before unblinding (October 12/19, 2012)

- Primary endpoint: change from baseline to Week 24 in 6MWT distance (mean of duplicate assessments per visit). Secondary endpoints: change from baseline to Week 24 in 3MSCT rate, and percentage change from baseline to Week 24 in normalized urine KS (single central laboratory)

- Sample size: approximately 162 patients (54/arm) were planned for >90% power to detect a 40-meter mean-change difference in 6MWT between each active dose and placebo, assuming a common SD of 65 meters (deliberately conservative relative to the SD observed in the similar population subset of the supportive Phase 1/2 study MOR-002) at an overall two-sided α=0.05 with the Hochberg method for multiplicity; the trial was declared positive if both active doses beat placebo at p<0.05, or if one dose beat placebo at p<0.025; 177 patients were ultimately randomized (176 in the ITT set; 1 excluded pre-treatment for an unconfirmed diagnosis)

- Analysis populations: ITT (all randomized subjects dosed at least once, analyzed as randomized) was primary; Per-Protocol and All-Randomized sets were sensitivity analyses. Primary/secondary analyses used ANCOVA models (Week 24 change from baseline, or percentage change for urine KS) with treatment, baseline 6MWT category, and age group as factors (plus the relevant baseline value as a covariate for 3MSCT and urine KS)

- Result: the 2 mg/kg once-weekly dose showed a statistically significant 6MWT treatment effect (LS mean difference vs. placebo 22.5 m, 95% CI 4.0-40.9, p=0.0174); the once-every-other-week dose did not (0.5 m, 95% CI -17.8-18.9, p=0.9542). Because the once-every-other-week dose failed at the first (primary-endpoint) step, all subsequent hypothesis testing on secondary endpoints was, per the applicant's own (FDA-criticized) multiplicity rule, exploratory; neither dose showed a 3MSCT effect (both doses' 95% CIs crossed zero), while both doses showed large, nominally significant reductions in urine KS (not supported by a controlled hypothesis test given the upstream 3MSCT failure)

- A special/exploratory subgroup finding identified during FDA's review cycle — patients with baseline 6MWT ≤200 meters — showed a substantially larger once-weekly-dose treatment effect (LS mean difference 40.4 m, 95% CI 11.0-69.8, p=0.0074) than the >200-meter subgroup (10.8 m, 95% CI -12.8-34.4, p=0.3657); FDA concluded this more-severely-affected subgroup "seems to drive" the overall positive result, but treated the finding as exploratory only

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary, p.3]* — "There appears to be sufficient evidence to support efficacy claims on improving the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance for the VIMIZIM (BMN 110; elosulfase alfa) 2.0 mg/kg/week dose... Overall, the design of study MOR-004 was deemed adequate from a statistical perspective, and the applicant's corresponding statistical analysis plan deemed appropriate. There were no statistical review issues identified for this application. However, currently there is no consensus regarding the clinical meaningfulness of the primary study endpoint of 6MWT distance."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §2.1 Overview, p.4]* — "Biomarin then submitted their single pivotal phase 3 study (trial MOR-004) through the Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) regulatory pathway on December 3, 2010. DGIEP subsequently issued a No-Agreement letter on January 20, 2011. Biomarin chose not to pursue the SPA any further but attempted to reach agreements on the outstanding clinical and statistical issues by an additional advice meeting held on July 9, 2012."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.1 Study Design and Endpoints]* — "Approximately 162 patients (54 patients in each group) would be enrolled into the study to have more than 90% power to detect a difference of 40 meters in mean change in the 6MWT distance between each of the BMN 110 groups and the placebo group, assuming that the common standard deviation (SD) was 65 meters at an overall 0.05 two-sided significance level, α, with the Hochberg method for multiplicity adjustment... Study MOR-004 would be considered positive if both comparisons of the drug regimens to placebo render p-values less than 0.05 or the comparison of one of the drug regimens to placebo results in a p-value less than 0.025."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.2 Multiplicity Adjustment]* — "This step-down procedure was pre-specified in a dubious manner by the applicant. By not specifically stating if the step-down begins at the primary analysis level one could speculate that the applicant had assumed that formal hypothesis testing could still be conducted on the secondary efficacy endpoints after spending all of the Type I error rate on the primary endpoint comparisons. Consequently, the pre-specified step-down procedure was inherently flawed; however, study conclusions were not affected as neither BMN 110 dose was found to be statistically significant... for the first secondary endpoint."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.3 Primary Endpoint Analysis]* — "The primary analysis of the 6MWT distance was an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model of the Week 24 change from baseline in the 6MWT measurement with treatment, baseline 6MWT categories (≤ 200 meters and > 200 meters), and age groups (5-11, 12-18, and ≥ 19 years old) as factors."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.5 Handling of Dropouts/Missing Data]* — "For subjects with missing 6MWT or 3MSCT data who had not died and were physically able to perform the test(s), and for subjects with missing urine KS data, the Multiple Imputation (MI) approach was conducted while assuming that these data were missing at random (MAR)... The sampling utilized a Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC) chain with five sets of imputations from SAS PROC MI. The imputation was performed for each treatment group separately using the randomly selected seed 38867."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.4 Results and Conclusions, Table 4]* — "It can be observed that the BMN 110 2.0 mg/kg/week dose showed superior improvement in the change from baseline for 6MWT at Week 24 when compared to placebo while the BMN 110 2.0 mg/kg/qow dose failed to show a statistically significant treatment difference when compared to placebo."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §5.3 Conclusions and Recommendations, p.29]* — "An additional subgroup of patients who had a 6MWT distance of ≤ 200 meters at baseline were identified during the review cycle. This subgroup, which represents patients with greater morbidity, seems to drive the significant 6MWT efficacy results, and this suggests that these patients may respond better to the BMN 110 2.0 mg/kg/week dose than the patients with less morbidity at baseline. This finding, however, is exploratory in nature and thus cannot be used to support an efficacy claim in the ≤ 200 meters subgroup population. Consequently, if the results regarding this subgroup are to be included in the product labeling, they should be presented in a descriptive manner."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, Deputy Division Director Review, §9 Advisory Committee Meeting]* — "Although 6-MWT is an assessment of multiple organ systems involved in MPS IVA, I do not agree that the efficacy endpoint completely assesses the impact of Vimizim on the consequences of this disease. It is likely a measure of some treatment benefit in this patient population but the medical community is encouraged to identify more suitable endpoints for assessment especially in the underserved pediatric population that might be treated off label with this treatment. Until a more appropriate functional measure specific to MPS IVA patients becomes available, one should consider carefully the interpretability of the 6MWT as a definitive measure of clinical benefit."

**Reverse-engineered SAP** *(inferred — no genuine sponsor SAP/protocol document is publicly posted; MOR-004's own SAP text is not available on ClinicalTrials.gov or Drugs@FDA, so these points reconstruct SAP mechanics not explicitly spelled out even in FDA's detailed statistical-review paraphrase above)*

- **Full endpoint-family step-down structure with nested Hochberg gates** [inferred from combining the review's statement that "results...correspond to the endpoint testing order specified in section 3.2.1" (i.e., 6MWT → 3MSCT → urine KS) with its separate description of the Hochberg method being "nested within each step/endpoint testing when comparing each of the two doses to placebo"]: the SAP's intended decision algorithm was almost certainly (1) apply Hochberg step-up to the two dose-vs-placebo 6MWT comparisons; (2) only if *both* doses cleared 6MWT at p<0.05 (or one cleared at p<0.025 per the family-wise rule), proceed to apply the same Hochberg step-up structure to the 3MSCT comparisons; (3) repeat for urine KS — a fixed-sequence-of-Hochberg-gates design that FDA never had to fully test in practice because the once-every-other-week dose failed at 6MWT.

- **Origin of the ≤200m/>200m baseline stratification cutoff** [inferred from the review noting the assumed SD of 65 meters was "somewhat conservative when compared to the standard deviation associated with the similar population subset found within study MOR-002," combined with the trial's 30-325m eligibility window]: the 200-meter cutoff (used both as a randomization stratification factor and, later, as the subgroup found to drive the primary result) plausibly reflects a natural near-midpoint split of the eligible 30-325m range informed by MOR-002's Phase 1/2 experience, though neither document states the cutoff's derivation explicitly, so this remains a plausible reconstruction rather than a confirmed fact.

- **Unresolved counterfactual in the multiplicity flaw** [inferred from the review's statement that the flawed step-down rule "did not affect study conclusions" only because the once-every-other-week dose was already non-significant at 3MSCT]: had the once-weekly dose's already-significant 6MWT result been paired with a *significant* 3MSCT result for that same dose (while the qow dose remained null), the SAP as pre-specified does not resolve whether formal (alpha-controlled) secondary testing should have continued for the qow dose or been entirely halted — this ambiguity is described by FDA but not actually resolved by any document reviewed, and cannot be reconstructed further from public sources.

---

### 5. Eliglustat (Cerdelga) — NDA 205494

**Sponsor:** Genzyme Corporation (a Sanofi company)

**Indication approved:** Long-term treatment of adult patients with Gaucher disease type 1 (GD1) who are CYP2D6 extensive metabolizers (EMs), intermediate metabolizers (IMs), or poor metabolizers (PMs), as detected by an FDA-cleared test

**Approval date:** August 19, 2014

**Pivotal trial:** GZGD02507 (ENGAGE), NCT00891202 — pivotal, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, treatment-naïve patients; GZGD02607 (ENCORE), NCT00943111 — key supportive, randomized, open-label, active-controlled non-inferiority trial in patients switching from enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (ENGAGE, treatment-naïve GD1 patients); Randomized, open-label, active-controlled (ENCORE, non-inferiority switch-from-ERT design against imiglucerase/CEREZYME); Small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (ENGAGE N=40; ENCORE N=160; GD1 worldwide incidence estimated at 1 in 50,000-100,000 births per the FDA Summary Review) — ENGAGE recruitment stalled at 16/36 target patients 18 months into enrollment, prompting an April 2011 Type C meeting where the sponsor unsuccessfully proposed shifting the pivotal-efficacy burden to ENCORE

- *Endpoints:* Percentage change from baseline in spleen volume (in multiples of normal, MN) at Week 39, ENGAGE primary endpoint, tested in a pre-specified order ahead of three secondary endpoints (hemoglobin, liver volume, platelet count); composite binary "stable" responder endpoint at Week 52, ENCORE primary endpoint, requiring simultaneous maintenance of hemoglobin (no decrease >1.5 g/dL), platelets (no decrease >25%), spleen volume (no increase >25% MN), and liver volume (no increase >20% MN), each from baseline, with treatment failures adjudicated by a blinded Independent Adjudication Board

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA model (treatment plus baseline spleen-severity stratum, with baseline value added as a covariate for secondary endpoints) for each of ENGAGE's four ordered continuous endpoints, reporting LS-mean treatment differences with 95% CIs (the taxonomy's only ANCOVA row, "ANCOVA with normality-contingent fallback to a non-parametric test," requires a pre-specified non-parametric fallback that eliglustat's SAP did not include; this is a plain ANCOVA with no fallback); for ENCORE's primary non-inferiority comparison, a Mantel-Haenszel-weighted (per randomization stratum) Agresti-Caffo adjusted Wald confidence interval for the difference in binomial "stable" proportions between eliglustat and CEREZYME (distinct from the taxonomy's Newcombe-method and Miettinen-Nurminen rows, neither of which is the Agresti-Caffo construction actually used here)

- *Multiplicity:* Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing for ENGAGE's four endpoints (spleen volume→hemoglobin→liver volume→platelet count), where a later endpoint's comparison to placebo remained confirmatory only if every earlier endpoint in the order reached p<0.05, all four of which did; ENCORE pre-specified no multiplicity adjustment at all, so the FDA statistical review deemed every non-primary analysis — including the sponsor's own supplemental, DGIEP-requested non-inferiority test on percentage change in spleen volume — exploratory (Unadjusted secondary/supportive testing (single formal primary endpoint))

- *Missing data/bias:* Last observation carried forward (LOCF) for ENGAGE's Week-39 efficacy endpoints among patients with missing data or early withdrawal, with a no-change-from-baseline imputation as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis missing-data-as-treatment-failure imputation for ENCORE's binary primary stability endpoint among patients missing Week-52 assessments or who withdrew (distinct from the taxonomy's diary-specific non-responder-imputation row); ENGAGE and ENCORE each had only 1/40 and 4/160 dropouts respectively, so FDA concluded neither trial's conclusions were sensitive to the imputation method

- *Regulatory:* Pharmacogenomic patient-selection and dose-differentiation requirement — the approved indication and recommended dosage (84 mg BID for EMs/IMs, 84 mg once daily for PMs) are explicitly conditioned on CYP2D6 genotype "as detected by an FDA-cleared test," with ultra-rapid metabolizers excluded as a Limitation of Use and indeterminate metabolizers left without a recommended dose (Companion diagnostic co-approval, extended here from a tumor-mutation-selection context to a metabolizer-genotype dosing/eligibility gate — flagged as an atypical use of this term); FDA-disputed non-inferiority margin left unresolved at approval — the FDA statistical review states plainly that neither ENCORE's primary 25% margin nor its supplemental 15% margin was ever agreed to by the Division, yet approval proceeded on the totality of the ENGAGE and ENCORE evidence; Orphan Drug Designation (September 17, 2008) and Priority Review under PDUFA V; postmarketing requirements under FDCA §505(o) for dedicated renal- and hepatic-impairment PK trials; no REMS required; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting is mentioned in the Statistical, Summary, or Cross-Discipline Team Leader reviews for this application

**Trial design & endpoints**

- ENGAGE (GZGD02507) was a multinational (12 countries), multicenter (18 sites), randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase 3 trial in treatment-naïve adult and adolescent (≥16 years) GD1 patients, stratified by screening spleen-volume severity (≤20 MN vs. >20 MN) and randomized 1:1 to eliglustat or placebo for a 39-week Double-Blind Treatment Period, followed by an Open-Label Treatment Period; eliglustat dosing began at 50 mg BID with a Week-4 PK-guided escalation to 100 mg BID. Sample size: approximately 36 patients (1:1) were planned, allowing a 20% dropout rate, to yield ≥28 evaluable patients, assuming a 25% vs. 5% mean decrease in spleen volume for eliglustat vs. placebo, common SD of 15%, two-sided two-sample t-test, 5% alpha, 92% power; 40 patients were ultimately randomized (20/20) after a mid-trial recruitment shortfall (16 patients enrolled 18 months into a planned 2-year recruitment period) triggered an April 2011 Type C meeting, at which FDA declined the sponsor's proposal to shift pivotal-efficacy responsibility to ENCORE and instead required continued ENGAGE recruitment, with within-treatment-group (uncontrolled) analyses added by SAP amendment as a contingency that was ultimately not needed.

- ENGAGE primary endpoint: percentage change from baseline in spleen volume (MN) at Week 39, analyzed by ANCOVA (treatment, baseline spleen-severity stratum) in the Full Analysis Set (all dosed, as-randomized), with Per-Protocol and Week-39-Completer sets as pre-specified sensitivity analyses. Secondary endpoints (absolute change in hemoglobin, percentage change in liver volume, percentage change in platelet count, each at Week 39) were tested only if the preceding endpoint in the pre-specified order was significant at p<0.05 (fixed-sequence step-down). Result (FDA's reviewer table, Tables 5-8): spleen volume LS-mean difference (eliglustat − placebo) −30.03% (95% CI −36.82, −23.24; p<0.0001); hemoglobin +1.22 g/dL (0.57, 1.88; p=0.0006); liver volume −6.64% (−11.37, −1.91; p=0.0072); platelet count +41.06% (23.95, 58.17; p<0.0001) — all four steps of the hierarchy reached significance, so none of the testing fell back to exploratory status. Only 1 of 40 randomized patients discontinued.

- ENCORE (GZGD02607) was a multinational (12 countries), multicenter (34 sites), randomized, open-label, active-controlled, parallel-group Phase 3 non-inferiority trial in adult GD1 patients previously stabilized on ERT for ≥3 years, stratified by pre-study CEREZYME dose (<35 vs. ≥35 U/kg/QOW) and randomized 2:1 to eliglustat (oral, dose-titrated by CYP2D6-guided PK) or continued CEREZYME (IV, at stable pre-study dose) for a 52-week Primary Analysis Treatment Period, followed by a Long-Term Treatment Period. The trial's primary objective was changed from a within-group descriptive assessment to a comparative non-inferiority design by a major protocol amendment (Amendment 2, October 2009) after parallel discussions with EMA and DGIEP, before first-patient dosing. Sample size: approximately 150 patients (2:1) were planned to yield ≥120 evaluable, assuming a 95% (CEREZYME) vs. 85% (eliglustat) stability rate from the Phase 2 GZGD00304 study, 85% power, one-sided alpha 0.025, a 25% non-inferiority margin, and 20% non-evaluable/dropout; 160 patients were randomized (106 eliglustat : 54 CEREZYME).

- ENCORE primary endpoint: proportion of patients "stable" (composite of hemoglobin, platelet, spleen-volume, and liver-volume criteria above) at Week 52 in the Per-Protocol Set (per ICH E9 guidance for non-inferiority designs), with FAS, All-Randomized, and Week-52-Completer sets as sensitivity analyses; non-inferiority was to be declared if the lower bound of the Mantel-Haenszel-stratum-weighted, Agresti-Caffo-adjusted 95% CI for the eliglustat-minus-CEREZYME difference in stability rate excluded a 25-percentage-point deficit. Result (PP set, FDA Table 11): 84/99 (84.8%) eliglustat patients vs. 44/47 (93.6%) CEREZYME patients stable at Week 52; difference −8.8% (95% CI −17.6%, 3.3%) — lower bound above −25%, so eliglustat was declared non-inferior. A DGIEP-requested supplemental (exploratory, non-pre-specified-margin) non-inferiority analysis of percentage change in spleen volume at Week 52, using a 15% margin the Division never formally endorsed, also favored non-inferiority (FAS treatment difference −1.73%, 95% CI −6.72, 3.25; PP −2.83%, 95% CI −8.14, 2.47 — both upper bounds under 15%). FDA's statistical review states explicitly that neither the primary 25% margin nor this supplemental 15% margin was ever agreed to by the Division and that assay sensitivity could not be assessed absent a placebo-controlled CEREZYME trial (which has never been conducted), yet the review concluded the design was "adequate from a statistical perspective" overall and recommended no changes precluding approval. Only 4 of 160 randomized patients discontinued (2 per arm).

- CYP2D6 metabolizer-status subgroup analyses (a pre-specified special population of clinical interest per FDA's review) showed both trials were dominated by extensive metabolizers (36/40 in ENGAGE; 122/159 in ENCORE), with poor and ultra-rapid metabolizer cells too small for independent inference (e.g., ENGAGE had a single intermediate-metabolizer and a single ultra-rapid-metabolizer patient per arm); this sparsity is the statistical backdrop for the label's PM/EM/IM dosing distinction and its "specific dosage cannot be recommended" limitation for indeterminate metabolizers, both of which rest primarily on Clinical Pharmacology PK/PD modeling (PBPK, QTc) rather than on the efficacy trials' subgroup power.

- A third Phase 3 trial, GZGD03109 (EDGE), compared once-daily vs. twice-daily eliglustat dosing regimens and, together with the open-label Phase 2 study GZGD00304 (the 26-patient trial that generated ENCORE's non-inferiority margin assumptions), provided supportive but non-pivotal efficacy/safety data reviewed alongside ENGAGE and ENCORE.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.1, p.8]* — "The original statistical analysis plan (SAP) was finalized on October 28, 2010. An amendment to the SAP was made on August 11, 2011. This amendment incorporated additional inferential analyses for assessing the change from baseline at Week 39 in the four efficacy parameters of interest... exclusively within the eliglustat treatment group without comparison to the placebo group. These additional analyses were deemed exploratory by the review team."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.1.2.2 "Multiplicity Adjustment," p.17]* — "In order to control the overall study-wise type I error rate, a step-down/closed sequential testing procedure was pre-specified by the applicant... Starting with the primary endpoint, the applicant stated that the step-down could only be carried to the next endpoint... if and only if the current endpoint/step was found to be statistically significant in the comparison of eliglustat to placebo (i.e., p-value less than 0.05)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.1.1, p.13]* — "Allowing for a drop-out rate of 20%, approximately 36 male and female patients would have to be randomized in this study in a 1:1 ratio to receive eliglustat or placebo in order to yield at least 28 evaluable patients... This sample size was estimated under the assumption of a 25% decrease in spleen volume in MN for eliglustat and a 5% decrease in spleen volume in MN for placebo at 39 weeks, a common standard deviation of 15% with a two-sided two-sample t-test using a 5% level of significance and 92% power."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.1, p.33-34]* — "Approximately 150 male and female patients were planned to be randomized in this study in order to yield at least 120 evaluable patients at the end of 52 weeks. This sample size was based on expected responder/stability rates of 95% for the CEREZYME treatment group and 85% for the eliglustat treatment group... a power of 85%, a one-sided significance level of 0.025, a non-inferiority margin of 25%, and a 20% non-evaluable/drop-out rate."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.2.3 "Primary Endpoint Analysis," p.36]* — "The applicant specified that if the lower-bound of the 95% CI for the difference was within the non-inferiority margin of 25%, then eliglustat treatment would be declared non-inferior to CEREZYME treatment. The aforementioned 95% CI for the difference... was estimated using the method of Agresti and Caffo's adjusted Wald confidence intervals... The overall estimate was based on a weighted combination of the differences... with the scaled Mantel-Haenszel weights for each randomization stratum."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.2.2 "Multiplicity Adjustment," p.36]* — "As stated above in Section 3.2.2.1, the applicant did not pre-specify a multiplicity adjustment for controlling the overall study-wise type I error. Consequently all subsequent (i.e., non-primary) analyses were considered exploratory."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.1, p.29 and Executive Summary, p.4]* — "One issue pertaining to the ENCORE study is the non-inferiority margin of 25% that was pre-specified for the primary efficacy assessment. This margin was deemed clinically unacceptable by the clinical review team. There was also no agreement on the non-inferiority margin of 15%, proposed for the additionally requested assessment of percentage change from baseline in spleen volume... Neither of these margins was acceptable from a statistical perspective."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §5.1-5.3 "Summary and Conclusions," p.60-61]* — "Overall, the designs of both the ENGAGE and ENCORE studies were deemed adequate from a statistical perspective for the proposed indication, and the applicant's corresponding statistical analysis plans deemed appropriate. There were no statistical review issues identified for this application that would preclude product approval... There is sufficient evidence in supporting the proposed efficacy claims for eliglustat, and the claims reflected within the applicant's submitted product labeling are supported by the results presented in this review."

*[inferred, from FDA Statistical Review Tables 20-21 and the approved label's dosing/limitations language, §2.1-2.2 and §1]* — The label's CYP2D6-genotype-gated indication (EM/IM/PM eligible; URM excluded as a Limitation of Use; indeterminate metabolizers given no recommended dose) is not itself a statistical hypothesis test result from ENGAGE or ENCORE — both trials' non-extensive-metabolizer subgroups were too small (e.g., single-digit N per cell) for independent inference — and instead reflects Clinical Pharmacology PK/PD and PBPK modeling of eliglustat exposure and QTc effect by genotype, layered on top of the efficacy trials' predominantly extensive-metabolizer populations.
