### 6. Cholic acid (Cholbam) — NDA 205750

**Sponsor:** Asklepion Pharmaceuticals, LLC (the underlying compassionate-use research program and Investigator IND 45,470 were held by James E. Heubi, MD, and Kenneth D.R. Setchell, PhD, at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (CCHMC) from 1994; the IND was transferred to Asklepion in May 2007, and Drs. Heubi and Setchell continued treating patients under it thereafter; ClinicalTrials.gov now lists Mirum Pharmaceuticals, Inc. as sponsor of record post-acquisition)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of bile acid synthesis disorders due to single enzyme defects (SEDs); adjunctive treatment of peroxisomal disorders (PDs), including Zellweger spectrum disorders, in patients who exhibit manifestations of liver disease, steatorrhea, or complications from decreased fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Limitation of use: safety and effectiveness on extrahepatic manifestations of either SEDs or PDs (including Zellweger spectrum disorders) have not been established.

**Approval date:** March 17, 2015 (original approval letter dated March 17, 2015; a replacement approval letter was issued the same effective date to correct a labeling error)

**Pivotal trial:** CAC-91-10-10 (NCT00007020), "Investigation in the Pathogenesis of Liver Disease in Patients With Inborn Errors of Bile Acid Metabolism" — single-center, open-label, non-randomized treatment/compassionate-use protocol at CCHMC, 1992-2009, N=85 (ITT: 54 SED, 31 PD); supportive: extension trial CAC-002-01 (NCT01438411), open-label continuation, 2010-2016, N=53 (31 rollover + 10 de novo per the FDA Statistical Review's Table 1, growing to 53 total by study completion per ClinicalTrials.gov); also supportive: CAC-001-01 (NCT01115582), a small open-label formulation-bridging study (N=16) comparing the to-be-marketed capsule against the CCHMC-compounded capsule used in CAC-91-10-10

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md, §1) — estimated US prevalence of <100 total patients per the Office of Orphan Products Development designation (2007); multi-decade investigator-held-IND compassionate-use/expanded-access treatment protocol (1992-2009), begun purely as an academic research program with no initial intent to seek marketing approval, later retrospectively reconstituted (via a sponsor-created "Paper CRF" transcribed from patient charts starting in 2007) into the pivotal efficacy/safety dataset for an NDA; sponsor-submitted literature-derived historical control cohort found non-comparable to the treated population and rejected by FDA as an adequate control; open-label continuation/extension trial (CAC-002-01) submitted late in the review cycle and used to materially revise the peroxisomal-disorder efficacy conclusion

- *Endpoints:* no single pre-specified primary endpoint; continuous biochemical/growth measures (urinary bile acids by FAB-MS, ALT/AST, total/direct bilirubin, height/weight percentile, liver histology) compared pre- to post-treatment, summarized largely as median-to-median, mean-to-mean, and last-pre-treatment-to-last-post-treatment changes; a composite, explicitly **post hoc** responder definition combining survival, growth, and biomarker-normalization criteria was constructed by FDA's clinical reviewer during the review cycle, not specified in advance by the sponsor's protocol; survival/mortality assessed against sponsor-submitted historical-control and published natural-history (Poll-The et al. 2004) cohorts

- *Primary analysis:* descriptive single-arm response-rate analysis (point estimate, largely without formal confidence intervals) (Keyword_Taxonomy.md, §3); Kaplan-Meier estimation of survival, compared between treated patients and historical/natural-history controls; Fisher's exact test and a (unstratified) log-rank test used by the sponsor for the treated-vs-historical-control mortality comparison, with FDA's own reviewers disputing whether the log-rank/Kaplan-Meier framework was even an appropriate method for literature-derived comparator data; FDA's Statistical Review explicitly states the submitted study results "did not rely on appropriate inferential statistics or trial designs that would be considered adequate and well-controlled to support specific endpoint testing"

- *Missing data/bias:* pervasive, multi-decade missing/unavailable data from non-GCP, chart-abstracted compassionate-use records (1992-2007) with no prospective visit schedule, confirmed by an FDA Office of Scientific Investigations field inspection at the CCHMC site; sponsor's retrospective-literature-review historical control rejected by FDA reviewers as inadequately matched to the treated cohort on diagnosis, demographics, and baseline severity; FDA's Cross-Discipline Team Leader identified and corrected a misclassified historical-control patient's survival status and disputed the clinical meaningfulness of the sponsor's survival comparison in the PD population

- *Regulatory:* reviewer-vs-reviewer statistical dispute documented within a single review (Keyword_Taxonomy.md, §7) — the primary Medical Officer (Dr. Wen-Yi Gao) recommended accelerated approval (21 CFR 314.510) for the SED population only and a Complete Response for the PD population based on an initial responder analysis showing 0 PD responders, while the Cross-Discipline Team Leader (Dr. Lara Dimick-Santos) and the Division Deputy Director (Dr. Andrew Mulberg) disagreed, incorporating later-submitted extension-trial (CAC-002-01) growth and coagulopathy data to identify 10-11 PD responders and granting full/regular approval (not accelerated) for both populations, with the PD indication narrowed in labeling to patients exhibiting hepatobiliary manifestations; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened ("outside expertise was not deemed necessary"); Orphan Drug Designation (2007) for an ultra-rare inborn-error-of-metabolism population; Postmarketing Requirement under FDCA §505(o) for a prospective, long-term (≥10-year) observational registry study (≥55 patients) in lieu of a randomized confirmatory trial, given the impracticality of randomization in a disease this rare; priority review under PDUFA V, with the review cycle extended roughly five months past the original PDUFA goal date (October 21, 2014 to March 17, 2015) specifically to incorporate the extension-trial data

**Trial design & endpoints**

- CAC-91-10-10 was a single-center, open-label, non-randomized treatment protocol at CCHMC enrolling infants, children, and (less commonly) adults with cholestasis (conjugated bilirubin >2 mg/dL or elevated serum bile acids) and urine FAB-MS analysis positive for atypical bile acid metabolites consistent with a bile acid synthesis disorder (SED cohort), or a sub-study (CAC-92-8-19) enrolling patients with peroxisomal disorders on the basis of a neurologic evaluation plus elevated serum very-long-chain fatty acids (phytanic acid ≥4 µmol/L) and positive urine FAB-MS (PD cohort); the protocol began enrolling in 1992 and continued for 18 years, ultimately dosing 85 patients (per the Statistical/Summary Reviews' ITT accounting: 54 SED, 31 PD; per the Medical Review's "safety set" as of a later data cut: 79 patients, 50 SED + 29 PD — the discrepancy across FDA documents itself reflects the trial's rolling, chart-based data collection rather than a fixed database lock at a single planned analysis).

- Cholic acid was dosed at 10-15 mg/kg/day (11-17 mg/kg/day in patients with concomitant familial hypertriglyceridemia), administered orally as 50 mg or 250 mg capsules (compounded at the CCHMC pharmacy for CAC-91-10-10; a "to-be-marketed" (TBM) commercial capsule was bridged against the compounded capsule in a separate small study, CAC-001-01/NCT01115582, N=16) or as a liquid formulation.

- There was no pre-specified primary efficacy endpoint in the traditional sense. FDA's Medical Review reconstructed the evidentiary basis using a post hoc "responder" analysis: a **baseline cholestasis** definition (≥2 of: ALT/AST >50 U/L; total bilirubin >1 mg/dL or direct bilirubin >0.3 mg/dL; cholestasis on liver biopsy; urinary FAB-MS score >2) and a **responder** definition (≥2 biomarker criteria plus survival, or ≥1 biomarker criterion plus body-weight increase and survival), where biomarker criteria were ALT/AST reduced to <50 U/L (or reduced ≥80% from baseline), total bilirubin reduced to ≤1 mg/dL, and no cholestasis on repeat liver biopsy, and clinical criteria were body weight increased ≥10% (or stable at >50th percentile) and survival (initially "alive at last follow-up," later revised during review to "survival for ≥3 years on treatment, or alive at the end of" the extension trial).

- Per the approved label's final accounting (combining CAC-91-10-10 ["Trial 1"] and CAC-002-01 ["Trial 2"]): in the SED population, 28 of 44 efficacy-evaluable patients (64%) were responders (3β-HSD 22/37; AKR1D1 3/4; CTX 2/2; AMACR 1/1), and 41 of 62 SED patients overall (67%) survived >3 years from trial entry; in the PD population, 11 of 24 efficacy-evaluable patients (46%) were responders (neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy 3/6; generalized PD 1/1; Refsum disease 3/4; Zellweger syndrome 3/8; PD type unknown 1/5), while "no evidence of improvement in survival over that seen in historical controls could be demonstrated from the data presented" and only 13 of 31 PD patients (42%) survived >3 years.

- The sponsor also submitted a Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and Fisher's exact comparison of CAC-91-10-10 patients' survival against a literature-derived historical control; FDA's Medical Officer found the treated-vs-control overall death-rate difference non-significant (48% vs. 68%, Fisher's exact p=0.183) but time-to-death significantly longer in treated patients (129 vs. 9 months, log-rank p=0.01) — a result FDA's own Cross-Discipline Team Leader considered method-inappropriate ("the Kaplan-Meier method of analysis is likely not appropriate to this literature review data") and, separately, the published natural-history comparator (Poll-The et al. 2004, 31 PD patients) showed *higher* 4-year survival among untreated milder-PD patients than in CAC-91-10-10 (77% vs. 60%), a discrepancy the CDTL attributed partly to a misclassified historical-control patient and to the small numbers involved rather than to a true survival deficit from treatment.

- FDA's Statistical Review support was almost entirely process-oriented rather than a traditional analysis: the primary statistical reviewer helped the clinical team draft Information Requests, confirmed responder-analysis results, and helped identify a historical-control-inadequacy problem, rather than conducting an independent inferential analysis, because "this individual clinical study was identified as not being the proper basis for traditional confirmatory efficacy review" and "the rarity of this disease would have made a randomized controlled trial impractical even if that was to be the original objective of the study."

- FDA's three senior reviewers reached different regulatory conclusions from the same dataset: the Medical Officer (Dr. Wen-Yi Gao) recommended accelerated approval under 21 CFR 314.510 for SEDs only, with a Complete Response for PDs (his initial responder analysis, before the extension-trial data were incorporated, found zero PD responders); the Cross-Discipline Team Leader (Dr. Lara Dimick-Santos) and the Division Deputy Director (Dr. Andrew Mulberg) instead favored full/regular approval for both populations, after incorporating growth and coagulopathy data from the later-submitted CAC-002-01 extension trial that raised the PD responder count to 10-11 of ~24-30 evaluable patients; the final approved label restricts the PD indication to patients "who exhibit manifestations of liver disease, steatorrhea or complications from decreased fat soluble vitamin absorption," reflecting this compromise.

- A Postmarketing Requirement under FDCA §505(o) mandates a prospective, long-term (≥10-year) observational registry study of ≥55 patients (≥25 on cholic acid, ≥30 not on cholic acid, including ≥20 PD patients) to assess long-term safety and, implicitly, gather further effectiveness data in routine clinical use, given that a randomized confirmatory trial was considered infeasible in a population this small.

**Reverse-engineered SAP**

- *[inferred]* No formal hypothesis-testing framework, alpha-control, or pre-specified statistical analysis plan governed the primary efficacy claim, despite the Statistical Review's filing checklist marking "Endpoints and methods of analysis are specified in the protocols/statistical analysis plans" as satisfied — the substance of every other statistical/clinical/CDTL document instead describes efficacy being assessed via a responder definition constructed **during FDA's review of the data** (explicitly labeled "post-hoc" in the Medical Review), inferred from the fact that the responder criteria's survival component was itself revised mid-review (from "alive at last follow-up" to "survival ≥3 years on treatment, or alive at end of Trial 2") to accommodate the extension trial's longer follow-up.

- *[inferred]* The effective "primary analysis" was a within-patient, pre- vs. post-treatment comparison of continuous biomarkers (ALT/AST, bilirubin, urinary bile acid FAB-MS score) and growth (height/weight percentile) summarized as median-to-median, mean-to-mean, and last-to-last changes — inferred from the FDA Statistical Reviewer's Table 2 documenting a sequence of Information Requests that progressively asked the sponsor to reformat its own results into these three comparison structures for each biomarker in turn (bilirubin, then ALT/AST/height/weight, then graphical patient profiles), indicating no single pre-agreed comparison method existed at submission.

- *[inferred]* The differential regulatory outcome for the SED vs. PD populations (regular approval with no restriction for SED; regular approval but label-restricted to hepatobiliary-manifestation patients for PD) is inferable directly from the responder-rate magnitude and consistency across sub-defect groups reported in the label (SED responder rates ranging 59-100% across four enzyme defects, all directionally favorable, vs. PD responder rates ranging 20-100% across five disorder subtypes with the largest PD subgroups — Zellweger syndrome and PD-type-unknown — showing the weakest response, 38% and 20% respectively) — i.e., the label's restriction to PD patients "who exhibit manifestations of liver disease, steatorrhea, or complications from decreased fat-soluble vitamin absorption" operationalizes exactly the hepatobiliary-disease subgroup that the Division Deputy Director's review states responders in the PD group were drawn from.

- *[inferred]* The 10-15 mg/kg/day dosing regimen was not established via a dedicated dose-ranging trial but was carried forward unchanged from decades of empirical titration in the CCHMC compassionate-use program — inferable from the absence of any dose-response or dose-finding analysis in the Statistical or Clinical Reviews, and from the Division Deputy Director's Summary Review explicitly noting "There are no data provided in this application to justify fully the final dose of what is currently recommended in labeling," while nonetheless endorsing the dose based on decades of institutional clinical experience monitoring hepatic safety markers.

- *[inferred]* Liver-biopsy histology was treated as a supportive/tertiary biomarker rather than a quantitatively analyzed endpoint, inferable from the small, inconsistent denominators reported for this measure (6 SED patients and 9 PD patients with paired pre/post biopsies, out of efficacy-evaluable populations of 44 and 24 respectively) relative to the ALT/AST/bilirubin/weight measures reported for nearly all evaluable patients — indicating liver biopsy was available too sparsely across this decades-long, non-protocolized program to serve as more than a descriptive corroborating data point within the composite responder definition.

### 7. Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) — NDA 206038

**Sponsor:** Vertex Pharmaceuticals Incorporated

**Indication approved:** Treatment of cystic fibrosis (CF) in patients 12 years of age and older who are homozygous for the F508del mutation in the CFTR gene

**Approval date:** July 2, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** Two replicate Phase 3 trials — TRAFFIC (VX12-809-103), NCT01807923, and TRANSPORT (VX12-809-104), NCT01807949

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group design; two replicate 24-week Phase 3 trials (TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT), each with 3 arms (placebo, LUM 600mg qd/IVA 250mg q12h, LUM 400mg/IVA 250mg q12h), stratified randomization by age (<18 vs. ≥18), sex, and ppFEV1 severity at screening (<70% vs. ≥70%); biomarker-selected/enriched population (enrollment restricted to CF patients homozygous for the F508del-CFTR mutation, confirmed by genotype — Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1, analogous to KEYNOTE-024's PD-L1 selection and FLAURA's EGFR selection); no lumacaftor-monotherapy or ivacaftor-monotherapy arm was included in either pivotal trial, so FDA assessed lumacaftor's own contribution to the combination post hoc via a cross-study "synthesis method" comparing the pivotal trials' placebo-controlled effect against a separately-reviewed ivacaftor-monotherapy phase 2 trial (Study 770-104, from NDA 203-188) under a non-inferiority framework and an untestable "constancy assumption" (contribution-of-components assessment via cross-trial non-inferiority synthesis, used because no monotherapy arm existed in the pivotal trials themselves)

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint was absolute change from baseline in percent predicted FEV1 (ppFEV1) at Week 24, assessed as the average of the treatment effects at Week 16 and Week 24 (continuous pulmonary-function change-from-baseline endpoint, averaged across two visit windows — Keyword_Taxonomy.md §2 has no existing row for a spirometric/lung-function endpoint); five pre-specified key secondary endpoints tested in a fixed order (relative change in ppFEV1; absolute change in BMI; absolute change in the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R) respiratory domain score; responder rate, ≥5% relative-ppFEV1 improvement; number of pulmonary exacerbations through Week 24)

- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with subject as a random effect, treatment/visit/treatment-by-visit interaction as fixed effects, adjustment for sex/age-group/ppFEV1-severity strata, an unstructured covariance structure, and Kenward-Roger denominator degrees of freedom (Keyword_Taxonomy.md's MMRM row is defined around a sandwich variance estimator [Nirogacestat]; this trial instead used unstructured covariance/Kenward-Roger, definition flexed accordingly); Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test, stratified by sex/age-group/ppFEV1-severity, for the ≥5%-responder key secondary endpoint; negative binomial regression with an exposure-time offset for pulmonary exacerbation rate; ANCOVA-with-multiple-imputation and a stratified Wilcoxon rank-sum test used as primary-endpoint/exacerbation sensitivity analyses, respectively

- *Multiplicity:* Bonferroni split of the overall two-sided alpha (0.05) across the two active-dose arms (0.025 each), each compared separately to placebo; within each dose, fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing of the primary endpoint and the five key secondary endpoints in a pre-specified order, stopping at the first endpoint failing to reach p<0.025, after which all subsequent endpoints were reported as descriptive/nominal only (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §4, Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing)

- *Regulatory:* FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee, May 12, 2015; voted 12-1 to recommend approval even though members were split 3-4-6 on whether the data adequately established lumacaftor's own contribution to the combination, and unanimously felt the ivacaftor-monotherapy data were insufficient to conclude efficacy in this genotype); reviewer-documented data-coding discrepancy — the FDA statistical reviewer identified stratification-variable coding errors via two Information Requests and independently reproduced the primary and key-secondary analyses using corrected covariate values from the clinical database (FDA reviewer-conducted independent re-analysis correcting stratification-variable coding errors identified via Information Requests)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- TRAFFIC (809-103) and TRANSPORT (809-104) were near-identical 24-week, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trials conducted at over 90 centers in North America, Europe, and Australia, enrolling CF patients aged 12 and older, homozygous for F508del-CFTR, with 40%-90% ppFEV1 at screening and clinically stable disease; subjects were stratified by age (<18 vs. ≥18), sex, and ppFEV1 severity at screening (<70% vs. ≥70%) and randomized equally to placebo, LUM 600mg qd/IVA 250mg q12h, or LUM 400mg/IVA 250mg q12h, on top of usual CF background therapy.

- Primary endpoint: absolute change from baseline in ppFEV1 at Week 24, assessed as the average of the treatment effects at Week 16 and Week 24 (baseline defined as the most recent non-missing measurement, scheduled or unscheduled, before the first dose).

- Five key secondary endpoints, in pre-specified testing order: (1) relative change from baseline in ppFEV1 at Week 24 (same averaging convention); (2) absolute change from baseline in BMI at Week 24; (3) absolute change from baseline in CFQ-R respiratory domain score at Week 24; (4) responder rate (≥5% relative-ppFEV1 improvement) at Week 24; (5) number of pulmonary exacerbations through Week 24 (exacerbation defined identically to the phase 2 ivacaftor-monotherapy trial: new/changed antibiotic therapy for ≥4 of a defined list of signs/symptoms).

- Sample size/power: each trial planned to enroll 501 subjects (167 per arm), sized on the primary ppFEV1 endpoint assuming a 5-percentage-point treatment difference, a common SD of 8%, a 10% missing-data/dropout rate, a 2-sided 2-group t-test, and alpha=0.025 per active dose (to preserve overall two-sided Type I error at 0.05 across the two doses) — yielding ~99% power to detect a 5-point difference for either dose vs. placebo; no interim analysis was conducted in either trial. Actual enrollment was higher than planned: 1,122 subjects randomized across the two trials (559 in TRAFFIC, 563 in TRANSPORT), of whom 1,108 received ≥1 dose and 1,082 completed the trial.

- Statistical methods: primary and continuous key-secondary endpoints (relative ppFEV1, BMI, CFQ-R) were analyzed by MMRM (subject as random effect; treatment, visit, and treatment-by-visit interaction as fixed effects; adjusted for sex, baseline age group, and ppFEV1 severity at screening; unstructured within-subject covariance; Kenward-Roger denominator degrees of freedom), including both on-treatment measurements and measurements collected after early treatment discontinuation, with no imputation for missing MMRM data. The ≥5%-responder endpoint was analyzed by a stratified (sex/age-group/ppFEV1-severity) Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test; pulmonary exacerbations by negative binomial regression with the same covariates. Multiplicity was controlled by a Bonferroni split of alpha=0.05 into 0.025 per active dose, with a fixed-sequence hierarchical test of the primary endpoint followed by the five key secondaries (in the order listed above) within each dose, stopping at the first non-significant step. Analyses were conducted on the Full Analysis Set (all subjects who received any study drug, as randomized), with the Per-Protocol Set used only as a supportive analysis; sensitivity analyses included on-treatment-only MMRM, ANCOVA with multiple imputation (primary endpoint), a rank-based ANCOVA, and a stratified Wilcoxon rank-sum test (exacerbations).

- Results: in both trials, both LUM/IVA doses produced statistically significant improvement over placebo in absolute ppFEV1 at Week 24 — TRAFFIC: +4.0 points (600mg qd dose, 95% CI 2.6-5.4, p<0.0001) and +2.6 points (400mg dose, 95% CI 1.2-4.0, p=0.0003); TRANSPORT: +2.6 points (600mg qd dose, 95% CI 1.2-4.1, p=0.0004) and +3.0 points (400mg dose, 95% CI 1.6-4.4, p<0.0001). Of the five key secondary endpoints, only relative-ppFEV1 change replicated significance for both doses in both trials; the hierarchical procedure then halted at BMI in TRAFFIC (not significant for either dose) and at CFQ-R in TRANSPORT (not significant for either dose), so the responder-rate and exacerbation-rate results — though numerically favorable (e.g., exacerbation rate ratios of 0.6-0.7 vs. placebo) — were downgraded to descriptive/nominal per the pre-specified testing rule. Missing data were minimal (2.2%-2.5% study discontinuation) and results were consistent across sensitivity analyses, PPS, and demographic/regional/severity subgroups.

- FDA's separate cross-study "contribution of lumacaftor" analysis (statistical reviewer David Petullo) found that a synthesis-method 95% CI for the difference between LUM/IVA (integrated across TRAFFIC/TRANSPORT) and ivacaftor monotherapy (from phase 2 trial 770-104) did not exclude zero for ppFEV1 (e.g., 0.6 [-3.3, 4.5] for baseline ppFEV1 40-90%), meaning superiority of the combination over ivacaftor alone was not statistically established — a finding the Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee (PADAC) discussed at length before voting 12-1 to recommend approval anyway, given the combination's benefit over placebo and the unmet need in this genotype.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, ClinicalTrials.gov API, `documentSection` field for both NCT01807923 and NCT01807949]* — `null` (no sponsor protocol or Statistical Analysis Plan is posted in the Documents tab for either pivotal trial; the excerpts below are drawn instead from the FDA Statistical Review, which describes the pre-specified SAP content in detail).

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Lan Zeng review, §2.1.2 "History of Drug Development"]* — "The Division and the applicant agreed that for the pivotal Phase 3 studies, Lumacaftor monotherapy and ivacaftor as monotherapy was not required for the phase 3 studies; Data through the end of treatment (24 weeks) should be submitted for review; The primary efficacy endpoint was absolute change from baseline in percent predicted FEV1 (ppFEV1). Relative change in ppFEV1 could be a key secondary endpoint; The proposed mixed effects model with repeated measures (MMRM) was reasonable as long as the amount of missing data with respect to the primary endpoint was minimal; The proposed hierarchical testing strategy with Bonferroni correction was adequate for the control of Type I error."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Lan Zeng review, §3.2.2 "Statistical Methodologies"]* — "Each study planned to enroll 501 subjects (167 subjects for each treatment group) which were based on the protocol-defined efficacy endpoint of absolute change from baseline in ppFEV1 at Week 24, with the following assumptions: A treatment difference of mean absolute change from baseline in ppFEV1 of 5% between the active and placebo treatment groups, and a common standard deviation (SD) of 8%; A 10% missing data/drop-out rate; A 2-sided, 2-group, t-test of equal means; An alpha of 0.025 to address the multiplicity across the 2 active doses and ensure an overall Type I error of 0.05. These studies had approximately 99% power to detect a treatment difference of 5% in absolute change of ppFEV1 between either dose of LUM/IVA and placebo."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Lan Zeng review, §3.2.2]* — "The MMRM analysis included subject as a random effect, treatment, visit, and treatment-by-visit interaction as fixed effects, with adjustment for sex, age group at baseline, and ppFEV1 severity at screening. An unstructured covariance structure was assumed to model the within-subject errors. A Kenward-Roger approximation was used for the denominator degrees of freedom... To account for the comparison of two doses of LUM/IVA to placebo, a Bonferroni correction was applied to control the overall Type I error rate at 0.05. Within each individual trial, a hierarchical testing procedure was used for the primary and key secondary endpoints at α = 0.025 for each active treatment arm separately. The order of testing for the key secondary endpoints was as follows: Absolute change in ppFEV1, relative change in ppFEV1, absolute change in BMI, absolute change in CFQ-R, response rate based on improvement in ppFEV1, and pulmonary exacerbations. At each step, the comparison was considered statistically significant if the p-value < 0.025 and all previous tests also met this level of significance. If a test failed, all results from subsequent tests were considered descriptive (nominal p-values)."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Lan Zeng review, §3.2.4 "Results," on stratification-variable data errors]* — "During my review, I noted some discrepancies between the coding for the stratification variables and the actual value for these measurements in the clinical datasets. Information Requests were sent to the applicant on February 23, 2015 and March 10, 2015, respectively... To evaluate the impact of the stratification errors, I conducted a set of alternative analyses by including the actual values for baseline age, sex, and ppFEV1 at screening from the clinical database."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, David Petullo "Contribution of Lumacaftor" review, §1.1 "Overview"]* — "The applicant submitted the results from two phase 3 efficacy studies, VX12-809-103 (809-103) and VX12-809-104 (809-104) that evaluated placebo and two doses of lumacaftor/ivacaftor (LUM/IVA) in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients homozygous for the F508del mutation. These studies demonstrated a statistically significant treatment benefit in improving lung function (FEV1). However, these studies did not evaluate either lumacaftor or ivacaftor as monotherapies... The Pulmonary, Allergy, Drugs Advisory Committee convened on May 12, 2015 to discuss this application and whether they believed sufficient evidence was present to evaluate the contribution of lumacaftor to the combination product and overall approval of Orkambi. Even though the majority of Committee members agreed that there was not sufficient evidence to establish that the combination product was any better than ivacaftor monotherapy, they voted 12–1 to recommend approval of the combination product."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, David Petullo review, §2.2 "Statistical Methodologies"]* — "To evaluate the contribution of lumacaftor, I continued with the NI approach to test if LUM/IVA was superior to ivacaftor with respect to ppFEV1 and pulmonary exacerbations utilizing the synthesis method... A 95% confidence (CI) for the difference between ivacaftor and LUM/IVA was derived. If this CI excluded 0 (1 for exacerbations), one could conclude with 95% confidence that LUM/IVA was superior to placebo if one is willing to accept that the effect of ivacaftor in study 770-104 was similar to that in studies 809-103 and 809-104... Superiority was not established."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, §9 "Advisory Committee Meeting"]* — "The committee members opined that the current data for ivacaftor monotherapy are not sufficient to conclude efficacy for CF patients with the F508del mutation, and the data are not adequate to assess comparative clinical efficacy of the lumacaftor plus ivacaftor combination product to ivacaftor alone. Some committee members noted that they are placed in a difficult or impossible position in trying to determine clinical contribution of individual components and similar situations should be avoided in the future."

**Reverse-engineered SAP**

- *[inferred]* The MMRM's inclusion of both on-treatment measurements and post-discontinuation measurements (per FDA Statistical Review §3.2.2: "Both on-treatment measurements and measurements after treatment discontinuation... were included in primary analyses") implies a treatment-policy-like estimand strategy for intercurrent events (treatment discontinuation), rather than an on-treatment/hypothetical estimand — consistent with the minimal missing-data rate (2.2%-2.5%) the review reports and its conclusion that "missing data was minimal and was not a concern."

- *[inferred]* The Full Analysis Set (all FAS subjects analyzed as randomized) rather than an as-treated population was used for the primary analysis, inferred from the review's Table 1 patient-disposition structure distinguishing "All Subjects Set," FAS, PPS, and Safety Set, and the statement that "the primary analysis and analysis of key secondary endpoints were performed on the FAS," with the PPS reserved for supportive analyses only.

### 8. Uridine triacetate (Xuriden) — NDA 208169

**Sponsor:** Wellstat Therapeutics Corporation

**Indication approved:** Uridine replacement therapy for the treatment of hereditary orotic aciduria (HOA), an autosomal recessive uridine monophosphate synthase (UMPS) deficiency

**Approval date:** September 4, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** Study 401.13.001 ("Open-Label Study of Uridine Triacetate in Pediatric Patients With Hereditary Orotic Aciduria"), NCT02110147, open-label, single-arm/single-group, baseline-controlled, Phase 3, N=4

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* single-arm, open-label trial (no randomized concurrent control) in an ultra-rare monogenic disease — small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md, §1); reviewed under Section 505(b)(2) because dose selection and the efficacy case relied in part on decades of published literature on oral uridine (the drug's active metabolite, to which the sponsor held no right of reference) rather than on a company-run comparator arm — a 505(b)(2), literature-bridged historical-control approval built on physiological/pharmacological reasoning rather than a formal PK-equivalence bridging trial to an already-approved reference product; within-patient, baseline-controlled comparison for 3 of the 4 patients (each was already on chronic oral uridine and was switched to uridine triacetate, serving as their own historical control), plus a single treatment-naïve patient; the trial's 4 enrolled patients were reported by the sponsor to represent all HOA patients identifiable in the United States at the time, out of only ~20 cases (roughly 15 well-documented) ever reported worldwide in the medical literature.

- *Endpoints:* individualized (patient-specific) primary endpoint — each patient's own pre-existing abnormal hematologic parameter was designated in advance as that patient's personal primary endpoint (neutrophil count/percent for Patient 1, white blood cell count for Patient 2, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) for Patients 3 and 4), rather than one common endpoint across patients; for the 3 patients transitioning from uridine, success was defined as stability of that parameter at Days 28/42 vs. Day 0 baseline, while the treatment-naïve patient (Patient 4) required improvement; shared secondary endpoints across all 4 patients were urinary orotic acid and orotidine concentrations (pharmacodynamic markers of the enzymatic defect) and, in the 3 pediatric patients, growth (height/weight and height/weight-velocity z-scores).

- *Primary analysis:* descriptive patient-level case-series analysis — no pooled response rate, confidence interval, p-value, or formal hypothesis test was computed for any endpoint, individually or pooled, anywhere in the sponsor's submission, FDA's statistical review, or the approved label; FDA's clinical review states plainly that "the applicant provided descriptive statistics for efficacy and safety analyses" and that sample size "was not based on formal statistical considerations" (more minimal even than the taxonomy's existing "descriptive single-arm response-rate analysis," since no aggregate rate or interval was ever constructed); no multiplicity adjustment was applied across the 4 patients' distinct individualized endpoints, each analyzed as an independent case rather than for pooled cross-patient inference.

- *Missing data/bias:* undocumented pre-treatment baseline value limiting interpretability of a within-patient stability claim — the approved label discloses that documentation of Patient 2's white blood cell count prior to uridine initiation was not available, so "stability" after switching to uridine triacetate could not be benchmarked against a true pre-uridine baseline for that patient.

- *Regulatory:* Orphan Drug Designation (August 9, 2013), Breakthrough Therapy Designation (April 30, 2014), and an 8-month PDUFA Priority Review were granted; a Rare Pediatric Disease priority review voucher under FDCA §529 was awarded at approval; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened; the application was exempt from the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) by virtue of the orphan designation; no REMS was required; postmarketing commitments required a 2-year continuation of extension-study follow-up and development of a revised drug-product dissolution method.

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study 401.13.001 was an open-label, single-arm, two-center (Children's Hospital of Michigan, Detroit; Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh of UPMC) Phase 3 trial with a 42-day ("6-week") Main Study followed by an open-ended Treatment Extension in which patients continued uridine triacetate with safety/efficacy monitored roughly every 6 months; 3 of the 4 enrolled patients had previously been treated with oral uridine (obtained under compassionate-use/expanded-access arrangements from a supplier that discontinued the product in December 2012 — the shortage that prompted FDA to recruit Wellstat as a replacement manufacturer, per the FDA Summary Review) and were switched at Day 1 to oral uridine triacetate at a starting dose of 60 mg/kg/day, escalatable per protocol to a maximum of 300 mg/kg/day, though no patient in the trial received more than 120 mg/kg/day; the 4th patient was treatment-naïve; patients were 3 male, 1 female, ages 3 to 19 years (per the approved label).

- Primary endpoint (individualized per patient, as pre-agreed with FDA in December 2013/January 2014 meetings): neutrophil count/percent (Patient 1), white blood cell count (Patient 2), and MCV (Patients 3 and 4); for the 3 transitioning patients, success required stability of that parameter at Days 28 and 42 versus Day 0 baseline; for the treatment-naïve Patient 4, success required improvement in MCV.

- Secondary endpoints (shared): urinary orotic acid and orotidine concentrations, and (in the 3 pediatric patients) growth parameters (height/weight and height/weight-velocity z-scores).

- Sample-size rationale: none — per the FDA Summary Review, the 4 enrolled patients "represent all patients with HOA that have been identified in the US by the applicant," and the FDA Clinical Review states directly that the trial's sample size "was not based on formal statistical considerations" (§5.3.10).

- Statistical methods used: purely descriptive tabulation of each patient's values at Baseline/Day 28/Day 42/6-month extension against pre-specified thresholds (age-specific normal ranges and a fixed "stability" margin of ~15-30% deterioration from baseline); the FDA statistical reviewer (Min Min, PhD; concurring Yeh-Fong Chen, PhD) independently recomputed the sponsor's percent-change figures from raw data but applied no additional inferential test.

- Result at 6 weeks (Main Study): Patients 1 and 3 met their pre-specified stability criteria; Patient 2's WBC count remained within range after switching, though the label notes documentation of Patient 2's pre-uridine WBC count was unavailable; Patient 4 (treatment-naïve) did not meet the pre-specified improvement criterion for MCV; no adverse events were attributed to uridine triacetate.

- Result at 6 months (Treatment Extension): hematologic parameters were stable or improved in all 4 patients — Patient 1's neutrophil percent and count rose into the normal reference range for the first time in the patient's life after dose increases (60→95→120 mg/kg/day); urinary orotic acid/orotidine remained stable in 3 patients, while one patient's orotic acid rose more than twofold during the extension (per the FDA Statistical Review); all patients showed growth stability or improvement.

- FDA's clinical reviewer (Carla Epps, MD, MPH) explicitly concluded that the 6-week Main Study data alone were insufficient — only the neutropenic patient (Patient 1) showed a change clearly attributable to treatment — and that FDA's efficacy conclusion instead rested on combining the 6-month extension data with "the totality of evidence" from the published historical case-report literature on oral uridine (the active moiety), which established HOA's natural history (rapid relapse of hematologic abnormalities and orotic aciduria within weeks of treatment interruption) as the implicit historical control, plus a physiological/pharmacokinetic "scientific bridge" connecting uridine triacetate dosing to historically effective uridine doses (150-300 mg/kg/day of uridine ≈ 60-120 mg/kg/day of the more bioavailable prodrug).

- FDA's statistical/clinical reviewers separately critiqued the sponsor's fixed percentage-based "stability" margin as not calibrated to each hematologic parameter's known intra-patient biological variability, citing published NHANES-based reference data (~20% day-to-day variability in neutrophil count vs. ~2% in MCV) and concluding, after applying that variability benchmark instead of the sponsor's flat threshold, that the observed within-patient changes were consistent with genuine clinical stability rather than measurement noise.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, Executive Summary, p.3]* — "The sponsor submitted one open-label phase 3 study with four patients to demonstrate the maintenance effect of uridine triacetate as uridine replacement therapy in pediatric patients with hereditary orotic aciduria (HOA)... Among the four patients, one was treatment-naïve and the other three who had been treated with uridine before the study had experienced positive therapeutic responses to uridine."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §2.1 Overview, p.3-4]* — "HOA is a rare congenital autosomal recessive disorder, and only about 20 cases of this rare disorder have been documented worldwide."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §2.1, "features initially agreed to by the FDA," p.4-5]* — "The primary efficacy endpoints in the trial were hematologic and individualized for each patient. Secondary endpoints were based on urinary orotic acid and uridine exposure (PK)... Demonstration of a 'stable response' as assessed by clinical efficacy endpoints in Protocol 401.13.001 was acceptable to support marketing approval."

*[verbatim, FDA Clinical Review, §5.3.10 "Statistical Analysis Plan," p.~27-28]* — "The applicant provided descriptive statistics for efficacy and safety analyses. Determination of Sample Size: The trial sample size was not based on formal statistical considerations."

*[verbatim, FDA Clinical Review, §1.2 Risk Benefit Assessment, p.6-7]* — "The benefit-risk analysis of uridine triacetate for the proposed indication is favorable. This is based on a review of retrospective case studies of 18 patients with HOA treated empirically with other unapproved uridine formulations and clinical review findings for four patients enrolled in the single pivotal trial (Study 001). The published case studies and the pivotal trial patients represent all confirmed cases of patients with this disorder."

*[verbatim, FDA Clinical Review, §1.2, p.7]* — "Although all three patients who transitioned from uridine maintained stable hematologic parameters after 6 weeks of treatment, based on the prior evidence (or lack thereof) of a hematologic response with uridine, only the neutropenic patient can be considered to have demonstrated sustained clinical benefit. No improvement in hematologic status was observed in the treatment-naïve patient. Therefore, based on the primary efficacy findings for Study 001 alone, there is not sufficient evidence to support efficacy for uridine triacetate."

*[verbatim, FDA Clinical Review, §5.3.10 "Reviewer Comments," p.~28-29]* — "the applicant's definition of clinical stability (any deterioration in value was not more than 15% to 30% worse than the baseline value) for patients with baseline abnormal values is inadequate for identifying clinically significant deterioration in hematologic status... Published analyses of hematology laboratory values in healthy adults reported about a 20% day-to-day individual variability in neutrophil count... compared to a 2% variability in MCV. Therefore, the appropriate margin of change to establish clinical stability should be based on the expected range of intrapatient variability for a particular hematologic parameter."

*[verbatim, FDA Clinical Review, §5.3.10, p.~28]* — "The trial design for Study 001 meets the regulatory requirements for adequate and well-controlled trials as delineated in 21 CFR 314.126... The use of individualized hematologic endpoints is appropriate for evaluation of HOA due to the clinical heterogeneity of the disease... interruption or withdrawal of adequate uridine replacement therapy in patients with baseline abnormalities in hematologic parameters is known to result in worsening status within several weeks. Thus, the six-week study duration should be sufficient to evaluate for clinical stability."

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §4 "Summary and Conclusions," p.13]* — "The sponsor submitted one open-label phase 3 study with 4 patients to demonstrate the maintenance effect of uridine triacetate as uridine replacement therapy in pediatric patients with hereditary orotic aciduria (HOA). The primary endpoints included Neutrophils, WBC count and MCV, and each patient had his/her own primary endpoint. The statistical reviewer confirmed the sponsor's efficacy findings."

*[verbatim, FDA Summary Review, Division Director Review, §9 "Advisory Committee Meeting," p.16]* — "This application did not require an Advisory Committee meeting. The clinical program was designed with FDA input, there were no efficacy or safety issues identified in the review of this application."

*[verbatim, approved Package Insert, §14 Clinical Studies]* — "For patients switched from oral uridine to oral XURIDEN (Patients 1, 2, and 3), the primary endpoint was stability of the hematologic parameter; for the treatment-naïve patient (Patient 4), the primary endpoint was improvement of the hematologic parameter... Patient 4 did not meet the pre-specified endpoint of improvement of the hematologic parameter."

**Reverse-engineered SAP** (no genuine sponsor SAP/protocol document is public; the points below infer analytic logic not spelled out verbatim in any single source, each traced to a specific reported result):

- [inferred] The sample size of 4 was not derived from any power or precision calculation but was fixed entirely by disease epidemiology — the sponsor is inferred to have designed the trial as an exhaustive case series (enroll every identifiable US patient) rather than a sampled cohort, traceable to the FDA Summary Review's statement that the 4 patients "represent all patients with HOA that have been identified in the US by the applicant."

- [inferred] The SAP is inferred to have pre-specified a per-patient endpoint-assignment rule — assign whichever hematologic parameter was abnormal at trial entry as that patient's individualized primary endpoint — rather than one common endpoint, traceable to the distinct per-patient endpoint assignments reported in Table 4 of the label (neutrophils for Patient 1, WBC for Patient 2, MCV for Patients 3-4).

- [inferred] The ~15-30% "stability" deterioration threshold is inferred to have been a sponsor-chosen decision rule not grounded in a formal biological-variability calculation, since FDA's own clinical reviewer subsequently had to construct the appropriate variability benchmark (NHANES-based ~20% neutrophil vs. ~2% MCV day-to-day variability) after the fact to check whether the sponsor's flat thresholds were clinically meaningful — traceable to the Clinical Review §5.3.10 reviewer comments quoted above.

- [inferred] No inferential statistic (CI, p-value, hypothesis test) was ever planned at any level, individual or pooled — inferred from the complete absence of any such statistic in the label's Table 4, the Statistical Review's Table 3.3, or the Clinical Review's efficacy narrative, consistent with FDA's characterization of the analysis as providing only "descriptive statistics."

- [inferred] The ultimate efficacy conclusion's reliance on 6-month extension-phase data plus the published historical case-report literature, rather than the 6-week Main Study primary analysis alone, is inferred to reflect a post hoc widening of the evidentiary base beyond what the original 6-week primary analysis was designed to support — traceable directly to the clinical reviewer's statement that "based on the primary efficacy findings for Study 001 alone, there is not sufficient evidence to support efficacy for uridine triacetate."

### 9. Asfotase alfa (Strensiq) — BLA 125513

**Sponsor:** Alexion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (development originated under Enobia Pharma Inc., IND 100,619 opened June 2008; Alexion acquired Enobia and notified FDA of the transfer on February 7, 2012)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of patients with perinatal/infantile- and juvenile-onset hypophosphatasia (HPP)

**Approval date:** October 23, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** No single randomized pivotal trial; two indication-specific open-label trial programs, each compared against a separately extracted retrospective natural-history historical-control cohort — perinatal/infantile-onset HPP: ENB-002-08 (NCT00744042, N=11) with long-term extension ENB-003-08 (NCT01205152), pooled with ENB-010-10 (NCT01176266, N=59; combined qualifying N=68) vs. natural-history control ENB-011-10 (NCT01419028, N=48); juvenile-onset HPP: ENB-006-09 (NCT00952484, N=8 juvenile-onset patients of 13 enrolled) with extension ENB-008-10 (NCT01203826) vs. natural-history control ALX-HPP-502 (NCT02104219) and its substudy ALX-HPP-502s (NCT02235493, N=6, gait subset)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1) — cohorts of 11 (ENB-002-08), 59 (ENB-010-10), and 8-of-13-enrolled (ENB-006-09) patients; two independently dosed company trials in the same indication pooled post hoc into one primary efficacy population for perinatal/infantile-onset HPP (ENB-002-08/ENB-003-08 + ENB-010-10, combined N=68), related to but not an exact match of the taxonomy's "Cross-trial pooled/integrated analysis (independently conducted, separately sponsored/protocoled trials)" (§1), since both trials share a sponsor/drug and the pooling plan was negotiated with FDA well into trial conduct; primary efficacy analysis compared against a non-randomized, non-concurrent historical control drawn from a separately conducted, eligibility-matched retrospective natural-history chart-review study rather than a randomized concurrent arm — no existing taxonomy term precisely covers this design ("retrospective natural-history chart-review historical control"); a sponsor-proposed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-arm confirmatory trial for juvenile-onset HPP (ENB-014-12, ~30 patients planned) was never conducted after FDA gave the sponsor the option to substitute the historical-control approach instead

- *Endpoints:* perinatal/infantile-onset — primary endpoint overall survival (time to death from birth to point of last contact), secondary endpoint invasive ventilator-free survival, both endpoints and the pooling/historical-control plan agreed with FDA only after trial conduct was underway (Type C meeting April 16, 2013; Type B meeting September 3, 2013); juvenile-onset — the primary efficacy analysis as actually conducted was change in gait (modified Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment-Gait, mPOMA-G, an instrument not validated in HPP), though ENB-006-09's original SAP specified change in HPP-related rickets severity (Radiographic Global Impression of Change [RGI-C] and Rickets Severity Score [RSS]) as primary; growth (height/weight z-scores) ultimately became the "chief clinical parameter" driving FDA's approval decision for juvenile-onset HPP, with RGI-C radiographic response, the 6-Minute Walk Test, and gait serving as supportive parameters

- *Primary analysis:* perinatal/infantile-onset — Kaplan-Meier estimation, unstratified log-rank test, hazard ratio with 95% CI (proportional-hazards assumption checked graphically via log(-log(estimated survival)) vs. log(time)), Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs on point survival-rate estimates, all pre-specified as exploratory/supportive because the historical-control comparison was formalized only during trial conduct; FDA's statistical reviewer additionally ran a Nelson-Aalen sensitivity analysis and a "worst-case" imputation (censored patients counted as failures at last contact), both concordant with the primary result; juvenile-onset — purely descriptive comparison (change-from-baseline shift tables, means/medians, RGI-C responder proportions at a ≥2-point threshold) between ENB-006-09/ENB-008-10 (n=8) and ALX-HPP-502/ALX-HPP-502s (n=32 growth/radiographic, n=6 gait), with no confidence intervals or formal hypothesis tests on the primary comparisons

- *Missing data/bias:* survival analysis population for perinatal/infantile-onset HPP restricted to the 68 of 70 treated patients (97%) who happened to meet the ENB-011-10 natural-history study's eligibility criteria; a post hoc sensitivity subgroup limited to the 46 (of 68) patients who received the eventual labeled 6 mg/kg/week regimen without dose modification was consistent with the overall result; FDA's statistical reviewer explicitly identified the standard historical-control biases — confounding from unmeasured/latent baseline variables absent a randomization mechanism, and retrospective selection bias in which patients were extracted for chart review (potentially yielding an overly optimistic historical event rate) — as inherent, unresolved limitations rather than analyses correctable post hoc

- *Regulatory:* no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (Medical Review §9.3: "No advisory committee was held for this submission"); Orphan Drug Designation (September 2008), Fast Track Designation (May 2009), Breakthrough Therapy Designation (May 2013), Rare Pediatric Disease Designation (voucher issued at approval), Priority Review (extended 3 months for a major amendment, per PDUFA V); PREA requirements waived given orphan designation; three postmarketing requirements imposed under FDCA §505(o), including a ≥5-year prospective observational safety registry for hypersensitivity, ectopic-calcification, and immune-complex-mediated-reaction risk; the primary FDA statistical reviewer's write-up explicitly disagreed with the Division's decision to let the sponsor substitute the historical-control approach for the previously discussed randomized, placebo-controlled juvenile-onset trial (ENB-014-12) that the sponsor had been "willing to conduct"

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Two parallel development streams, one per HPP severity phenotype, each anchored by open-label company trial(s) plus a separately conducted retrospective natural-history historical control; no randomized concurrent-control trial was conducted for either indication.

- Perinatal/infantile-onset HPP: ENB-002-08 (NCT00744042) — phase 1/2, multinational, multicenter, open-label, single-arm, 24-week trial, N=11 (ages 3 weeks to 39.5 months at entry, severe disease defined by rachitic chest deformity, vitamin-B6-dependent seizures, or failure to thrive), with long-term extension ENB-003-08 (NCT01205152, up to 5 years); patients received a 2 mg/kg loading infusion then 1 mg/kg SC three times weekly with escalation up to 3 mg/kg three times weekly. ENB-010-10 (NCT01176266) — phase 2/3, multinational, multicenter, open-label, single-arm, 4-year trial (N=59 in the FDA statistical review's efficacy population; 69 total enrolled per ClinicalTrials.gov), dosed at 6 mg/kg/week as either 1 mg/kg six times weekly or 2 mg/kg three times weekly. Combined, 70 perinatal/infantile-onset patients were treated across the two trials; 68 (97%) met ENB-011-10's eligibility criteria and were included in the primary survival analysis.

- Historical control: ENB-011-10 (NCT01419028) — international, multicenter, retrospective chart-review natural-history study, N=48 extracted patients with perinatal/infantile-onset HPP, matched to trial eligibility criteria; for patients alive as of the last chart record, the treating physician was contacted to confirm current survival status.

- Primary endpoint (perinatal/infantile-onset): overall survival (time to death from birth to point of last contact). Secondary endpoint: invasive ventilator-free survival (time to start of invasive ventilation or death). Both endpoints, the cross-trial pooling, and the ENB-011-10 historical-control comparison were negotiated between Alexion and FDA's Division of Gastroenterology and Inborn Errors Products (DGIEP) at a Type C meeting (April 16, 2013) and a Type B meeting (September 3, 2013) — after the trials were already underway, so FDA's statistical review designated the resulting hypothesis tests as post hoc/exploratory rather than confirmatory.

- No formal sample-size calculation was performed for any of the perinatal/infantile-onset or juvenile-onset trials: "There was no planned enrollment for any of these studies given the paucity of this patient population; all efforts were made to enroll/extract as many patients as possible" (FDA Statistical Review).

- Juvenile-onset HPP: ENB-006-09 (NCT00952484) — phase 2, multinational, multicenter, open-label, randomized (2 mg/kg vs. 3 mg/kg three times weekly), parallel-dose, 24-week trial; 13 patients enrolled and treated (8 juvenile-onset, 5 perinatal/infantile-onset patients also included in this trial and analyzed with that cohort instead), with long-term extension ENB-008-10 (NCT01203826, up to 3.5 years).

- Historical control: ALX-HPP-502 (NCT02104219) and its substudy ALX-HPP-502s (NCT02235493) — retrospective chart-review natural-history study of juvenile-onset HPP patients, N=32 for the growth/radiographic comparison, N=6 for the gait/mPOMA-G comparison subset.

- The ENB-006-09 protocol was amended mid-conduct, as agreed with FDA, to change its primary efficacy analysis from change in HPP-related rickets severity (by RGI-C and RSS scores) to change in gait (mPOMA-G score) versus the ALX-HPP-502s historical control; this became the pre-specified "primary efficacy analysis" FDA's clinical reviewer formally evaluated, but it was judged insufficient on its own — limited by its post hoc nature, an unvalidated instrument in the HPP population, baseline disease-severity differences between cohorts, and a re-reading methodology (videos originally filmed for other ambulation assessments). FDA's approval decision instead rested predominantly on growth (height/weight z-scores) as the "chief clinical parameter," with RGI-C radiographic response, the 6-Minute Walk Test, and gait as supportive.

- A sponsor-proposed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-arm, 24-week confirmatory trial for juvenile-onset HPP (ENB-014-12, ~30 patients, 15 per arm) was discussed as an alternative at the same September 3, 2013 Type B meeting; DGIEP instead gave Alexion the option to rely on the historical-control comparison, and ENB-014-12 was never conducted — a choice the primary FDA statistical reviewer explicitly stated he disagreed with.

- Statistical methods (perinatal/infantile-onset): Kaplan-Meier survival curves, unstratified log-rank test, hazard ratio with 95% CI (proportional-hazards assumption checked graphically), Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs on point survival-rate estimates; FDA-reviewer-generated results were overall survival HR 0.089 (95% CI 0.039–0.202, log-rank p<0.0001) and invasive ventilator-free survival HR 0.278 (95% CI 0.162–0.478, log-rank p<0.0001), both against the ENB-011-10 historical control (N=48); sensitivity analyses using a Nelson-Aalen estimator, a "worst-case" censoring-as-failure imputation, and a subgroup limited to patients dosed at the eventual labeled 6 mg/kg/week regimen without modification (46/68) were all concordant with the primary result. All hypothesis tests were designated exploratory/supportive, and the statistical reviewer stated "no inferential statistics should be presented within the final product labeling" — a recommendation the approved label did not fully follow (see below).

- Statistical methods (juvenile-onset): purely descriptive — shift tables of change-from-baseline height/weight z-score category (>+0.5 improvement / -0.5 to +0.5 stable / <-0.5 worsening), mean/median change-from-baseline comparisons for growth, and RGI-C responder proportions (≥2-point improvement on the 7-point scale) — with no confidence intervals, formal hypothesis tests, or pre-specified covariate adjustment for the primary comparisons (a sponsor post hoc RSS-baseline-adjusted RGI-C analysis was also presented after treated and control cohorts turned out to differ in baseline rickets severity). FDA's statistical reviewer concluded this evidentiary approach was "not adequate from a statistical perspective," while the clinical review team based its recommendation on "the totality of descriptive data."

- A discrepancy between sources: the approved label's Table 7 reports a perinatal/infantile-onset survival hazard ratio of 0.14 (95% CI 0.05–0.39), footnoted as "adjusted for year of diagnosis," versus the FDA statistical reviewer's own unadjusted reviewer-generated HR of 0.089 (95% CI 0.039–0.202) for the same comparison — indicating the label reflects a distinct (year-of-diagnosis-adjusted) sponsor analysis rather than the reviewer's independently reproduced unadjusted Kaplan-Meier/log-rank result, and that inferential statistics (HR, CI) were in fact included in the final label despite the statistical reviewer's recommendation against doing so.

(applied to the label's reported hazard ratio of 0.14, 95% CI 0.05–0.39, for overall survival — the sponsor's own labeling analysis, distinct from the FDA reviewer's unadjusted reviewer-generated HR of 0.089 above.)

**Reverse-engineered SAP** (no genuine sponsor SAP or protocol is publicly posted for any of the eight ClinicalTrials.gov records associated with this BLA; the following points are inferred from the FDA review documents and label rather than quoted from a sponsor SAP)

- *[inferred]* The differing hazard-ratio point estimates for perinatal/infantile-onset overall survival — label HR 0.14 (95% CI 0.05–0.39, "adjusted for year of diagnosis") versus the FDA statistical reviewer's own unadjusted HR 0.089 (95% CI 0.039–0.202) — suggest the sponsor's actual primary/label survival analysis specified a Cox proportional-hazards model with year-of-diagnosis as a covariate (plausibly to account for improving neonatal/respiratory supportive care over the multi-decade span covered by the pooled trial and natural-history cohorts), distinct from the simpler unadjusted Kaplan-Meier/log-rank approach the FDA reviewer used to independently reproduce the result; this is inferred solely from the label's footnote and the numeric discrepancy, since no sponsor SAP language describing the covariate model is available.

- *[inferred]* The height/weight z-score change-from-baseline cut-point of ±0.5 used to categorize perinatal/infantile- and juvenile-onset growth "shift" results as worsened/stable/improved was most likely a threshold specified in an SAP or SAP amendment during BLA review rather than in the original trial protocols, since the FDA statistical review attributes the choice directly to review-team judgment ("The z-score cut-point of 0.5 was chosen due to it being considered clinically meaningful by the clinical review team") rather than to a pre-specified, externally validated cutoff — consistent with a post hoc analysis-plan element negotiated with FDA rather than a protocol-specified endpoint definition.

- *[inferred]* The RGI-C responder threshold (≥+2 on the 7-point scale) functioned as the de facto primary skeletal-response criterion presented in the label for perinatal/infantile-onset HPP (50/68, 74% responders by last assessment), even though RGI-C was never part of the FDA-agreed primary/secondary endpoint set (overall survival/ventilator-free survival) for that indication; this is inferred from the label's §14.1 presentation of RGI-C data as a purely single-arm descriptive result immediately following the formal survival endpoints, with the label stating plainly "No comparative data were available from historical controls" for this specific analysis — unlike the juvenile-onset RGI-C comparison, which did have a historical-control arm (2/32, 6% responders) and functioned as a genuine (if post hoc) between-cohort comparison.

### 10. Sebelipase alfa (Kanuma) — BLA 125561

**Sponsor:** Alexion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (BLA originally filed October 21, 2014 by Synageva BioPharma Corporation, which Alexion acquired in 2015 prior to approval)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of patients with a diagnosis of Lysosomal Acid Lipase (LAL) deficiency, encompassing both the rapidly progressive infantile-onset form historically called Wolman disease (presenting within the first 6 months of life) and the later-onset form historically called Cholesteryl Ester Storage Disease (CESD)

**Approval date:** December 8, 2015

**Pivotal trial:** Two pivotal studies supported full approval under 21 CFR Part 601 for two distinct patient populations — LAL-CL02 / ARISE ("Acid Lipase Replacement Investigating Safety and Efficacy"), NCT01757184, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in children/adults with CESD; and LAL-CL03, NCT01371825, open-label single-arm dose-escalation phase 1/2 trial in infants with rapidly progressive Wolman-disease-phenotype LAL deficiency, compared against a historical control extracted from the retrospective natural-history study LAL-1-NH01

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 trial (LAL-CL02/ARISE; 1:1 randomization via IVRS/IWRS, stratified by age <12/≥12 years, screening ALT <3×ULN/≥3×ULN, and baseline use of lipid-lowering medication), 20-week double-blind period followed by an open-label extension to 130 weeks; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §1) for LAL-CL03 (9 treated infants); historical natural-history-cohort comparison for a survival endpoint in a single-arm ultra-rare-disease trial, full-approval pathway under 21 CFR Part 601 rather than a threshold-based historical-control comparison (distinct from the taxonomy's existing "non-inferiority analysis against a fixed historical-control threshold," since this used a directly matched external cohort analyzed by log-rank test/Cox HR rather than a fixed rate threshold)

- *Endpoints:* LAL-CL03 primary endpoint was an age-anchored survival endpoint — time to death from birth up to Month 12 — compared against an external historical-control cohort rather than a within-trial randomized comparator; LAL-CL02/ARISE primary endpoint was a biochemical/enzyme-normalization responder endpoint (normalization of ALT at Week 20), with 8 pre-specified secondary endpoints in a fixed testing order (% change from baseline in LDL-c, non-HDL-c, AST normalization, triglycerides, HDL-c, liver fat content by MRI-PDFF, improvement in liver histopathology, and liver volume by MRI)

- *Primary analysis:* Kaplan-Meier estimation and unstratified log-rank test with Cox-model hazard ratio (LAL-CL03, survival vs. historical control); exact/Clopper-Pearson-type binomial confidence intervals for survival rates and responder proportions; Fisher's exact test (unstratified, LAL-CL02/ARISE primary ALT-normalization analysis) with Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test and Breslow-Day homogeneity test as FDA sensitivity analyses; Wilcoxon rank-sum test (unstratified) as the sponsor's pre-specified analysis for continuous lipid/imaging secondary endpoints, with ANCOVA (adjusting for the three randomization strata plus baseline value) as the FDA statistical reviewer's sensitivity analysis

- *Multiplicity:* Fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §4) across the 9 pre-specified LAL-CL02/ARISE endpoints (ALT→LDL-c→non-HDL-c→AST→triglycerides→HDL-c→liver fat content→liver histopathology→liver volume), each step gated on statistical significance (p<0.05) of the prior step; the chain ran successfully through liver fat content (7th step, p<0.0001) before failing at liver histopathology improvement (8th step, p=0.4216), which by the pre-specified rule rendered the final step (liver volume) exploratory only

- *Interim/alpha-spending:* Data Monitoring Committee (DMC/DSMB) (Keyword_Taxonomy.md §5) — an Independent Data Monitoring Committee operated under a charter for both LAL-CL02 and LAL-CL03 to review safety data and approve dose escalations; no formally planned interim efficacy analyses were conducted in either trial

- *Missing data/bias:* Worst-case ("failure") imputation for censored patients in the LAL-CL03 survival analysis and for missing binary responder data (ALT/AST normalization, liver histopathology) in LAL-CL02, plus no-change-from-baseline imputation for missing continuous secondary endpoints (adapting the taxonomy's "non-responder imputation for missing binary/diary efficacy data" concept to a survival/biochemical-responder context rather than a patient-diary context); FDA statistical reviewer noted the historical-control comparison's inherent risks of selection bias (retrospective cohort selection) and confounding from unmeasured baseline imbalances, magnified by very small sample size

- *Regulatory:* No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened ("the safety profile is acceptable ... the application did not raise significant safety or efficacy issues that were unexpected for a biologic of this class," per the approval letter); Orphan Drug Designation (July 1, 2010), Fast Track Designation (June 14, 2011), Breakthrough Therapy Designation for Wolman disease (May 13, 2013), Priority Review under PDUFA V, and a Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Voucher awarded concurrently with approval; FDA clinical-review rejection of a sponsor's statistically significant primary endpoint (ALT normalization) as insufficient on its own to support the CESD approval, substituting lipid secondary endpoints (LDL-c foremost) as the basis for the labeled efficacy claim (analogous in structure to the pattern flagged in the Pozelimab/Veopoz entry)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- **LAL-CL02 (ARISE):** multinational (17 countries, 55 sites), randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 trial in treatment-naïve children/adults with CESD (ages 4-58; 66 randomized, 36 sebelipase alfa/30 placebo); patients stratified by age (<12/≥12 years), screening ALT (<3×ULN/≥3×ULN), and lipid-lowering-medication use, then randomized 1:1 to IV sebelipase alfa 1 mg/kg or matching placebo every other week for a 20-week double-blind period, followed by open-label sebelipase alfa (all patients) to Week 150.

- Sample-size rationale (FDA Statistical Review, §3.2.2.1): assuming a 71% ALT-normalization response rate on sebelipase alfa vs. 17% on placebo, 50 randomized patients (~25/arm) would provide 97% power to detect a significant difference via Fisher's exact test at two-sided α=0.05; actual enrollment (66) exceeded this target.

- LAL-CL02 primary result: ALT normalization at Week 20 in 11/36 (30.6%) sebelipase alfa vs. 2/30 (6.7%) placebo, treatment difference 23.9% (95% CI 6.4%-41.4%), Fisher's exact p=0.0271 (CMH-adjusted p=0.0242, Breslow-Day homogeneity p=0.178). Per the pre-specified step-down procedure, this triggered formal testing of LDL-c (LS-mean difference in % change from baseline -22.4%, 95% CI -31.24 to -13.56, p<0.0001), non-HDL-c (-21.0%, p<0.0001), AST normalization (41.7% vs 3.3%, difference 38.4%), triglycerides (-12.9%, p=0.0435), HDL-c (+18.5%, p<0.0001), and liver fat content by MRI-PDFF (-27.4%, p<0.0001) — all statistically significant — before the chain stopped at liver histopathology improvement (62.5% vs 40.0%, Fisher's p=0.4216, not significant), rendering the final pre-specified endpoint (liver volume) exploratory.

- **LAL-CL03:** multinational (9 countries, 12 sites), open-label, single-arm, intra-patient dose-escalation phase 1/2 trial in infants with rapidly progressive Wolman-disease-phenotype LAL deficiency (growth failure within the first 6 months of life), ≤8 months of age at first infusion; starting dose 0.35 mg/kg QW escalated to 1 mg/kg QW (and up to 3-5 mg/kg QW for disease progression). The 6th protocol amendment (April 5, 2012) changed the primary objective from safety/tolerability to survival at 12 months of age vs. baseline-matched historical-control infants from the retrospective natural-history study LAL-1-NH01; of 35 LAL-1-NH01 patients extracted, 21 were adjudicated appropriate comparators. Of 11 LAL-CL03 infants screened, 2 died during screening (severe liver failure); 9 were enrolled, treated, and analyzed (Primary Efficacy Analysis Set), all ≤8 months of age at first infusion.

- LAL-CL03 primary result (FDA Statistical Review, Table 4): 6/9 (66.7%, 95% CI 29.9-92.5%) sebelipase alfa-treated infants alive at Month 12 vs. 0/21 (0%, 95% CI 0-16.1%) historical-control infants; hazard ratio 0.141 (95% CI 0.040-0.496), log-rank p=0.0006. Result was robust to a Per-Protocol Set sensitivity analysis, a worst-case ("failure") imputation of censored patients, a Nelson-Aalen sensitivity analysis, and a repeat analysis using time to death from birth up to point of last contact (same HR/CI/p-value).

- Statistical reviewer conclusion (FDA Statistical Review, §5.1): both study designs, and the corresponding sponsor SAPs, were "deemed adequate from a statistical perspective," with no statistical review issues precluding approval; for LAL-CL03 specifically, "the determination of the clinical effectiveness of sebelipase alfa will rely more on clinical judgment than on the statistical rigor usually required for larger randomized controlled studies," given the extreme rarity of Wolman disease (estimated ~600 total US patients) and the inherent limitations of a retrospective historical-control comparison.
