### 31. Odevixibat (Bylvay) — NDA 215498

**Sponsor:** Albireo Pharma, Inc. (original NDA applicant; Ipsen acquired Albireo in 2023 and is the current marketing sponsor)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of pruritus in patients 3 months of age and older with progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC); labeled limitation of use that odevixibat may not be effective in PFIC type 2 patients with ABCB11 variants resulting in non-functional or complete absence of bile salt export pump (BSEP-3) protein

**Approval date:** July 20, 2021

**Pivotal trial:** Trial A4250-005 (PEDFIC 1), NCT03566238

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=62, three arms)
- *Endpoints:* diary-based composite pruritus responder endpoint (caregiver-reported ObsRO scratching score); serum bile acid (sBA) responder rate as a region-specific co-primary endpoint later downgraded to exploratory
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA on least-squares means for the responder-proportion primary endpoint; mixed model for repeated measurements (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance matrix and multiple imputation for a supportive continuous secondary endpoint
- *Multiplicity:* closed testing procedure (combined-dose vs. placebo gatekeeper at one-sided α=0.025, then individual-dose comparisons)
- *Missing data/bias:* non-responder imputation for missing diary-based pruritus assessments; multiple imputation under both missing-at-random (MAR) and missing-not-at-random (MNAR) assumptions as a sensitivity analysis for a continuous secondary endpoint
- *Regulatory:* FDA constructed and relied on an endpoint definition alternative to the sponsor's prespecified primary endpoint, outside the pre-specified testing hierarchy, to resolve interpretability concerns ("FDA-substituted post hoc primary-endpoint definition outside the formal testing hierarchy"); FDA approved only the lower of two studied doses despite the sponsor proposing the higher dose for labeling, based on a benefit-risk tradeoff rather than an oncology dose-optimization program ("FDA dose down-selection outside Project Optimus/oncology context")

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Trial A4250-005 (PEDFIC 1) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, international phase 3 trial in children with PFIC types 1 and 2, consisting of a 35- to 56-day screening period, a 24-week double-blind treatment period, and a 4-week follow-up period; 62 patients were randomized 1:1:1 to odevixibat 40 mcg/kg/day (N=23), odevixibat 120 mcg/kg/day (N=19), or matching placebo (N=20) at 28 sites (5 US, 15 Europe, 8 rest-of-world), stratified by PFIC class (type 1 vs. 2) and age group (6 months-5 years, 6-12 years, 13-18 years)
- Prespecified primary endpoint (US): the mean percentage of caregiver-reported (ObsRO) pruritus assessments over the 24-week treatment period classified as "positive," where a positive assessment was a scratching score ≤1 or at least a 1-point drop from a biweekly AM/PM baseline average; a global protocol also specified a different primary endpoint for the EU and rest-of-world regions — proportion of patients with ≥70% reduction in fasting serum bile acids (sBA) from baseline or reaching ≤70 micromole/L at 24 weeks — but FDA determined the bioanalytical method used for sBA had not been adequately validated per 2018 FDA bioanalytical-method-validation guidance, so sBA results were treated as exploratory/supportive rather than primary
- FDA raised substantive concerns with the sponsor's prespecified primary endpoint definition (comparing a same-day integer score to a rounded biweekly average baseline, and treating an unvalidated "1-point drop" criterion as clinically meaningful) and, outside the formal testing hierarchy, independently analyzed an alternative endpoint (percentage of assessments with a scratching score ≤1, with no baseline-drop criterion) plus a supportive endpoint (change in Worst Weekly Scratching Score from baseline to Weeks 21-24)
- Secondary/exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in monthly average scratching scores (overall, daytime, nighttime, worst-daily), sBA change from baseline, growth parameters (height/weight/BMI Z-scores), and ALT; none of the secondary/exploratory endpoints were adjusted for multiplicity
- Sample size: protocol planned ~60 patients; no formal interim analysis was described for this trial
- Primary statistical method: ANCOVA model with treatment arm, AM baseline pruritus score, PM baseline pruritus score, and the randomization stratification factors (PFIC class, age class) as covariates/fixed effects; LS means, LS mean differences, 95% CIs, and one-sided p-values were reported for each active dose vs. placebo
- Multiplicity control: a closed testing procedure first compared the average effect of the pooled 40 mcg/kg and 120 mcg/kg dose groups against placebo at one-sided α=0.025; only if that combined comparison was significant were the two individual doses tested against placebo (each also at one-sided α=0.025), with the individual dose's adjusted p-value taken as the maximum of the combined-dose p-value and its own unadjusted p-value
- Missing-data handling: all missing pruritus assessments, and all assessments scheduled after an intercurrent event (premature discontinuation, death, rescue treatment initiation), were classified as "negative" (non-responder) pruritus assessments for the primary composite endpoint; for the continuous Worst Weekly Scratching Score secondary endpoint, FDA compared four missing-data handling approaches under an MMRM model — no imputation (MAR), multiple imputation (MI) under MAR, the Applicant's MI under an MNAR assumption restricted to imputed values in the observed scoring range (0-4), and an Agency MI variant relaxing that range restriction
- Reported primary-endpoint result (ITT, N=62): LS mean percentage of positive assessments was 30.1% (placebo) vs. 58.3% (40 mcg/kg) and 51.8% (120 mcg/kg); LS mean differences vs. placebo were 28.2 percentage points (95% CI 9.8-46.6, one-sided p=0.0016 unadjusted/0.0019 adjusted) for 40 mcg/kg and 21.7 points (95% CI 1.9-41.5, p=0.0163) for 120 mcg/kg. Under FDA's alternative endpoint definition, only the 40 mcg/kg dose retained statistical significance (LS mean difference 22.2 points, 95% CI 4.7-39.6, p=0.0069); the 120 mcg/kg dose showed a numerically smaller, non-significant effect (16.9 points, 95% CI -2.0-35.7, p=0.0390 nominal but outside the CI-based significance threshold FDA emphasized)
- Dosing decision: because 120 mcg/kg/day did not show better efficacy than 40 mcg/kg/day on FDA's endpoint and was associated with more liver-test abnormalities and diarrhea requiring interruption, FDA approved only the 40 mcg/kg/day starting dose as safe and effective, despite the sponsor having proposed 120 mcg/kg/day for labeling

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Integrated Review, Section 6.2.1.1 "Design, Trial A4250-005," p.27]*

> "Trial A4250-005 (NCT03566238) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of odevixibat compared to placebo in children with progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis types 1 and 2... The protocol planned to enroll approximately 60 eligible patients who were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive 40 mcg/kg/day of odevixibat, 120 mcg/kg/day of odevixibat, or a matching placebo. The protocol specified that randomization was stratified according to PFIC class (types 1 and 2) and age group (6 months to 5 years, 6 to 12 years, and 13 to ≤18 years)."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.3 "Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial A4250-005," p.32]*

> "The protocol specified that for the primary endpoint (proportion of positive pruritus assessments at the patient level over the 24-week treatment period), the comparisons between the treatment groups is evaluated using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model. The model includes treatment arm, AM baseline pruritus score, PM baseline pruritus score, and the randomization stratification factors, i.e., PFIC class and age class... The protocol/SAP (statistical analysis plan) specified a multiple testing procedure to control the type I error rate for evaluating the primary efficacy endpoint for each of the two dose groups compared to the placebo group. In the closed testing procedure, the average effect of the 40 mcg/kg/day and 120 mcg/kg/day dose groups was first compared with the placebo group. If the one-sided p-value was ≤0.025, the one-sided p-values are calculated for the comparisons of the 40 mcg/kg/day dose versus placebo and the 120 mcg/kg/day dose versus placebo... No adjustments were specified for multiple comparisons when testing secondary and exploratory efficacy variables."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.3.2 "Uncertainty of Primary Efficacy Endpoint," p.44]*

> "The prespecified primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of 'positive pruritus assessments' at the patient level over the 24-week treatment period, where a positive pruritus assessment for each patient on each assessment day was a dichotomous outcome defined as occurring when one or both of the following two criteria were met: 'a scratching score of ≤1 or at least a 1-point drop from baseline on the Albireo ObsRO instrument'... The Agency had concerns about the Applicant's definition of a positive pruritus assessment."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.3.1 "Conclusions," p.43]*

> "The main source of evidence to support the approval came from one adequate and well controlled trial, i.e., Trial A4250-005... Whether the efficacy was evaluated by the Applicant's prespecified primary endpoint or by FDA's alternative endpoint, treatment with odevixibat demonstrated statistically persuasive results in improvement of pruritus... Therefore, the Agency accepts a single adequate and well-controlled trial with confirmatory evidence as sufficient to support a recommendation for approving odevixibat for 'treatment of pruritus.'"

*[verbatim, same source, Table 14, p.37]*

> "Prespecified primary endpoint: Mean percentage of assessments that are ≤1 or at least a 1-point drop from baseline — LS mean (SE): Placebo 30.1 (9.1), 40 mcg/kg/day 58.3 (8.6), 120 mcg/kg/day 51.8 (9.5); LS mean difference (SE): 28.2 (9.2) and 21.7 (9.9); 95% CI: (9.8, 46.6) and (1.9, 41.5); one-sided unadjusted p-value: 0.0016 and 0.0163."

### 32. Avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt (Nexviazyme) — BLA 761194

**Sponsor:** Genzyme, a Sanofi Company

**Indication approved:** Treatment of patients 1 year of age and older with late-onset Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase [GAA] deficiency)

**Approval date:** August 6, 2021

**Pivotal trial:** Trial EFC14028 (COMET), NCT02782741

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial (avalglucosidase alfa vs. alglucosidase alfa, not placebo); non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchy; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=100)
- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in percent-predicted forced vital capacity (FVC), upright position, at Week 49 (primary); change from baseline in 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance at Week 49 (key secondary)
- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measurements (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance matrix, estimating a treatment-policy estimand
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (non-inferiority on primary → superiority on primary → formal superiority test of key secondary gated on primary superiority)
- *Missing data/bias:* tipping-point analysis (multiple imputation) to test robustness of the non-inferiority conclusion to departures from the missing-at-random assumption; ANCOVA and Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney sensitivity analyses using last-observation-carried-forward-style handling of missing Week 49 values
- *Regulatory:* FDA-derived non-inferiority margin based on reanalysis of a historical placebo-controlled trial (LOTS/AGLU02704) of the active comparator, not a concurrent placebo arm; approval granted on a met non-inferiority result after the pre-specified superiority test on the primary endpoint narrowly missed significance (p=0.0626)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Trial EFC14028 (COMET) was a phase 3, randomized (1:1), double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, multicenter, multinational trial comparing avalglucosidase alfa to alglucosidase alfa (the previously approved enzyme replacement therapy) in treatment-naive adults and adolescents with late-onset Pompe disease; 100 patients were randomized (51 avalglucosidase alfa, 49 alglucosidase alfa), mean age 48.1 years, 94% White, both drugs dosed every other week for a 49-week primary analysis period (PAP) followed by an open-label extension treatment period (ETP) in which all patients received avalglucosidase alfa
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline to Week 49 in percent-predicted FVC in the upright position, analyzed as a treatment-policy estimand ("the difference between avalglucosidase alfa treatment and alglucosidase alfa in mean FVC (% predicted) change from baseline to week 49 regardless of whether intercurrent events have occurred") via MMRM including baseline FVC, age, gender, treatment group, visit, and treatment-by-visit interaction, with visits at Weeks 13, 25, 37, and 49 and an unstructured covariance matrix; analysis population was the modified intent-to-treat (mITT) set (all randomized patients receiving ≥1 infusion, which in this trial was all randomized patients)
- Key secondary endpoint: change from baseline to Week 49 in 6MWT distance, analyzed via an analogous MMRM including baseline 6MWT distance and baseline FVC as additional covariates; formal superiority testing of this endpoint was gated on the primary endpoint achieving superiority
- Other secondary endpoints (all via MMRM, no multiplicity adjustment): change from baseline in maximal inspiratory/expiratory pressure (MIP/MEP), lower-extremity muscle strength composite score, Quick Motor Function Test (QMFT) total score, and SF-12 Physical/Mental Component Summary scores (PCS/MCS)
- Non-inferiority margin: -1.1%, derived by FDA/sponsor from a reanalysis of the historical placebo-controlled trial AGLU02704 (LOTS), in which alglucosidase alfa's treatment effect over placebo on the same FVC endpoint at 52 weeks had a 95% CI lower bound of 1.7% (point estimate 3.7%, 95% CI 1.7-5.6; a sensitivity analysis using different missing-data handling gave 3.6%, 95% CI 1.4-5.8); because both lower bounds exceeded 1.1%, FDA considered a -1.1% NI margin (preserving at least half of the historical effect) acceptable
- Testing hierarchy: non-inferiority was assessed first via the two-sided 95% CI for the MMRM treatment difference (NI met if the lower bound exceeded -1.1%); only if NI was met would a two-sided superiority test at alpha=0.05 be performed on the same primary endpoint, and only if that superiority test was significant would a formal superiority test of the key secondary (6MWT) be conducted
- Missing-data handling: the primary MMRM analysis performed no explicit imputation, relying on a missing-at-random (MAR) assumption; sensitivity analyses included (1) a tipping-point analysis using multiple imputation to identify how large a shift against avalglucosidase alfa would be needed to overturn the NI conclusion, (2) an ANCOVA model using each patient's last available value for missing Week 49 assessments, and (3) a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test with missing Week 49 values imputed as the worse of baseline or last assessment; a supportive linear mixed-effects model (random intercept and slope) was also specified
- Reported primary result (mITT, N=100): LS mean change in FVC (% predicted) from baseline to Week 49 was 2.89% (avalglucosidase alfa) vs. 0.46% (alglucosidase alfa); estimated treatment difference 2.43 percentage points (95% CI -0.13 to 4.99). Because the CI lower bound (-0.13) exceeded the pre-specified NI margin (-1.1%), the trial met non-inferiority; the superiority p-value was 0.0626, narrowly missing the pre-specified two-sided alpha=0.05 threshold, so the formal (alpha-controlled) superiority claim and the gated formal test of the 6MWT key secondary were not met — FDA's review nonetheless treated the endpoint's broader profile (safety, secondary endpoints, unmet medical need in a serious ultra-rare disease) as supporting approval on the strength of the non-inferiority finding
- FDA sensitivity work: the review team additionally excluded each trial site one at a time from the MMRM to check for a single-site effect, and separately confirmed the primary result was not being driven by a baseline FVC imbalance between arms

As the lower bounds of the 95% CIs were larger than 1.1%, the proposed NI margin of -1.1% was considered acceptable by the Agency."

As the lower bound of the 95% CI for the difference is larger than the prespecified NI margin of -1.1%, the trial met noninferiority for the primary efficacy endpoint. The p-value for the superiority test was 0.06, slightly larger than the prespecified significance level of 0.05."

### 33. Maralixibat (Livmarli) — NDA 214662

**Sponsor:** Mirum Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of cholestatic pruritus in patients with Alagille syndrome (ALGS) 1 year of age and older

**Approval date:** September 29, 2021

**Pivotal trial:** Trial LUM001-304 (ICONIC), NCT02160782

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized-withdrawal design (open-label run-in followed by a double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal period); small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=31 enrolled, 29 randomized)
- *Endpoints:* serum bile acid (sBA) responder-based composite as the sponsor's protocol-specified primary endpoint; diary-based observer-reported pruritus endpoint (ItchRO(Obs)) as the endpoint FDA actually relied on for approval
- *Primary analysis:* descriptive comparison of mean change and 95% CI in fasting sBA and in ItchRO(Obs) scores between randomized-withdrawal arms (no formal hypothesis test framework was pre-specified as controlling for the endpoint FDA ultimately used)
- *Missing data/bias:* multiple summaries of daily pruritus scores (morning-only, evening-only, average) checked for consistency as an informal robustness/sensitivity approach
- *Regulatory:* FDA declined to accept the sponsor's protocol-specified primary endpoint (sBA responder change) as a validated surrogate or adequate basis for a clinical-benefit claim, and instead grounded approval in its own analysis of secondary pruritus endpoints in the full randomized-withdrawal population ("FDA approval grounded in the Agency's own analysis of a secondary/exploratory endpoint after the sponsor's protocol-specified primary endpoint was rejected as an unvalidated surrogate"); approved for ages 1 year and older despite the pivotal trial enrolling no adults, based on unmet need and a presumed common mechanism/biology across ages

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Trial LUM001-304 ("ICONIC") was a Phase 2 study in patients with Alagille syndrome and pruritus, consisting of an 18-week open-label run-in period, a 4-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized drug-withdrawal (RWD) period, a subsequent 26-week open-label after-randomized-withdrawal (ARW) period, and an optional long-term extension; 31 patients enrolled, 29 completed the open-label run-in and were randomized 1:1 at Week 18 to continue maralixibat (400 mcg/kg, N=13) or switch to placebo (N=16) for the 4-week RWD period (all patients remaining at Week 18 were randomized, not only sBA responders); randomization was stratified by whether the patient had achieved a >50% sBA reduction from baseline to Week 12 (under earlier protocol versions) and by study site
- Sponsor's protocol-specified primary endpoint: mean change from Week 18 to Week 22 (i.e., across the RWD period) in fasting sBA levels, restricted to the subset of patients who had already responded to open-label maralixibat with a ≥50% sBA reduction from baseline to Week 12 or Week 18 — a modified intent-to-treat (MITT) population of only 15 of the 29 randomized patients (5 maralixibat, 10 placebo)
- FDA rejected reliance on this endpoint, stating sBA change is "not a validated surrogate endpoint that can be used to demonstrate clinical benefit," and noting sBA is "distal from disease course and clinical outcomes" (it does not reflect hepatocellular bile-acid levels, the presumed mediator of liver damage); pruritus, a secondary endpoint family in the protocol, had no single prespecified primary definition and no multiplicity adjustment across its multiple operationalizations
- FDA instead analyzed several ItchRO(Obs)-based pruritus endpoints in the full 29-patient randomized population as the basis for its efficacy conclusion, emphasizing the weekly average of the worst daily ItchRO(Obs) score at Week 22 and its change from Week 18 to Week 22; these analyses were checked for consistency using different daily-score summaries (morning-only, evening-only, and averaged scores)
- Reported result (RWD period, N=29): weekly average worst-daily ItchRO(Obs) score at Week 22 was 1.6 (95% CI 1.1-2.1) for maralixibat vs. 3.0 (95% CI 2.6-3.5) for placebo; change from Week 18 to Week 22 was 0.2 (95% CI -0.3 to 0.7) for maralixibat vs. 1.6 (95% CI 1.2-2.1) for placebo, a between-arm mean difference of -1.4 (95% CI -2.1 to -0.8); after the RWD period, patients who had been on placebo resumed maralixibat and returned to a similar level of pruritus improvement as those continuously treated
- No formal alpha-controlled hypothesis-testing hierarchy governed the pruritus endpoints FDA relied on; the reported comparisons were treated as descriptive/estimation-based (means and 95% CIs) rather than a pre-specified primary-endpoint significance test, consistent with the endpoint not having been the protocol's designated primary analysis
- Age extrapolation: the trial enrolled only pediatric patients, but FDA approved the drug down to age 1 year and did not restrict the indication to the trial's enrolled ages, reasoning that ALGS biology and the ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT) mechanism of action are shared across ages
- Safety database: 86 patients total (31 from LUM001-304 plus 55 from supportive lower-dose studies), median 32.3 months exposure, almost entirely open-label; the 4-week RWD period was the only placebo-controlled exposure window in the entire program

### 34. Vosoritide (Voxzogo) — NDA 214938

**Sponsor:** BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.

**Indication approved:** To increase linear growth in pediatric patients with achondroplasia who are 5 years of age and older with open epiphyses; approved under accelerated approval based on improvement in annualized growth velocity (AGV), with continued approval contingent on verification and description of clinical benefit (final adult height) in confirmatory trial(s)

**Approval date:** November 19, 2021

**Pivotal trial:** Study 111-301, NCT03197766

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=121); pre-trial natural-history run-in period used to establish each subject's own baseline growth rate (Study 111-901) rather than an in-trial placebo run-in
- *Endpoints:* annualized growth velocity (AGV), change from baseline at Week 52, as an intermediate/surrogate primary endpoint (not a validated surrogate, per FDA); height Z-score and upper-to-lower body segment ratio as key secondary endpoints
- *Primary analysis:* analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with treatment, stratum (sex × Tanner stage), baseline age, baseline AGV, and baseline height Z-score as covariates
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing across key secondary endpoints, gated on the primary endpoint
- *Missing data/bias:* pre-specified multiple imputation approach (using post-discontinuation height data from same-arm discontinuers) could not be applied because too few subjects discontinued; the Applicant instead extrapolated each subject's own baseline AGV forward to impute missing standing/sitting height, and FDA ran a conservative sensitivity analysis assuming zero growth during any missing-data period
- *Regulatory:* accelerated approval (21 CFR 314.500 pathway) granted on a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial rather than the more typical single-arm design, because the primary endpoint (AGV) itself was judged an unvalidated surrogate requiring confirmatory final-height data ("Accelerated approval on a surrogate endpoint despite a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal design"); FDA Advisory Committee (joint Pediatric Advisory Committee/Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee) shaped the endpoint and design choice before the pivotal trial began, but did not review the completed NDA; external natural-history comparator data (AchNH study) used to contextualize long-term open-label follow-up growth in the extension studies ("External natural-history comparator arm to support long-term/uncontrolled follow-up efficacy assessment")

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study 111-301 was a 52-week, randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial of vosoritide 15 µg/kg/day (subcutaneous) vs. placebo in children with achondroplasia (ACH) ages 5-18 years with open epiphyses; randomization was stratified by sex and Tanner stage of pubertal development (stratum: male Tanner I, female Tanner I, male Tanner >I, female Tanner >I); subjects were required to have at least 6 months of prospectively collected baseline growth data from a preceding non-interventional natural-history study (Study 111-901) before enrolling, so that each subject's own pre-treatment AGV served as an individual baseline rather than relying on an in-trial placebo run-in or an external population norm
- FDA treated this single trial as the pivotal adequate and well-controlled study, explicitly invoking the rare/serious-disease unmet-need standard: "Because ACH is a serious and rare disease with an unmet medical need, FDA accepted the single adequate and well-controlled Study 111-301... to demonstrate efficacy"
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline in AGV (cm/year) at Week 52, where AGV = (height at Date 2 − height at Date 1) / (interval length in days) × 365.25; baseline AGV was calculated using the standing height from at least 6 months prior to Study 111-301 enrollment (measured in Study 111-901) versus the Study 111-301 baseline height
- Key secondary endpoints (hierarchically tested, gated behind the primary): change from baseline in height Z-score (age/sex-standardized against CDC average-stature reference data) at Week 52, and change from baseline in upper-to-lower body segment ratio (sitting height / [standing height − sitting height]) at Week 52 — the latter chosen because a decreasing ratio (less disproportionality) was considered beneficial while an increasing ratio was flagged as a potential risk signal (e.g., reduced mobility)
- Sample size: 55 subjects per arm were planned for ~90% power to detect a 1.75 cm/year AGV difference, assuming a pooled SD of 2.80 cm/year, using a two-sided two-sample t-test at alpha=0.05; 121 subjects were ultimately randomized (60 vosoritide, 61 placebo) and 119/121 completed the study
- Missing-data handling: the pre-specified plan was multiple imputation using post-discontinuation height measurements from other same-arm discontinuers, but only 2 vosoritide-treated subjects discontinued (and both left the study entirely), making that approach infeasible; the Applicant instead imputed missing standing/sitting heights at Week 52 by projecting each subject's own baseline AGV forward from their last observed height, and FDA additionally ran a conservative sensitivity analysis assuming no growth at all during the missing-data window, which produced a smaller but consistent treatment-difference estimate
- Subgroup analyses (sex, age group, race, baseline AGV, height Z-score, Tanner stage) used the same ANCOVA model with added subgroup and subgroup-by-treatment terms, supplemented by a Bayesian hierarchical shrinkage model for subgroup estimates
- Reported primary result (FAS, N=121): LS mean AGV change from baseline to Week 52 was 1.40 cm/year (95% CI 1.15-1.66) for vosoritide vs. -0.17 cm/year (95% CI -0.42 to 0.08) for placebo; LS mean difference 1.57 cm/year (95% CI 1.22-1.93, p<0.0001). The effect was detectable by Week 13 and maintained through Week 52; FDA attributed the pronounced early effect partly to a catch-up-growth phenomenon and cautioned that short-term AGV gains do not by themselves establish an effect on final adult height
- Regulatory basis: FDA and the Medical Policy and Program Review Council (MPPRC, June 16, 2021) agreed the data constituted substantial evidence of effectiveness for AGV improvement, but concluded AGV is an intermediate clinical endpoint rather than a validated surrogate in this disproportionate-short-stature population (unlike GH-deficiency/Turner-syndrome/idiopathic-short-stature settings where AGV-to-final-height translation is established), because no final-height data or validated growth-prediction model existed for ACH; the Council specifically favored the accelerated-approval pathway with a postmarketing requirement (rather than a postmarketing commitment) "to generate reliable data on final height," given PMCs are "not always robust, reliable, or followed through"

No second Advisory Committee meeting was convened to review the completed NDA; FDA's review states the 2018 meeting "adequately addressed the important elements of the clinical development program."

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

> "The Applicant conducted 1 randomized, double-blind, controlled trial. Because ACH is a serious and rare disease with an unmet medical need, FDA accepted the single adequate and well-controlled Study 111-301 conducted in subjects ages 5 to 18 years to demonstrate efficacy of the drug in patients with ACH ages 5 to 18 years... The subjects were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive vosoritide 15 µg/kg or placebo. The randomization was stratified by sex and Tanner stage of pubertal development. The subjects were required to have at least 6 months of baseline growth data collected in observational Study 111-901 prior to enrollment in Study 111-301."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.3 "Statistical Analysis Plan, Study 111-301," p.27]*

The baseline AGV was established in the observational run-in period of Study 111-901, based on the standing height at least 6 months prior to enrollment to Study 111-301. An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model was used to determine the treatment difference between vosoritide and placebo at Week 52. It included the following baseline factors: Treatment group; Stratum: Male Tanner Stage I, Female Tanner Stage I, Male Tanner Stage > I, Female Tanner Stage > I; Age at baseline; AGV at baseline; Height Z-score at baseline... The key secondary endpoints were analyzed using a similar ANCOVA model as the primary efficacy endpoint. Hierarchical testing was used to control the type I error."

*[verbatim, same source, "Sample Size Calculation," p.27]*

> "With 55 subjects planned in each group (vosoritide and placebo), the power to detect a difference between them of 1.75 cm/year in change from baseline in AGV at 12 months was approximately 90%. This assumes the pooled standard deviation (SD) of the change from baseline in AGV is 2.80 using a two-sided two-sample t-test at the 0.05 significance level."

*[verbatim, same source, Table 10 and surrounding text, Section 6.2.1.4.2, p.30-31]*

> "The vosoritide-treated group demonstrated superiority to placebo in terms of change in AGV from baseline to Week 52... The difference in LS mean change from baseline between the 2 groups was 1.57 cm/year (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.22, 1.93; p-value<0.0001)."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.3.4 "Use of AGV as Surrogate Marker...," p.52]*

> "The team considers AGV to be an intermediate clinical endpoint and not a validated surrogate endpoint in this population with disproportional growth, because sufficient data on final height was not provided... to validate the use of AGV in this population, and no predictive validation model exists... Thus, based on these limitations, the submitted data support accelerated approval, but data on final height are needed to confirm that changes in the intermediate clinical endpoint of AGV ultimately translate into the intended clinical benefit of improved final adult height."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 11 "Advisory Committee Summary," p.113]*

> "Joint public advisory committee meeting of the PAC and EMDAC was held on July 30, 2018... The Advisory Committee members agreed that the AGV can be used as a primary endpoint; however, final height is a key goal of treatment in the intended population... All Committee members agreed that a randomized, placebo-controlled study design is optimal to provide statistically and clinically significant efficacy data and sufficient safety data."

### 35. Ganaxolone (Ztalmy) — NDA 215904

**Sponsor:** Marinus Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of seizures associated with cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) deficiency disorder (CDD) in patients 2 years of age and older

**Approval date:** March 18, 2022

**Pivotal trial:** Study 1042-CDD-3001 (Marigold), NCT03572933

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=101)
- *Endpoints:* percent change from baseline in 28-day major motor seizure frequency (diary-based); ≥50% responder rate; Clinical Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I)
- *Primary analysis:* Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Hodges-Lehmann estimator of location shift; supportive ANCOVA on log-transformed seizure frequency
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (primary → 2 key secondary endpoints, in protocol-specified order, gated on primary significance)
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design with O'Brien-Fleming boundaries for up to 2 planned interim analyses; Data Monitoring Committee (DMC/DSMB) agreed the second interim analysis was unnecessary once full enrollment occurred before the first interim look
- *Missing data/bias:* two pre-specified sensitivity analyses for subjects who permanently stopped seizure diary recording — one imputing placebo-quartile-matched values, one imputing the median of the 5 highest placebo-group seizure counts (a conservative/worst-case-style approach); FDA separately investigated an eDiary programming error that created duplicate seizure entries and a nontrivial volume of caregiver-proxy diary entries, concluding neither materially affected the result
- *Regulatory:* FDA reviewer flagged that the SAP did not pre-specify the alpha-level for the key secondary endpoints under the group-sequential design, noting that testing them at the full two-sided 0.05 level (as the sponsor's plan implied) would inflate the overall type I error (reviewer-documented statistical-methodology gap, distinct from the sponsor executing a different analysis than agreed); ganaxolone is a CNS-active neuroactive steroid subject to DEA controlled-substance scheduling, supported by a dedicated human abuse-potential (HAP) study using lorazepam as a positive control and Drug Liking VAS as the endpoint

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study 1042-CDD-3001 ("Marigold") was a phase 3, global, double-blind, randomized (1:1), placebo-controlled trial of adjunctive ganaxolone (added to existing anti-seizure medications) in children and young adults 2-21 years old with CDKL5 deficiency disorder; the double-blind (DB) phase comprised a 6-week prospective baseline, 4 weeks of titration, and 13 weeks of dose maintenance (17 weeks total), followed by an open-label extension; 101 subjects were randomized (51 placebo, 50 ganaxolone)
- Primary endpoint: percent change from baseline in 28-day frequency of "major motor seizures" (the CSR's term for the protocol's "primary seizures": bilateral tonic, generalized tonic-clonic, bilateral clonic, atonic/drop, or focal-to-bilateral-tonic-clonic seizures) during the 17-week DB treatment phase, based on caregiver electronic seizure diaries
- Key secondary endpoints (tested in a pre-specified order, gated on the primary endpoint's significance): (1) proportion of subjects with a ≥50% reduction from baseline in major motor seizure frequency (analyzed via Fisher's exact test), and (2) Clinical Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I) at the last scheduled DB visit (analyzed via ordinal logistic/proportional-odds regression with treatment group as a factor); the FDA reviewer noted the protocol/SAP did not specify whether CGI-I referred to the clinician- or caregiver-rated version, and the CSR reported both
- Analysis population: intention-to-treat (ITT), all randomized subjects who received ≥1 dose of study drug (N=101; 1 ganaxolone subject with missing baseline seizure data was excluded from the primary-endpoint analysis, N=100 analyzed)
- Primary statistical method: Wilcoxon rank-sum test on percent change from baseline in 28-day major motor seizure frequency, with the Hodges-Lehmann estimator used for the location-shift point estimate and CI; the primary analysis used all available diary data regardless of treatment discontinuation or rescue-medication use (an intention-to-treat-consistent, non-imputation-based approach for observed data)
- Group-sequential design: up to 2 formal interim analyses were planned (at 50 and 75 subjects reaching 17 weeks post-randomization) using O'Brien-Fleming boundaries (one-sided nominal boundary 0.0001 at IA1, 0.0012 at IA2, implying a final two-sided alpha of approximately 0.048); because enrollment outpaced the interim-analysis schedule and all patients were already randomized by the time the first interim analysis was run, the sponsor and DMC agreed the second interim analysis was unnecessary
- Missing-data handling: caregivers were instructed to keep recording seizures even after a subject's early drug discontinuation, to minimize missingness; for the rarer case of subjects who stopped recording entirely, two sensitivity analyses imputed missing periods either using placebo-arm data matched to the subject's own baseline quartile, or (a more conservative/worst-case approach) using the median of the 5 highest placebo-group seizure counts
- Data-integrity issue: an eDiary software error caused caregivers to be incorrectly prompted about "missing" entries that had actually been recorded, leading to 1,217 duplicate seizure entries across 65 subjects (<2% of all seizures) as of the original database lock; a corrected data snapshot was issued, and FDA additionally found a non-trivial number of seizure diary entries recorded by site-staff proxy rather than caregivers directly — FDA's review concluded neither issue raised a major concern about study integrity or changed the result
- Reported primary result (ITT, N=100 analyzed): median percent change in 28-day major motor seizure frequency was -30.7% (ganaxolone) vs. -6.9% (placebo); Hodges-Lehmann location-shift estimate -27.1% (95% CI -47.9 to -9.5), Wilcoxon p=0.0036. A supportive ANCOVA sensitivity analysis on log-transformed seizure frequency (log baseline as covariate) showed a 35.2%-36.2% relative reduction favoring ganaxolone (log-scale LS mean difference -0.45, 95% CI -0.79 to -0.12, p=0.0084). The interim analysis (52 subjects) produced p=0.003, which did not cross the O'Brien-Fleming efficacy boundary, so the trial continued to its final analysis. Key secondary endpoints showed numerically favorable but not formally tested-to-significance results (the FDA reviewer noted the trial "was not powered to show statistical significance for these secondary endpoints" and separately flagged that the SAP's silence on the secondary endpoints' alpha allocation risked inflating type I error if tested at the full 0.05 level)

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review and Evaluation, Section 2.1 "Overview," p.5]*

> "Study 1042-CDD-3001 (referred to as Study 3001) is the single pivotal efficacy study to support the approval of ganaxolone for the treatment of seizures associated CDD. The study is a double-blind (DB), randomized, placebo-controlled study in patients aged 2 to 19 years. The primary endpoint is the percent change from baseline in 28-day major motor seizure frequency during the 17-week DB treatment phase."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 3.2.2 "Statistical Methodologies," p.7]*

> "The primary efficacy endpoint of percent change from baseline in 28-day seizure frequency was analyzed using the Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test. The primary analysis used all available data, even if they were collected after the subject stopped taking study medication, regardless of whether the subject took rescue medication... Up to two formal interim analyses were planned on the primary endpoint. They were to be conducted when 50 subjects and 75 subjects were at least 17 weeks post randomization. O'Brien-Fleming boundaries would be used based on the actual number of subjects at the times of the interim analyses. The (one-sided) boundary was 0.0001 at the first IA and 0.0012 at the 2nd IA. The two-sided p-value at the final analysis would be approximately 0.048."

*[verbatim, same source, "Multiplicity Adjustment," p.7]*

> "If the null hypothesis was rejected for the primary efficacy endpoint at the 2-sided α-level allocated to the final analysis of the primary endpoint, then statistical hypothesis testing would be performed on the 2 key secondary endpoints in the order listed in section 3.2.1. Reviewer's note: the SAP didn't explicitly specify the α-level for testing the key secondary endpoints. For group sequential design, the secondary endpoints cannot be tested at the full 2-sided 0.05 significance level without inflating the overall type I error."

*[verbatim, same source, Table 3 and surrounding text, Section 3.2.4, p.10]*

> "During the 17-week double-blind treatment phase, there was a statistically significant difference of -27.1% in the median percent change from baseline in seizure frequency (-30.7% for subjects in the ganaxolone group and -6.9% for the placebo group; p = 0.0036)."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 3.1 "Data and Analysis Quality," p.5]*

> "There was a programming error that caused the eDiary to provide incorrect prompts of missing entries several days after they had in fact been entered by the parent or caregiver, who then re-recorded the seizure and medication information creating duplicate entries... At the time of double-blind data lock (01 September 2020) a total of 1217 duplicate seizures were identified for 65 subjects (34 ganaxolone and 31 placebo) within the double-blind phase of the trial accounting for <2% of the seizures... This issue does not raise a major concern on the study integrity as the error was discovered and corrected prior to the database lock."

### 36. Vutrisiran (Amvuttra) — NDA 215515

**Sponsor:** Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of the polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR amyloidosis) in adults

**Approval date:** June 13, 2022

**Pivotal trial:** Study ALN-TTRSC02-002 (HELIOS-A), NCT03759379; external control drawn from the APOLLO trial (NCT01960348, patisiran)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized (3:1), open-label, active-controlled trial (vutrisiran vs. patisiran as a concurrent reference/active comparator) combined with an external placebo control drawn from a different, previously completed trial (APOLLO) of the related approved drug patisiran; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=164 randomized in HELIOS-A; N=77 external APOLLO placebo)
- *Endpoints:* modified Neuropathy Impairment Score +7 (mNIS+7), change from baseline at Month 9 (primary); Norfolk Quality of Life-Diabetic Neuropathy (Norfolk QoL-DN) total score, change from baseline at Month 9 (key secondary); serum transthyretin (TTR) percent reduction as a non-inferiority endpoint vs. the internal patisiran arm
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA with multiple imputation (MI) comparing patient-level HELIOS-A vutrisiran data against patient-level historical APOLLO placebo data
- *Missing data/bias:* prespecified imputation for missing mNIS+7 sub-component items; FDA reviewer conducted an independent joint rank test (joint ranking of survival time together with mNIS+7 change among survivors) as a sensitivity analysis, to avoid treating deaths as ignorable/ordinary missing data on a functional-impairment endpoint ("Joint rank test combining survival time and a continuous functional-impairment score, used when death cannot be treated as ignorable missingness on a functional endpoint" — related to, but distinct in mechanics from, the Finkelstein-Schoenfeld hierarchical composite test already in the taxonomy); COVID-19-related visit-window extensions and a dedicated sensitivity analysis imputing delayed assessments with a poor outcome
- *Regulatory:* cross-trial external-control design explicitly reviewed under the FDA statistical reviewer's own keyword classification "External Control; Single Study; Rare Disease" (distinct from the taxonomy's existing "cross-trial pooled/integrated analysis" and "post hoc recombination" entries, which describe combining data within one sponsor's own multi-trial program rather than borrowing an already-completed, differently-designed trial's placebo arm as an external comparator for a new drug); FDA statistical reviewer explicitly flagged material baseline imbalances between the external-control and treatment populations (race, genotype, sex, disease severity) as a reliability concern, but concluded the totality of evidence (large effect size, concordance with the internal active-comparator arm, and consistency with the historical patisiran-vs-placebo effect in APOLLO) was "sufficiently compelling" despite the single-trial, externally-controlled evidentiary basis

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study ALN-TTRSC02-002 ("HELIOS-A") was a global, Phase 3, randomized (3:1), open-label trial of vutrisiran 25 mg subcutaneous every 3 months vs. patisiran 0.3 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks (an approved reference/active comparator targeting the same transthyretin mechanism) in adults with hATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy; randomization was stratified by TTR genotype (V30M vs. non-V30M) and baseline Neuropathy Impairment Score (NIS <50 vs. ≥50); 164 patients were randomized (122 vutrisiran, 42 patisiran) at 57 sites in 22 countries
- Because there was no concurrent placebo arm within HELIOS-A, FDA had agreed to let the sponsor compare the vutrisiran arm's Month 9 outcomes against the placebo arm from APOLLO (NCT01960348), the completed Phase 3 trial that had originally registered patisiran; efforts to minimize cross-trial differences included similar inclusion/exclusion criteria, overlapping study sites/global footprint, and identical efficacy assessment methods, rater training, and central laboratory for mNIS+7
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline to Month 9 in the modified Neuropathy Impairment Score +7 (mNIS+7), a composite of five components (muscle weakness [NIS-W], reflexes [NIS-R], quantitative sensory testing [QST], a 5-nerve-conduction sum [Σ5 NCS], and postural blood pressure), ranging 0 (no impairment) to 304 (maximum impairment), compared between the HELIOS-A vutrisiran arm and the external APOLLO placebo arm; the patisiran arm within HELIOS-A was analyzed only descriptively against vutrisiran for this endpoint (except for the TTR endpoint, where vutrisiran was compared directly to patisiran within HELIOS-A under a non-inferiority framework)
- Key secondary endpoint: change from baseline to Month 9 in Norfolk QoL-DN total score (range -4 to 136, lower is better), compared the same way (HELIOS-A vutrisiran vs. external APOLLO placebo)
- Sample size/power: assuming an APOLLO placebo-arm mean (SD) mNIS+7 change of 15 (17) points and a vutrisiran mean change of 0, the design had >90% power for a two-sided t-test at alpha=0.05; a parallel calculation for Norfolk QoL-DN (APOLLO placebo mean [SD] change 11.5 [19.2], assumed vutrisiran mean change -4) also gave >90% power
- Censoring/data-handling rules: for consistency with APOLLO, both studies' mNIS+7 and Norfolk QoL-DN analyses censored assessments after a patient initiated a TTR-stabilizing agent (e.g., tafamidis, diflunisal) for >14 days or received a liver transplant; HELIOS-A additionally censored after initiation of any TTR-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (e.g., inotersen) or (for the vutrisiran arm) patisiran; COVID-19-related visit delays of up to 6 months beyond the protocol-defined window were still included as the Month 9/18 assessment, per a protocol amendment
- Reported primary result (mITT): LS mean mNIS+7 change from baseline to Month 9 was -2.24 points (vutrisiran, improvement) vs. +14.76 points (external APOLLO placebo, worsening); LS mean between-group difference -17.00 points (p<0.0001). A separate within-HELIOS-A comparison found the patisiran-vutrisiran difference was only -0.06 points (SE=2.75), i.e., the two active-drug arms performed similarly, consistent with a shared mechanism of action
- Independent FDA analysis and concerns: the reviewer's own comparison (Table 9) found the external APOLLO placebo arm's baseline mNIS+7 (mean 74.6) was materially higher (worse) than the HELIOS-A vutrisiran arm's baseline (mean 60.6), alongside imbalances in race, genotype, sex, and cardiac-subpopulation proportions between the two separately conducted trials, and stated plainly that "comparison to an external control with such clear differences in patient composition is not likely to be reliable"; the reviewer nonetheless found the totality of evidence persuasive because the vutrisiran-vs.-APOLLO-placebo effect size closely tracked the historical patisiran-vs.-APOLLO-placebo effect and the internal vutrisiran-vs.-patisiran comparison, both of which help validate the external-control design against a shared benchmark
- Missing-data/death handling: because there were 2 vutrisiran-arm deaths before the Month 9 visit (and 2 in the external APOLLO placebo arm), and functional-scale missingness caused by death is not equivalent to ordinary missingness, the FDA reviewer ran an independent joint rank test (joint ranking of survival time and mNIS+7 change among survivors, an approach the reviewer noted is "typically the recommended primary analysis in ALS" trials) as a sensitivity analysis; this analysis (N=186, t=6.11, p<0.0001) also favored vutrisiran, though the reviewer cautioned this sensitivity analysis still could not correct for the underlying cross-trial baseline imbalance. A separate sensitivity analysis assuming the worst-case mNIS+7 outcome (+20 points) for the 13 vutrisiran patients whose Month 9 assessment was delayed 3-6 months due to COVID-19 did not change the conclusion
- FDA's "Collective Evidence" assessment explicitly noted this was a single controlled efficacy study ("Collective evidence is not considered in this review since there was only one trial"), and the final conclusion accepted the single externally-controlled trial as sufficient given the rare, serious disease and unmet need

> "The Division had agreed to allow the sponsor to compare the investigational treatment Vutrisiran, to the placebo arm from the sponsor's APOLLO trial involving the approved predecessor product, Patisiran, which was also used as an active control in the current HELIOS-A trial. The APOLLO placebo and HELIOS-A Vutrisiran arms seem to have several notable differences in patient characteristics... ### 37. Olipudase alfa (Xenpozyme) — BLA 761261

**Sponsor:** Genzyme, a Sanofi Company

**Indication approved:** Treatment of non-central nervous system manifestations of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD) in adult and pediatric patients

**Approval date:** August 31, 2022

**Pivotal trial:** Trial DFI12712 (ASCEND), NCT02004691; supported by Trial DFI13803 (ASCEND-Peds)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a crossover extension (placebo-arm subjects crossed over to active treatment after the primary analysis period); small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=36)
- *Endpoints:* co-primary endpoint family of (1) percent change in %-predicted DLCO (diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide) at Week 52, and (2) a two-part combination endpoint of percent change in spleen volume (MRI, multiples of normal) plus change in Splenomegaly-Related Score (SRS, an eDiary-based symptom/impact score)
- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance matrix and Kenward-Roger degrees-of-freedom approximation, for each primary-endpoint component
- *Multiplicity:* Hochberg step-up procedure across the DLCO and spleen-volume components, with a distinct rule folding the SRS component into whether the combination endpoint counted as significant, under an overall "either endpoint wins" (OR-based) trial-success criterion ("OR-based (either-or) win criterion across two co-primary endpoint families," as opposed to the taxonomy's existing AND-based co-primary or hierarchical structures) — FDA confirmed in DARRTS that it had agreed to this win criterion in advance
- *Missing data/bias:* no imputation in the primary MMRM analyses (relying on the model's implicit missing-at-random handling); supportive pattern-mixture model to assess robustness to the MAR assumption; Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test with last-observation-carried-forward imputation as a non-parametric sensitivity analysis; responder-analysis thresholds pre-specified for each primary-endpoint component
- *Regulatory:* FDA's primary statistical analysis population deviated from the sponsor's own SAP-specified population (mITT) to a narrower one (mITT-C, excluding 5 subjects who received an analytically distinct, non-to-be-marketed manufacturing process of the drug), because the reviewer judged the two manufacturing processes "analytically incomparable" and process C was the to-be-marketed formulation

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Trial DFI12712 (ASCEND) was a Phase 2/3, multicenter, randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled, repeat-dose trial of IV olipudase alfa every 2 weeks in adults (≥18 years) with ASMD type B, with a 52-week primary analysis period (PAP) followed by an extension treatment period (ETP) in which placebo-arm subjects crossed over to active treatment; 36 subjects were randomized (18 olipudase alfa, 18 placebo), with dose escalation (true for the active arm, mock/sham for placebo, to preserve blinding) from 0.1 up to a target 3 mg/kg over the first 14 weeks
- Eligibility required documented acid sphingomyelinase (ASM) deficiency with ASMD type B, DLCO ≤70% predicted, spleen volume ≥6 multiples of normal (MN), and SRS ≥5 at baseline
- Co-primary endpoint 1: percent change from baseline to Week 52 in %-predicted DLCO (adjusted for hemoglobin and ambient barometric pressure)
- Co-primary endpoint 2 (a two-component combination endpoint): percent change from baseline to Week 52 in spleen volume by MRI, combined with change from baseline to Week 52 in the Splenomegaly-Related Score (SRS; a 5-item, 0-10 daily symptom/impact eDiary score covering abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, early satiety, body-image dissatisfaction, and difficulty bending down, drawn from the Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form)
- Secondary endpoints (no formal multiplicity adjustment, tested only if both primary endpoints were significant, then in sequence): percent change in liver volume, percent change in platelet count, Brief Fatigue Inventory item 3, Brief Pain Inventory item 3, and FACIT-Dyspnea score, all at Week 52
- Statistical methods: each of the three primary-endpoint components (DLCO, spleen volume, SRS) and all secondary endpoints were analyzed via MMRM including baseline value, baseline age, treatment arm, visit, and a visit-by-treatment interaction, with an unstructured covariance matrix and Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom; responder-analysis thresholds were pre-specified (≥30% spleen-volume decrease, ≥15-point absolute DLCO improvement, ≥12.5-point SRS decrease)
- Multiplicity/win criterion: DLCO and spleen-volume p-values (each from its own MMRM) were compared using a Hochberg-style procedure — if the larger of the two two-sided p-values was <0.05, both were significant; if only the smaller was <0.025, only that one was; otherwise neither was. The combination endpoint (spleen volume + SRS) was significant only if spleen volume was significant AND the SRS p-value was <0.15 (a relaxed threshold reflecting SRS's supportive/patient-reported role). The trial was deemed an overall "win" if either the DLCO endpoint or the combination endpoint was significant — FDA's review notes the Agency had pre-agreed to this criterion (referenced DARRTS Reference ID 3897521 under IND 12757)
- Analysis population: FDA's primary analysis used the mITT-C population (mITT excluding 5 subjects who received an earlier, analytically distinct "process B" formulation of olipudase alfa), departing from the sponsor's SAP-designated mITT population, because process B and the to-be-marketed process C were determined analytically incomparable and only process C data were used to inform labeling
- Reported results (mITT-C, N=18 placebo/N=13 olipudase alfa at Week 52): DLCO percent change from baseline was 3.08% (placebo) vs. 24.2% (olipudase alfa); MMRM LS mean difference in percentage change 15.48 points (95% CI 7.99-22.97; absolute-scale LS mean difference 7.07% predicted, 95% CI 4.29-9.84, p<0.0001; confirmed by Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney, p=0.0008). Spleen volume percent change at Week 52 was +0.42% (placebo) vs. -38.77% (olipudase alfa); LS mean difference -39.22 percentage points (95% CI -44.73 to -33.70, p<0.0001 by both MMRM and WMW). The SRS component did not reach significance, so per the pre-specified rule the combination endpoint itself was not declared significant — but because the DLCO endpoint alone met the win criterion, the trial was deemed an overall success
- ASCEND-Peds (Trial DFI13803), a single-arm, open-label pediatric extension/bridging study, provided supportive percent-predicted-DLCO and other efficacy data used to extend the indication to pediatric patients, but did not itself carry an independent randomized comparison

> "The primary objective of the trial was to evaluate the efficacy of olipudase alfa by assessing changes from baseline to Week 52 in: (1) infiltrative lung disease as measured by DLCO and (2) spleen volume as measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in association with subject perception related to spleen volume as measured by SRS... The protocol proposed to analyze two primary efficacy endpoints (one of which was a two-part combination endpoint): Percentage change in DLCO at Week 52; Combination endpoint: Percentage change in spleen volume at Week 52, Change in splenomegaly-related score (SRS) at Week 52."

If the spleen volume was significant..., then the combination endpoint was significant if the SRS component p-value (as determined by the MMRM) was <0.15; but insignificant otherwise. The trial was considered a 'win' if either the DLCO or combination endpoint were significant in the agreed SAP... Reviewer's Comment: According to the information in DARRTS, FDA agreed on the win criteria (IND12757 - Reference ID: 3897521)."

### 38. Velmanase alfa-tycv (Lamzede) — NDA 761278

**Sponsor:** Chiesi Farmaceutici S.p.A. (trial rhLAMAN-05 was originally conducted by Zymenex A/S, later acquired by Chiesi)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of non-central nervous system manifestations of alpha-mannosidosis (AM) in adult and pediatric patients

**Approval date:** February 16, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** Trial rhLAMAN-05, NCT01681953; supported by Trial rhLAMAN-08 and the rhLAMAN-10 integrated long-term analysis

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized (3:2), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=25); trial conducted entirely outside the US (EU, supporting a 2018 EMA approval) with no FDA input into its design, later repurposed as the single pivotal trial for a US BLA after a planned US confirmatory trial (SHAMAN) was abandoned pre-enrollment due to COVID-19
- *Endpoints:* co-primary endpoints of serum oligosaccharide reduction (disease-specific biomarker) and 3-minute stair climb test (3MSCT, clinical function); key secondary endpoints of forced vital capacity (FVC%) and 6-minute walk test (6MWT)
- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA on relative (percent) and absolute change from baseline at Week 52
- *Interim/alpha-spending:* non-binding interim analysis at Week 26 with a lower bar for declaring success than the final analysis (see below)
- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption specified for the primary endpoints only (not for key secondary endpoints); FDA reviewer independently re-derived relative-change results using non-transformed data after finding the sponsor's back-transformation formula for log-scale ANCOVA estimates was not adequately justified; FDA excluded the sponsor's own responder analyses from its efficacy assessment because no clinical-meaningfulness rationale was provided for the response thresholds
- *Regulatory:* traditional (regular, non-accelerated) approval granted despite the clinical/functional co-primary endpoint (3MSCT) and both key secondary endpoints failing to reach statistical significance, resting on a statistically significant biomarker endpoint (serum oligosaccharides) plus a pre-specified "trend" (not significance) criterion for the functional endpoints, supported by FDA's "confirmatory evidence" framework — well-understood single-enzyme disease pathophysiology, a clear mechanism of action, evidence the drug reaches its target tissue, and evidence of an exposure-response relationship on the biomarker ("Regular approval resting on a non-statistically-significant clinical/functional endpoint trend, supported by a significant biomarker endpoint and the confirmatory-evidence doctrine in lieu of a second adequate trial"); efficacy in patients <6 years old was extrapolated from the pivotal trial (which enrolled only ages 6-35) using supportive PK/PD data from a separate open-label trial in children 3 to <6 years

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Trial rhLAMAN-05 was a multicenter, double-blind, randomized (3:2), placebo-controlled, 52-week trial of velmanase alfa in patients with AM aged 6-35 years, conducted at European sites (Poland, Spain, Germany, France, UK, and others) between September 2012 and May 2014; 26 patients were screened, 25 randomized (15 velmanase, 10 placebo), none discontinued; this trial had already supported EMA approval of velmanase in the EU in 2018, years before an IND for velmanase was opened with FDA (August 2019)
- The originally planned US pivotal trial (SHAMAN, NCT04031066) was stopped in October 2020, before any subject was screened or enrolled, due to COVID-19-pandemic-related issues; the sponsor then proposed reusing the completed European rhLAMAN-05 trial to support a US BLA, initially under the accelerated approval pathway
- At a Type C "surrogate endpoint" meeting (January 31, 2022), the sponsor proposed instead submitting under the traditional approval pathway, with accelerated approval (treating serum oligosaccharides as a surrogate reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit) as a fallback if serum oligosaccharides could not be validated as a true surrogate; FDA acknowledged a "reasonable scientific basis" for using serum oligosaccharides as a surrogate and that a traditional-approval submission "appeared reasonable," while reserving final judgment for full BLA review
- Co-primary endpoints, both evaluated as percent (and, as a sensitivity analysis, absolute) change from baseline to Week 52: (1) serum oligosaccharide concentration, and (2) the 3-minute stair climb test (3MSCT, steps climbed in 3 minutes); key secondary endpoints: forced vital capacity (FVC, % predicted) and the 6-minute walk test (6MWT, meters)
- Statistical methods: ANCOVA models were specified for both relative-change (on log-transformed data) and absolute-change analyses at Week 52, producing adjusted means, adjusted between-arm differences, 95% CIs, and p-values; the SAP specified multiple imputation for missing primary-endpoint data (assuming missing-at-random) but did not define a missing-data method for the key secondary endpoints
- FDA's reviewer-level corrections: (1) the sponsor's SAP specified ANCOVA on log-transformed data for relative-change endpoints but did not adequately justify its back-transformation formula ({exp(mean)-1} × 100) for reporting untransformed relative-change estimates, so FDA independently reanalyzed relative change using non-transformed data; (2) for 4 subjects with FVC values deemed unreliable due to poor spirometry maneuver quality, FDA ran two additional analyses (treating them as no-change, and excluding them) that produced results similar to the sponsor's multiple-imputation-based handling; (3) FDA declined to credit the sponsor's responder analyses (using thresholds such as ≥70% oligosaccharide reduction or ≥10% 3MSCT increase) because no rationale for the clinical meaningfulness of those specific thresholds was provided
- Pre-specified success criteria (from the protocol/SAP, applied without FDA's prior input since the trial predated the IND): efficacy would be considered established if EITHER (a) serum oligosaccharides showed a statistically significant improvement at alpha=0.025 AND 3MSCT showed significance at alpha=0.05, both at the non-binding Week 26 interim analysis, OR (b) at the Week 52 final analysis, serum oligosaccharides reached significance at alpha=0.025 while 3MSCT and either FVC or 6MWT showed merely a favorable "trend" (not a formal significance requirement)
- Reported results (Week 52, adjusted treatment difference, velmanase n=15 vs. placebo n=10): serum oligosaccharides showed a relative reduction of -55.6 percentage points beyond placebo (95% CI -69.3 to -41.9, p<0.001); 3MSCT relative change difference was +3.4% (95% CI -9.5 to 16.3, p=0.59, not significant); FVC% relative change difference was +7.4% (95% CI -5.7 to 20.5, p=0.25, not significant); 6MWT relative change difference was +1.6% (95% CI -7.2 to 10.4, p=0.71, not significant). Despite only the biomarker endpoint reaching formal significance, FDA's review concluded "the results for the clinical endpoints..., which consistently favored velmanase and were supported by a statistically significant reduction in serum oligosaccharides..., were sufficient to establish the efficacy of velmanase"
- Supportive confirmatory evidence (in lieu of a second adequate/well-controlled trial): FDA's benefit-risk assessment explicitly invoked (1) well-understood single-enzyme disease pathophysiology, (2) a clear, targeted mechanism of action (enzyme replacement), (3) evidence the enzyme reaches its target tissue, (4) evidence of drug effect on the biomarker, and (5) evidence of an exposure-response relationship for the biomarker, as adequate confirmatory evidence supporting regular approval from a single placebo-controlled trial
- Extrapolation to pediatric patients <6 years: Trial rhLAMAN-08, a single-arm, open-label PK/PD and safety study in 5 children aged 3 to <6 years (24 months of treatment, no patients younger than 3 years), supplied supportive PK/PD data; efficacy in this age group was otherwise extrapolated from rhLAMAN-05 given shared disease biology across ages, while safety in patients <6 years was assessed as adequate down to birth based on rhLAMAN-05, rhLAMAN-08, and postmarketing global-use data combined

> "The review team concluded that the results for the clinical endpoints in Trial rhLAMAN-05 (the primary endpoint of 3MSCT and the key secondary endpoints of 6MWT and FVC%), which consistently favored velmanase and were supported by a statistically significant reduction in serum oligosaccharides with velmanase, were sufficient to establish the efficacy of velmanase in the treatment of AM."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 3.1.1.2 "Adequacy of the Confirmatory Evidence," p.14]*

> "The following lines evidence constitute adequate confirmatory evidence of treatment benefit: (1) well-understood underlying disease pathophysiology (i.e., AM is known to be caused by a single enzyme deficiency); (2) clear, targeted mechanism of action (MOA) of velmanase (i.e., replacement of the deficient enzyme); (3) evidence velmanase reaches its target tissue; (4) evidence of drug effect on the pharmacologically relevant biomarker; and (5) evidence of exposure-response (biomarker)."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.4, p.29-30]*

> "The SAP pre-specified an interim analysis using Week 26 data. The interim analysis was not binding, in that the trial could continue even if efficacy had been established based on the pre-specified definition. Demonstration of efficacy was pre-specified in the protocol and SAP as: A statistically significant improvement in serum oligosaccharides and 3MSCT, at the significance levels of 0.025 and 0.05 respectively, at the interim (Week 26) analysis, or A statistically significant improvement in serum oligosaccharides at the significance level of 0.025 and a trend for improvement in the 3MSCT and either FVC or 6MWT at the final (Week 52) analysis... Trial rhLAMAN-05 was conducted outside of the United States and its protocol and SAP were not submitted to the FDA prior to study initiation or completion."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.5 "Results of Analyses" and Table 9, p.31]*

> "The treatment difference of the Week 52 change from baseline in serum oligosaccharides produced a statistically significant p-value of < 0.001 in favor of velmanase. The estimated treatment differences of the Week 52 changes from baseline in 3MSCT, FVC%, and 6MWT favored velmanase, compared to placebo. Based on their pre-specified criteria for demonstration of efficacy..., the Applicant concludes that efficacy of velmanase has been established in Trial rhLAMAN-05."

### 39. Sparsentan (Filspari) — NDA 216403

**Sponsor:** Travere Therapeutics, Inc.

**Indication approved:** To reduce proteinuria in adults with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) at risk of rapid disease progression, generally a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≥1.5 g/g; approved under accelerated approval based on a reduction in proteinuria, with continued approval contingent on verification and description of clinical benefit (slowing of kidney function decline) in a confirmatory clinical trial — label states plainly "it has not been established whether Filspari slows kidney function decline in patients with IgAN"

**Approval date:** February 17, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** Study PROTECT, NCT03762850 (single trial serving as both the accelerated-approval interim-analysis study and its own confirmatory trial at final analysis)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized (1:1), double-blind, active-controlled trial (sparsentan vs. irbesartan, an ARB — not placebo, since background ACEI/ARB therapy could not ethically be withheld); single trial with a planned unblinded interim analysis used for accelerated approval and the same trial's final analysis used as the confirmatory trial ("Single trial serving as both the accelerated-approval basis and its own confirmatory trial via a pre-planned interim-then-final-analysis structure," distinct from the taxonomy's existing "Accelerated approval based on a randomized, non-registrational Phase 2 trial," where the confirmatory trial is a separate, later study)
- *Endpoints:* urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UP/C), percent/geometric-mean-ratio change from baseline at Week 36 (surrogate endpoint for accelerated approval); eGFR total slope and chronic slope over 110 weeks (clinical/confirmatory endpoints for full approval)
- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) on log-transformed UP/C for the surrogate endpoint; mixed-model random-coefficients (random intercept and slope) analysis of eGFR slope for the confirmatory endpoints
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing across a pre-specified ordered sequence (UP/C at Week 36 → eGFR 2-year total slope → eGFR 2-year chronic slope → other secondary endpoints), with only the first tested at the (interim) accelerated-approval analysis and the remainder held for the final analysis — a gatekeeping structure spanning two separate, temporally staggered analyses of the same trial
- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption via a Bayesian multivariate-normal MCMC model (SAS PROC MI), separately handling intermittent missing values before discontinuation vs. missing values after discontinuation
- *Regulatory:* accelerated approval (21 CFR 314.500 pathway) granted on a surrogate proteinuria endpoint from a randomized, active-controlled trial (not a single-arm trial, the more typical accelerated-approval design), with the same trial's long-term eGFR-slope analysis at 110 weeks serving as the pre-specified confirmatory endpoint for full approval — a two-stage endpoint structure explicitly built into a single protocol/SAP rather than requiring a second, independently designed confirmatory trial

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study PROTECT was a randomized (1:1), double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled trial of sparsentan vs. irbesartan in adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, urine protein excretion ≥1.0 g/day, eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73m², on a stable maximally tolerated ACEI/ARB dose; randomization was stratified by baseline eGFR (30 to <60 vs. ≥60 mL/min/1.73m²) and baseline urine protein excretion (≤1.75 vs. >1.75 g/day). Background ACEI/ARB therapy was discontinued before randomization since the trial itself substituted the study drug (sparsentan or irbesartan) for that background therapy; patients were treated for a 110-week double-blind period, then washed out for 4 weeks and returned to their entry ACEI/ARB regimen. The trial fully enrolled 406 subjects by May 26, 2021
- Two-stage endpoint design, built into a single protocol/SAP from the outset: a pre-specified unblinded interim analysis at Week 36 (after ≥280 subjects reached that timepoint) evaluated the primary endpoint for accelerated approval — change from baseline in UP/C — while the same trial's full 110-week follow-up was pre-designated to generate the confirmatory endpoint for full approval — the rate of change (slope) of eGFR
- Interim-analysis (accelerated-approval) endpoint: percent/geometric-mean-ratio change from baseline in UP/C (24-hour urine collection) at Week 36, analyzed via MMRM on log-transformed data (log baseline UP/C, treatment, time, treatment-by-time interaction, and the 4-level randomization stratum as fixed effects, subject as random effect, unstructured covariance matrix), with estimates back-transformed via [exp(LS mean log-change) - 1] × 100
- Confirmatory (full-approval) endpoints: eGFR total slope (Day 1 to Week 110) and eGFR chronic slope (Week 6 to Week 110, i.e., excluding the initial ~6-week acute hemodynamic effect of treatment), each via a mixed-model random-coefficients analysis (random intercept and random slope per subject) with baseline eGFR, time, treatment-by-time interaction, and randomization strata as fixed effects; eGFR was calculated via the CKD-EPI (Levey 2009) formula
- Multiplicity/testing sequence (for the FDA analysis specifically; a different procedure applied for non-US regulators): a fixed-sequence gatekeeping procedure tested, in order, (1) UP/C at Week 36, (2) eGFR total slope at 110 weeks (2-year), (3) eGFR chronic slope at 110 weeks (2-year), then (4) other secondary endpoints — only the first step was tested (at full two-sided alpha=0.05) at the interim analysis; if any step failed to reach significance, all subsequent steps were treated as descriptive/exploratory only
- Sample size (interim analysis): 280 randomized subjects gave ≥90% power assuming a true relative treatment effect on UP/C of ≥30% (sparsentan vs. irbesartan), an SD of 0.92 for log-scale change from baseline, and two-sided alpha=0.05; the SAP additionally stated that, per an external IgAN patient-registry analysis, a 30% UP/C treatment effect was estimated to predict a 6.4 mL/min/1.73m² difference in 104-week eGFR total slope (95% CI 0.83-12.44) — an explicit, pre-specified quantitative bridge from the surrogate to the confirmatory clinical endpoint
- Reported interim result (interim analysis set, N=281; 140 irbesartan, 141 sparsentan): adjusted geometric mean UP/C at Week 36 was 85.1% of baseline (irbesartan) vs. 55.2% of baseline (sparsentan); ratio of geometric-mean-relative-to-baseline between arms was 0.65 (95% CI 0.55-0.77) — i.e., UP/C was 35% lower with sparsentan than irbesartan (95% CI 23%-45% lower, p<0.0001) — the result supporting accelerated approval
- At the time of accelerated approval, the eGFR-slope confirmatory analysis had not yet matured (110-week follow-up was still ongoing for later-enrolled subjects); the label explicitly disclaims established benefit on kidney-function decline pending that confirmatory readout from the same trial

*[verbatim, FDA Integrated Review, "Application Information" summary table, p.i]*

> "Filspari is indicated to reduce proteinuria in adults with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) at risk of rapid disease progression, generally a urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≥1.5 g/g.
