*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.1, p.24]*

> "The protocol prespecified an unblinded interim analysis performed 36 weeks after randomization of at least 280 subjects to evaluate the primary efficacy endpoint (i.e., endpoint for accelerated approval) based on change in proteinuria at Week 36. The same study will be used to verify and describe the clinical benefit. The confirmatory endpoint will evaluate the rate of change of eGFR over 110 weeks following initiation of randomized therapy and will be evaluated in the full study population."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.4 "Endpoints, Study PROTECT," p.26]*

> "The primary efficacy endpoint for the interim analysis was the change from baseline (Day 1) in the UP/C based on a 24-hour urine sample at Week 36 (i.e., endpoint for accelerated approval)... Endpoints for the Confirmatory Trial: The confirmatory endpoint to verify the clinical benefit is the rate of change in eGFR over a 110-week (approximately 2 years) period following the initiation of randomized therapy... The confirmatory analysis will include the following key secondary endpoint that will be included within the testing strategy: the rate of change in eGFR over a 104-week (approximately 2 years) period following the initial acute effect of randomized therapy."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 6.2.1.5 "Statistical Analysis Plan, Study PROTECT," "Multiplicity Adjustment," p.27]*

> "At the interim analysis, only the primary endpoint of UP/C at Week 36 was to be tested at a full alpha of 0.05, and no formal testing was to be conducted on the eGFR rate of change over 6 to 58 weeks. The full testing sequence is as shown below. Only the first endpoint was to be tested at the interim analysis; the other endpoints were to be tested at the final analysis: UP/C at 36 weeks; eGFR rate of change at 110 weeks (2-year total slope); eGFR rate of change over 6 to 110 weeks (2-year chronic slope); Other secondary endpoints at final analysis. If at any step, the statistical comparison was not statistically significant at the specified significance level of 0.05, then the remaining comparisons would be considered descriptive and exploratory."

*[verbatim, same source, "Sample Size," p.28]*

> "For the primary endpoint UP/C at the interim analysis, a total of 280 randomized subjects will provide at least 90% power assuming the following: True relative treatment effect on UP/C, sparsentan versus irbesartan, is at least 30%. Standard deviation of the log change from baseline in proteinuria at Week 36 is 0.92. Two-sided alpha level is 0.05. The SAP also assumes, based on analyses of an IgAN patient registry database, that a 30% treatment effect on UP/C predicts a difference in eGFR total slope at 104 weeks of 6.4 mL/min/1.73 m2, with a 95% CI of (0.83, 12.44)."

*[verbatim, same source, "Primary Efficacy Endpoint, IAS," p.34]*

> "At Week 36, the UP/C geometric mean was 85.1% and 55.2% of the baseline value for subjects in the irbesartan and sparsentan groups, respectively. The ratio of the geometric mean relative to baseline between the two groups was 0.65 (95%CI: 0.55, 0.77), i.e., the geometric mean relative to baseline at Week 36 was 35% lower (95%CI: 23% lower to 45% lower; p-value<0.0001) for the sparsentan arm compared to the irbesartan arm."

### 40. Omaveloxolone (Skyclarys) — NDA 216718

**Sponsor:** Reata Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (original NDA applicant; Biogen acquired Reata in 2023, after this approval)

**Indication approved:** Treatment of Friedreich's ataxia (FA) in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older

**Approval date:** February 28, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** Study 408-C-1402, Part 2, NCT02255435

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, stratified by pes cavus status, nested within a larger 2-part study (Part 1 was a separate dose-ranging stage); small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (N=103 randomized, 82 in the primary efficacy analysis set)
- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale (mFARS) at Week 48 (primary); Patient/Clinician Global Impression of Change (PGIC/CGIC) as key secondaries; 9-hole peg test, timed 25-foot walk, fall frequency, peak work, and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) score as other secondaries
- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with an unstructured covariance matrix
- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing (mFARS → PGIC → CGIC → 9-HPT → T25-FWT → falls → peak work → ADL, each gated on the previous endpoint's significance)
- *Missing data/bias:* imbalanced missingness between arms (6/40 omaveloxolone vs. 1/42 placebo missing the Week 48 assessment) prompted control-based and treatment-based multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses and a tipping-point analysis; a late-discovered data-entry error in the primary endpoint dataset required a CSR addendum, though FDA found it did not change the efficacy conclusion; reviewer-documented mid-trial SAP amendment adding "site" as a model covariate in the final SAP version shortly before study completion, which FDA confirmed did not materially change the result
- *Regulatory:* full/traditional (not accelerated) approval granted from a single Phase 2 trial with a p-value close to the 0.05 boundary (p=0.014) on the primary endpoint, whose two key secondary endpoints (PGIC, CGIC) and 4 of 5 other secondary endpoints were not statistically significant, supported cautiously by a natural-history-study comparison the reviewer viewed as weak evidence given heavy missing data ("Full/traditional approval on a single trial with a narrowly-significant primary endpoint and failed key secondaries, supported only by a skeptically-received natural-history comparator"); FDA explicitly rejected the sponsor's post hoc global rank test combining endpoints as a basis for supporting efficacy, citing the FDA multiple-endpoints guidance's requirement that pre-specified multiplicity procedures, not post hoc combinations, control the overall Type I error

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study 408-C-1402 was conducted in two parts: Part 1 was a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, dose-ranging study (doses from 2.5 mg to 300 mg) to select the Part 2 dose; Part 2 (the pivotal trial for this NDA) was a randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial of omaveloxolone 150 mg once daily for a 48-week double-blind treatment phase (after a 4-week screening period), in patients 16-40 years old with genetically confirmed FA and a baseline mFARS score of 20-80; randomization was stratified by pes cavus status (a foot deformity), with patients with pes cavus capped at ≤20% of Part 2 enrollment
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline to Week 48 in the modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale (mFARS; range 0-99, the full neurologic FARS assessment minus the peripheral-nervous-system section), assessed at 6 post-baseline timepoints (Weeks 4, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48); analyzed via MMRM including treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, and baseline-mFARS-by-visit interaction as fixed effects, with baseline mFARS value and site as covariates, subject as a random effect, and an unstructured covariance matrix
- Analysis population: the Full Analysis Set (FAS) was defined as randomized, treated patients without pes cavus with ≥1 post-baseline efficacy assessment — i.e., the efficacy analysis population itself excluded the pes-cavus stratum entirely (83 of 103 randomized patients had no pes cavus; 82 of those 83 were included in the FAS)
- Sample size/power: ~100 subjects planned (1:1), ~45 per arm expected in the efficacy dataset after ~10% dropout, giving ~80% power to detect a 2-point mFARS treatment difference assuming a common SD of 3.5
- Multiplicity: type I error was controlled via fixed-sequence hierarchical testing, each endpoint tested at the 0.05 level only if the prior endpoint in the sequence was significant: mFARS (primary) → PGIC → CGIC → 9-hole peg test → timed 25-foot walk test → fall frequency → peak work during exercise testing → Activities of Daily Living (ADL) score
- SAP amendment: the SAP was revised 3 times close to the end of the study, with "site" added as a covariate to the primary MMRM model only in the final version; FDA verified the model produced very similar results whether or not site was included (p=0.0141 with site vs. 0.0196 without), so did not consider this late change to materially affect interpretability
- Missing-data handling: missingness at Week 48 was imbalanced between arms (6 of 40 omaveloxolone patients missing vs. 1 of 42 placebo patients, largely due to adverse events and, in 2 cases, patients leaving early to catch flights), which FDA flagged as a potential bias concern in a trial this small; sensitivity analyses used control-based and treatment-based multiple imputation (both confirmed the primary result) and a tipping-point analysis, which found the result would flip from significant to non-significant only if a shift of about 2 points (mFARS) were applied — a magnitude FDA noted was comparable to a full year of untreated disease progression
- Data-entry error: a data-entry error in the primary endpoint dataset was discovered late in review, prompting a CSR addendum with corrected results; FDA found the corrected results nearly identical to the original (p=0.0138 vs. 0.0141) and concluded the error did not alter the efficacy conclusion
- Reported primary result (FAS, N=82): LS mean change in mFARS from baseline to Week 48 was -1.55 (omaveloxolone) vs. +0.85 (placebo); LS mean difference -2.40 (95% CI -4.31 to -0.50, p=0.0141; -2.41, p=0.0138 after the data-entry-error correction). The two key secondary endpoints were not significant: PGIC LS mean difference -0.43 (p=0.13); CGIC LS mean difference -0.13 (p=0.53); because the hierarchy broke at the first key secondary, all subsequent secondary endpoints (9-HPT, T25-FWT, falls, peak work, ADL) were formally non-significant regardless of their nominal p-values, though the review noted the ADL endpoint alone had a nominal p=0.042
- Supportive (non-confirmatory) evidence considered: the sponsor submitted a single published natural-history study (Patel et al. 2016, ~820 patients at baseline declining to 290 by Year 5, substantial missing data) showing an average 1-2 point/year mFARS worsening in a similar-aged population, which FDA noted was roughly consistent with both the trial's placebo-arm worsening (+0.85 over 48 weeks) and the tipping-point shift (2 points), but the reviewer explicitly stated heavy missingness in the natural-history data meant it "could [not] provide additional strong support." The sponsor also submitted post hoc "delayed-start" and "baseline-controlled" analyses using the open-label extension, which FDA found uninterpretable because well under half of Week-48 completers had extension data at Week 72, breaking the randomized comparison; and a post hoc global rank test combining primary and secondary endpoints (p=0.0124, or 0.0041 combined with the ADL endpoint), which FDA rejected as not controlling the family-wise Type I error and not pre-specified

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2023/216718Orig1s000ltr.pdf

- Package Insert / Label (original, 2023) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/216718s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Statistical Review and Evaluation — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/216718Orig1s000StatR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov record — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02255435 (no protocol/SAP document posted in the Documents tab; record confirms randomized, double-masked, parallel design, actual enrollment 172 across both parts of the study)

- Protocol / SAP: no sponsor-posted protocol/SAP found on ClinicalTrials.gov; the FDA Statistical Review quotes SAP methodology and documents its 3 late amendments directly (see below)

- Pivotal publication: Lynch DR, Chin MP, Delatycki MB, et al. "Safety and Efficacy of Omaveloxolone in Friedreich Ataxia (MOXIe Study)." *Ann Neurol.* 2021;89(2):212-225. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/ana.25934), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33068037/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Safety%20and%20Efficacy%20of%20Omaveloxolone%20in%20Friedreich%20Ataxia%20MOXIe%20Study)

- No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was identified for this NDA.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, "Executive Summary," p.4]*

> "The efficacy evidence for RTA408 (Omaveloxolone oral dissolving capsule 50-mg strength at 3 capsules per day) is based on one Phase II study 408-C-1402-PT2... This study provided statistical evidence to support that RTA408 is efficacious in patients with for FA based on change from baseline mFARS (modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale) score at week 48."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 3.1 "Data and Analysis Quality," p.6]*

> "On face, this study was statistically positive on the primary endpoint with a p-value of 0.0141 and effect size of about -2.4 points. The two key secondary endpoints had p values 0.1300 and 0.5259, respectively... For the primary endpoint, 1 patient in the placebo group and 6 in the drug group had missing data. Such 'imbalance' in missingness is a potential issue for bias, since this is a relatively small study with about 40 patients randomized in each group to start with... Data entry error regarding primary endpoint was discovered late in the review, although it did not alter the efficacy conclusion and the impact was minimal."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 3.2.2 "Statistical Methodologies," p.9]*

> "The primary endpoint was analyzed using a mixed effect repeated measures (MMRM) model that included treatment group, mFARS score at baseline, site, visit, baseline-by-visit and the treatment-by-visit interactions, using analysis visits 4, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 48, and assuming an unstructured covariance matrix. The study SAP was changed 3 times close to the end of study, and site was added to be a covariate in the model in the last version of SAP. The model produced very similar result whether including site as covariate or not."

*[verbatim, same source, Table 5 and surrounding text, Section 3.2.4.1, p.13]*

> "The primary analysis of mFARS included 82 patients. There was a statistically significant greater mean reduction in the mFARS score from baseline to week 48 of the 48-week double-blind treatment phase for RTA408 compared with placebo. The difference in least squares mean (LSM) (95% CI) was −2.4 (−4.3, −0.5) for RTA408 vs placebo (p = 0.014)."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 5.1 "Statistical Issues and Collective Evidence," p.19]*

> "There is only one single natural history study with its result summarized in Patel [2016]... In sum, the primary endpoint result of the pivotal trial is statistically significant with p = 0.0141. Given the well-known possible issues with use of natural history data, we do not see that Patel [2016] with heavy missing data could provide additional strong support."

*[verbatim, same source, same section, on the post hoc global test, p.19-20]*

> "We have concerns with such global testing. First, all these analyses are post-hoc and do not follow the pre-specified multiplicity adjustment procedure... It does not control the overall type I error probability associated with testing the pre-specified set of endpoints (FDA Guidance for Industry, Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials)... Such a global testing result adds little to help interpretation for strength of statistical evidence."

*[verbatim, same source, Section 5.2 "Conclusions and Recommendation," p.20]*

> "The efficacy results obtained from the statistical analyses of the one pivotal study (408-C-1402-PT2) support the conclusion that RTA408 at 150 mg is effective in treating patients with episodic FA, based on change from baseline in the primary endpoint mFARS at Week 48."

### 41. Pegunigalsidase alfa-iwxj (Elfabrio) — BLA 761161

**Sponsor:** Chiesi Farmaceutici S.p.A. (sponsor of record on the BLA per FDA's Drugs@FDA overview page; pegunigalsidase alfa was originated by Protalix BioTherapeutics/Protalix Ltd., which manufactures the enzyme and is sponsor of record for the pivotal trial on ClinicalTrials.gov; Chiesi USA, Inc. distributes the product in the US under license from Protalix)

**Indication approved:** Long-term enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) in adult patients with a confirmed diagnosis of Fabry disease

**Approval date:** May 9, 2023 (traditional/regular approval, not accelerated approval — see regulatory history below)

**Pivotal trial:** BALANCE (Protalix protocol PB-102-F20), NCT02795676 — a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled switch trial in ERT-experienced Fabry patients; FDA's review ultimately treated BALANCE as confirmatory evidence rather than the sole "adequate and well-controlled" trial, with that role instead filled by the single-arm renal-biopsy trial PB-102-F01/F02 (part of the same early-phase dose-ranging program registered as NCT01678898)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, switch/continuation-of-therapy design (all patients ERT-experienced on agalsidase beta ≥1 year before randomization), small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population, regular approval grounded in a single-arm histological-surrogate trial (renal Gb3/BLISS score) as the sole adequate and well-controlled study, with a randomized active-controlled trial downgraded from primary to confirmatory evidence after FDA rejected the sponsor's non-inferiority margin

- *Endpoints:* annualized rate of change (slope) in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, CKD-EPI) as primary endpoint (continuous renal-biomarker slope endpoint), renal biopsy Gb3 inclusion count (BLISS score) as a surrogate histological primary endpoint in a companion single-arm trial, plasma/urine Lyso-Gb3 and Gb3 concentrations, left ventricular mass index (LVMI) by cardiac MRI, Fabry Clinical Events (FCE) composite (cardiac/cerebrovascular/renal events plus non-cardiac death), patient-reported outcomes (Brief Pain Inventory, Mainz Severity Score Index, EQ-5D-5L)

- *Primary analysis:* two-stage slope analysis — per-patient linear regression of eGFR on time, followed by a group-level comparison of the individual slopes — using quantile regression (SAS PROC QUANTREG) on median slopes as the sponsor's final primary model, with a random-intercept-random-slope (RIRS) longitudinal mixed model and a two-stage ANCOVA on mean slopes as competing/supportive models; within-patient permutation test and exact McNemar's test for the single-arm histological endpoint

- *Multiplicity:* unadjusted secondary/supportive testing (single formal primary endpoint)

- *Interim/alpha-spending:* unblinded interim analysis at Month 12, pre-specified only to support an EU Marketing Authorization Application, not intended to trigger stopping/adaptation for FDA purposes and given no formal alpha penalty at the Month-24 final analysis — but retrospectively linked to the sponsor's post-unblinding change to the primary analysis method and endpoint (unblinded-interim-informed post-hoc primary-analysis change)

- *Missing data/bias:* missing-at-random assumption for eGFR-slope estimation, reference-based multiple imputation and tipping-point sensitivity analyses planned in the original (pre-unblinding) SAP for the superiority framing but dropped once the primary switched to non-inferiority, AKI-episode eGFR values treated as missing/excluded from slope estimation

- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval, FDA rejection of a sponsor's proposed non-inferiority margin as unsupported, downgrading a randomized trial from primary to confirmatory evidence, original accelerated-approval pathway foreclosed by the reference product's own accelerated-to-traditional-approval conversion occurring before the BLA's action date

**Trial design & endpoints**

- BALANCE (PB-102-F20): randomized (2:1), double-blind (quadruple-masked), active-controlled Phase 3 trial in adults 18-60 years with Fabry disease and impaired renal function (screening eGFR 40-120 mL/min/1.73m², evidence of renal-function decline of at least -2 mL/min/1.73m²/year), all previously treated with agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme) for ≥1 year and on a stable dose for ≥6 months; no more than 50% of enrolled patients could be female; randomization stratified by urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) <1 vs. ≥1 g/g; patients continued on 1 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks of either PRX-102 (pegunigalsidase alfa) or agalsidase beta, blinded to identity

- Primary efficacy endpoint: the annualized rate of change (slope) in eGFR, assessed over 104 weeks (24 months) of treatment and derived from serial serum creatinine via the CKD-EPI equation — described as a comparison of *mean* slopes (via a longitudinal mixed model) in the SAP's endpoint-definition sections (2.2.1, 3), but ultimately analyzed as a comparison of *median* slopes via quantile regression in the SAP's primary-analysis section (9.2), an internal inconsistency left over from the sponsor's post-unblinding SAP revision

- Secondary endpoints: change from baseline in plasma Lyso-Gb3, LVMI by cardiac MRI, plasma Gb3, urine Lyso-Gb3, UPCR, pain-medication frequency, exercise stress test, Brief Pain Inventory, Mainz Severity Score Index, EQ-5D-5L; Fabry Clinical Events (FCE, a composite of cardiac, cerebrovascular, and renal events plus non-cardiac death); achievement of pre-specified Fabry Kidney Disease therapeutic goals

- Sample size/power: as originally planned under a superiority framing, ~66 evaluable patients (78 randomized allowing 15% dropout, 2:1 ratio) gave ~80% power to detect a 1.1 mL/min/1.73m²/year slope difference at two-sided alpha 0.05 (assumed SD 1.5 in each arm); the same N gave ≥90% power for a later-added one-sided, alpha-0.025 non-inferiority test against a margin of -3.0 mL/min/1.73m²/year, first used at the Month-12 interim analysis submitted only to EMA; 78 patients were ultimately randomized (53 PRX-102, 25 agalsidase beta) and 77 received at least one dose (ITT population)

- Statistical methods: the original SAP (dated September 24, 2020, pre-dating any unblinding) specified a superiority test of mean eGFR slope via an RIRS mixed model adjusted for the UPCR stratification factor, with a two-stage ANCOVA (per-patient linear-regression slopes compared by ANCOVA) as the FDA-recommended key supportive analysis from a 2019 pre-BLA meeting; after an April 2021 unblinded interim analysis conducted to support an EU MAA submission, the sponsor's final SAP (dated January 25, 2022) changed the primary analysis to a two-stage approach with quantile regression on the median slope (SAS PROC QUANTREG), declaring non-inferiority if the lower bound of the 95% CI for the PRX-102-minus-agalsidase-beta difference was ≥ -3.0 mL/min/1.73m²/year; FDA's statistical review declined to accept this as the controlling analysis, instead treating the pre-unblinding RIRS/ANCOVA specification as "the Applicant's primary analysis" for interpretive purposes, running its own post-hoc two-stage ANCOVA adjusted for continuous UPCR, and rejecting the sponsor's -3.0 non-inferiority margin outright for lack of any placebo-controlled agalsidase-beta data in a population comparable to BALANCE's (treatment-experienced, milder renal impairment) — concluding BALANCE could not support a formal non-inferiority claim and using its comparable-slope result only as confirmatory evidence alongside the single-arm PB-102-F01/F02 renal-biopsy trial, which FDA treated as the "one adequate and well-controlled study" via a large reduction in kidney Gb3 inclusions (BLISS score, assessed by light microscopy across ~300 peritubular capillaries per biopsy) analyzed with paired t-tests (sponsor) and non-parametric permutation/exact McNemar's tests (FDA, given n=14)

- Notable secondary-endpoint caveat: the FCE composite numerically favored agalsidase beta over PRX-102, but FDA's review found this "especially problematic" because the blinded medical monitor's FCE classifications were not adjudicated by specialists and because all patients who experienced an FCE had been on prior ERT for 4 years to over a decade versus a comparatively short PRX-102 exposure at the time of the event — FDA concluded it could not attribute the imbalance to drug, prior treatment, disease progression, or chance

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/761161Orig1s000Approv.pdf

- Package Insert / Label — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/761161s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Multi-Discipline Review (bundles the Summary Review, Clinical Review [Mehul Desai, MD], and Statistical Review [Yared Gurmu, PhD], all dated May 8, 2023, in one combined PDF distinguished internally by separate "Reference ID" page groupings; no stand-alone Statistical Review PDF is posted separately) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/761161Orig1s000MultidisciplineR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov record (BALANCE) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02795676

- Protocol (PB-102-F20, Version 5, July 14, 2017) — https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/76/NCT02795676/Prot_000.pdf

- Statistical Analysis Plan (final version, January 25, 2022) — https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/76/NCT02795676/SAP_001.pdf

"Head-to-head trial of pegunigalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta in patients with Fabry disease and deteriorating renal function: results from the 2-year randomised phase III BALANCE study." *J Med Genet.* 2024;61(6):520-530. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1136/jmg-2023-109445), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37940383/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Head-to-head%20trial%20of%20pegunigalsidase%20alfa%20versus%20agalsidase%20beta%20in%20patients%20with%20Fabry%20disease%20and%20deteriorating%20renal%20function)

**Other resources**

- Labeling discrepancy noted: the approved Package Insert's Section 14 ("Clinical Studies") describes the randomized active-controlled trial as "Trial 2 (NCT03566017)," but NCT03566017 is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as a single-group, open-label extension study, while the randomized, double-blind trial matching the label's description (77 randomized/dosed patients, 52 PRX-102/25 agalsidase beta, 104-week eGFR-slope endpoint) is unambiguously BALANCE/PB-102-F20/NCT02795676 — this appears to be a labeling citation error rather than a reference to a genuinely different trial

- Neither Chiesi nor Protalix appears in Vivli's published member list or the YODA Project's current data-partner list as of this research pass; Chiesi instead describes its own EFPIA/PhRMA-aligned "Chiesi Clinical Study Register" and a direct clinical-trial data-request portal rather than participation in a third-party IPD platform — trial-specific data availability for BALANCE was not otherwise confirmed

- No FDA advisory committee meeting was held for this BLA resubmission

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

The FDA regulatory history is unusually detailed and directly bears on how to read the SAP: the original BLA (submitted May 27, 2020) sought accelerated approval on the strength of the single-arm PB-102-F01/F02 renal-biopsy trial alone; FDA issued a Complete Response Letter on April 27, 2021 citing a manufacturing deficiency and, separately, ruling that accelerated approval was no longer available because the comparator (Fabrazyme) had itself converted from accelerated to traditional approval before PRX-102's action date, foreclosing the surrogate pathway unless PRX-102 showed a therapeutic advantage. In the resubmission, the sponsor leaned on BALANCE (then newly unblinded at its Month-12 interim look) to support traditional approval instead.

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, regulatory-history section (Ref ID 5170483), p.9 — FDA's September 2021 Type A meeting response, quoted within the review]* — "Yes, your plan to evaluate for PRX-102 non-inferiority to Fabrazyme on eGFR slope at 2 years may be a reasonable approach provided that adequate justification and strong evidence support such a statistical approach. We agree that a meeting prior to data lock will be important in order to discuss and come to agreement on the criteria to demonstrate non-inferiority and associated statistical considerations. We remind you that if substantial evidence of efficacy will be based on a single adequate and well-controlled trial, additional confirmatory evidence must also be provided to support substantial evidence of effectiveness."

*[verbatim, Statistical Analysis Plan (Protocol PB-102-F20, dated January 25, 2022), Section 9.2 "Primary Efficacy Analysis – Two Stage with Quantile Regression," p.27]* — "At the 2nd stage, the annualized mean change (slope) of the eGFR between the two treatment arms will be compared using quantile regression estimating the median slopes. The dependent variable will be the slope of each individual patient and the model will include the following covariates: Intercept; Treatment arm (PRX-102; agalsidase beta)... Non-inferiority will be declared if the lower bound of the confidence interval for the treatment difference (PRX-102 minus agalsidase beta) is greater or equal to -3.0 mL/min/1.73 m2/year."

*[verbatim, same SAP, Section 13.2 "Changes from Interim Analysis SAP to Final Analysis SAP," p.47]* — "1. Following the full approval of agalsidase beta, the final analysis was changed to non-inferiority. 2. The primary analysis was changed to the two-stage with quantile regression, and the RIRS (primary analysis for the interim analysis) is now a supportive analysis. This change was discussed and agreed with the FDA... 3. In the FDA interaction, the agency suggested to remove UPCR from the model."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Statistical Review "Summary and Conclusions," Section 4.1 (Ref ID 5170483), p.52]* — "The review team does not agree with the Applicant's proposed non-inferiority margin because there are no data to support this margin for agalsidase beta in the setting of Trial PB-102-F20 (see Appendix 3 for review team's evaluation on the Applicant's NI margin justification). The design of Trial PB-102 F20, therefore, does not allow for inference regarding non-inferiority of PRX-102 to agalsidase beta."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Clinical Review "Efficacy Results – Primary Endpoint" (Ref ID 5170365), p.33]* — "In summary, the applicant's SAP pre-defined primary analysis was a random intercept and random slope mixed effect model (RIRS) that compared the mean eGFR slope between PRX-102 and agalsidase arms adjusting for the randomization stratification factor of UPCR... Based on the Applicant's primary analysis adjusted for the binary baseline proteinuria (< 1 vs ≥ 1 gr/gr), the estimated mean eGFR slope between the two arms were comparable (-2.4 for PRX-102 and -2.3 for agalsidase beta), and the estimated treatment difference was -0.1 (95% CI: -2.3, 2.1) mL/min/1.73 m2/year."

Note a cross-document inconsistency in the same treatment-difference CI: the Summary Review (Ref ID 5170550, p.19) reports the identical point estimate with a different lower bound — *[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Summary Review, p.19]* — "the treatment difference was -0.1 (95% CI: -2.2, 2.1) mL/min/1.73 m2/year" — versus -2.3 in the Clinical Review and in the approved label; both are reproduced here as written rather than reconciled.

*[verbatim, approved Package Insert, Section 14 "Clinical Studies," p.16, describing Trial 2/BALANCE]* — "The primary efficacy endpoint was the annualized rate of change in eGFR (eGFR slope) assessed over 104 weeks. The estimated mean eGFR slope was -2.4 and -2.3 mL/min/1.73 m2/year on ELFABRIO and agalsidase beta respectively. The estimated treatment difference was -0.1 (95% CI: -2.3, 2.1) mL/min/1.73 m2/year."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Statistical Review, Section 3.2.2 (Ref ID 5170483), p.17, describing the single-arm PB-102-F01/F02 renal-biopsy endpoint FDA ultimately treated as the "adequate and well-controlled" primary evidence]* — "Given the single-arm design of PB-102-F01/F02/F03, inferential analysis of change from baseline to 6-month in Gb3 BLISS score rests on the assumption that spontaneous decline in Gb3 deposition is unlikely at the population level... This comparison was conducted using both a two-sample t-test and permutation test for each of the 14 individual patients."

*[verbatim, approved Package Insert, Table 6, p.16, reporting the PB-102-F01/F02 result]* — Mean Change at Week 26 (95% CI), All Patients (N=14): "-3.1 (-4.8, -1.4)" Gb3 inclusions per renal peritubular capillary.

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Summary Review "Efficacy Conclusion" (Ref ID 5170550), p.21]* — "According to the Statistical review dated May 8, 2023: 'From a statistical perspective, the team recommends traditional approval of PRX102.' We concur with this recommendation."

### 42. Palovarotene (Sohonos) — NDA 215559

**Sponsor:** Ipsen Biopharmaceuticals, Inc. — palovarotene was originally developed by Clementia Pharmaceuticals Inc. (which licensed the compound from Roche and held the IND from 2014), and Clementia was acquired by Ipsen in April 2019; Ipsen is the applicant of record on NDA 215559 (FDA Integrated Review, Reference ID 5227463, p.2, Table 1: "Applicant — Ipsen Biopharmaceuticals, Inc.")

**Indication approved:** Reduction in volume of new heterotopic ossification (HO) in adults and pediatric patients aged 8 years and older for females and 10 years and older for males with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) — a narrower claim than the "prevention of HO" indication originally proposed

**Approval date:** August 16, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** Study PVO-1A-301 ("MOVE" trial), NCT03312634, with Clementia's separately conducted natural history study PVO-1A-001 (NCT02322255) serving as the external untreated-comparator cohort

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (~800 confirmed FOP cases worldwide); Phase 3, multicenter, open-label, single-arm study using a non-concurrent natural-history-study cohort as an external control for the primary efficacy comparison, rather than a randomized or placebo comparator (no existing taxonomy row covers an external natural-history control design); partial clinical hold on a specific age-defined pediatric subgroup imposed mid-trial for an emergent safety signal, with treatment never resumed in that subgroup

- *Endpoints:* annualized change in new heterotopic ossification (HO) volume assessed by low-dose whole-body CT (WBCT), a continuous imaging-volumetric endpoint unique to this census; key secondary endpoint of proportion of subjects with any new HO at Month 12; flare-up rate per participant-month of exposure (negative binomial regression with an exposure-time offset)

- *Primary analysis:* Bayesian compound Poisson distribution model — a two-part mixture model separately estimating (1) the rate of body regions developing new HO and (2) the volume of new HO conditional on its occurring, with a square-root transformation of the volume component; post hoc Bayesian reanalysis of the same model omitting the square-root transformation; post hoc weighted linear mixed-effects model (wLME) using each subject's longest-follow-up observation (distinct from MMRM); FDA's independent frequentist reanalyses — generalized estimating equations (GEE) "landmark" analyses at Month 12, a random-slope mixed model, and covariate-adjusted ordinal logistic regression on ranked annualized HO

- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design with three interim analyses and a final analysis; one-sided overall alpha of 2.5%; Lan-DeMets alpha-spending function, revised from Pocock to O'Brien-Fleming parameterization at FDA's request; non-binding futility boundary (beta-spending) crossed at the second interim analysis without the trial actually stopping; Data Monitoring Committee (DMC)

- *Missing data/bias:* differential efficacy-assessment schedule between the treatment arm (6-month WBCT intervals) and the external natural-history control arm (12-month intervals), which FDA and the sponsor concluded interacted with the primary endpoint's square-root transformation to bias the prespecified primary analysis against palovarotene; negative (net-shrinkage) HO volume changes set to zero rather than treated as evidence of regression; missing-at-random assumption with no imputation for missing WBCT timepoints in the primary analysis

- *Regulatory:* Complete Response Letter (CRL) followed by resubmission and approval (original NDA submitted March 31, 2021, withdrawn by the sponsor August 21, 2021 for data-integrity issues involving missing WBCT scan readings; resubmitted April 29, 2022; CRL issued December 23, 2022 for insufficient evidence of effectiveness; complete response to the CRL submitted February 16, 2023); FDA Advisory Committee meeting held (June 28, 2023; committee name not confirmed in the reviewed documents); regular approval granted on FDA's own post hoc reanalysis of a trial that missed its prespecified primary endpoint, after FDA itself determined the prespecified analysis was invalid/biased; boxed warning added covering both embryo-fetal toxicity and premature physeal closure, the latter driving an age/sex-restricted approved population

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Study PVO-1A-301 (MOVE) was a Phase 3, multicenter, open-label, single-arm trial in patients ≥4 years old with a clinical diagnosis of FOP and no flare-up symptoms in the prior 4 weeks; the trial was explicitly designed with no randomized comparator, instead using data from Clementia's separately conducted natural history study (NHS, PVO-1A-001, NCT02322255) as the external control — per the SAP: *[verbatim, SAP v1.3.1, §1.5, p.7]* — "This is an open-label study, with the comparator arm being subject data from the NHS. The efficacy of palovarotene treatment in the MOVE Trial, as measured by the change in new HO volume (the primary efficacy endpoint), will be compared to that observed in untreated subjects who participated in the NHS."

- The "Principal Analysis population" (for comparability with the NHS) was restricted to subjects with the classic R206H ACVR1 mutation and no prior palovarotene exposure (~99 of ~110 total enrolled subjects); an additional ~11 subjects with other FOP-associated mutations or prior Phase 2 trial participation were enrolled but analyzed only in a "Supplementary" population. Dosing consisted of chronic daily palovarotene (5 mg) plus an escalated flare-up regimen (20 mg/day for 4 weeks, then 10 mg/day for 8 weeks, extendable) for FOP flare-ups; the trial was structured in Part A (24-month core treatment), Part B (24-month extension), and Part C (up to 2-year post-treatment safety follow-up for skeletally immature subjects who discontinued early)

- Primary efficacy endpoint: annualized change in new HO volume, assessed by low-dose whole-body CT (WBCT) excluding the head, at baseline/Month 6/12/18/24 in MOVE versus baseline/Month 12/24/36 in the NHS, read by two independent blinded readers with a third-reader adjudication; net-negative volume changes in a body region (from bone remodeling/measurement variability) were set to zero rather than treated as regression

- Key secondary endpoint: proportion of subjects with any new HO at Month 12; other secondary endpoints included number of body regions with new HO, flare-up rate/proportion of subjects with flare-ups (negative binomial regression), range of motion (CAJIS), physical function (FOP-PFQ), and PROMIS Global Health

- Sample size (~110 subjects total, ~99 in the Principal Analysis population) was determined by simulation using NHS WBCT data (65 subjects' paired 1-year scans) and observed Phase 2 palovarotene effect sizes, assuming a one-sided overall type I error rate of 2.5%; three formal interim efficacy analyses (with futility assessed at the second and third) plus a final analysis were planned, using a Lan-DeMets alpha-spending function initially specified with Pocock parameterization and later revised to O'Brien-Fleming "based on FDA scientific advice" *[verbatim, SAP v1.3.1, §1.9.1, p.11]*

- Prespecified primary analysis: a Bayesian compound Poisson distribution model jointly modeling (a) the number/rate of body regions developing new HO (Poisson, subject-level gamma-distributed rate) and (b) the square-root-transformed HO volume within regions with new HO (normal), with palovarotene's multiplicative treatment effect on each component (θ₁, θ₂) combined into an overall efficacy ratio γ = θ₁×θ₂; posterior probability that γ<1 (i.e., palovarotene reduces HO) was the basis for declaring statistical significance at each interim/final analysis

- The trial crossed its prespecified futility boundary at the second interim analysis (using the square-root-transformed model); the DMC unblinded the sponsor to determine whether the study should stop, but flagged that identical post hoc analyses without the square-root transformation showed apparent benefit, and recommended additional analyses rather than a definitive futility call — the study continued, with dosing interrupted and later resumed only in subjects ≥14 years old, per a partial FDA clinical hold (December 4, 2019) on dosing in children <14 imposed for premature physeal closure (PPC) that was never lifted for that age group

- At the resulting third interim analysis (treated by the sponsor as the de facto final efficacy analysis given the prolonged dosing interruptions), the Applicant's prespecified Bayesian analysis (with square-root transformation) failed to demonstrate efficacy — posterior probability of benefit 0.65, 95% credible interval for the annualized-HO ratio 0.74-1.22 — while the same Bayesian model without the square-root transformation showed posterior probability >0.99, and a post hoc weighted linear mixed-effects (wLME) model using each subject's longest available follow-up reached nominal significance (least-squares mean difference -10.9 cm³/year, 95% CI -21.2 to -0.6, nominal p=0.039). FDA's own frequentist GEE "landmark" reanalyses at Month 12 (avoiding the constant-rate-of-change assumption of the wLME) were directionally and statistically consistent (e.g., difference -15.3 cm³/year, 95% CI -28.5 to -2.1, nominal p=0.0229), as were a random-slope mixed model and a covariate-adjusted ordinal logistic regression intended to rule out a result driven by outliers/skewness

- FDA's Integrated Review concluded the prespecified square-root-transformed Bayesian model was biased against palovarotene because of the more frequent (6- vs. 12-month) WBCT assessment schedule in MOVE relative to the NHS, and that the post hoc analyses (by both sponsor and FDA) were the more appropriate basis for an efficacy conclusion — an unusual instance of FDA affirmatively substituting a post hoc reanalysis for a missed prespecified primary endpoint rather than merely supporting it as sensitivity evidence

- Supportive/confirmatory evidence came from a similarly designed but non-randomized/non-pivotal Phase 2 extension (Study 202C, same dosing regimen) compared against the NHS via propensity-score matching (mean annualized new HO 16.1 cm³/year with palovarotene vs. 28.4 cm³/year untreated), and from within-subject comparisons of HO accrual during on-treatment vs. dosing-interruption ("pause") periods

- Safety: premature physeal closure (PPC) occurred in 14/25 (56%) of the youngest pediatric subjects (<8y girls/<10y boys) and 13/39 (33%) of early adolescents (≥8/10 to <14y) across Studies 301 and 202B/C, versus none of 38 older adolescents (≥14 to <18y); PPC was associated with reduced growth in standing height and knee height. This safety signal — first observed on scheduled radiographs in 2019 — led to the December 2019 partial clinical hold and ultimately to the approved population being restricted to females ≥8 years and males ≥10 years, with a boxed warning for premature physeal closure alongside embryo-fetal toxicity

### 43. Pozelimab-bbfg (Veopoz) — BLA 761339

**Sponsor:** Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Treatment of CD55-deficient protein-losing enteropathy (CHAPLE disease) in adult and pediatric patients 1 year of age and older

**Approval date:** August 18, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** R3918-PLE-1878, NCT04209634, open-label, single-arm, phase 2/3

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* single-arm, open-label trial (no randomized concurrent control) in an ultra-rare monogenic disease (worldwide patient count in the low tens at time of filing); FDA-accepted external-control design under 21 CFR 314.126, using two historical-control sources — a published 14-patient uncontrolled case series of eculizumab-treated CHAPLE patients (Ozen 2021; Kurolap 2019), and each enrolled subject's own pre-treatment medical-chart history — rather than a concurrent placebo arm, which the sponsor and FDA agreed would be unethical given prior evidence that C5 inhibition (eculizumab) resolves life-threatening manifestations; small single-arm or small randomized trial in an ultra-rare disease population (Keyword_Taxonomy.md, §1); within-patient (pre-treatment vs. on-treatment) comparison as a secondary analytic frame for hospitalization, growth, and other objective endpoints

- *Endpoints:* multi-component (composite) primary endpoint requiring both (1) normalization of serum albumin between Weeks 12-24 (≥70% of measurements ≥3.5 g/dL, no single value <2.5 g/dL, no albumin infusion required) and (2) improvement without worsening, at Week 24, in 4 pre-specified clinical signs/symptoms (abdominal pain frequency, bowel movement frequency, facial edema, peripheral edema) among those evaluable for improvement at baseline; FDA's clinical review concluded the symptom-based component's clinical outcome assessments (COAs) were not fit-for-purpose (proxy-reported pain scale, unreliable pediatric e-diary reporting, inconsistent local-vs-central edema grading) and instead centered its efficacy conclusion on serum albumin normalization plus secondary/objective endpoints (hospitalization days, albumin-transfusion requirement, height/weight z-scores)

- *Primary analysis:* responder proportion with 90% exact (Clopper-Pearson) confidence interval, analyzed in the Full Analysis Set and repeated in the Per-Protocol Set; pre-specified success criterion (from the SAP's sample-size section) was a Beta-Binomial Bayesian comparison (Jeffreys prior, Beta(0.5,0.5)) of the pozelimab responder rate against the historical eculizumab cohort's 0/14 pre-treatment response rate, with ≥4/6 evaluable active-PLE patients meeting the primary endpoint pre-specified as providing >99% posterior probability that pozelimab's response rate exceeds the untreated historical rate — FDA explicitly stated it "did not agree with this criterion" as a sample-size justification and pushed the sponsor (via repeated Type C meeting/IR feedback) to enroll as many subjects as feasible; final enrollment was 10 subjects, all with active disease

- *Missing data/bias:* estimand for the primary endpoint used a composite strategy (discontinuation for lack of efficacy or an adverse event counted as non-responder); non-responder imputation used as a sensitivity analysis for subjects with fewer than 5 of 7 planned Week 12-24 albumin measurements; FDA-requested sensitivity analysis substituting centrally-read (photograph-based) edema assessment for local investigator assessment collapsed the "100% efficacy" primary-endpoint result to 20% efficacy (2/10, 90% CI 3.7-50.7%), illustrating the reliability problem FDA flagged in the symptom-based component (FDA-driven post hoc reader-concordance sensitivity analysis overturning a sponsor's primary responder-endpoint result)

- *Regulatory:* No FDA Advisory Committee meeting was convened (FDA's review states one "was not convened to discuss this application," while noting the sponsor had itself questioned whether an AdComm was warranted); approved as the first product for this recently described ultra-rare monogenic disease; no REMS required; no post-marketing requirements at approval, though post-marketing commitments were agreed

**Trial design & endpoints**

- R3918-PLE-1878 was an open-label, single-arm, 144-week treatment study (screening up to 4-10 weeks; follow-up to Week 164) in patients ≥1 year old with a CD55 loss-of-function mutation and clinically active PLE (hypoalbuminemia ≤3.2 g/dL plus ≥7 days of qualifying symptoms/signs in the prior 6 months, off eculizumab); patients received a single 30 mg/kg IV loading dose on Day 1, then weekly subcutaneous weight-based dosing; a minimum of 6 and up to ~20 patients were planned, with the primary analysis timed to when ~6 active-PLE patients had reached 24 weeks of treatment; the protocol was amended 6 times.

- Sample-size rationale (per the posted SAP, v4, dated June 20, 2022, §2.2): historical eculizumab data (Ozen 2021, Kurolap 2019) showed 0/14 patients met the primary-endpoint definition before eculizumab treatment (90% exact CI 0.00-0.19) and 14/14 met it on eculizumab (90% exact CI 0.81-1.00); the sponsor calculated that observing ≥4/6 pozelimab-treated responders would yield a 90% exact CI (0.27, 0.94) clearly excluding the historical untreated upper bound, and — via a Beta-Binomial Bayesian analysis with a Jeffreys Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior — would give >99% posterior probability that pozelimab's true response rate exceeds the untreated historical rate, and 90% posterior probability the rate is ≥0.37 higher; FDA's Multi-Disciplinary Review states this was not a hypothesis-testing design (no formal sample-size/power calculation) and that FDA "did not agree with this criterion," repeatedly urging maximal enrollment; 10 subjects were ultimately enrolled and treated.

- Primary analysis population: Full Analysis Set (all dosed subjects), repeated in a Per-Protocol Set; primary endpoint proportion summarized with a 90% exact (Clopper-Pearson) CI.

- Result (FDA-replicated, Table 24 of the Multi-Discipline Review, from the sponsor's Clinical Study Report Table 14): 10/10 (100%) subjects met the pre-specified multi-component primary endpoint (90% CI 74.1-100%) — all 10 achieved serum albumin normalization and all 10 showed improvement/no worsening on all 4 symptom components. FDA's clinical/statistical review determined the symptom-based COAs were not fit-for-purpose (unvalidated proxy-reported pain measure, unreliable multi-reporter pediatric bowel-movement e-diary, and — critically — a sponsor-conducted sensitivity analysis substituting centrally-read photographic edema grading for local investigator grading that collapsed the composite responder rate to 2/10 (20%, 90% CI 3.7-50.7%)). FDA therefore based its efficacy conclusion primarily on the objective albumin-normalization component (10/10, 100%) plus secondary/objective endpoints.

- Supportive secondary/objective results emphasized by FDA: hospitalization days fell from 268 days across 9/10 subjects in the 48 weeks pre-treatment to 7 days across 2/10 subjects on treatment; growth (height/weight z-scores) and other biochemical parameters (immunoglobulins, vitamin B12, iron indices) were tracked as secondary endpoints with change-from-baseline summaries rather than formal hypothesis tests.

- FDA's statistical review (Tae Hyun Jung, PhD, Statistical Reviewer; Paul Imbriano, PhD, Statistical Team Leader) concluded that despite the small, non-randomized, single-arm design and the inadequacy of the symptom-based COAs, the magnitude and consistency of the albumin-normalization and hospitalization/objective results, combined with a well-understood disease mechanism (complement dysregulation via CD55 loss) and the historical-control comparison, supported substantial evidence of effectiveness for this ultra-rare, previously untreatable monogenic disease.

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, ClinicalTrials.gov-posted Statistical Analysis Plan, v4 (June 20, 2022), §1.1]* — "R3918-PLE-1878 is an open-label study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of pozelimab in 6 to 20 patients with active CD55-deficient PLE, as an addition to standard-of-care therapies (excluding eculizumab). The hypothesis is that pozelimab treatment will result in normalization of serum albumin and improvement in clinical signs and symptoms in CD55-deficient PLE/CHAPLE disease... This study does not include a randomized, concurrent placebo control group... a trial design involving the withholding of active therapy from some trial subjects, as a control group, is not considered acceptable. These eculizumab data have been used to provide an external control to enable interpretation of the results from our open-label study, as per guidance in 21CFR 314.126."

*[verbatim, posted SAP, §2.2]* — "The study is regarded as successful if at least 4 of 6 evaluable patients with active PLE achieve the primary endpoint... By a Bayesian analysis, a comparison between 4 of 6 pozelimab-treated patients achieving the primary endpoint and 0 of 14 in the historical data by a Beta-Binomial analysis with the Jefferys prior of Beta(0.5, 0.5) would conclude that there is a >99% posterior probability that pozelimab has a greater response rate than untreated patients."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, "Sample size considerations," p.89]* — "As the study did not include hypothesis testing, there was no formal method to estimate the sample size... FDA did not agree with this criterion and repeatedly encouraged the Applicant to enroll as many subjects as possible to ensure adequate data were available in the BLA to assess safety and efficacy."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, "Study Endpoints," p.82]* — "The Division did not agree with the symptom-based component of the multi-component endpoint. There were multiple limitations to these assessments that rendered the data inadequate / uninterpretable to support efficacy... These concerns were communicated multiple times to the Applicant prior to submission of the BLA (Type C meeting dated October 6, 2021, IRs dated August 6, 2020, and August 2, 2021)."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, "Efficacy Results – Primary Efficacy Endpoint," p.94]* — "Based on the pre-specified multi-component primary endpoint, all 10 (100%) subjects with active disease at baseline achieved normalization of serum albumin and demonstrated improvement in clinical signs and symptoms evaluable for improvement at baseline, without worsening of the others after 24 weeks of treatment, indicating 100% efficacy (90% CI: 74.1%, 100%)... As noted in Section 16.4.8, the Division did not agree with the symptom-based component of the multi-component endpoint. Therefore, the assessment of efficacy in this review will primarily focus on other endpoints that were considered to be more objective and interpretable."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, §16.4.8.3 "Sensitivity Analysis of Edema Assessment in Primary Endpoint," p.308]* — "The Applicant's sensitivity analysis using centrally read assessments of edema resulted in 20% efficacy (90% CI: 3.7%, 50.7%). This dramatic difference in the response rate for the sensitivity analysis compared to the primary analysis is attributed to the lack of concordance between physician (local site) assessment of edema, and centrally read assessment of edema based upon photographs."

*[verbatim, FDA Multi-Discipline Review, Summary Review, p.~360]* — "While CHAPLE disease is a recently identified very rare monogenic disease, its etiopathogenesis is well-understood, supporting the mechanistic rationale of using pozelimab and providing confirmatory evidence to substantiate the results of the single trial... Pozelimab will be the first product to be approved for use in this recently described very rare monogenic disease."

### 44. Cipaglucosidase alfa-atga (Pombiliti) — BLA 761204

**Sponsor:** Amicus Therapeutics (co-reviewed and co-approved in parallel with NDA 215211 for Opfolda/miglustat, the obligate co-administered oral chaperone, also an Amicus product incorporating Zavesca/miglustat safety data by reference from Actelion's NDA 021348)

**Indication approved:** Long-term enzyme replacement therapy, co-administered with miglustat, for adult patients with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) weighing ≥40 kg who are not improving on their current enzyme replacement therapy — a second-line-therapy indication, not first-line, per FDA's explicit labeling recommendation

**Approval date:** September 28, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** ATB200-03 / PROPEL, NCT03729362

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, active-controlled (vs. non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa co-administered with oral placebo), parallel-group, multicenter, international phase 3 trial; 2:1 randomization, stratified by baseline 6MWD category and ERT status (ERT-experienced vs. ERT-naive), not stratified by center

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint change from baseline to Week 52 in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD); six pre-specified, hierarchically ordered key secondary endpoints (sitting FVC % predicted; lower-extremity manual muscle test score; Week 26 6MWD; PROMIS Physical Function; PROMIS Fatigue; GSGC composite score)

- *Primary analysis:* MMRM (mixed model for repeated measures) on the ITT-OBS (observed-cases) population as the primary analysis for 6MWD, with a pre-specified ANCOVA/ITT-LOCF sensitivity analysis; one-sided superiority test at alpha=0.025

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (gatekeeping) hierarchical testing — primary endpoint tested first at one-sided alpha=0.025; each of the 6 ordered key secondary endpoints tested at the same alpha only if every endpoint above it in the sequence was significant; testing stopped at the first non-significant step, converting all endpoints below it to descriptive/nominal-only results

- *Missing data/bias:* MMRM under a missing-at-random assumption for the primary ITT-OBS analysis, cross-checked against an ITT-LOCF/ANCOVA sensitivity analysis; a pre-specified "control-based imputation" tipping-point-style sensitivity analysis (missing values imputed by averaging 15 randomly resampled Week-52 values from the active-comparator arm) to probe MAR validity; FDA's own re-analysis additionally excluded a single outlying comparator-arm subject as a post hoc sensitivity check

- *Regulatory:* substantial evidence of effectiveness established from a single adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence (established Pompe disease mechanism/etiology and Gaa-knockout-mouse pharmacology data) under FDA's "one trial plus confirmatory evidence" framework, despite the trial's primary endpoint failing its pre-specified superiority test — approval restricted to second-line use as a direct consequence; no Advisory Committee meeting held

**Trial design & endpoints**

- ATB200-03 (PROPEL) was a phase 3, double-blind, randomized, parallel-group, multicenter, international trial in adults (≥18y, ≥40 kg) with LOPD, enrolling both ERT-experienced (on alglucosidase alfa ≥24 months) and ERT-naive subjects; eligibility required sitting FVC ≥30% predicted and specific 6-minute walk test (6MWT) screening criteria (both screening 6MWD values ≥75 m and ≤90% predicted, within 20% of each other)

- Subjects were randomized 2:1 to IV cipaglucosidase alfa (20 mg/kg Q2W) + oral miglustat (weight-based dose) versus IV alglucosidase alfa (20 mg/kg Q2W, a non-U.S.-approved comparator product) + oral placebo, over a 12-month double-blind treatment period, with an open-label extension (ATB200-07) offered afterward; randomization was stratified by baseline 6MWD category (75-<150m, 150-<400m, ≥400m) and ERT status, not by center

- Sample size: planned for ~110 randomized (99 evaluable) subjects, powered (per the SAP, nQuery 8) at ~90% to detect a standardized effect size of 0.7 for the primary endpoint using a 2-group t-test at one-sided alpha=0.025 with 2:1 allocation; actual enrollment per ClinicalTrials.gov was 125

- Primary efficacy analysis: MMRM (SAS PROC MIXED, REML, unstructured covariance, Kenward-Roger degrees-of-freedom adjustment) on the ITT-OBS population, with fixed terms for treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, ERT status, gender, and continuous covariates for baseline 6MWD, age, weight, and height

- Result: the primary endpoint (Week-52 change in 6MWD) did not meet its pre-specified one-sided alpha=0.025 significance threshold. In the full ITT population, LS-mean difference was 14.21 m favoring cipa-mig (95% CI −2.6, 31.02; one-sided p=0.048, i.e., short of the 0.025 bar); in the FDA statistical reviewer's alternate presentation (raw observed means including all subjects), the estimated treatment difference was 5.33 m (95% CI −15.2, 25.9; p=0.608), described by FDA as "heavily influenced by the presence of an outlier in the comparator arm." A post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding that outlier gave an MMRM difference of 14 m (95% CI −2.6, 31; p=0.1) and a Wilcoxon rank-sum p=0.07 — still short of formal significance, though FDA characterized the direction as "convincing evidence" of a clinically meaningful numerical benefit

- Because the primary endpoint did not reach significance, the hierarchical gatekeeping procedure formally stopped there: the first key secondary endpoint (Week-52 FVC % predicted, LS-mean difference 2.32%, 95% CI 0.02-4.62, p=0.0484/nominal p=0.048) was reported only as "nominal statistical significance," not a formally controlled secondary claim, and no subsequent key secondaries were formally tested. A post hoc Wilcoxon rank-sum global test combining 6MWD and FVC endpoints gave p=0.022

- FDA's Integrated (Multi-Discipline) Review concluded substantial evidence of effectiveness rested on this one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence (well-established LOPD etiology/mechanism and Gaa-knockout-mouse pharmacology), explicitly noting the data were "not adequate to support use as first-line therapy given the lack of statistical significance for superiority and the inherent increased risk of two products over one" — the review team, at the February 2022 mid-cycle communication and April 2022 late-cycle meeting, negotiated the eventual second-line-only indication as the regulatory resolution of the missed primary endpoint

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

*[verbatim, ClinicalTrials.gov-posted SAP, ATB200-03 Statistical Analysis Plan Final v3.0, §3.3.1/§3.3.2, p.12]* — "The primary efficacy endpoint of this study is the change from baseline to Week 52 in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) measured in meters... The key secondary efficacy endpoints, in hierarchical order of importance, are: Change from baseline to Week 52 in sitting FVC (% predicted); Change from baseline to Week 52 in the manual muscle test (MMT) score for the lower extremities; Change from baseline to Week 26 in 6MWD; Change from baseline to Week 52 in the total score for [PROMIS] – Physical Function; Change from baseline to Week 52 in the total score for the PROMIS – Fatigue; Change from baseline to Week 52 in the total score for the GSGC."

*[verbatim, SAP §4.3, p.16]* — "Using a 2-group t-test with a 1-sided significance level of 0.025 and a 2:1 randomization ratio, a total of 99 subjects (66 subjects in the ATB200/AT2221 group and 33 subjects in the alglucosidase alfa/placebo group) would yield approximately 90% power to detect a clinically meaningful standardized effect size of 0.7 between the 2 groups in a superiority test for the primary endpoint."

*[verbatim, SAP §8.4, p.33]* — "The study has 6 key secondary efficacy endpoints which are ordered. The family-wise Type I error rate (FWER) for the statistical tests of the primary and key secondary endpoints will be controlled at 0.025... To strongly control the FWER at this level, a gate-keeping approach will be utilized in which each family of statistical tests... will be conducted in a sequential manner... If at any point the null hypothesis fails to be rejected, then that comparison and any other comparison below it cannot be claimed as successful."

*[verbatim, SAP §8.5.1, p.35]* — "The primary efficacy endpoint (change from baseline to Week 52 in 6MWD) will be analyzed using an MMRM model to compare between treatment and control on the ITT-OBS population... SAS PROC MIXED will be used for the analysis, with restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) and unstructured within-subject covariance structure. The Kenward-Roger approximation will be used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom."

*[verbatim, SAP §8.3.2 (MAR sensitivity), p.33]* — "In addition, a 'control group imputation' algorithm based on data sampled from the control group (alglucosidase alfa/placebo) will be implemented to replace missing data at the post-baseline visit... a random sample of 15 values will be selected (with replacement) from the available set of data in the control group at Week 52. The average of these 15 values will then be used to replace the missing value."

*[verbatim, FDA Integrated Review §6.2.1.4.2, p.44]* — "The estimated treatment difference was 2.3% (95% CI: 0.02 to 4.6; p=0.0484) favoring the cipa-mig arm... However, as the superiority test for the primary endpoint did not meet the significance level of 0.05, no formal superiority test was conducted for the FVC (% predicted) endpoint."

*[verbatim, FDA Integrated Review §1, Summary of Regulatory Action, p.3]* — "Substantial evidence of effectiveness for cipaglucosidase alfa coadministered with miglustat in patients with LOPD was established using data from one adequate and well-controlled trial with confirmatory evidence (CE)... While the one adequate and well-controlled trial with CE were adequate to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness, the data were not adequate to support use as first-line therapy given the lack of statistical significance for superiority and the inherent increased risk of two products over one."

*[verbatim, FDA Integrated Review, Administrative/regulatory history, p.~46]* — "The mid-cycle communication was held between Amicus and FDA on February 1, 2022, during which the review issue of the primary endpoint in trial ATB200-03 not having reached statistical significance for superiority on the primary endpoint of 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) was discussed... During the late cycle meeting, the FDA discussed its recommendation that cipa-mig be indicated as a second-line therapy because of the lack of statistical significance for superiority over available enzyme replacement therapy."

Note on Keyword_Taxonomy.md: the trial design/regulatory pattern here — a randomized active-controlled trial whose primary endpoint misses its pre-specified significance threshold, with FDA nonetheless finding substantial evidence of effectiveness via the "one trial plus confirmatory evidence" pathway and resolving the shortfall by narrowing the approved indication to second-line use only — does not appear to already be captured in Keyword_Taxonomy.md's Trial design or Regulatory sections. Flagged here as "": *Missed primary endpoint resolved via indication-narrowing (second-line-only approval) rather than trial failure*.

### 45. Nedosiran (Rivfloza) — NDA 215842

**Sponsor:** Novo Nordisk, Inc., c/o Dicerna Pharmaceuticals, Inc. — Dicerna Pharmaceuticals originated and developed nedosiran (internal code DCR-PHXC) and ran the pivotal trial as lead sponsor of record on ClinicalTrials.gov; Novo Nordisk A/S acquired Dicerna in December 2021, and the NDA itself (submitted September 30, 2022) lists Novo Nordisk, Inc. as the applicant, with Dicerna staff handling regulatory correspondence

**Indication approved:** To lower urinary oxalate levels in children 9 years of age and older and adults with primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1) and relatively preserved kidney function (e.g., eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m²); the label states too few PH2 patients were enrolled in the pivotal trial to evaluate efficacy in that population, so the approved indication is PH1-only even though the trial enrolled both PH1 and PH2 patients aged 6 and older

**Approval date:** September 29, 2023

**Pivotal trial:** PHYOX2 (sponsor protocol DCR-PHXC-201), NCT03847909

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group; small ultra-rare-disease trial population (35 randomized: 23 nedosiran, 12 placebo); covariate-adaptive minimization randomization (2:1 ratio, 80%/20% biased-coin allocation to the treatment minimizing imbalance across age-category and eGFR-category strata) (not currently a distinct row in Keyword_Taxonomy.md § Trial design)

- *Endpoints:* AUC-of-percent-change continuous urinary-biomarker endpoint (area under the curve, Days 90-180, of percent change from baseline in 24-hour urinary oxalate) (distinct from the taxonomy's existing PK/PD activity-threshold and lipid percent-change endpoint rows; FDA's statistical review specifically critiques this AUC construction's order-dependence and single-imputation properties, see SAP section below); key secondary responder endpoint (proportion normalized/near-normalized 24-hour urinary oxalate)

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA (fixed effects for age category, eGFR category, baseline urinary oxalate) (a single-timepoint/AUC-window ANCOVA, distinct from the taxonomy's existing "Repeated-measures ANCOVA" row); Fisher's exact test (key secondary); Wilcoxon rank-sum test (secondary stone-burden/plasma-oxalate endpoints); mixed model with random intercept and slope (eGFR rate of decline); exact Poisson regression with an exposure-time offset (exploratory stone-event rate)

- *Multiplicity:* fixed-sequence (step-down) hierarchical testing, 6 endpoints deep (AUC urinary oxalate → normalized/near-normalized Uox → plasma oxalate → kidney stone number → kidney stone surface area → eGFR rate of change), each gated at one-sided alpha 0.025

- *Interim/alpha-spending:* group-sequential design with alpha-spending planned at the sample-size-calculation stage (for a possible sample-size re-estimation interim look after two-thirds enrollment) but never executed because of slow enrollment; independent DSMC (three voting members) monitored unblinded safety/efficacy data periodically, including age-de-escalation gates before enrolling 6-11-year-olds

- *Missing data/bias:* multiple imputation under missing-at-random (FCS regression, 50 imputed datasets, SAS PROC MI/MIANALYZE, Rubin's rules) as the primary approach; MNAR control-based pattern imputation as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis; FDA-conducted independent tipping-point sensitivity analysis (sponsor did not provide one); FDA-conducted rerandomization/permutation test to validate p-values under covariate-adaptive minimization randomization (not currently in Keyword_Taxonomy.md § Primary analysis method); FDA-conducted post hoc covariate-adjusted sensitivity analysis (baseline imbalance) for a race imbalance (all Asian participants randomized to nedosiran) and an eGFR/disease-severity imbalance

- *Regulatory:* Orphan drug designation (granted May 15, 2018); Breakthrough Therapy designation for PH1 (granted July 2, 2019; a companion Breakthrough Therapy request for PH2 was denied December 30, 2020); Standard (not Priority) review; rare pediatric disease priority review voucher request denied because the application was not eligible for priority review; no FDA Advisory Committee meeting held; FDA statistical review documents a substantive methodological critique of the sponsor's AUC-based primary endpoint (temporal-order dependence, single-imputation bias) and required an additional, more interpretable LS-mean-percent-change endpoint in labeling alongside AUC (not currently in Keyword_Taxonomy.md § Regulatory process tags)

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Phase 2, randomized (2:1 active:placebo), quadruple-blind (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor), placebo-controlled (sterile normal saline injection), parallel-group trial in patients aged 6 years and older with genotype-confirmed PH1 or PH2, estimated GFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m², plasma oxalate ≤30 µmol/L, and no systemic oxalosis, dialysis, or organ transplant; randomization used a minimization algorithm (not simple block randomization) stratified by age category and eGFR category, assigning each new participant with 80% probability to whichever treatment arm would minimize cross-arm imbalance and with 20% probability to the other arm

- Primary efficacy endpoint: area under the curve (AUC) from Day 90 to Day 180 of percent change from baseline in 24-hour urinary oxalate excretion (BSA-adjusted for participants <18 years), with baseline defined as the average of two screening 24-hour collections and the AUC computed via a trapezoidal-rule variant that signs area above/below the zero line so a net decrease from baseline is a negative AUC

- Key secondary endpoint: proportion of participants achieving normalized (<0.46 mmol/24h) or near-normalized (≥0.46 to <0.60 mmol/24h) 24-hour urinary oxalate on at least two consecutive visits beginning Day 90

- Other secondary endpoints (tested in a fixed hierarchical sequence behind the key secondary): percent change in plasma oxalate to Day 180 (adults only), percent change in number of kidney stones (ultrasound), percent change in summed kidney-stone surface area (ultrasound), rate of change in eGFR; tertiary/exploratory endpoints included stone-event rate, SF-36/EQ-5D-5L/PedsQL quality-of-life scores, and spot-vs-24-hour urinary oxalate correlation

- Sample size: powered for 36 participants (24 active, 12 placebo) to give ~94% power for a one-sided superiority test at alpha=0.025, assuming AUC=0 in placebo and AUC=-3600 (a 40% decrease over 90 days) in the active arm; a planned interim analysis to re-estimate sample size after two-thirds of participants completed the study was in the original design but was not performed because of slow enrollment; the trial ultimately randomized 35 participants (23 nedosiran, 12 placebo)

- Analysis populations: primary/key-secondary analyses were specified on the modified intent-to-treat (mITT) population (randomized patients with ≥1 post-Day-90 efficacy assessment); FDA's statistical reviewer independently re-ran the primary analyses on the ITT population (all randomized patients with ≥1 post-baseline assessment) because it judged mITT could fail to preserve the original randomization, and used ITT as the basis for its own conclusions throughout the review

- Statistical methods: one-sided ANCOVA-based comparison of AUC percent-change (fixed effects: treatment, age category, eGFR category, baseline urinary oxalate) at alpha=0.025; missing 24-hour urinary oxalate values (8.3%-26.1% of observations by timepoint) imputed via a fully-conditional-specification multiple-imputation model (50 imputations) under a missing-at-random assumption, combined via Rubin's rules; because randomization used a covariate-adaptive minimization algorithm rather than simple/block randomization, FDA additionally ran a 13,500-replication rerandomization (permutation) test to confirm that the sponsor's classical p-values were not invalidated by the adaptive allocation scheme
