### 2. Indacaterol (Arcapta Neohaler) — NDA 022383

**Sponsor:** Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corp.

**Indication approved:** Long-term, once-daily maintenance bronchodilator treatment of airflow obstruction in patients with COPD (75 mcg once-daily strength only; the originally proposed 150 mcg strength received a Complete Response in this same review cycle)

**Approval date:** July 1, 2011

**Pivotal trial:** Study B2336 ("INVOLVE," NCT00567996), Study B2346 (NCT00624286), Study B2354 (NCT01072448), and Study B2355 (NCT01068600) — randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (B2336 also active-controlled with salmeterol), parallel-arm Phase 3 trials in COPD, conducted as part of a resubmission following a 2009 Complete Response Letter; dose-selection trials B2223 and B2357 (asthma) and B2356 (COPD) were conducted specifically to address the CRL's dosing deficiencies

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (add-on active-controlled with salmeterol in B2336), parallel-arm; original NDA (150/300 mcg once daily) received a Complete Response Letter on October 16, 2009 citing excess cardiovascular/cerebrovascular serious adverse events versus placebo/formoterol and possible asthma-related deaths versus salmeterol, plus inadequate dose/frequency justification; FDA's End-of-Review meeting explicitly directed the sponsor to re-characterize dose and dosing frequency first in asthma patients (considered more sensitive to LABA-related adverse effects) before further COPD development — a "regulator-mandated re-sequencing of dose-finding through a more adverse-effect-sensitive population before the intended target population, following a safety-driven Complete Response Letter" not currently in the taxonomy

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint 24-hour post-dose trough FEV1 after 12 weeks of treatment; key/secondary endpoints included St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total score and "days of poor control" (DOPC); in Study B2336, DOPC was pre-specified in the original protocol as the key secondary endpoint but was changed to SGRQ before database lock and unblinding (Mid-trial SAP amendment changing endpoint status)

- *Primary analysis:* mixed-effects model with treatment as fixed effect, baseline pre/post-salbutamol and pre/post-ipratropium reversibility measures as covariates, smoking status as a fixed effect, and study center as a random effect (nested within country for the multinational B2336); SGRQ responder analysis (≥4-unit improvement) via logistic regression with the same covariates; missing trough-FEV1/SGRQ values imputed by last-observation-carried-forward

- *Multiplicity:* in Study B2336, multiple testing across the (reordered) secondary endpoints was controlled by a hierarchical procedure following the DOPC→SGRQ endpoint-status change

- *Missing data/bias:* primary analysis used LOCF; reviewer additionally analyzed SGRQ without imputation and with baseline-observation-carried-forward (BOCF) as sensitivity analyses because LOCF risked bias for patients withdrawing due to lack of efficacy or adverse events; no direct head-to-head comparison of the two approved-dose candidates (75 mcg vs. 150 mcg) existed in any single Phase 3 trial — the only cross-dose comparison came from a 10-study pooled "COPD three-month efficacy population," which showed no statistically significant difference among doses on SGRQ

- *Regulatory:* Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee (PADAC) meeting held March 8, 2011 — committee voted 13-4 to recommend approval of the 75 mcg dose but 5-12 against approval of the 150 mcg dose (concluding added benefit over 75 mcg was not demonstrated), and split 10-7 on whether SGRQ data supported efficacy for the 75 mcg dose; FDA's action followed the Committee's dose-specific split exactly — Approval for 75 mcg, a further Complete Response for 150 mcg — an instance of "FDA approval action tracking an Advisory Committee's split, dose-specific vote rather than a single up/down recommendation for the whole application"; consumer advocacy group Public Citizen raised ethical-conduct concerns regarding the placebo-controlled COPD trials during the meeting's open public forum

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Studies B2354 and B2355 (12 weeks, US-only) each had two arms (indacaterol 75 mcg once daily vs. placebo, ~160 patients/arm); Study B2336 (26 weeks, ex-US) had three arms (indacaterol 150 mcg once daily, salmeterol 50 mcg twice daily, placebo, ~300 patients/arm); Study B2346 supported the 150 mcg dose

- Dose-selection trials conducted to satisfy the CRL: B2223 (asthma, 3 indacaterol dosing regimens + placebo), B2357 (asthma, 4 indacaterol doses + placebo + salmeterol), and B2356 (identical design to B2357 but in COPD patients) — B2356 showed 18.75 mcg once daily was sub-clinically-meaningful (0.07 L vs. placebo, below the sponsor's 0.12 L MCID) and that dose separation among 37.5/75/150 mcg was not clear by week 2

- In Study B2336, trough FEV1 improvement for indacaterol 150 mcg over placebo was 0.17 L (95% CI 0.13-0.20 L), exceeding the 0.12 L MCID and statistically superior to salmeterol (p<0.001); in Studies B2354/B2355, trough FEV1 improvement for indacaterol 75 mcg over placebo was 0.12 L (95% CI 0.08-0.15 L) and 0.14 L (95% CI 0.10-0.18 L) respectively, each meeting or exceeding the MCID

- SGRQ improvement over placebo at 150 mcg was -4.8 (95% CI -7.2, -2.4) in B2346 and -6.3 (95% CI -8.2, -4.3) in B2336, both exceeding the 4-unit MCID; at 75 mcg and other doses, pooled SGRQ improvement (-3.6 to -4.1) fell short of or near the MCID, and no dose showed a statistically significant SGRQ advantage over another dose in pooled analysis

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2011/022383s000ltr.pdf

- Package Insert / Label (original, 2011) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/022383s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Statistical Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022383Orig1s000StatR.pdf

- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2011/022383Orig1s000SumR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov records — B2336/INVOLVE: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00567996 ; B2346: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00624286 ; B2354: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01072448 ; B2355: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01068600

- Protocol / SAP — not identified as individually posted on ClinicalTrials.gov for these trials; FDA's Statistical Review quotes and summarizes the pre-specified statistical methodology in detail, cited above as verbatim FDA-review text

- Pivotal publication (B2346): Feldman G, Siler T, Prasad N, et al. Efficacy and safety of indacaterol 150 microg once-daily in COPD: a double-blind, randomised, 12-week study. *BMC Pulm Med*. 2010;10:11. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2466-10-11), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20211002/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy%20and%20safety%20of%20indacaterol%20150%20microg%20once-daily%20in%20COPD)

- Supporting publication (B2354/B2355): Kerwin EM, Gotfried MH, Lawrence D, Lassen C, et al. **Other resources**

- No trial-specific IPD/dataset access program (Vivli, YODA, Project Data Sphere) confirmed for Novartis or this program

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID: 2904218), §1.1]* "My review of the statistical evidence suggests support for the claim. However, based on the data from the dose and regimen selection trials submitted, there were no clear separation among the doses and regimens studied. Multiple doses and regimens worked equally well in terms of efficacy. Which dose and regimen to approve is up to discussion at the advisory committee meeting."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §3.1.4]* "The primary (24-hour post-dose trough FEV1 after 12 weeks treatment) and secondary (SGRQ scores) efficacy endpoints included in this review were analyzed using a mixed effect model... To reflect the randomization scheme, the model also included the smoking status as fixed effects with center as a random effect."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, results narrative]* "In Study B2336, the 'days of poor control' (DOPC) were specified as the key secondary efficacy endpoint in the original protocol, but was changed into SGRQ before the database lock and unblinding. Multiple testing was controlled by a hierarchical procedure. The protocol change did not affect the study conduct, but does change data interpretation as it modified the order of how the secondary efficacy endpoints were tested."

- *[verbatim, FDA Summary Review (Reference ID: 2968845), §9]* "The Committee by majority voting concluded that efficacy for 75 mcg dose was demonstrated, that the 75 mcg was safe for use in COPD patients, and recommended approval of the 75 mcg dose (votes were 13 yes and 4 no). Regarding the 150 mcg dose, the Committee concluded that added benefit of the 150 mcg dose was not demonstrated, and balancing the overall efficacy and safety data, recommended against approval of the 150 mcg dose (votes were 5 yes and 12 no)."

### 3. Lucinactant (Surfaxin) — NDA 021746

**Sponsor:** Discovery Laboratories, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Prevention of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants at high risk of RDS

**Approval date:** March 6, 2012 (fifth review cycle; original submission filed April 13, 2004)

**Pivotal trial:** Study KL4-IRDS-06 — a multinational (Europe and Latin America), multicenter (50 sites), randomized, masked, active-controlled (Exosurf and Survanta), prophylaxis superiority trial in premature neonates; no NCT identified (trial conducted circa 1998-2000, predating ClinicalTrials.gov); supportive Study KL4-IRDS-02 (non-inferiority vs. Curosurf) was rejected by FDA as a basis for efficacy and was reviewed for safety only

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, masked, active-controlled (three-arm: lucinactant/Surfaxin, colfosceril palmitate/Exosurf, beractant/Survanta), prophylaxis-of-RDS superiority trial with a "short-term" efficacy/safety phase (36 weeks post-conceptual age) and a "long-term" outcomes/safety phase (6 and 12 months corrected age); the approval itself is an unusual regulatory pattern — efficacy on the single pivotal trial (KL4-IRDS-06) was accepted as early as the original 2004-2006 review cycles, but approval was withheld for three further review cycles (2006-2012) entirely on Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) grounds (drug-substance impurities, release/stability specifications, and — the final outstanding issue — validation of the fetal-rabbit bioassay used to confirm biological activity of drug product lots), a "multi-cycle approval delay driven entirely by unresolved CMC/bioassay-validation deficiencies after efficacy was already accepted" pattern not currently in the taxonomy; FDA separately rejected the sponsor's proposed non-inferiority design for the supportive trial KL4-IRDS-02 (vs. Curosurf) as statistically unsupportable, citing insufficient historical data to estimate the active-comparator effect and inappropriate margin justification, and required it be treated as safety-only evidence

- *Endpoints:* co-primary(-adjacent) efficacy endpoints — RDS incidence at 24 hours of age, and RDS-related mortality through 14 days of age (the sponsor's own framing of a second endpoint as one composite vs. two separate endpoints was itself a source of reviewer confusion, addressed in the FDA review); secondary/exploratory endpoints included the composite of RDS mortality by 14 days or air leak by day 7, and all-cause mortality by 14 days

- *Primary analysis:* stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test (stratified by center and birthweight), per the Agency-agreed, protocol-specified analysis, for RDS incidence and RDS-related mortality; sponsor's own analysis used logistic regression stratifying on the same factors, giving concordant results

- *Missing data/bias:* a central finding of FDA's review was a large discrepancy between the trial's blinded Adjudication Committee's assessment of RDS incidence/mortality and the site investigators' case-report-form (CRF) data — the CRF data did not support the magnitude of the RDS-mortality finding seen in the adjudicated dataset; FDA's reviewer also found that the reduction in RDS-specific mortality with lucinactant was offset by a numerically higher non-RDS-related mortality, such that all-cause mortality differed little between arms, and this pattern held in both the European and Latin American regions of the trial

- *Regulatory:* Approvable Letter issued February 11, 2005 on efficacy/safety grounds tied to the adjudication-vs-CRF discrepancy and clinical interpretation of the mortality trade-off; subsequent review cycles (through the fifth, approved March 6, 2012) turned entirely on unresolved CMC deficiencies, most persistently the validated bioassay demonstrating batch-to-batch biological activity in a fetal-rabbit RDS model

**Trial design & endpoints**

- KL4-IRDS-06 randomized premature neonates at risk of RDS to lucinactant, colfosceril palmitate (Exosurf), or beractant (Survanta) for RDS prophylaxis, with adjudicated (committee-determined) and investigator-CRF-reported RDS incidence/mortality outcomes collected in parallel

- Based on the adjudicated dataset, lucinactant showed a statistically significant 17% relative reduction in RDS incidence at 24 hours (95% CI 5%-28%, p=0.007 by the Agency-agreed stratified CMH test; p=0.005 by the sponsor's logistic-regression model) and a 52% relative reduction in RDS-related mortality by 14 days (95% CI 24%-69%, p=0.001) versus Exosurf; these findings were not consistently reproduced in the investigator CRF data

- All-cause mortality by 14 days showed little difference between lucinactant and Exosurf; non-RDS-related mortality was significantly higher with lucinactant, largely offsetting the RDS-specific mortality benefit — FDA's reviewer explicitly flagged that "clinical input is needed to determine whether... the reduction of RDS mortality is a relevant clinical benefit for Surfaxin" given this trade-off

- KL4-IRDS-02 (supportive, vs. Curosurf/poractant alfa) was terminated early for stated economic reasons, which FDA noted further limited its ability to support long-term safety conclusions; FDA declined to accept its non-inferiority efficacy framing on the grounds that a single placebo-controlled historical trial provided inadequate information on between-trial variability of the active-comparator (Curosurf) effect

- ClinicalTrials.gov record — none identified; KL4-IRDS-06 was conducted circa 1998-2000, predating ClinicalTrials.gov (established 2000, mandatory registration phased in later)

- Protocol / SAP — not publicly posted; FDA's Statistical Review quotes and summarizes the pre-specified analysis plan in detail, cited above as verbatim FDA-review text

- Pivotal publication: Moya FR, Gadzinowski J, Bancalari E, Salinas V, Kopelman B, Bancalari A, Kornacka MK, Merritt TA, Segal R, Schaber CJ, Tsai H, Massaro J, d'Agostino R; International Surfaxin Collaborative Study Group. However, there was a large discrepancy between the Adjudicated Committee's assessment and CRF reporting in terms of these incidence rates. The case report form (CRF) data did not support the RDS mortality finding."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review, §1.1]* "All cause mortality by 14 days showed little difference between Surfaxin and Exosurf. Non-RDS related mortality was significantly larger for Surfaxin. Such pattern was observed consistently in both the European region and the Latin American region. The reduction of RDS mortality and the increase of non-RDS mortality with Surfaxin seem to balance each other out."

The clinical recommendation for the original submission was Approval; however, there were and continued to be major CMC deficiencies that led to complete response actions on previous review cycles."

### 4. Aclidinium bromide (Tudorza Pressair) — NDA 202450

**Sponsor:** Forest Laboratories, Inc.

**Indication approved:** Long-term maintenance treatment of bronchospasm associated with COPD, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema

**Approval date:** July 23, 2012

**Pivotal trial:** ATTAIN (Study M/34273/34, NCT01001494), ACCORD COPD I (Study LAS-MD-33, NCT00891462), and ACCORD COPD II (Study LAS-MD-38, NCT01045161) — randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trials of aclidinium bromide 200 mcg and 400 mcg twice daily

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-arm (three trials: ATTAIN 24 weeks, ex-US; ACCORD COPD I and II 12 weeks each, North America); two Phase 2 crossover dose-ranging trials (M23, M29) conducted in Germany/Belgium preceded the Phase 3 program

- *Endpoints:* primary endpoint 24-hour post-dose trough FEV1 change from baseline at week 12; secondary endpoints included peak FEV1, TDI focal score (ATTAIN only), and SGRQ total score responder analysis (≥4-point improvement)

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA with treatment and sex as factors, baseline and age as covariates; a pre-specified MMRM sensitivity analysis (unstructured covariance, observed-case data) supported the primary ANCOVA result; binary responder endpoints (TDI, SGRQ) analyzed by logistic regression

- *Multiplicity:* Hochberg step-up procedure used both (a) across the two aclidinium dose arms (200/400 mcg) within the primary endpoint, and (b) within each step of a pre-specified sequential-gatekeeping procedure across secondary endpoints (peak FEV1 → TDI responder → SGRQ responder), with testing continuing to the next step only if at least one dose was significant at the prior step

- *Missing data/bias:* primary analysis used last-observation-carried-forward per the sponsor's SAP; in February 2011 (during trial conduct, after unblinding of an earlier Phase 3 study) FDA informed the sponsor that its pre-specified LOCF imputation strategy was "not acceptable," but the sponsor noted the data were already unblinded and could not be prospectively amended; the reviewer's independent judgment was that missing data was not a materially confounding issue here because results were consistent and highly significant across analytical methods and imputation strategies (LOCF, BOCF, MMRM) — an instance of a reviewer-documented FDA objection to a sponsor's pre-specified missing-data method raised after unblinding, without a design change resulting ("Post-unblinding FDA objection to a pre-specified imputation method, with no resulting SAP amendment because data were already unblinded")

- *Regulatory:* Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee (PADAC) meeting held February 23, 2012 — voted 14-0 that substantial evidence of efficacy existed for aclidinium bromide 400 mcg twice daily, 10-3 (1 abstention) that safety had been adequately assessed, and 12-2 in favor of overall approvability

**Trial design & endpoints**

- ATTAIN (M34): 24-week trial in Europe/South Africa, three arms (aclidinium 200 mcg, 400 mcg, placebo), ~280 patients/arm

- ACCORD COPD I (M33) and ACCORD COPD II (M38a): identically designed 12-week trials in Canada/USA, three arms each (aclidinium 400 mcg, 200 mcg, placebo), ~180 patients/arm

- Aclidinium 400 mcg twice daily produced statistically significant trough-FEV1 improvements over placebo in all three trials, ranging from 72 to 124 mL; 200 mcg showed smaller but also statistically significant improvements; only ATTAIN's 400 mcg arm showed an SGRQ improvement meeting the 4-point MCID versus placebo, a finding not replicated in the two 12-week trials

- Overall COPD exacerbation rates were low across all three trials, which the reviewer stated made definitive assessment of an exacerbation-rate benefit difficult

This finding was not replicated in the other two trials."

### 5. Fluticasone furoate/vilanterol (Breo Ellipta) — NDA 204275

**Sponsor:** GlaxoSmithKline

**Indication approved:** Long-term, once-daily maintenance treatment of airflow obstruction in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), including chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema, and reduction of exacerbations in COPD patients with a history of exacerbations

**Approval date:** May 10, 2013

**Pivotal trial:** Studies HZC112206 (NCT01053988) and HZC112207 (NCT01054885), two 24-week lung-function trials; Studies HZC102871 (NCT01009463) and HZC102970 (NCT01017952), two 12-month exacerbation-rate trials

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter trials; prespecified factorial combination-product design in which the fixed-dose combination, each individual monotherapy component, and placebo were all randomized from trial inception, specifically to satisfy 21 CFR 300.50's requirement to demonstrate each component's contribution (**"Prespecified factorial combination-product design (combination + each monotherapy component + placebo randomized from inception, per 21 CFR 300.50)"**; seen in Studies 2206/2207 here and in the companion umeclidinium/vilanterol program below)

- *Endpoints:* co-primary/primary trough FEV1 change from baseline at Day 169 (lung-function trials 2206/2207); annual rate of moderate/severe COPD exacerbations (exacerbation trials 2871/2970, dosed against a vilanterol-monotherapy internal comparator rather than placebo alone)

- *Primary analysis:* mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM)-based ANCOVA with covariates for treatment, smoking-status stratification factor, visit, and baseline-by-visit and treatment-by-visit interactions

- *Multiplicity:* step-down procedure across treatment comparisons and key endpoints in Studies 2206/2207, judged by FDA to provide strong control of the Type I error rate

- *Missing data/bias:* three imputation approaches compared — sponsor's last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) sensitivity analysis, explicitly rejected by FDA as non-conservative and potentially biased; multiple imputation under a Missing-at-Random (MAR) assumption via a Bayesian multivariate-normal MCMC model; and multiple imputation under a Copy-Differences-from-Control (CDC) assumption, both following the Carpenter-Roger-Kenward framework for longitudinal trials with protocol deviation

- *Regulatory:* Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee (PADAC) met April 17, 2013; voted 12-1 that substantial evidence of efficacy for airflow obstruction had been shown, 8-5 for exacerbation reduction, and 9-4 on overall approvability for airflow obstruction

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Studies 2206 (HZC112206, NCT01053988) and 2207 (HZC112207, NCT01054885): 24-week, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group trials in patients ≥40 years old with COPD, each testing the fixed-dose combination (fluticasone furoate/vilanterol, FF/VI) against each monotherapy component and placebo, all randomized from inception — a factorial-style design used to isolate each component's individual contribution as required by 21 CFR 300.50. Study 2206 tested FF/VI 50/25 mcg and 100/25 mcg (with FF 100 mcg and VI 25 mcg monotherapy arms and placebo); Study 2207 tested FF/VI 100/25 mcg and 200/25 mcg (with FF 100 mcg, FF 200 mcg, VI 25 mcg monotherapy arms and placebo). Primary endpoint: change from baseline in trough FEV1 at Day 169.

- Studies 2871 (HZC102871, NCT01009463) and 2970 (HZC102970, NCT01017952): 12-month, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group exacerbation trials testing FF/VI 50/25, 100/25, and 200/25 mcg against vilanterol 25 mcg monotherapy as the internal comparator (rather than placebo alone), with a 4-week run-in. Primary endpoint: annual rate of moderate/severe COPD exacerbations.

- Three further active-comparator studies (2352/NCT01323621, 3109/NCT01323634, 3107/NCT01342913) compared FF/VI against fluticasone propionate/salmeterol or similar active comparators on change-from-baseline trough FEV1; these informed labeling and safety but were not the primary basis for the efficacy claim.

- Primary statistical model across the lung-function trials: an MMRM-type ANCOVA with treatment, the smoking-status stratification factor, visit, and baseline-by-visit and treatment-by-visit interaction terms. FDA's Statistical Review states there was "a strong control of the Type 1 error for the primary endpoints," achieved via a step-down procedure across treatment comparisons and key endpoints in Studies 2206 and 2207.

- Missing data handling was an explicit point of methodological disagreement: the sponsor's LOCF sensitivity analysis was rejected by FDA on grounds that it assumes a discontinuing patient's outcome stays constant over time, understating uncertainty and not necessarily conservative; two multiple-imputation alternatives (MAR-based Bayesian MCMC, and Copy-Differences-from-Control) were preferred, both following the Carpenter-Roger-Kenward analytic framework for longitudinal trials with protocol deviations.

- The Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee met April 17, 2013, and voted 12-1 that substantial evidence of efficacy for airflow obstruction in COPD had been demonstrated, 8-5 that substantial evidence of efficacy for exacerbation reduction had been demonstrated, 10-3 that safety was adequately demonstrated, and 9-4 on overall approvability for the airflow-obstruction claim (8-5 for the exacerbation-reduction claim). The committee's Division of Scientific Investigations audited clinical sites in the pivotal COPD studies as part of its review.

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2013/204275Orig1s000ltr.pdf

- Package Insert / Label (original, 2013) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2013/204275s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3278249) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204275Orig1s000StatR.pdf

- FDA Summary Review (Reference ID 3306249) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204275Orig1s000SumR.pdf

- ClinicalTrials.gov records — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01053988 (2206), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01054885 (2207), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01009463 (2871), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01017952 (2970)

- Protocol / SAP — not posted on ClinicalTrials.gov for any of the seven studies reviewed (documentSection field empty via the ClinicalTrials.gov API for all); FDA's Statistical Review extensively quotes and paraphrases the underlying protocols and SAPs

- Pivotal publication (Studies 2206/2207, lung function): Dransfield MT, et al., and companion reports in *Respiratory Medicine* 2013;107(4):550-569, covering the dose-ranging FF/VI lung-function results — Study 2206 (50/25 and 100/25 mcg arms), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rmed.2012.12.014), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23352226/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=randomised%20trial%20of%20fluticasone%20furoate%20vilanterol%2050%2025%20100%2025%20on%20lung%20function%20in%20COPD); Study 2207 (100/25 and 200/25 mcg arms), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rmed.2012.12.016), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23332861/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=fluticasone%20furoate%20vilanterol%20100%2025%20200%2025%20improves%20lung%20function%20in%20COPD)

- Pivotal publication (Studies 2871/2970, exacerbations): Dransfield MT, Bourbeau J, Jones PW, et al. Once-daily inhaled fluticasone furoate and vilanterol versus vilanterol only for prevention of exacerbations of COPD: two replicate double-blind, parallel-group, randomised controlled trials. *Lancet Respir Med*. 2013;1(3):210-223. [DOI](<https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-2600(13)70040-7>), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24429127/), [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Once-daily%20inhaled%20fluticasone%20furoate%20and%20vilanterol%20versus%20vilanterol%20only%20for%20prevention%20of%20exacerbations%20of%20COPD)

**Other resources**

- GlaxoSmithKline participates in ClinicalStudyDataRequest.com (CSDR) for patient-level data sharing on its trials generally; trial-specific listing for these seven studies was not individually confirmed, stated here plainly rather than asserted

- Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee meeting held April 17, 2013 (voting detail above)

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3278249)]* "There was a strong control of the Type 1 error for the primary endpoints. Studies 2206 and 2207 used a step-down procedure to account for multiplicity across treatment comparisons and key endpoints."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3278249)]*, on LOCF: "The Division generally does not accept LOCF as an imputation strategy because this implies patients who discontinue treatment will have the same outcome over time. This may lead to a biased standard error estimates since we are ignoring inherent uncertainty in the imputed values. In addition, this approach may not be conservative in terms of the patient's imputed outcome."

- *[verbatim, FDA Summary Review (Reference ID 3306249)]*, on the April 17, 2013 PADAC meeting: "Overall, members felt that GSK had conducted an extensive, rigorous, and well-designed program."

- **Reverse-engineered SAP** (for details the excerpted FDA-review text does not fully resolve): *[inferred]* the exact control-arm structure of Studies 2871/2970 (vilanterol monotherapy as the sole internal comparator, without an additional placebo arm) is traced to the FDA Statistical Review's Table 1 study-arm listing and the published Lancet Respiratory Medicine report's stated design, rather than to a directly quoted SAP passage.

### 6. Umeclidinium/vilanterol (Anoro Ellipta) — NDA 203975

**Sponsor:** GlaxoSmithKline

**Indication approved:** Long-term, once-daily maintenance treatment of airflow obstruction in patients with COPD, including chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema

**Approval date:** December 18, 2013

**Pivotal trial:** Study 113373 (NCT01313650, the pivotal-dose placebo-controlled trial at the approved 62.5/25 mcg dose); supportive Studies 113361 (NCT01313637), 113360 (NCT01316900), and 113374 (NCT01316913)

**Keywords:**

- *Design:* randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, 24-week trials; prespecified factorial combination-product design (combination + each monotherapy component + placebo randomized from inception, per 21 CFR 300.50; also seen in the Breo Ellipta program above) for Studies 361/373; active (tiotropium)-controlled factorial design for Studies 360/374; supportive incomplete-block randomized crossover exercise-endurance trials (Studies 417/NCT01328444 and 418/NCT01323660) with co-primary endpoints

- *Endpoints:* change from baseline in trough FEV1 at Day 169 (primary, all four core efficacy trials); weighted mean FEV1 0-6h post-dose at Day 168 (secondary); exercise endurance time and trough FEV1 at 12 weeks (co-primary, crossover trials 417/418); St George's Respiratory Questionnaire dyspnea score reclassified mid-program from a prespecified secondary endpoint to an "Other Efficacy Endpoint"

- *Primary analysis:* ANCOVA-type model for trough FEV1; log-rank/parametric analysis for exercise endurance time in the crossover trials

- *Multiplicity:* ordered pairwise comparisons (combination vs. each monotherapy vs. placebo in 361/373; combination vs. tiotropium vs. monotherapy in 360/374, high dose tested before low dose); FDA noted the applicant did not control for multiplicity across other efficacy endpoints (SGRQ, SOBDA, rescue medication use, exacerbation rate) in any of the four core trials

- *Missing data/bias:* three named sensitivity-imputation approaches — Missing at Random (MAR) multiple imputation, Copy Differences from Control (CDC), and Last Mean Carried Forward (LMCF, assuming either a flat or a -25 mL/year declining post-withdrawal trend) — all of which gave treatment-effect estimates roughly 20-30% smaller than the primary analysis

- *Regulatory:* Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee met September 10, 2013, voting 13-0 on substantial evidence of efficacy and 11-2 on overall approvability; FDA explicitly discussed FEV1 as a surrogate endpoint requiring subjective/patient-reported corroboration

**Trial design & endpoints**

- Four primary efficacy studies, all Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, 24 weeks, in patients with ≥10 pack-year smoking history, %predicted FEV1 ≤70%, post-salbutamol FEV1/FVC <0.7, and mMRC dyspnea score ≥2. Study 361 (NCT01313637): placebo-controlled, 3:3:3:2 randomization to umeclidinium/vilanterol (UMEC/VI) 125/25 mcg, UMEC 125 mcg, VI 25 mcg, and placebo (N=1463 planned, 90% power, 58-68 mL minimal clinically important difference assumptions). Study 373 (NCT01313650): the pivotal-dose trial, same design at UMEC/VI 62.5/25 mcg, UMEC 62.5 mcg, VI 25 mcg, and placebo — the only one of the four core trials providing a direct placebo comparison at the approved 62.5/25 mcg dose. Study 360 (NCT01316900) and Study 374 (NCT01316913): tiotropium-active-controlled, 1:1:1:1 designs comparing UMEC/VI (125/25 mcg) against tiotropium and each monotherapy component.

- Primary endpoint across all four core trials: change from baseline in trough FEV1 at Day 169 (mean of 23h/24h post-dose values on Day 168). Secondary endpoint: weighted mean FEV1 0-6h post-dose on Day 168. The St George's Respiratory Questionnaire dyspnea (SOBDA) score, originally a prespecified secondary endpoint, was reclassified mid-program to an "Other Efficacy Endpoint."

- Two supportive crossover trials, Study 417/"Study A" (NCT01328444) and Study 418/"Study B" (NCT01323660): 2-period, 12-week-per-period, incomplete-block randomized crossover designs with co-primary endpoints of exercise endurance time (endurance shuttle walk test) and trough FEV1 at 12 weeks, both required to reach significance at two-sided α=0.05. In Study 418, the trough FEV1 co-primary endpoint was met at both doses (vs. tiotropium and vs. placebo), but the high-dose exercise-endurance-time comparison failed, which under the pre-specified testing hierarchy limited formal claims for lower-priority comparisons in that trial.

- Multiplicity: FDA's Statistical Review states plainly that "the applicant did not control for multiplicity across other efficacy endpoints (e.g., SGRQ, SOBDA, rescue medication use, exacerbation rate) in any of the studies," even though the primary and immediately adjacent comparisons used ordered hierarchical testing.

- Missing data: three named sensitivity approaches were used — Missing at Random (MAR) multiple imputation based on per-arm mean/covariance estimation; Copy Differences from Control (CDC), assuming post-withdrawal trajectories mirror control-arm completers; and Last Mean Carried Forward (LMCF), assuming either a flat (0 mL/year) or declining (-25 mL/year) mean trend from the last observed value. FDA's review states these "demonstrated consistent evidence of superiority to placebo, but provided estimated treatment effect sizes of approximately 20-30% less than the primary analyses."

- FDA framed the entire effectiveness case as substantially anchored on the single placebo-controlled comparison in Study 373 at the approved dose (UMEC/VI 62.5/25 mcg vs. placebo, trough FEV1 improvement of 0.167 L, 95% CI 0.128-0.207), supplemented by supportive evidence from the other three core trials and the two crossover trials, and discussed at length why FEV1 is a surrogate endpoint that "does not directly measure how a patient functions or feels in daily life," making corroborating patient-reported/subjective endpoints important to the overall judgment of clinical meaningfulness.

- The Pulmonary-Allergy Drugs Advisory Committee met September 10, 2013, and voted 13-0 that substantial evidence of efficacy for airflow obstruction had been demonstrated, 10-3 that safety was adequately demonstrated, and 11-2 on overall approvability, while expressing some concern about the size of the cardiovascular safety database.

**Documents**

- FDA Approval Letter — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2013/203975Orig1s000ltr.pdf

- Package Insert / Label (original, 2013) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2013/203975s000lbl.pdf

- FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3358394) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/203975Orig1s000StatR.pdf

- FDA Summary Review — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/203975Orig1s000SumR.pdf

**SAP — exact text / key excerpts**

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3358394)]* "The applicant did not control for multiplicity across other efficacy endpoints (e.g., SGRQ, SOBDA, rescue medication use, exacerbation rate) in any of the studies."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3358394)]*, on missing-data sensitivity: "Missing data sensitivity analyses demonstrated consistent evidence of superiority to placebo, but provided estimated treatment effect sizes of approximately 20-30% less than the primary analyses."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3358394)]*, on the surrogate nature of the primary endpoint: "We consider FEV1 to be a surrogate endpoint, because it does not directly measure how a patient functions or feels in daily life, or how long a patient survives (Fleming 2012)... because they do not directly measure the COPD symptoms... that are important to patients, the claim of effectiveness based on the primary analyses relies on the conclusion that the treatment effect on FEV1 will reliably predict effects on a clinically meaningful endpoint."

- *[verbatim, FDA Statistical Review (Reference ID 3358394)]*, framing the effectiveness case: "we must evaluate whether results from this single study, combined with supportive data from additional studies, meet the standard for substantial evidence of effectiveness," referring to Study 373 as the sole direct placebo-controlled comparison at the approved dose.

- **Reverse-engineered SAP** (for details not fully resolved by the excerpted FDA-review text): *[inferred]* Study 359's exact NCT registration was not independently confirmed in this research pass; it is referenced here only as a 52-week, safety-only trial (2:2:1 randomization to UMEC/VI 125/25, UMEC 125, and placebo) and is not part of the primary efficacy basis, consistent with its absence from FDA's efficacy-focused Statistical Review discussion.

## Cross-cutting observations (pilot findings — original 10-drug scope; see Master_Index.md for current overall coverage)

### Oncology

- Two of five submissions (osimertinib/FLAURA, pembrolizumab/KEYNOTE-024) had a genuine sponsor SAP or combined Protocol+SAP document publicly posted on ClinicalTrials.gov. One (venetoclax/CLL14) had a protocol with a real but less detailed statistical section, with the standalone SAP referenced but not separately posted. One (olaparib/SOLO-2) had no posted SAP/protocol but an unusually detailed FDA statistical review that describes the SAP second-hand, including reviewer pushback on how it was executed. One (enzalutamide/PREVAIL) had neither, requiring full reverse-engineering from the label.
- All four trials with real SAP detail used a group-sequential / alpha-spending approach for at least one endpoint (Hwang-Shih-DeCani for KEYNOTE-024; Lan-DeMets/O'Brien-Fleming for FLAURA; gamma-family spending for CLL14; an unspecified but likely similar approach can be inferred for SOLO-2's two-stage design). This appears to be the market-standard approach for Phase III oncology trials with event-driven co-primary or hierarchical secondary endpoints in this period.
- FDA's own review documents (SOLO-2, CLL14) are a genuinely rich secondary source — in the SOLO-2 case, arguably richer than a static SAP document, because they document where FDA caught the sponsor deviating from an agreed-upon analysis approach after the fact.

### Cardiovascular / metabolic

- Only one of five submissions (semaglutide/SELECT) had a genuine sponsor SAP and protocol posted on ClinicalTrials.gov — and even that came with an extraction complication (see the SELECT entry's caveat) rather than a clean verbatim source. The other four relied entirely on FDA statistical/clinical reviews (empagliflozin, sacubitril-valsartan, dapagliflozin) or, for evolocumab/FOURIER, a fully reverse-engineered reconstruction — the opposite mix from oncology, where ClinicalTrials.gov postings were the stronger source.
- Where FDA reviews were available (empagliflozin, sacubitril-valsartan, dapagliflozin), they were exceptionally detailed — more so than in oncology — because CVOTs of this kind almost always involve group-sequential monitoring, non-inferiority-then-superiority hierarchies, or (dapagliflozin) a genuine mid-trial elevation of a secondary endpoint to co-primary status that FDA had to specifically evaluate for integrity.
- Three of five trials (EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DECLARE-TIMI 58, and implicitly PARADIGM-HF) used the same broad statistical pattern: non-inferiority safety margin tested first, then a hierarchical/recycled-alpha path to superiority — a structure essentially unseen in the oncology batch, which instead centered on direct superiority testing with PFS/OS hierarchies. This reflects the regulatory history of the class (post-2008 FDA guidance requiring CV safety exclusion for diabetes drugs), not a random difference between areas.
- Dapagliflozin/DECLARE-TIMI 58 is the standout example in this pilot of a testing hierarchy actually mattering to the outcome: the primary MACE endpoint only reached non-inferiority (not superiority), but the pre-planned "alpha recycling" rule let the trial's dual-primary HHF/CV-death endpoint absorb the full alpha and reach significance — which is the entire basis for the approved indication.
- Two submissions (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) were found via a working pattern worth reusing at scale: search `accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/<year>/<ApplNo>Orig1s<supp>.pdf` even when Drugs@FDA's own supplement-overview page lists only a label and approval letter — FDA appears to have retroactively posted full combined review packages for at least some older efficacy supplements under later year-folders (2021 in both cases here) that aren't linked from the per-supplement overview page and don't surface via ordinary web search on the supplement number.

### General

- accessdata.fda.gov blocks unauthenticated automated requests without a browser-like User-Agent header (returns an Akamai "abuse detection" apology page); requests succeeded once a standard browser User-Agent string was set.
- At least one sponsor (Novo Nordisk, for SELECT) posts ClinicalTrials.gov documents through a redaction pipeline that destroys inter-word spacing in the underlying PDF text layer. This is a genuinely new failure mode relative to the oncology pilot's documents, and any future scaling of this census should budget time for manual word-boundary reconstruction (or an OCR-based re-extraction) when a posted document turns out to come from this sponsor/pipeline.
